Y'all,

Judith's reply to Robert is probably the only serious and
constructive piece of ufo debate I've seen
in UK email circles for weeks. Could peace be breaking out at
last?

I'll go for this discussion.......

I agree that 'on the ground' investigation is essential Judith, but never
discount
the relevance of musing from the Armchair - some of the most difficult
cases
have been cracked whilst drifting into the fabric.

As regards Rendlesham, I haven't been (though intend to do so as part of
research
for a book I and others have just secrured a contract for) so what people
say is both
intriguing and baffling.

>1) THE ORFORD NESS LIGHTHOUSE CANNOT BE
>IMPLICATED IN ANY UFO SIGHTING OR LANDING. If you visit the area

This way well be the case - but then why have former Rendlesham devotee
James Easton,
Jenny Randles and
Ian Ridpath, who have all been to the area, stuck to their belief that the
lighthouse
and lightship *were* responsible. Either they can or can't be seen Someone
is
right and someone is wrong. We need to know!

>Because of the intervening coastal ridge, the powerful horizontal beam of
the lighthouse is
> completely cut off to those viewing it >from a low position on land, thus
THE BEAM FROM THE LIGHTHOUSE DOES NOT >PENETRATE THE
FOREST AT ALL.

See above.

>2) As to the meteor theory, I personally don't believe that this even
holds water. We saw many meteors that night, literally >hundreds, high up
in the atmosphere, and they were beautiful to behold, whilst keeping a
respectful distance !

Never discount meteors! As I found in the Berwyn case there can be
nights when the universe goes meteor-bonkers- crazy. Have *thorough* checks
been done with astonomical associations, the bolide society in
Cornwall and the BGS in Edinburgh?

>Granted they were all traveling in a roughly E.- W. direction and it is a
possibility that one
>could drop from a decaying orbit, hit the earth's atmosphere, burn up and
come in to
>land over the coast of Suffolk . But wouldn't that be seen for exactly
what it was, even by American airmen ?

No it wouldn't - or not necessarily. The ufological literature
is littered with many cases where meteors have been misperceived - often by
multiple
witnesses - and seen as UFOs. Just because whatever it was was seen by
airmen means nothing. There is no such thing as an entirely 'credible'
witness.

>Low in the atmosphere, just before collision, it would be seen as an
orange/yellow ball
>of fire with a tail. It would make a tremendous rushing noise (enough to
waken people
>from their sleep), leave a trail of destruction in the treetops (first
point of impact),
>gouge out a tract of land and leave an appreciable crater commensurate
with its mass. I don't
>think this tallies with the description given by any of the witnesses, and
if it were indeed
>a meteorite impact, why all the mystery and stories of UFOs? Is it likely
that a meteor
> would fall to earth, two or three nights running, in the same place?

Not necessarily Judith! What colour a meteor is seen as is dependent
on several factors; what the composition of the meteor is will cause
different colours to be seen and all colours have been recorded.
Noise etc is entirely dependent on height (and wind direction) and how can
a witness
accurately judge that? What looks near can be far and vice versa.
As nothing has ever been *proved* to land at Rendlesham it is specious
to argue the likelihood of whether an unproved anything did anything at
all on 2-3 nights running. Sorry to be difficult but you've got to think
these
things through!

>If a meteor had landed, why was it not seismically recorded, not just
pinpointing
> the Rendlesham area, but anywhere in the British
>Isles, in case it had only "overflown" the area?

Has anyone checked the BGS for records of that night? And just
because something prosaic *wasn't* recorded doesn't mean it
tdidn't take place. The problem with Rendlesham-ites as with
all other adherents to 'exotic' UFO cases is that they don't seem
to understand the onus is on *them* to prove something weird
actually took place *not* on the rest of us. This isn't getting at
you Judith, just a general observation.

>And if it had just passed over and
>ditched somewhere in the Atlantic, why was a five mile diameter exclusion
zone
> imposed by the authorities as attested to by local residents? One man
living near
> Capel Green was refused permission by the police to leave his home.

Again, problems. Air Exclusion zones are imposed for a variety of reasons

Hi all

Only one aspect of interest to add below, most of which I tend to agree
with, and that's the 'the use of hypnosis invalidates the Godfrey case'
statement - this has no basis in scientific fact.

I know little of either Godfrey's complete statement or of the
information obtained through 'hypnosis' but I do know that regression
hypnosis has not been proven to be invalid.

I think this point has to be made as I see many people are obsessed with
damning a technique which has been used medically and non-medically to
elicit FACT. Recent scientific research suggests that the use of
'hypnosis' enhances ones memory of events dramatically. The researchers
found that subjects were able to substantially improve their recall of
events when hypnotic techniques were used.

To damn evidence that may be valid through prejudice or ill-conceived
assumption rather than scientific argument is of no use investigatively.
The evidence in Godfrey's case would have had to be considered as a
whole - direct, material, circumstantial and 'hypnotically-induced' -
with due consideration given to the probability of imagination and/or
false memory syndrome etc.

A moratorium on regression by BUFORA is commendable, no one wants
witnesses subjected to naive intervention using potentially dangerous
techniques of any kind - and one does not need to use hypnotic
regression to induce false-memory and recall - but let's not condemn a
modality that has shown itself to be very useful in the right hands.

>It is a fact of life that, IF 'abduction' is occurring - a large body
of circumstantial evidence supports this possibility despite alternative
opinion - and 'abductees' generally report loss of memory of related
events, the only means at present understood as having potential for
recovering those memories are either through hypnosis and related
modalities or a gradual return of memory as nature takes it's course. It
is also widely accepted that extreme trauma can inhibit memory, probably
for self-preservation. 'Regression techniques', safely and properly
administered, are possibly the only means of inducing early return of
memory recovery at this time.

Ipso facto, if one is not prepared to consider such techniques to
develop a case investigation where the modality may be the only way to
move forward, then one will reach the conclusion one expects ( and a
self-fulfilling prophesy ) - that 'abduction' does not occur. Is that
scientific?

John.

On the point of the lighthouse....

I have been there at night when the lighthouse has been active and you can
see it for many many miles. As the fog grew in it was seen as an errie light
of a set pattern and pulse so again would not be mistaken by those who live
or work in the area. Guards on a base would often be staring into the
darkness and have seen it - or asked others about it and been given the
reason.

The lighthouse from Bentwaters seems to arc across the sky like a clock hand
going from 10 oclock to 2 oclock in the sky (arc degrees equivalent that
is).

This could in no way have led to Halt and a team leaving the base under
those conditions.

So it "must" have been something else of a much more impressive nature.
If this helps....

Matthew

Hi All!!

Very interesting; hypnosis is OK and it isn't OK? So which is it/isn't
it......

I do not know of any registered medical personnel who use hypnosis to
recover memories and I'd really like to know which scientists have used
hypnosis to 'improve recall' (?) given that I have read several articles in
"New Scientist" by US academics studying the effects of hypnosis who
actually argue that it is all kidology!

Hmmmm....

I asked my sister about this - she's a real Doctor BTW. She said that
hypnosis is regarded as a dangerous fringe activity by many of her
colleagues. Eric Morris has come out totally against the use of hypnosis
having used it occasionally in the past - for reasons including the fact
that it was impossible to tell whether the witness was telling the truth.

Haven't people with no "abduction" experience made up such an event after
hypnosis?

So are you saying that hypnosis doesn't implant false memories and what
about those cases in the US?????

You say that hypnosis is a "potentially dangerous technique" - or is this
only in the 'wrong hands'.

Whose are the 'right hands'.......?

BTW - when asked on a TV interview Alan Godfrey seems to have argued that
there was some kind of a cover-up? Cover-up of what?

Next you'll be telling me that Godfrey was a "trained observer" - when
there is no such thing......I have little problem remembering things and
even if I didn't - perish the thought - there is NO way that I'd get
involved with hypnosis.

Some people claim to give up smoking after hypnosis. Why not just give up
anyway????

Tim X

Hello John,and everyone

I feel I must comment on this whole hypnosis issue. This is indeed a very
important area of concern on the problems of hypnosis being used as a
method to unlock memories of close encounter experiences. I feel the
medical literature so far on recovered and false memories and indeed memory
retrieval in general is indicating that this process does not give either
the researcher or witness any clear or useful information of what has
occurred. There is no doubt that there have been major problems with the
use of regression hypnosis in some claims of abduction and as far as I can
see the medical evidence presents clear guidelines and research on the
problems involved in using hypnosis as a tool to extract accurate, reliable
and indeed objective information about extraordinary human experiences.


>>I think this point has to be made as I see many people are obsessed with
>damning a technique which has been used medically and non-medically to
>elicit FACT

**Please quote some cases where hypnosis has been used to elicit FACT, which
can be totally backed up by independent witnesses?
. Recent scientific research suggests that the use of
>'hypnosis' enhances ones memory of events dramatically. The researchers
>found that subjects were able to substantially improve their recall of
>events when hypnotic techniques were used.

**I would appreciate more information on this recent scientific research
where the use of hypnosis enhanced memory of events so dramatically. Can
specific case studies be backed up by independent parties?>

>
>To damn evidence that may be valid through prejudice or ill-conceived
>assumption rather than scientific argument is of no use investigatively.

**Can we prove that it is valid though? The scientific research on hypnosis
and memory retrieval that I am familiar with very clearly defines the major
problems with hypnosis and memory retrieval.


>The evidence in Godfrey's case would have had to be considered as a
>whole - direct, material, circumstantial and 'hypnotically-induced' -
>with due consideration given to the probability of imagination and/or
>false memory syndrome etc.

Very possibly true. As far as I understand it from the coverage of Alan
Godfrey's experience, he never felt that he understood or agreed with what
he said under hypnosis, only what he consciously remembered
>
>A moratorium on regression by BUFORA is commendable, no one wants
>witnesses subjected to naive intervention using potentially dangerous
>techniques of any kind

Absolutely and there are certainly cases where hypnosis has caused problems
for the witnesses. I personally feel that UFO research should not involve
hypnosis as a tool for memory retrieval about their experiences. This, in
my view, leads to further problems at times and therefore cannot possibly be
in the best interests of the witness. Furthermore, it does not add to our
knowledge of the possibilities of what may be occurring, but beyond all of
this remains the well being of the witness which must be primary to us. I
fail to see how using hypnosis to define the nature of their experience is
helping or supporting the witness, particularly with the imagery and
scenarios that can emerge, which has been very frightening for some people.
I have first hand experience of a small percentage of these cases where
people have undergone hypnosis with another UFO organisation or as an
independent venture and they have , become very disturbed and frightened by
what emerged under hypnosis and therefore what they perceive may have
happened to them. The mind is more powerful than we could even begin to
imagine and I believe we must be extremely cautious and responsible to those
that contact our organisations about high strangeness events.
- and one does not need to use hypnotic
>regression to induce false-memory and recall -

This is true, which is why memory retrieval has been shown to be very much
less than accurate at times and to me would emphasise the point of not using
hypnosis in claims of UFO Encounters. Surely this would enhance the
fallibility of memory even more?!

Just a few thoughts.

Gloria

On the point of the lighthouse....

Standing in Caple Green it becomes evident that if the military were
scattered about the field then those to the right farthest corner of
the field away from track 10 would not even have been able to see the
light from lighthouse due to dense tree cover. If any of the military
had progressed through the forest and away from the beaten track then
it most unlikely they would have been able to see the light from the
lighthouse unless they were 50ft tall+. So when the Americans promote
their far-fetched claims of the sky being lit up on approach to the
landing site. Following their route there is no possible way that this
effect can be attributed to the light house.

On the subject of the meteor shower......
December is a good month for stargazing in East Anglia. Skies are
quite clear and you can bet that just about any night you pick you'll
see shooting stars (as Judith mentioned). I don't think that we can
write this one off as misperceptions of a meteor shower. Investigators
went onto Bentwaters to follow up on sightings during November and the
beginning of December. I'm sure that there was meteor activity during
these periods as well but sceptics haven't blamed it as an excuse for
these particular sightings. Why? Because they are lesser known.

I think something of import happened in Rendlesham Forest over the
night of the 27th of December. However until we can discount much of
the American BS and many of the natural alternatives that sceptics
have presented to the media without the need for solid research to
back up their theories then we'll simply be amidst a whitewash of
contradication and lies with little chance of eradicating the myth and
getting to the truth.

Dear all,

You are all aware of the recent reply to my PRIMEBASE BULLETIN No.1
elicited from British researcher Judith Jaafar
I feel her points require a detailed reply. This deabte rased some very
interesting points about my project, Rendlesham and other aspects of
British UFO research & investigation.

Ms. Jaafar's comments are noted with a ">" symbol.

[Snip < Text My Detailed reply to Tim Matthew's e-mail re PRIMEBASE
BULLETIN 1
dated 28th Jan 1999].
>Having read the above, and while applauding Robert's sterling efforts to
>make some sense of all the scattered data floating around, I feel it
>important to stress that armchair research is no substitute for "on the
>ground" investigation. This applies to all of us, and I myself am guilty
of
>coming to conclusions about cases on the strength of reports/ articles /
>books submitted by other researchers. Unfortunately, it is impossible for
>most of us to travel round the country to do our own investigations at UFO
>locations and we have to rely on the often shoddy, and downright
misleading
>research of others.

Reply:
Firstly, my reply to Tim (which mentioned Rendlesham not in any *great*
depth!) was hardly a "serious" research effort -
though the two case-examples I mentioned are worthy of some (minor)
consideration!
It was more of an "casual" excercise for PRIMEBASE, more than anything...

In regards to Ms. Jaafar's other points...
I would counter that *all* the best research is "done in an armchair"! The
process of validating (or otherwise) a case is *pure* "armchair" research.
 Aircraft movement checks, writing to weather stations, checking the
positions of astronomical bodies is all done from indoors (as is
interviewing witnesses - unless you (and them) want to get needlessly cold
and wet!). Even checking
the "folklore" of an area is library-chair based research. I have done all
this in my time as a Ufologist. Without it, any field work
is merely raw, unsubstantiated data!

If we adopt an attitude of ignoring (even demeaning) all past information,
we would end up with a subject that effectively "has no past". This is
indeed what *has* happened in recent years, where sensationalist
researchers have been allowed to "reinvent" Ufology for the "dancehouse
generation". Without work such as PRIMEBASE we would be unaware of the
statistical parameters of sightings, past trends and so on. Which, in
fact, we largely are, because of the disdain such research is viewed and
treated by many within the U.K UFO community.

HENCE THERE IS NO PROGRESS IN OUR UNDERSTANDING OF UFO
REPORTS!
  (An important fact to note in this bold fashion!!!)

 And, as I have said before, how can ufology have a future if it never had
a past? But, for ufology, the past holds lots of skeletons; ie reports of
UFOs resembling George Adamski's (mainly in the 1950's and early 1960's),
the changing face of British UFO entities (mainly tall blond-haired men
prior to the 1970's (Adamski again!) and then lots of "Greys" after about
1985(!) - is there a slight Budd Hopkins/ Communion influence here?), etc.
Many "classic" cases are (on closer examination) only "classic" mistakes!

In a climate such as this PRIMEBASE is vital, if only on a folkloric level!
 The more time I devote to this project the
more important I think it is, on a variety of levels.

As for the case-samples in PRIMEBASE itself being "shoddy.....and
....misleading", that is a matter of opinion! The degree to which a case
was investigated is shown, in the standard manner (ie through levels "D" to
"A"). The names of the investigators are also shown. PRIMEBASE includes
some of the best investigated cases in the U.K (and some of the
not-so-better researched ones,as well!). I would hardly think it is fair
or accurate to imply that the work of investigators such as Ken Philips,
Jenny Randles, R. Sandbatch, David Clarke, Andy Roberts, Gloria Dixon, Tony
Eccles, Paul Fuller, me(!),John Heptonstall......and Judith Jaafar herself
is "shoddy....and... misleading"! And - on noting these names - I am sure
she will have a higher opinion of PRIMEBASE's datasample! All these
people have been prime sources for diverse PRIMEBASE "entries". If my
database composed purely of rubbishy "shoddy" reports ripped off from cheap
paperbacks I would *never* have continued to proceed with this major
research effort! In fact, it is vital the work of these investigators
*are* recorded for the future, because of the great efforts they took!

Dear All,

Having actually enjoyed watching tonight's "Riddle of the Skies", (I'm
prejudiced having served as a consultant to the show) especially the less
frenetic and more low key approach, I was equally heartened to read Rob's
response to the latest Rendlesham debate.

I'm not entirely sure what benefits the activities of a local UFO research
group wondering around the woods some 18 years later are and I'm not at all
sure that anything more interesting than the lighthouse was responsible for
the major sightings. In any case, how can a triangular "craft" have landed
in the forest?

I think we should entirely discount Warren's testimony.

I didn't actually know that Steuart Campbell had matched the flashes (not
flashers!) in the woods to the lighthouse but I'll check it out.....In
addition Rob is right to state that a great deal of armchair research IS
required. Quite often visiting sites years after the event serve only to
encourage posturing and posing for the camera.....It's also a great deal
easier than speaking to witnesses and phoning airports and local
authorities.
On a general note I think continued interest in the clearly questionable
Rendlesham case is evidence of attempts to provide evidence of "UFO
Reality" by the "best-case scenario" whereby more localised reports and
mini UFO "flaps" are ignored. We tend to hear only about Roswell, Socorro,
Belgium, Mexico when it is not clear that the best evidence - either way -
comes from them and in fact one might argue that the financial/UFO
industrial motive serves to encourage and maintain myths that have grown up
around these "best cases".

In fact in terms of the Belgium case there are many problems with the
standard and accepted version of events and much like Rendlesham these are
almost never discussed; things like;

1 - FTs of the sort seen in Belgium were seen in the UK - around RAF
Boscombe Down - in March 1990.

2 - The radar on the two Belgian AF jets sent to intercept the "UFO" was
malfunctioning. The two jets' radar systems locked onto each other!

3 - Most of the "thousands of witnesses" did NOT see a triangle - just
lights.

4 - There is limited evidence of hoaxing.

5 - The Defence Intelligence community took a great interest in the
sightings indicating that certain of their number knew exactly what was
going on.

6 - The "triangular UFO" at no time displayed evidence of high performance
and its' characteristics were more akin to an advanced LTA hybrid than
anything else.

7 - The MOD lied about NADGE knowledge of the UFO reports, the faulty radar
and more besides.

8 - The little radar evidence from ground stations suggested that the "UFO"
travelled towards the English coast (!).

Oh yes - the intercept pilots NEVER SAW a triangular UFO.

One of the most dubious elements of the UFO evidence is radar which often
malfunctions. Ask anyone whose been involved with radar systems.....

No doubt these and more will be discussed in future......at least there is
evidence of reasoned UFO debate on this list!

Three of the lectures at our very excellent Conference on Sat 272/99 in
Southport will be along the lines of re-examining famous cases; the Peter
Day UFO film (Jenny Randles), Berwyn (Andy Roberts) and Howden Moors/"The
Sheffield Incident" (Dr. Dave Clarke) and this is clearly evidence of our
desire to provide a counterbalance to the host of misinformed propaganda
currently on TV and in the general media. I'll also be announcing further
information about our research into US disc programmes! Lots of new UFO
video footage is to be shown too!

>Very interesting; hypnosis is OK and it isn't OK? So which is it/isn't

Hypnosis is a modality that has been used for at least 100 years in the
UK since introduction by Mesmer when it was known as Mesmerism.

Hypnotherapy, as defined by the Oxford Dictionary, is 'the treatment of
disease by hypnotism'.

The techniques involve from deep trance when the subject has no
immediate memory of their hypnotic session to mild trance when the
subject is fully aware of everything that occurs; both these extremes
have been used in 'regressing' subjects. To quote from arch sceptic Sue
Blackmore in her book 'Beyond the Body' page 183 "Nowadays hypnotism is
an accepted part of medicine and psychology" - that about sums it up.

>I do not know of any registered medical personnel who use hypnosis to
>recover memories and I'd really like to know which scientists have used
>hypnosis to 'improve recall' (?)

I did not keep the article but it appeared only last week in the
National Press.

By the way, psychology - a la Sue Blackmore - is not a 'medical'
science. Psychologists and Psychiatrists ( who are medics ) amongst
others use hypnotism.

Let's not confuse 'medical' with 'knows everything about medicine' - the
two things are very mutually exclusive I can assure you and I do not
know any medics who would disagree with that point. Some of the most
hardened sceptics about anything they do not understand, despite more
than adequate scientific acceptability, are registered medical
personnel, it goes with the territory especially when asked to offer
opinions by patients. They are strapped by a system that dictates what
they are allowed to 'know'. Contrary to propaganda, their medicine is
largely not evidence-based, ( about 80% is not ), and Aussie Research
showed modern medicine to be the 3rd biggest killer after heart disease
and cancer, USA Research showed it to be the 4th after heart disease,
cancer and stroke; let's not confuse fact with opinion.

Surgical techniques have been carried out under hypnosis by medical
'scientists' in various parts of the world. People, especially children,
are often hypnotised or hypnotherapy is used on them by trained dentists
prior to dental surgery. etc. etc.

> given that I have read several articles in
>"New Scientist" by US academics studying the effects of hypnosis who
>actually argue that it is all kidology!
>
There are always the small number of sceptics who maintain the delusion
that anything they disagree with must be wrong or invalid; that's life.
I prefer to look at the overall scientific evidence and look objectively
at all situations, you can be sure they are in denial. New Scientist has
a record of sceptics editing; remember arch sceptic and long time editor
Bernard Dixon of CSICPS fame ( UKs version of CSICOPS, the USA group
with The Amazing Randi etc. ). In his book 'Dirty Medicine' Martin J.
walker describes CSICOP as practising 'scientific McCarthyism'.
Unfortunately it is easy to confuse scientific fact with many things
scientists say. I'm a scientist and I know of which I speak that is
opinion and that which currently is 'fact'.
>Hmmmm....
>
>I asked my sister about this - she's a real Doctor BTW. She said that

Do you mean by 'real doctor' ie. she has a PhD in a subject, or do you
mean she is a physician?

>hypnosis is regarded as a dangerous fringe activity by many of her
>colleagues.

As I said, some are in denial, some are prejudiced, and some know no
better; Hypnosis is a technique that has a scientific and medical
foundation. When 'fringe' people indulge themselves in the use of a
technique with which they put a subject at risk - that can be any aspect
of risk from emotional upset to physical or mental distress depending on
the situation - then it is dangerous. It can still be dangerous when
used by medical practitioners, just as 99% of all medical techniques are
themselves potentially dangerous - that goes with the biochemical
territory and surgical activity, but the perception is that 'physicians'
may be the 'safest pair of hands'. There is no evidence that this is
correct. I know of no studies which have compared such techniques of
intervention when used by medical against non-medical people who use
them.

>Eric Morris has come out totally against the use of hypnosis
>having used it occasionally in the past - for reasons including the fact
>that it was impossible to tell whether the witness was telling the truth.

That's the point I made in a previous e-mail; unless such techniques are
considered for use to move forward in an investigation, or to confirm or
introduce new evidence, they should not be considered; if the
information obtained during 'regression sessions' cannot be verified
it's of little use even if it may be true. It is easy to tell if the
witness is truthful if the evidence can be verified materially or
directly. The problems we have seen with such techniques used willy
nilly by Quest etc. is that information obtained by such means has been
taken as fact without any supporting evidence - that's ridiculous and
has led to much conjecture about 'regression'.

I was involved in research with 'hypnotherapy regression' some years ago
involving several subjects with various disorders; the sessions were
controlled by a very experienced hypnotherapist, myself and an
immunologist assisted her. Although the information obtained was
fascinating, it was not of a nature that would allow us to verify the
facts so I was left unconvinced. The research was geared at the type of
information produced as opposed to the validity of that info. so I did
not expect too much. It is certainly true that a vivid imagination can
affect the outcome. It is also true that, under the correct protocols,
scientists have proved the validity of the technique by gaining
substantially more accurate information during hypnosis than without -
look at the recent press.
>
>Haven't people with no "abduction" experience made up such an event after
>hypnosis?
>
I am sure they have; I read a few transcripts by 'regressionists' who
had obtained abduction details from subjects and to a one they had used
leading questions. Any such interviews must done without any form of
leading - just like a lawyer in court - or one puts ideas and words into
the mouth of the subject. Prior contamination must also be identified
and, I repeat, only information which is supported by other direct
and/or material and/or circumstantial evidence should be considered
potentially useful.

>So are you saying that hypnosis doesn't implant false memories and what
>about those cases in the US?????
>
False memories can be planted either through hypnosis or by prior
'impression' forming techniques. You can tell a child ( and some
impressionable adults ) facts about themselves that they had no
knowledge of with sufficient credibility and these may be recounted as
truth during any future interviews or sessions, whether under hypnosis
or not. That's life.

That is one 'danger' of any interview, not only under hypnosis, and it
has to be recognised as a potential 'side effect' of such techniques -
as any medical intervention has. One has to take it into consideration
when assessing results.

>You say that hypnosis is a "potentially dangerous technique" - or is this
>only in the 'wrong hands'.

It is a potentially dangerous technique, as is any intervention in
another's affairs, in any hands; some people will be more adept at this
than others, sensitivity and concern for the welfare of the subject
being paramount as opposed to any form of professional expertise.
>
>Whose are the 'right hands'.......?
>
Those trained in its use, and who gain experience in the safe and
effective practice of the modality. I would not ask a medic to prescribe
a homeopathic remedy, nor a spinal manipulation, nor an acupuncture
session unless I was sure he/she was qualified and experienced in said
forms of medical intervention; nor would I want a homeopath to prescribe
drugs. If I was to be regressed I would find someone recognised as
experienced in the techniques and having a recognised qualification in
either psychology or hypnotherapy, and most importantly, who I felt
comfortable allowing myself to be manipulated in such ways by. If that
person was medically qualified, and the other criteria were met, I would
be most comfortable.


>BTW - when asked on a TV interview Alan Godfrey seems to have argued that
>there was some kind of a cover-up? Cover-up of what?

I did not see the interview; nor do I know Godfrey, the fact he was a
police officer suggests he may have been of reasonable character -
though not always the case - so I do not know what 'cover-up' he spoke
of. Assuming he was 'abducted' during his shift ( not sure but did he
not say that he was with another officer when they both saw a UFO? - who
would support his own story presumably ) then there must have been
evidence that he went missing etc. If evidence was produced that was of
material value, and this was ignored or suppressed then he would have
presumed cover-up; he may KNOW that there was a cover-up. Best ask him.

If there is additional evidence of some 'exotic' occurrence in addition
to any regression data, there is a case to explore. I haven't the facts
have you?

I interviewed a police officer who, with three others, saw a UFO over
Wetherby about 20 years ago; he only reported to me as he was incensed
by sceptics on a radio program who said all UFO witnesses are deluded.
He was in the control room at midnight when a WPC banged on the door to
alert him about a 'saucer' they had chased towards York, handed over to
York Police, then chased it back as it followed the river to Wetherby
again in their squad car. The others would not comment but he did as he
was never interviewed by 'men who arrived from the MOD and told the
other 3 who were interviewed never to speak of the incident'. The three
were a sergeant, PC and WPC. The PC now works at Menwith Hill. I would
call that a 'cover-up'.
>
>Next you'll be telling me that Godfrey was a "trained observer" - when
>there is no such thing......I have little problem remembering things and
>even if I didn't - perish the thought - there is NO way that I'd get
>involved with hypnosis.
>
I don't know anything of Godfrey so can't tell whether he has developed
his observation techniques; it is a prerequisite for good policing
though not something always taken up. When I worked in criminal
intelligence I was involved with much OP work, hence many photos and
videos of targets, and did not necessarily see a target in the flesh
before having to apprehend him or operate against him. Despite this one
developed an exceptional ability to recognise targets from very limited
data. People working on satellite and other surveillance maps develop a
tremendous ability to see detail one may not normally see. I call all
this 'becoming a trained observer' but depends on what one is trained to
observe. As I said, it is incumbent on a police officer to develop
observational abilities, it doesn't always happen.
>Some people claim to give up smoking after hypnosis. Why not just give up
>anyway????
>
Having dealt with many people who wished to give up smoking I can state
that as an addiction it is not an easy task for addicts to give up; nor
is prozac, amitriptyline, vallium, heroin, crack- cocaine and opium.
Nicotine is a drug, giving-up usually induces withdrawal. Many people
testify to giving-up only through hypnosis, and having tried many and
varied ways without success, and unless I have reason to disbelieve them
I usually accept their word, after-all it was their experience.


Cheers


John.

>medical literature so far on recovered and false memories and indeed memory
>retrieval in general is indicating that this process does not give either

>occurred. There is no doubt that there have been major problems with the
>use of regression hypnosis in some claims of abduction and as far as I can
>see the medical evidence presents clear guidelines and research on the
>problems involved in using hypnosis as a tool to extract accurate, reliable
>and indeed objective information about extraordinary human experiences.

>
>>>I think this point has to be made as I see many people are obsessed with
>>damning a technique which has been used medically and non-medically to
>>elicit FACT

>**Please quote some cases where hypnosis has been used to elicit FACT, which
>can be totally backed up by independent witnesses?

Look at medical and psychological literature over the last 100 years; I
think we are focussing on 'regression' really as hypnosis has proved
itself over and again. As for 'regression' all we are talking about is
the facilitated memory of past events. Last week's press contained
details of recent research where researchers had specifically tested
memory with and without hypnosis as an aid; the latter made substantial
difference.

I think we have to stop confusing 'medical' advice, and 'medical'
opinion with scientific fact. John Mack is a medical doctor of some
repute and was so long before his sojourn into UFOlogy, who practices
psychiatry and he has used and supported regression.

Most prejudice is against the ET hypothesis and therefore any technique
which purports to provide evidence of 'ET' intervention will
automatically be considered invalid, without scientific argument. I am
excluding the obvious dangers associated with regression practised
without proper safeguards - and we could argue what they should be - but
medically I agree with the possibility that it can be dangerous. It can
be far less dangerous than many anti-psychotic drugs that 'abductees' no
doubt find themselves subjected to by medics who do not accept the
probability that their patient may have experienced an 'abduction'.

>
>. Recent scientific research suggests that the use of

>>found that subjects were able to substantially improve their recall of
>>events when hypnotic techniques were used.
>

>where the use of hypnosis enhanced memory of events so dramatically. Can
>specific case studies be backed up by independent parties?>

Look to last weeks press.
>>
>>To damn evidence that may be valid through prejudice or ill-conceived
>>assumption rather than scientific argument is of no use investigatively.
>
>**Can we prove that it is valid though? The scientific research on hypnosis
>and memory retrieval that I am familiar with very clearly defines the major
>problems with hypnosis and memory retrieval.
>
Memory retrieved through hypnosis is only questionable if not supported
by follow-up which proves the facts elicited by the recall process.
USA courts of law have excluded evidence gained through 'regression'
because it is still arguable whether it is valid or not; they are trying
to sort it out from opinion to scientific fact, that will take research.
They have not excluded the possibility that those recollections may be
completely valid. In such cases we are talking about courts of law where
another party is to suffer the consequences of the revelation e.g.
abused child etc. The court must satisfy itself that any information has
been obtained according to accepted methods, and that it is demonstrable
in court.
>

>>with due consideration given to the probability of imagination and/or

>he said under hypnosis, only what he consciously remembered

If it was 'hypnosis' and not light trance/hypnotherapy it is possible he
does not recollect what he said. If he does not recollect what he said,
and does not consciously remember certain facts that came out under
hypnosis, then how can he be sure if what he said is true or false?

It might be interesting to note here something that I came across in the
PRO over a year ago. All the obvious UFO files had already been pulled by
various researchers, so I opted for a lateral approach and homed in on a
report on Orfordness. It was massive and I only managed to take a rather
cursory look, but what I found certainly gave me food for thought. First of
all, Bentwaters/ Woodbridge was part of the experimentation that was going
on at Orfordness i.e. project "Cobra Mist"(amongst others), working on the
development of over - the - horizon radar. Questions had been asked by MPs
and in Parliament about what was going on, and the MOD had issued
instructions that the lie that they were only experimenting with sound-wave
propagation must be adhered to at all times, even to Ministers. This lie
may have had something to do with the fact that the military were becoming
increasingly concerned that their experimentation with microwaves was
causing shipping in the Suffolk coastal area to blow-up ! If questioned
about this, military personnel were instructed to say that the cause of
these mysterious explosions was sparks igniting empty fuel tanks.
Interesting, since this was exactly the same excuse that was used when that
civilian airliner came down a few years back just outside New York,
although witnesses said they had seen something like a missile whizzing
along just before the explosion.

Allegedly, "Cobra Mist" was closed down around 1970 for lack of government
funding, but some further research by Richard Conway has shown that it
actually continued under another name "Cold Shadow"(I think that's right),
under the leadership of guess who ?................. none other than our
old friend Ralph Noyes. (check with Richard for details). The files on this
are still classified under the 30yr rule.

And now here's something really interesting. In the Orfordness/Cobra Mist
file I came upon a memo from the head of the MOD to a top official in the
Pentagon. I don't have the photo copy I made to hand (I passed all this to
Richard), but I believe it was from 1968 or thereabouts. It "requested" in
rather unequivocal terms that the Americans desist from engaging in secret
research and experimentation from their bases in Suffolk
(Woodbridge/Bentwaters), research to which the British were not party, and
to which no official British Government sanction had been given. This had
been brought to light by a leak in security at the American bases, and the
British authorities were mightily displeased. What sort of research this
was I never discovered, but it leads one to wonder just what was going on
in rural Suffolk. Whether this could be connected to subsequent events at
Rendlesham Forest and other strange events in the area (Shingle Street ? )
I do not know, but it's worth a ponder.

I am aware that meteors can burn up in all different colours ( I myself
have witnessed a brilliant electric blue shower), but these colours are
normally seen when burning high up in the atmosphere, forty to eighty miles
up. If a meteor is sufficiently large to make it to earth without total
burn-out, the outer particles which give rise to these brilliant colours
have been burnt - off, leaving a core which is much more likely to resemble
a conventional ball of fire(colour-wise). But by far the most important
factor in determining whether we are dealing with a meteor, and
distinguishing it from space-debris re-entry (which has also been
postulated in this case) is the duration of the sighting. 80% of meteors
which have been misidentified as UFOs have had a viewing duration of less
than 10 seconds, and 50% less than five seconds, with bolides being visible
for only slightly longer. It would have come and gone in less time than
Col. Halt would have taken to get out of his pyjamas. If it was a bright
fireball meteor that gave rise to the initial sighting, then what were they
chasing through the woods? A mirage ? And don'tell me THE LIGHTHOUSE,
please !

Hello All,

Received the latest Nick Pope newsletter this morning. 'Nick Pope's Weird
World' it most certainly is!!

He actually had the gall to pull me up for complaining about the shoddy way
in which TV companies, and Granada specifically (Yes, round three of the
nightmare tonight folks!!) treat UFO researchers. They expect everything
for nothing and suppose that you go weak at the knees when talking to one
of their researchers.

In fact Mark Gorton of Granada - who is partly responsible for the awful
rubbish that is "Origin Unknown" emailed a colleague of mine and in his
defence could only argue that he had been TOLD to make the series "more
alien" and that factual errors are "just TV"!!

I kid you not.

Yes, we at Lancashire UFO Society do alot of hard work - as do all you out
there. You know - buying books, subscribing to magazines and journals,
making long phone calls, speaking to witnesses, visiting archives and
attending Conferences. Do we get rich? Do we make a profit even?

No we don't.

We're not all in this for the money but fair remuneration for services
rendered - ie; decent research - seems fair to me.

But Nick Pope thinks that there is a problem with this. Or so he claims in
his latest sleepfest ezine effort.

How much were we asking for? £100 for providing Granada with six witnesses
to triangle sightings, copies of reports, details of sightings, details on
stealth programmes that have taken four years to get hold of. Not to
mention having their researcher over to ours and spending time faxing and
generally running about.

We didn't intend to spend it all at once! (Just in case you were wondering
our good treasurer keeps my hands out of the money pot!!)

My view is that every TV company should pay a research fee - as they do to
everyone else bar Ufologists it would seem - when we are helping them make
a programme. Many groups already make such a legitimate demand and I would
encourage everyone to do the same. BUFORA has done this in the past and it
is to be hoped that the IUN will do so when it kicks into action.

Now let's get one thing straight. Pope is the man who asked, and was paid,
no less than £1,000 for speaking at a Quest International Conference. He
has been paid thousands for articles and appearances and is getting
£100,000 for his so-called "technothriller" (!) "Operation Thunderchild".

Hypocrisy doesn't even come close!

So who is making money from who?

It's the UFO industry folks - it's business - it's nothing to do with
effective and credible research!

This is what Nick 'The Millionaire' had to say;

"
    The High Moral Ground (Not!)

 A noted UFO "anorak" criticised the excellent new Grenada TV
series Watch the Skies in a recent Internet post, stating that he
and another UFO group had decided not to play any part in the
project because they didn't agree with the angle which they felt
the series was taking. Admirable, if true. Unfortunately for him,
he let the cat out of the bag a few lines later, with a sniffy comment
about how Grenada weren't prepared to pay a "research fee".
Oh dear!"

The guy can't even spell Granada properly - or get the title of the
programme
correct!!!!!!

Sniffy?

Don't think so!

Yet again Pope's blown it but then I exposed the truth about his pre-Air
Staff 2A
"UFO close encounter" on a live TV programme!

No doubt he is getting worried about the many people asking him searching
questions about the gloss he has put on his career at the MOD and the fact
that in terms of anything of significance, for instance a joint UK-US
stealth
programme, he was left well and truly out of the loop.

A very junior civil servant indeed.

I'm not perfect, far from it, but my UFO research is aimed at one thing and
one thing
only; finding out the truth about man-made UFOs and investigating all local
UFO sightings
in Lancashire and elsewhere to the best of my ability.

If Nick wants to donate some of his stash to our noble efforts then we'd be
happy
to receive it. We might be able to pay the phone bill.

Tim Matthews - Lancashire UFO Society - working in the voluntary
sector.......with y'all....

No, this makes the use of hypnosis under such circumstances a modality
which requires rigorous standards of provision.

In the Supreme Court of British Columbia a case REGINA v CARRIE SAVOY,
Nov 18th and 19th 1997; it was ruled that evidence produced by
regression hypnosis may be admitted if the following guidelines were
followed:-

1. The person conducting the interview should be a qualified
professional with training in the use of hypnosis and expertise in
psychiatry and clinical psychology.
2. The hypnotist (H) must be independent of the party requiring services
3. The H must be given only minimum amount of info. necessary to conduct
interview.
4. The entire interview between H and witness should be recorded
5. Only the H and subject must be present at that interview; if any
party needs to watch this has to be arranged via CCTV or other mechanism
5. Prior to hypnosis, the H should conduct a lengthy interview of the
subject to ascertain medical history, present/past use of drugs, and
judgement and intelligence of subject evaluated.
6 Prior to hypnosis, the H should elicit from the subject a detailed
description of the facts surrounding the subject matter of the hypnosis
session as the subject is able to recall them at that point in time.
7. The H should pay careful attention to the form and manner of
questions - the choice of words and avoidance of body language so that
he is not either intentionally or inadvertently providing the subject
with info.

These rules are self-explanatory and take into consideration important
facts such as - once the hypnosis session has elicited facts, whether or
not those facts are true they are likely to become permanent memory for
the witness. Hence a full interview to elicit any facts recalled must
occur prior to hypnosis for later comparison. No leading questions or
body language etc. to be given

They then realised that even these rules would not be fair to the
Defence as it presented a problem of the inability of the Opposition to
cross-examine the witness with original pre-hypnosis memory - no matter
whether it is true or false. This was a court of law. In our case we do
not face that problem, there is no requirement for cross-examination as
such, and hence the guidelines would be deemed sufficient.

>"I am also sure Ian Ridpath (who has also visited the site on several

You bet! We *know* that the airmen went chasing the lighthouse on the first
night, because two of them said so in their witness statements which James
Easton very resourcefully uncovered from the CAUS files (which, of course,
no UFO believer ever bothered to do).
We also know that the local police who were called to the location on the
first night said that the only light they could see was from the Orford
Ness lighthouse. This was an independent eyewitness account that the UFO
believers never managed to track down, and which many of them have also
conveniently never bothered to quote since I placed it in the public domain
15 years ago - I wonder why?

We can also easily deduce that the lighthouse was the culprit on the second
night, from Halt's own tape recording. On this, he conveniently gives the
compass bearing of the light, which shows he was looking in the direction
of the Orford Ness lighthouse, and he describes the flashing light as lying
"clear off to the coast". Hmm...

Also on the tape we can hear the airmen calling out the flash rate ("There
it is...there it is again") with a 5-second interval, which also matches
the flash rate of the Orford lighthouse.

Where was Halt observing from? In more recent statements, he has told us
that the flashing light was nearly in line with a farmhouse. As Judith J
points out in her posting:
>"The lighthouse ... can only be seen ... if you position yourself
carefully in direct line with a shallow dip in the ridge."<

Yes, indeed. As I have previously remarked (see for example James Easton's
web site), this is just the position from which the lighthouse can be seen
in line with the farmhouse. Coincidence, or what? (Another coincidence: how
many other UFOs are reported to have been flashing "like an eye winking at
you", as Halt put it on his tape? And how many were seen in the same
direction as a lighthouse?)

As for the positioning of the supposed "landing site" - how does *anyone*
know where this was? The airmen did not mark it on the first night. They
went out on the following morning and cast around until they found three
indentations which they thought could be interpreted as "landing marks". As
we know from the local police (who were called out *again* to look a them)
and the local forester Vince Thurkettle, these had all the appearance of
old rabbit scrapings - and when it comes to local knowledge of an English
pine forest, I would take the word of a local bobby and a local forester
over that of the US Air Force any day.

hypnosis.

entrenched in the psyche once revealed through hypnosis- whether true or
false - and therefore pre-hypnosis memory may be altered by hypnotically
enhanced recall

4. For the cross-examination this leaves the opposition without recourse
to the initial 'untainted' pre-hypnosis memory.

Preumably it would not be acceptable to allow the 'opposition' to
question/cross-examine the witness prior to hypnosis as this contradicts
other aspects of legal practice. Witness memory must remain as clear and
untainted by what would be traumatic cross-examination prior to the
court case. The process is, examination by your counsel, cross-
examination by opposition counsel, re-examination by your counsel to
clear-up any doubts introduced by clever cross-examination. That's the
law.

red, green, blue...

At that time I believed nearly everything
published in those skeptical books, and I told
myself: OK, that's a another UFO category which
becomes IFO (identified).

But, looking more often at the stars and
planets, I never, never, never saw a star
with changing colours.

My vision of colours is very good; not any
kind of daltonism. Apart from Mars (difficult
to see), which is frankly reddish, and Jupiter,
which I find yellowish, other astronomical
objects (stars, Venus) are just white or whitish.
Agreed, some stars look slightly bluish. But they
don't exhibit changing colours !

I know of this phenomenon called in French
"rayon vert" ("green flash" ?) which can be seen
at sunset, and which I myself observed several
times on the seaside (I even know the meteorological
conditions needed to see it, from the place where
I observe the sunset). This phenomenon exists,
it has been photographied and filmed (I have seen
photos).

Since stars appear at well known locations in
the sky, it would be easy to photography and
film these stars with changing colours (agreed,
it would depend on the meteorological conditions,
but with a little patience it would work). So
here is my question: what are the references for
these photos and films ? Maybe Ian Ridpath knows
these references ?

Without references, I think I will consider this
story of stars with changing colours as a legend.

Jean-Pierre Pharabod

Date: Sun, 21 Mar 1999 11:08:24 -0500
From: engima9 <ENGIMA9@compuserve.com>
Subject: An ETH variation!

UFO Research List

One of the problems with the ETH (other than a lack of *any* conclusive
evidence!) are the distances involved in travelling between the stars. For
many decades, everyone has come to accept that the ETH would involve
visitors from other, fairly distant star-systems. This would mean many,
many years of travel, and the utilisation of massive levels of energy
(*very* massive levels of energy in regards to "space-warp" travel!)

Where else could they be from; surely not from any of our nearby planets!
They are all hellholes incapable of supporting (virtually) any lifeforms.
Likewise, there is no evidence of any "Alien bases" (other than that which
can be explained in terms of TLP (or "TLP-type" events on other bodies
than the moon). And where's the evidence of ET mining, space-bases, etc,
on the other worlds of our solar system.... which doesn't depend on
conspiracy theories to sustain it's viability?

Likewise with all the near-earth stars akin to sol (ie Alpha Centauri & Tau
Ceti) . Where's the radio signals that such cultures should be
transmitting....transmissions we should have picked up decades ago! And,
all in all, 1.3+ parsecs is *still* a long way to travel (ie a round trip
at 0.5c (an reasonably viable speed for an STL starship) would take about
12 years to complete. By comparsion sailing ship explorations of our world
during the 16th-18th centuries took about 1-2 years in total - with (in
that case) plenty of hospitable places to stop along the way to pick up
supplies!.

So, what of *another* possibility.....

What if there was once a planet in orbit around our sun (or a nearby star)
 which was via a very severe collision event ( i.e impact with a very
large comet/asteriod or a moon-sized object) shifted from it's orbit and
ejected into interstellar space? What if this world originally existed
around the biozone of this star and had life?? And that life evolved and
developed a technical culture???

In our own solar system, the gap between Mars & Earth would be a suitable
location for such a "lost world".

Planets changing orbital positions are by no means impossible, likewise the
existence of "escaping" planetary bodies. In regards to the former,
Goldilocks (the super-massive world orbiting 51-Pegasi) is thought by some
astronomers to have been formed in one part of it's solar system and later
"transferred" to it's present location very close to 51-Pegasi. We also
know Jupiter can eject comets into interstellar space. And it is strongly
suspect that Miranda (one of the Moons of Uranus) was smashed appart by a
collision sometime in it's history and eventually reformed via accretion.
Many of the "gas giant" moons, the moons of Mars (and even, it is
suspected, Pluto) were "captured" bodies (albeit originally created by the
formation of our solar system). The early history of the solar system was
very definitely one of numerous collision events (the surface of the Moon,
Mercury and other worlds shows clear evidence of this).

Yes, of course, if such a world was "ejected" from it's solar system all
life on the surface would die. But there *could* also be survivors, living
undergound in artifical environments. If we accept that we could establish
a base in space (ie the Alpha spacestation or MIR) or on the Moon (the
postulated lunar colony proposed for the first two decades of the 21st
century), life could equally be sustained to this "ejected" planet by such
artifical means.

Living underground all radio communications could well be (logically)
channeled underground, and hence blocked by the planet's surface. This
would not therefore "leak" out into space and be subsequently detected by
our radio telescopes. A world without a sun it would not be visible
optically, with very little light falling on it's surface. If sufficiently
distant from it's originating solar system it would have *no* gravitational
effects on it's originating system, and hence NOT be detectable by any
gravational effects on that particular solar system.

No-one on Earth would be aware of the existance of that world if this
disaster happened before recorded history
(in a time before man?).

As time progressed, the survivors on this world could become more and more
adapted to their new environment, until they were as suited to their
current artifical biome as we on earth are suited to our natural one. It
may well be these entities would be cybernetic organisms, living off energy
rather than food and not requiring an atmosphere. Or they may have even
become extremely sensitive to airborne organisms present in a "natural"
atmosphere world like Earth, due to them living in an artifical biome. Is
this why some UFO entities are reported to wear "spacesuits....which could
also be part of a cybernetic body-structure).

According to this theory there would be no open contact between ourselves
and "them" (for what purpose, when such radical differences exist between
us and "them". They need nothing from us, and "they" can't (or won't!)
share anything with us.

The only reason to visit earth would be to assess our "threat potential"
and to document our progress. Why not use radio scanning-beams/lasers to do
this work you ask, rather than direct visitation? Answer; this would give
away "their" position in space. Space flights would not. If you were a
culture surviving on a very (over) specialised artifical biosphere with
finite resources (but advanced technology) would you want to give away your
position to another race with access to nuclear weapons, spaceflight and a
long, unfortunate history of using such techonology in a violent and
ruthless manner? And, worse still, they could reach your world, within a
few decades (if not already). Hence, the lack of any formal contact.

This theoretical world - rather than being the heavenly utopia beloved of
many contactees - would be a dour, dark and depressing place, with
limited (but adequate and technically advanced) resources.

The most notable thing about this theory is that (providing this
hypothetical world is positioned not *too* far from our solar
system) the speeds visually attributed to UFOs would be adequate for the
(fairly) short journeys between earth and this "world"! That is a
propulsion system that can move a craft from very close range to the size
of a pin-point in several seconds.....ie similar to the motions attributed
by witnesses to UFOs since 1947!!!

This is not to say that I feel that all "true UFOs" are ET in origin, by
any means! To begin with, this is *only* a theory. But we *do* have
reports of "exotics" (the "handful of the handful" of inexplicable
reports). Sightings of seemingly material devices. Earthlights/UAPs EHS,
astro-mirages, etc probably dispose of upto (at least) 90% of all "true
UFO" reports. It is foolish (and baseless) to deny otherwise.

But there are a few sightings of seemingly material objects, which seem to
be advanced, constructed devices. Providing they cannot be explained in
other ways (ie exotic subjective effects and man-made devices) we obviously
need a theory to account for them. So it does no harm to look at such
concepts, providing it is done in a sensible, balanced way, one guided by
evidential motives rather than sympathy for a "traditional" idea. But
these "exotic" reports do exist. It may be prudent to look at such ideas,
if only on a "what if" basis.

This is a simple and viable form of the ETH, which could be proved. Deep
radar/lidar scanning of the region outside of our solar
system would be able to locate this theoretical "dead-alive " world (but
would not be possible for many decades....probably
well into the 21st century or early into the 22nd century).

I would be interested in any comments you might have in regards to this.
Most importantly, can anyone help me with assessing the viability of this
concept; ie of a planet being "ejected" out of the solar system (or being
ejected from another one and (eventually) "drifting" close to our own).

Lastly, I would like to thank researcher Martin Rushe of Wiltshire who
originally proposed to me the possibility of some "exotic" UFOs originating
from an unknown world within our solar system. Although I disagreed with
him on the original form of this theory, his ideas inspired me to come up
with the concept of an ejected extra-solar world, which I feel is worthy of
some consideration.
Robert Moore,
East Huntspill,
England.
21st March, 1999.

Robert,

The scientific method involves formulation of TESTABLE THEORIES and
HYPOTHESES
that are tested against observational data, past, present and future, in order
to provide REALITY CHECKS that the theories are not due to error or self-
deception or outright fraud. These reality checks are where predictions,
"reproducibility" and/or "repeatability," and "falsifiability" come in. A
scientifically useful theory has to be "falsifiable" and it has to explain
more than any data set that one might have started with, i.e., it has
heuristic power to explain or predict UNEXPECTED events or phenomena. This
again provides a reality check against error or deception. The scientific
method is NOT restricted to only those things that can be tested in a lab
experiment -- that is merely one of the better ways to do scientific reality
checks but not the ONLY way. Lab experiment isn't a formal prerequisite for
science otherwise most of astrophysics and geophysics would have to be thrown
out because they deal with things that cannot be brought into the lab such as
the earth's core or a neutron star. The old saw that "an event is not
repeatable" is hogwash, since the universe is closed and every event has an
effect on its surroundings. These effects in principle at least are testable
at any time, though in practice distance and time blur distinctions -- but
this must be determined on a case-by-case basis not by some a prior decree
made in advance of even trying. Physical effects of many events of past
history are actually testable in a lab and are repeatable and reproducible
(geology does it all the time).

Right now, almost all of UFOlogy is in a pre-scientific mode of blindly
gathering data without exactly knowing WHAT data are ultimately relevant
because relevance is determined by the theories or hypotheses we're testing --
and we don't have ETH or anything else developed into an easily testable
formulation. I like your STL (Slower Than Light) and FTL (Faster Than Light)
models of ETH because these might be developed into TESTABLE hypotheses,
especially STL.

One serious defect of UFOlogy is its perverse insistence on going after
impossible or untestable ideas instead of doing the hard work of testing the
doable or testable. Many times I'll see someone propose an idea that can be
tested against a database only to be shot down by someone saying that aliens
MIGHT POSSIBLY be so far advanced as to be indistinguishable from magic
(paraphrasing Arthur C. Clarke's dictum) and that no theory can be devised to
test magic because to us it appears capricious. The result is that no one
does any testing of the lower-level TESTABLE theories. Basically no one in
UFOlogy wants to "do their homework" before graduating into "advanced" studies
of abductions, paranormal powers, etc.
My critique of your idea is not the same thing as what I just objected to
because my point is that there is little difference between travel technology
requirements of an alien civilization settled on a planet around a nearby star
(perhaps 4 to 10 light-years away) and a civilization on a cold planet thrown
out into interstellar space perhaps 1 to 5 light-years away (I don't think you
gave any distances but these need to be defined). At least the planet around
a star has a habitable environment and doesn't suffer from the severe extremes
of an escaped planet. I could be wrong. But you need to define your distance
regimes.

Regards,

Brad Sparks

There's a further issue related to events in the WSA, which
surprisingly hasn't, to my knowledge, received publicity, even in
the 'UFO' magazines.

In 'Left at East Gate', co-authored by Larry Warren and Peter
Robbins, they publish [pages 351-366] the transcript of an
interview with Halt, apparently recorded with permission.

At some points, Halt asks for the tape recorder to be switched
off, e.g., "One of the most interesting things.. You want to turn
the tapes off?".

Warren and Robbins write how they were later dismayed and angered
when in July 1994, Halt gave a lecture in the UK, during which he
dismissed Warren's story, claiming that Warren hadn't been
involved at all.

I believe the lecture was given in Leeds, when Halt was in the UK
to film an interview for the ITV 'Strange But True?' documentary
on the case.

Considering Halt's actions a "breach of confidence" following his
discussions with them, Warren and Robbins retaliate by disclosing
claims which Halt had allegedly made to them in confidence.

One of these was allegedly that, "Light beams had penetrated the
hard-core bunkers of Bentwaters' weapons-security area".


During a 1997 CompuServe conference with Warren and Robbins, I
had the opportunity to ask them about this and the CompuServe
library transcript records:

James Easton: You claim Halt revealed that beams of light
penetrated the weapons storage area and damaged the nuclear
weapons. He has now confirmed that the "pencil thin" beams were
seen _near_ the storage area., but that's all. Do you still
maintain he confirmed that nuclear weapons were compromised?

Larry & Peter: Yes -- he told us this face to face when we met
with him in Washington DC -- it is in the book as well.

Strictly, they didn't claim any weapons were damaged.


It's a second-hand story and maybe that's not exactly what Halt
said, possibly he only referred to the 'beams' being observed in
the WSA.

Only Halt has made any public statement about the 'beams' being
reported on radio as coming down near the WSA.
Randy has no knowledge of this, it was never mentioned in the
days afterwards and no-one ever interviewed him about the events.

observed 'objects'. A clue is in the taped conversation with
Warren and Robbins, when he says:

"None of the witnesses that I've talked to from the third night
[the second night as we know it - James] say there was anything
physical they could catch other than lights"

In which case, Randy's story could be a considerable surprise to
him.

We await developments.

Quite true..... in fact I agree with a lot of what you write in your
interesting reply!
To be honest, I first I wanted to see whether such an exotic idea (as I
proposed) was worth bothering with to begin with! Hence my decision to
put it out for discussion. Obviously, defining the distances relating to
this theory (and it's viability!) is going to be one of the *main* aims of
future research into this concept.

For a start, I need to determine whether the concept of an "escaping"
planet is scientifically plausible to begin with!
It if turns out it's *NOT * then the concept is dead in the water! This
will obviously entail a lot of writing, reading and research..........
But we have some interesting instances from our solar system (and others -
ie 51-Pegasi) which shows that solar systems
can be very violent and dynamic places. More so than astronomers even ten
years ago *ever* suspected

Basically, my - and Martin Rushe's - "near world theory" (to give it a
name) is an attempt , foolish or otherwise, to come up with an ETH
concept that does *not* involve very long travel times between a
(hypothetical) world of origin and earth. This is the "bane" of many
versions of the ETH at present , unless you allow for the possibility of
high performance (and easy-to-use) FTL drive systems ( Which you probably
have to!). This theory also needed to "fit in" with a situation of
protracted non-"open" contact, a lack of radio-communication contact, but
also one where (repeat) physical visits to earth would nonetheless occur.
 I am also trying to keep the theory as *much* based on scientific fact as
I can. This may seem " limited" to some on this list (!), but it does *no*
harm to do this as a theoretical excercise (I'm watching those possible
"technological ceilings" I alluded to in a previous posting).

After I've examined *this* idea in depth, maybe then I will look at the
various FTL concepts.......

One factor where this theory *does* does go "out" a bit is in proposing a
highly advanced propulsion system, using concepts that (most of) science
currently rejects. But - that said - I based this drive-system on the
reported attributes of UFOs. Given that some "True UFO" reports DO
involve "machines", this would suggest a (repeatedly?) reusable
stage-to-orbit vehicle, with (seemingly) very good endurance and superb
flight attributes. In essence UFO flight-aspects seem to encompass
*everything* we would ever want from one of "our" aircraft; fast speeds
(with no sonic booms, making it possible to fly over bodies of land and
inhabited areas in "supersonic" mode) protracted hoverings, and instant
accelerations and decelerations. Also the "drive-system" concerned appears
to be fairly "clean" and doesn't slag the surroundings like one of our
rockets would do!
Incidentally, This *might* be because the propulsion-system in question
only requires a very small rate of thrust, utilising an "inertialess" drive
system. This also fits in with the lack of sonic booms, etc....

I would guess (at present) that this - *very* hypothetical - world would be
located less than 1 light year or so from our solar system. It would need
to be positioned at a distance where it would have *no* gravational effect
on the rest of the solar system. Otherwise the existence of such a world
would *already* be a well-accepted scientific fact!

Unless, of course, my research DOES uncover evidence of possible anomalous
gravational influences on bodies within the solar system. Then it could be
closer! But I am not aware of any such evidence at present.

It could very likely turn out to be (near solar-system?) moonshine. But at
least this concept can - maybe even *should* - be looked into, and the
research into it (whatever the results) can be preserved for future
reference and debate.

Like you said - lets see how well this theory withstands further research
and standards of scientific logic and reasoning, and whether it can be
shown to be viable (or otherwise)!

Regards,

Robert Moore

Jean-Pierre,

I've discussed related aspects with Ian Ridpath.

Ian believes that from Randy's description of their positions,
the right-hand star was Rigel, the one to the left was Saiph
(Kappa Orionis) and to the far left was Sirius.

I pointed out to Ian:

"James McGaha (CSICOP) suggested that the lights Halt observed -
two in the north and one to the south - were Vega, Deneb and
Sirius, respectively.

That makes five stars, minimum, being mistaken for 'UFOs',
described by several witnesses at two separate locations to be
*rapidly* accelerating and at least one of them reportedly
sending down a beam of light.

The problem with attributing stars as a cause is that even if
it's not the explanation, there are always going to be 'nearby
stars' which can 'fit'".
Substantiating the argument, it was also noted that when I first
told Steuart Campbell about the descriptions from those
original witness statements and trusting he won't mind if I
mention it, Steuart wrote:

"the reports you now quote are not of a flaming/descending
craft, but of a stationary flashing light in red and blue.

Naturally one has to ask what astronomical objects could have
been seen at that time in that direction. Until now there has
been no need to ask this question. However, I've just made a sky
check, with the following results:
     Input: 0300Z; 1980 Dec 26; 1.5degE/52deg3'N
    Output: Saturn and Jupiter in close conjunction at about
22deg.alt. and azimuth 126/127deg (SE). 1st mag. stars Spica
 (8deg.alt/121deg.azi); Arcturus (25deg.alt/91deg22'azi).

The report of a flashing object is consistent with a bright star
(not a planet) scintillating at low altitude. The only candidate
is Spica, incidentally in the same area of sky as the fireball.
Scintillation is usually also accompanied by colour
differentiation. Since Spica is a predominantly blue star, this
should be the dominant colour. But differentiation would also
show red. As I explained in my book (p. 52) the red component
will appear *below* the blue. A mirage can enlarge and enhance
the image and this effect.
[End]


All good and well, however, Steuart failed to appreciate the red
and blue lights were being reported within the forest, not in the
sky.

He still found an explanation for them as stars though!


Looking at the overall situation, we still have to account for
the initial red and blue lights seen within the forest that first
night, the source of which hasn't been explained, plus 'Tom's'
testimony that when they went in search of Burroughs, Cabansag
and Penniston:

I could clearly see the lights from the gate, just outside the
back gate (East gate). It was next to the road.

They were intermittent lights, very bright, 15-20 feet above the
ground.
They were pulsating and from what I recall there were 3 lights,
red green and blue.

It made no noise, but it defied gravity. It was really weird and
scary. We all knew what we were looking at, but no one really
came out and said it.

I saw them, so did Amn Beachum, Amn Hartman, Amn Hernandez.
[End]


This is the first time I've publicly disclosed these names.

I don't see any reason now why this can't be done.


It's illustrative of the main problem; I know the names of
approx. 10-15 people who participated in both nights events and
have never been interviewed. Any one of these participants may in
turn be able to identify someone else we're unaware of.

How can this be resolved?

Most, if not all, will have long since returned to the US and
many will now be civilians. Generating significant publicity in
the US and which might result in new information seems the only
solution.

Some twenty years on, it had occurred that Randy's story offers
an opportunity which, short of Halt publishing his own book, may
be the proverbial 'last shot'.


Although a 'newsworthy' item, is the story sufficiently credible
to be taken seriously by the media?

If we first await answers from Randy to questions raised and any
comments from Charles Halt, that will maybe determine itself.

Subject: 'List Housekeeping'

UFO Research List

Dear list members,

As there are now, I'm pleased to say, over 50 list subscribers,
to recap on the 'housekeeping rules':

1. The 'UFO Research List' is intended to provide a focused forum
for any related topics which recognise the need for a scientific
and evidential foundation.

It's that twilight zone which is devoid of abject nonsense and
where objectivity replaces resolute 'religious', or sceptical,
dogma.


2. The list is also primarily intended to enable secure
discussions and as subscribers may request feedback on new data
or privately debate controversial, sensitive issues, etc., ALL
contributions are therefore 'LIST ONLY - IN CONFIDENCE' unless
otherwise denoted.

If it appears on this list, it shouldn't be seen anywhere else
without the originator's permission.


3. The list address for any mail is:

UFORL@listbot.com


4. With some e-mail software, using 'reply' may not send a
response to the list, it will be sent ONLY to the address shown
in the 'From' heading, which is the person who sent the mail.

Using 'reply to all', as recommended by the ListBot notes, may
send a reply to both the list and the person who sent the mail,
if that's required.

It's recommended that the destination of your reply is therefore
checked before sending and should always be:

UFORL@listbot.com


5. Archives of messages posted to the list can be viewed on the
ListBot server, at URL:

http://www.listbot.com/


Log in as a list member under:

contents - log in - list member

You will require the password provided by the list server when
you subscribed.

If that's been mislaid, use the 'Lost yours?' link above the
password field.


6. You can also use the member log-in to:

- unsubscribe

- change your password

- change the e-mail address where you wish mail to be sent (very
useful and this can be done regularly)

- add e-mail aliases, i.e., provide additional addresses you
might send mail from

- update your member profile, i.e., any information you may have
provided when you joined the list.


7. The standard mailing list code applies and messages should be
no more than 65 characters in length.


8. The list software also requires that each posting is no larger
than 10k in size (approx. 1500 words maximum) and larger postings
should be broken down into sections.


9. Strict 'Netiquette' rules apply and all postings are expected
to be cordial, ensuring the list is always a pleasant
environment.


10. Any related queries should be addressed to:

UFORL-owner@listbot.com
James (Easton).
E-mail: pulsar@compuserve.com
