Joel et al,

The article "The truth is out" by Ren Hoek and Marco P. Van der Valk
appeared in the March 97 issue of Air Forces Monthly (AFM). In 10 pages it
dealt with the Boscombe Down incident. AFM is, and always has touted
itself as, a serious journal on military aviation. I have always found it
to be accurate and well written (apart from some bollocks about TWA800
last year)

The "truth is out" article was seen by many as an anomaly, indeed it is
without precedent in AFM's lifetime. The article postulated that an
aircraft called ASTRA (Advanced Stealth Technology Reconnaissance
Aircraft) had crash landed at Boscombe Down, the Defence Research Agency
airfield near Salisbury in southern England. The article placed great
emphasis on registration and scanner interceptions as proof that something
had happened. It generated a lot of interest, then nothing. AFM offered
£1000 reward for any photos of the ASTRA, but no contenders came forward.

The authors were Dutch spotters and scanner enthusiasts. Now, in the UK as
spotter is some-one who collects numbers, as opposed to the older meaning
of one who identifies aircraft (what I do. I don't do numbers, I see
enough at work). The term "Spotter" in particular Train Spotter is, in
common parlance, quite derogatory, implying a person obsessed with
minutiae.

Spotters are, however, very thorough and keep meticulous records. They
also have this odd habit of not believing that something exists until they
have the tail number. This is, I believe, why many of the spotters will
have nothing whatsoever to do with UFOs or black aircraft.

That is why the AFM article was so strange. A pair of Dutchmen (who are
probably the most pedantic spotters of the lot) come out of the woodwork,
put forward a totally off the wall theory (for spotters anyway) and back
it up with tail numbers and scanner frequencies. It was very strange
indeed. Since then (two years) nothing has been seen or heard of ASTRA.

Their expertise would be an asset to what we are trying to do, but the
spotters won't get into it. For example: I posted a question on a spotter
net a few years back. It was:
Can anyone give me any information on KC-135 movements through Mildenhall
on the three days either side of the 26th of August 1989.

I got nothing back, apart from one guy (who might be on this list) who
suggested that some of the local chaps would know.

I know that Mildenhall has a 24hr spotter patrol and network of comms to
alert the boys. I also know these guys can nail a particular aircraft to a
particular place on a particular date and time. They are very good at what
they do.

Why won't the spotters get involved in this? But why did they produce an
article on something that even Bill Sweetman gave a body swerve for lack
of hard data? We knew about this incident the day after it happened and
almost everything in the article happened: closed off roads, unusual
aircraft, dodgy bizjets clearing customs at odd entry points. Everything
checked out. BUT we heard it was the aircraft formerly known as the TR-3A
that had gone "tech" and came into Boscombe.

As a footnote, when Sweetman and I were taken to Boscombe for a spot of
filming, there was a BAe Hawk doing circuits of the airfield. A quick
squint through the bins revealed, in 6 inch letters "ASTRA".

You can Email the editor of AFM, Alan Warnes, at edafm@keymags.demon.co.uk

I'd be interested in what he has to say about it, I reckon AFM were left
with, as we say over here, egg on face.

Chris (definitely not a spotter)

Joel et al,

Machrihanish? Movements? Wouldn't like to try something a bit easier would
you? I expect you have looked at a map and seen where Machrihanish is. It
is not exactly on the beaten track. Probably the reason it was used for
nefarious activities.

There has been a lot of nonsense talked about Machrihanish over the years
and what it does now is still a bone of contention. Even back in the late
eighties there was very little activity at Machrihanish, so the spotters
would be loath to go there as there were very few tail numbers. It also
had some serious security due to it being a nuclear storage site. It seems
close enough to Ireland to be used as a jumping off point (May I add that
this is an OBSERVATION on my part and NOT to be taken as fact.) for ops.
Questions about Machrihanish tend to get strange answers. Officially it's
mothballed since 96 and only a local airport now. But I have seen photos
taken since showing Pave Lows parked on the ramp.

The locals split into two groups. The first say they'd heard the roar etc
and the second say its all nonsense and avoid answering or if they do,
won't go on the record, even after being dosed liberally with 12 year old
truth serum. My brother went to Cambelltown last year and asked a few
questions, went to the local paper etc. His impression was that something
was in and out of Machrihanish, but he got nothing in the way of hard
evidence for his outlay of truth serum. I also read an interview with a
couple of golfers who said that they would see anything flying in and out
of Machrihanish as the golf course is at the end of the runway and the
flight path goes over the town on Cambletown. I think an outbound Snark
would put one off one's putt.

There is however, the story about the guy who took the photos of a UFO
near Dumfries. He reported a UFO and that he had photos. Lo and behold his
photos "didn't come out" after telling his visitors his photofinisher's
address. Dumfries is about 100miles ESE from Machrihanish. Mind you it's
even closer to West Freugh, my bet for dodgy goings on in SW Scotland.
Incidently, draw a line between Machrihanish and Dumfries, project it over
the North Sea and where do we arrive?

As I said before, I asked about boring old tanker movements at Mildenhall
and got nothing back, so asking about Machrihanish will be the same. The
spotters would piss themselves laughing at such a request. Unless we have
an insider on the list. Any volunteers?

Here's a mention of an FT from 1952. Any ideas on the origin of the report?

----------------------------------------------------------------------------
------------

REVIEW OF THE WEEK: 'SAUCERS' OVER THE PENTAGON

For years, the standard technique for explaining our political institutions
has been to relate them to the feelings they might evoke from a Man from
Mars. The happenings of the past fortnight could hardly have failed to make
the thoughtful Washingtonian speculate that, perhaps, the Man from Mars had
at last come down to see for himself.

These happenings, of course, had to do with sightings hereabouts of strange
objects in the sky and on radar scopes. Were they flying saucers or merely
illusory things like reflections, mirages, St. Elmo's Fire and electronic
interference? Were they weather balloons ... as some scientists have
suggested? Or were they real aircraft, and if so, were they Ours or Theirs -
or something from outer space?

....

If all that is said about saucers is true, they are by far the hottest
performers ever seen in earthly skies. A synthesis of reports indicates that
the strange craft can travel at speeds up to several miles a second or down
to 35 miles an hour. They can hover motionless at any altitude. They can
ascend to heights of 50 miles or more. They can climb vertically at speeds
equal to their horizontal velocities.

They can turn on literally no more than a dime and streak away instantly in
another direction. They can come instantly to a halt from high speed, or
accelerate almost infinitely fast from a standing position. They can streak
soundlessly through the skies at speeds greater than those which make
artillery shells sound like express trains.

Obviously none of those feats is within the scope of known aircraft.
Supersonic planes cannot move slowly; helicopters cannot reach very high
altitudes. Planes as we know them travel more slowly in a vertical climb
than when in level flight. Quick turns and jackrabbit starts and stops are
quite impossible for real-life planes and pilots alike. Noise is always a
companion of speed in any kind of aircraft we know.

In appearance, too -- assuming they exist -- the saucers are unlike anything
in our experience. Some of them look, as the name implies, like flat
discs -- Lewis Carroll's "tea tray in the sky." Others are like cigars. At
least one, reported in Spain, resembled a flying triangle. Still another
bore a resemblance to an ice cream cone with a ball of fire where the ice
cream ought to be....

craft. Amond saw the craft between Ernage and

Sambre is about 10 kilometers. And Amond said
that, at the end of his observation, the craft
went away at high speed towards the South, i.e.
towards Jemeppe-sur-Sambre. Since Amond saw the
craft around 18 h 45, during 8 or 10 minutes, and
since the other witnesses saw the "detaching
central light" slightly after 18 h 50, it was
very probably the same craft. In a sense, each of
the two testimonies (two witnesses each) gives
coherence to the other.

we French people often laugh at them with our "blagues
belges" (needless to say, I don't really believe this

Chris,

Coincidentally, I've just come back from a few days on the Isle
of Mull and had contemplated a detour, via Oban, to Machrihanish
on the return journey.

Even being 'relatively' close, as Machrihanish is situated at the
end of that extensive peninsula it's still a long way to go and I
doubt if there's anything now which is likely to justify the
trip.


I have access to the 'Scotsman' newspaper archives and had kept
on file some publications re Machrihanish.

One of the newspaper articles, although it relates to 'Aurora'
speculation, might be of interest and I'll append it for general
information.

I presume it's now accepted that 'Aurora' as a theorised SR-71
replacement was always a misconception, arising from an unrelated
project named 'Aurora' in a 1986 US Procurement Program document?


>There is however, the story about the guy who took the photos of
>a UFO near Dumfries. He reported a UFO and that he had photos.
>Lo and behold his photos "didn't come out" after telling his
>visitors his photofinisher's address. Dumfries is about 100miles
>ESE from Machrihanish. Mind you it's even closer to West Freugh,
>my bet for dodgy goings on in SW Scotland.

West Freugh is featured in a separate 'Scotsman' article which
notes it was the centre of Scotland's "most famous UFO sighting"
and also mentions the speculative 'Aurora' connection:

Date: 20/10/1995
Headline: Blast at top secret MoD base injures two scientists
Byline: NIC OUTTERSIDE

Article: AN EXPLOSION at a top secret military base in south-
west Scotland seriously injured two scientists yesterday.

[...]
West Freugh is one of the MoD's most secret research
establishments, and the full facts surrounding the explosion may
never emerge.

The base, five miles from Stranraer, borders an RAF bombing
range, and in 1957 it was at the hub of Scotland's most famous
UFO sighting, when staff tracked an unidentified flying object
across the Borders to the Irish coast. The incident remained on
secret files until four years ago.

It has also been reported that the base, which extends to several
thousand acres on land and sea, has been involved in the
development of the US Air Force's new secret spy plane, codenamed
the Aurora.

West Freugh employs 200 workers, mostly under contract to the
MoD. It specialises in trials for aircraft weapons systems, and
is linked to other DERA research at Boscombe Down in Dorset. Its
range is bordered by a danger area where short-range surface-to-
air missiles are tested. The neighbouring Luce Bay is a licensed
MoD and NATO bombing range.
[End]


A possible West Freugh/'triangular craft' connection was also
suggested in the following, from John Locker:

From: satcom@mail.cybase.co.uk (John Locker)
To Mailing List: EURO-SCANNER@PEGASUS.CH
Date: Friday 14th February 1997

FLYING TRIANGLE OVER THE EAST COAST

Some time ago you may recall that I circulated details of a
triangular craft flying over the North West of England.

Sighting reports have been frequent in the area between Liverpool
and West Freugh...

My findings are as follows...

This is an unmanned triangular craft, unmanned, about 30-50 foot
span...a UAV. Very often it is seen in the company of two
Tornados, as in the latest sighting, just 2 days ago at 1458 over
Mablethorpe.

If I am correct the craft is flown from the rear cockpit of one
of the Tornados using a virtual cockpit setup, and microwave
video link. Powerplant is difficult...witnesses describe a
humming sound , possibly created by an electro-magnetic field,
however in such close proximity to other a/c I doubt this is the
case....the motor is certainly not conventional.

The sighting over Mablethorpe is important as I think the 3 a/c
may have been heading for the ACMI...so if any of you out there
have the ACMI in "range" it may be worth listening in to the
special tasks cells for any unusual activity.

Officials say this craft does not exist...in fact...they seem
quite happy for the rumours of UFOs to go from strength to
strength!

The ACMI playground frequencies are listed in the usual
publications.....I would be interested to hear from anyone who
gets a visual on the triangle.
[End]

That proven 'visual', outwith perhaps the 'Petit-Rechain' image
(the 'Trent' photograph of 'triangular UFOs'?), remains elusive.

Comparatively, were there any 'amateur' photographs of the
Stealth airplanes before their public unveiling?


Whilst on Mull, I did see demonstrations of extraordinary, tree-
top level, hovering, slow moving, then rapidly accelerating
flight from several aerial objects.

They were positively identified as Skylarks though!


James.
E-mail: voyager@ukonline.co.uk

__________

Date: 16/01/1995
Headline: Fresh claims surface over secret US jets
Byline: By Nic Outterside

Article: NORWEGIAN authorities are worried that a secret US spy-
plane flying from a Scottish airbase has caused avalanches along
some of its coastal fjords. New claims have surfaced that sonic
booms from the top- secret Aurora aircraft, which can fly at
three times the speed of sound, are responsible for the sudden
avalanches and an earthquake in the Netherlands as well as
unexplained radar blips, eerie noises and isolated UFO sightings
in Scotland. The Aurora is surrounded by secrecy. It has never
been photographed and the US defence department denies it exists,
in much the same way the first stealth bombers and fighters were
denied even after they entered service. British specialists say
the aircraft has operated test flights out of Machrihanish
airfield in Argyll for three years while hi-tech tracking
equipment at Benbecula and Fylingdales monitor its progress.

Reporters from a Norwegian national newspaper have visited
Scotland to collate evidence of the plane's activities between
Britain and mainland Europe. They say they have received numerous
complaints of sudden bass-like booms from isolated fishing
communities and farmsteads between Trondheim and Narvik, followed
by sudden avalanches of snow.

The Scotsman understands that Norwegian Government officials are
now concerned about the Aurora's flights, damage caused by the
sonic booms and the lack of consultation from their US NATO
allies. A government spokesman said they were carrying out long-
standing research into the causes of avalanches and they were
aware of the concern over test flights by military jet aircraft
from the UK. A spokesman for Norwegian Defence High Command said:
"We always receive a number of complaints from people over low-
flying aircraft and sonic booms - and it is probably true that
sonic booms could cause avalanches." However, he refused to
comment on the existence or activities of the Aurora. Dutch
scientists have blamed the 5,000 mph jet for causing a sudden
earth tremor which jolted the north coast of the Netherlands.

The reports are mirrored by 30 similar official recordings of
"low pitched sonic booms" in another test area in California, in
America. Evan Wiley, a military aircraft specialist, said
Scottish close encounters with the Aurora have tailed off after a
spate of sightings two years ago. However, a north of Scotland
RAF base tracked a very fast radar blip early last year but when
the incident was reported to RAF Buchan, superior officers denied
all knowledge of it. "The whole Aurora project has been shrouded
in secrecy," said Mr Wiley. He added that Machrihanish's 10,000
feet isolated runway was a logical base for the aircraft and the
Highlands and Islands and northern corridors are an ideal
European testing ground. An MoD spokesman said he knew nothing
about the aircraft. A spokesman for the US defence department
said: "I think you have been reading too many science fiction
magazines."

Bill Sweetman, the technical editor of Jane's Information Group
and a specialist in stealth technology said that it was natural
for British and American military spokesman to deny the existence
of the plane. "Put it this way, in 1988 the US Air Force had 50
F-117 Stealth aircraft operating in Nevada and still denied they
existed," he said.
[End]

- it also has a comparable 'antenna'

- the dark 'blobs' visible may be photographic artefacts - I
don't know

- for convenience, all images have been rotated to appear
horizontal.


The 'new' image is from a bona-fide 'UFO' photograph (as such),
taken many years ago.

If it's considered how that object would appear if in the same
profile as the Trent photographs, it looks like it would be a
close match.

Coincidence?

Dear all,

1) I think the budget line actually mentioned "air-breathing reconnaissance" rather
than SR-71. So that could cover anything with a engine operating withing the
atmosphere. ie UAVs, big blimps, airships, aircraft, pigeons with Minoxes (Minoxi?)

2) My brother got a load of articles from the Campbletown local paper, so I have them
at home if you're interested. Mostly COs denying all knowledge and saying things
like "If it was on my base, I'd know about it" (All US installations in the UK have a
British CO, but I'll leave it at that) I've been told by a couple of people about odd
movements of unlit aircraft after dark through Mach'h. Apocryphal tales of course.

3) West Freugh - Considering you can drive past West Freugh and as long as you
don't stop, you'll get no hassle. It is after all a research installation and therefore
subject to the same security as any business' research place, ie you don't want the
competition see what you have. I live next to Bruntingthorpe Airfield where Jaguar
cars test their new models. I've been asked to leave at least once and there have been
loose dogs running about the perimeter. So the security is commensurate with the job
in hand I would say, Jaguar chase you with a big dog, the MOD shoot you. Big boys
games, big boys rules.

Mind you, when we had our collars felt at Boscombe Down, the Plod were very nice
to us.

Perhaps Tim will elaborate on his claim (UFORL passim) to know where the deltas
are made and operate from? My money isn't on West Freugh.

Chris

This is a very strange point you raise here James, for reasons I'll
explain:

According to Bill Sweetman:

Due to an apparent slip of the censor's pencil, a DoD budget request in '85
called for production funding in '87 under the code name Aurora. The line
item appeared below the SR-71 & U-2 recon. a/c. (Bill Sweetman's Aurora
book & other sources)

According to Ben Rich:
" Aurora was the code name for the B-2 competition funding" [between
LockMart & Northrop.] (Ben Rich Leo Janus' Skunk Works book)

Now since Ben Rich then goes on to say that Northrop had the go-ahead in
Oct. 1981 to build the ATB [which was to become the B-2,] I don't follow
this line of thought for obvious reasons. The B-2 competition funding had
to be much earlier than the Aurora budget line we all know about.

Have I missed something here Chris ?

David

Confusion.

Chris wants to know as much as I do. I was told that the Martin Marietta
factory in Georgia, USA (?), was a candidate BUT....

...I repeat, that a couple of smaller triangles were living at Warton
(perhaps at the Projects Site, who knows?). I was told this by a guy who
actually worked there, had seen them in the hangars, and had the requisite
clearances. He showed me proof of this.
I'm not going to mention any details because it's his livelihood.

After all, these things were seen at Warton from very close range very
early on in the morning during 1996 - at the height of our local sightings
of a small FT seen accompanied by RAF Tornados...

I am still trying to get hold of BAe promotional material from the 1980s
which (not unlike the recent stuff we've got hold of) included some
details, and images, of future deltas. Several aviation buffs that I have
spoken to claim to have seen this material.

I wish I could be more specific.

We also have some fairly good information on the location for some
testing/flying of the larger models; Fort Drum, in Northern NY state (an

This 2nd photo is symetric, but this does not mean that the
object itself is symetric: if the photo is made while the
diameter on which is located the "peak" points towards the
photo apparatus, the "peak" will appear in a central position.
Therefore this would not enable to say that the object is
not the same. There are other small differences, in
particular it seems that there is something emerging
below the 2nd object. But, assuming the craft hypothesis,
it could be something retractable.

UFO Research List

[Forwarded to list]


I have been following your exchange about Flying Triangles and
also I was able to read Tim Mathews' book UFO REVELATION, so I
would like to give my opinion, no offense intended (please,
excuse my English).

It is really surprising the mutation on UFO forms during the last
two decades. Since the begining of the UFO Phenomena (in 1947) we
saw a preponderance of round and disc forms, or the famous cigar
"motherships". Of course, you can always find flying triangles
described (I am trying to trace that 1952 sighting in Spain) and
everybody now knows that the original Arnold's "flying saucers"
were not discs. But nowadays, the situation has changed and
almost all the UFOs described are triangular and dark.

I sincerely believe that the "secret prototype" hypothesis is
only good for a few cases, so the explanation of such a change
should go along psico-sociological paths. My proposal: In 1977
there was a famous film that was a big success, being imitated ad
nauseam in the following years: "Star Wars". And, what was the
initial scene of the film? A giant triangular spaceship flying
ominously over the spectator. Round forms were appropiate for the
benevolent or indiferent aliens of the 50s and 60s. The diabolic
greys "should" fly a different kind of vehicle.

Tim Mathews seems to suggest two complementary kind of
prototypes: for small UFOs at slow speed or hovering, he prefers
ULV or lighter-than-air dirigibles; for UFOS at great speed with
"stealth" tecnology, more advanced versions of 117A, etc. The
problem I find with this hypothesis is when you find cases that
combine both kind of characteristics.

Besides, we here in Spain have also noted a big increase in
triangular forms, specially around the Gibraltar Strait. A good
friend of mine defends that they are due to the use of ULV by the
Spanish militars, to monitor this sensitive border between Europe
and Africa. But there are too many cases, with variations in
speed and size, to simply accept that explanation. For instance,
a recent case near my town was explained as a refueling exercise.

In short, I do accept Mathews hypothesis for a small group of
cases around air bases, etc. but I do not think it should be
defended as THE answer to the UFO enigma.

Luis R. Gonzalez.

From: RB47Expert@aol.com
Subject: Re: Trent PhotographsMessage-id: <674fcfb4.24aa7e48@aol.com>

UFO Research List

Dear James, Jean-Pierre & List,

I've been offline most of the last several weeks so I've only caught snippets
of this discussion.

I've looked at the purported Schilling photo of 1977 and I don't see the
great similarity to the Trent object from 1950.

The Trent UFO has a very narrow "rim" or lip at the base, only about 3% of
the object diameter in width whereas the Schilling object's rim is much much
wider, about 10% of object diameter in width.

The Schilling "antenna" is much longer than the Trent "post." It is about
17% of object diameter in height whereas the Trent UFO's "post" is about 11%
of object diameter in height to the double notches at the top of the "post."

The Schilling object is asymmetrical in a way different than the Trent
object. The Schilling object's "platform" appears to be higher or thicker on
the right by about 30% than it is on the left. The Trent object's "platform"
is the same in height throughout to within +/- 5% or better (compensating for
the approximate 1 degree pitch down angle which makes the base and the
platform appear slightly curved).

I would do a similar analysis on the Max Standridge "Lausanne school" outdoor
light but my copies of the JPG's were corrupted by AOL and I haven't received
uncorrupted copies yet.

The lighting of the object in the Schilling photo appears to be backlit with
sun illumination from in front of the camera and above the scene. Foreground
vegetation likewise appears to have shadowing from a backlit sun, and
background trees similarly appear to be backlit. I can see no shadow of the
"UFO" and it wouldn't be to the right but approximately below the object and
nearer to the camera than the object (if not behind the camera and thus not
visible).

If the allegedly "30 foot" shadow in the Schilling photo is supposed to
indicate a UFO of nearly that size then we have a problem. There is a
distant fence in the background. The diameter of the "UFO" appears to be
about 5 times the height of the fence. If the fence is about 5-6 feet tall,
then a 30-foot UFO must be at approximately the same distance as the fence.
The purported shadow of the "UFO" would be cast down in the vicinity of the
fence and would not be visible in the grass at this distance and low camera
angle above the ground. Alternatively, if the "UFO" shadow does appear
relatively close to the camera, perhaps on a portion cropped off to one side
or other of the photo, then the "UFO" itself must be closer than the fence
and smaller than 30 feet. My general impression is the object appears to be
no more than several feet from the camera.

It is a joke to compare this one blurred photo to the stereo-pair sharp Trent
photos with their mass of fine detail visible down to almost the 5-10 micron
grain size, which has stimulated 30+ years of productive scientific analysis.


Brad Sparks

cc: Dr. Bruce Maccabee

Good news.

It seems that `ListBot' have now resolved the anomaly with
sending a `reply' to list mail.

Depending on your mail software, sometimes that reply would be
addressed directly to the person whose mail you were responding
to. It would not be sent to the list.


To reaffirm, this is what should happen now:

If you `reply' to a list message, your reply will appear on the
list.

If you `reply to all' a copy of your reply will also be forwarded
to the person who sent the mail you are responding to.


In a further development, it's possible to make this list
`public', via the mailing list's `home page' at:

http://UFORL.listbot.com/

The advantages?

- it allows any potentially interested subscribers to browse the
list discussions and subscribe on-line

- any message can be referred to by a unique URL, i.e., "please
see the following information at URL...", etc.

- it would be extremely useful to have this facility when the
material may also be of interest to other lists. Rather than a
time consuming re-post, a URL could be specified. For example, I
would like to mention the recent Bentwaters/Lakenheath
information, plus some queries about the Schilling photograph, on
the `Project 1947' list. Highlighting the relevant URLs from this
list would make that much easier.


Disadvantages?
- primarily that the discussions would be publicly accessible.

However, the ListBot mail service has an important facility not
available on other lists - it's possible to make any message
`PRIVATE', which prevents that message appearing in the public
archive. It is then effectively a `LIST ONLY' message.

If I mark my last `Flying Triangles' list posting as `PRIVATE',
the list server confirms:

"Message #270 is now hidden from the public archive. You can
always make the message public later".

As indicated here, it is possible to switch the `PRIVATE' setting
`on' or `off' for any message ever posted to the list.

In the public archives, the message heading simply doesn't show -
I marked messages 270 and 265 as `PRIVATE' and the public archive
(only briefly enabled for testing) appears thus (use fixed font):

Msg# Subject Time Sent
269 Re: Trent Photographs Tue Jun 29 15:54:35 1999 EDT
268 Re: Trent Photographs Tue Jun 29 15:54:07 1999 EDT
267 Re: Machrihanish Tue Jun 29 15:51:46 1999 EDT
266 Re: Flying Triangles Tue Jun 29 14:42:26 1999 EDT
264 Re: Machrihanish Tue Jun 29 13:08:51 1999 EDT


This seems to be an excellent compromise and enables the `best of
both worlds'.

If there are no strong objections - and please send any to myself
privately if preferred - I would like to proceed with this for a
trial period.

Before doing so, I will go through all of the archive list mail
and mark as `PRIVATE' any postings which were either `LIST ONLY',
refer to `LIST ONLY' mail, or which should be presumed as such,
erring greatly on the side of caution.

For example, the recent posting confirming names of subscribers,
would be flagged `PRIVATE' and not publicly accessible.


If there are strong objections, then this obviously needs to be
reconsidered.

From: joel carpenter <ufx@mindspring.com>
Subject: Tetrahedral balloonsMessage-id:
<007101bec4cb$767f9330$0100a8c0@mindspring.com>

UFO Research List - http://web.ukonline.co.uk/voyager/

Listmembers-

I'd like to point out again that a possible factor in the origin of the FT
phenomenon as a subset of the overall UFO phenomenon may have been the use
of scientific balloons of tetrahedral form, especially in Europe. An article
in "Space Science Reviews 13" (1972), "History of the Use of Balloons in
Scientific Experiments," by G. Pfotzer, is a pretty general treatment of the
subject, but it does have some interesting information. Here's the part on
the tetrahedral balloons:

"...The "Tetroon" represents an economical solution for certain purposes.
This balloon, shaped like a tetrahedron, was designed by W. F. Hutch and R.
Thorness at the University of Minnesota. It requires only straight line cuts
and sealing of flat [plastic] film. It is relatively cheap and a kind of
work horse. The shape approaches that of a sphere [when fully
inflated] but stresses are not evenly distributed. Such a 28 000 m3 balloon,
launched first by the University of Minnesota on September 7, 1956 ... and
reached an altitude of 44 000 m and had a flight duration of 3 days. "

I have a copy of Thorness' patent for the Tetroon. The shape is a little
hard to visualize, but you can make a model of one by rolling about half a
sheet of typing paper into a cylinder with the long edges touching. Tape the
edges together. Then flatten the top end and tape the edges together. Now
flatten and tape the bottom end of the tube _crossways_ to the top end. The
patent rights were assigned to the US Navy (naturally), suggesting military
applications were the primary US interest, although scientific organizations
in Germany and France are known to have used the design (and still do).


If you don't think these had an important effect on the evolution of the FT
phenomenon, I suggest a hard think about this:

"My first sighting of a UFO took place on the evening of 1 August 1963, when
together with other witnesses I observed a bright star-like object over
Beckenham. Through binoculars the stationary object looked tetrahedral in
shape, of a translucent or glass-like appearance. I learned that thousands
of people in London and the home counties had seen the object; that a US Air
Force F-100 Super Sabre from RAF/USAF Bentwaters and another plane from the
DeHavilland Aircraft Company had been sent up to investigate but were unable
to get anywhere near, owing to its great altitude (at least 90,000 feet);
and that an amateur astronomer from Bushey in Hertfordshire took a clear
photo.
The official explanation that the object was a balloon failed to satisfy me,
not least because identical objects seen and photographed elsewhere in
Europe in the 1960s have never been positively identified. One such
"balloon" was seen by thousands over Madrid on 5 September 1968....

I sent a print of the 1963 photo to the Max Planck Institute fur Aeronomie
in Germany, which had launched some of the balloons for cosmic ray research
in the 1960s. "Our institute launched some from near Gottingen," came the
reply, 'but I cannot confirm that the balloon you observed was indeed
launched from here....At that time many balloons were tetrahedral in shape.
They were built by a French factory. The volume of these balloons amounted
to about 4.000 to 10.000 m3. Your photo ... possibly shows a balloon, if you
turn it by 180 deg. Then you can also recognize the tetrahedral shape with
the flat side to the top....'

The object I saw in 1963, however, did not have a flat side to the top. Jan
Willemstyn, the amateur astronomer and former pilot who took the best
photograph of the object, told me that the base consisted of three triangles
with a common apex, the bases of the triangles forming a triangular
periphery roughly equilateral. At the top apex he observed a rodlike
extension with several transverse members - a detail confirmed by the
pianist John Bingham, living near me at the time, through his reflector
telescope. Jan Willemstyn said that the object was stationary in the field
of view of his four-inch refractor telescope for over two hours - an
impossible feat for a balloon."


The witness was Tim Good. Now let me make a couple of comments on this.
Firstly, take a look at Willemstyn's photo in "Above Top Secret." Clearly
the balloon is directly overhead, and the apex that Good describes as being
at the "top" is actually the BOTTOM, or payload suspension point, of the
tetrahedral balloon. The top isn't visible at all. The antennas that
Willemstyn saw were actually probably the primary payload of the device.
What about the stationary aspect? Well, by the early 1960s there had been a
lot of progress in balloon design. They could carry sophisticated ballast
systems that would allow a good degree of control. If you recall the recent
around-the-world balloon flights, remember that their primary navigation
method was to change altitude to intercept the wind currents that move in
different directions at different altitudes. Likewise with these big
Tetroons. If the balloon began to drift, ballast could be released by ground
controllers to cause it to enter a more favorable wind current. At the
altituded these balloons could reach, they could even encounter nearly
stationary airmasses and remain in one spot for a considerable time. (In the
caption to Willemstyn's photo, Good softens his argument significantly,
saying only that "While it is probable that it was a Tetrahedral balloon
released from Germany, its ability to remain stationary in the field of view
of a telescope is puzzling.")

The function of some these balloons may have been electronic intelligence.
If, say, GCHQ wanted to monitor something of interest on the Continent, or
maybe out at sea, they could hang antennas on a nice, slow-moving balloon
way up at 100,000 feet and suck signals up at will. Good might have fooled
himself about what he was looking at, but the Soviet Bloc countries knew
exactly what they were. In "UFOs

Subject: Re: Tetrahedral balloons

UFO Research List - http://web.ukonline.co.uk/voyager/

I note a lot of these tetrahedral balloons have been sighted in the FSU.
During the Cold War there was an major use of balloons for reconnaissance
by the United States (or some-one). This reached such an extent that the
Myasischev design Bureau was contracted to develop an aircraft
specifically to shoot down ballons.

This eventually became the Myasischev M-17 / M-55, ASCC reporting name
"Mystic". While originally seen on Sat imagery at what was then
Ramenskoye, they were thought to be analagous to the U-2. The Soviets had
discovered that the best way to destroy these ballons was by turret
mounted cannon on a slow flying high altitude aircraft. Apparently
balloons are rather difficult to shoot down.

An article in Air International outlines the programme (I can't give a
date, as I'm in Aberdeen, but Bill Rose has a copy I sent him. Any dates
Bill?).

Perhaps some of these tetrahedral balloons were used in this programme?

The balloon offensive reached a peak in 1981 if I recall correctly.

I was quite surprised by this, being aware that balloon reconnaissance
is rather hit and miss, but that it was done to such an extent as to
prompt a counter to it did really surprise me.

Chris

Barbara and I'm not sure if the program has been broadcast yet
in the US.

negatives fails to detect any trace of wires or how a hoax could
have been perpetrated.

the light and detail visible were not consistent with a 'close
up' model and did suggest a large, distant object.

Unfortunately, there was no comparison made with a 'test hoax',
where a model, suspended on a thin thread, was photographed in
the same context and these negatives then analysed.

Still, the score was Trents 1, sceptics 0.

I suspect it's not quite full-time though!

James & List,

The "Confirmation" program you mention was an NBC primetime special first
aired in the US on Feb 17, 1999. The Trent/McMinnville photos were featured
early on in the show and Rand Molnar of the Brooks Institute was the
on-camera analyst. (A careless error in the program gives the year of the
case as "1951" instead of 1950.) As I understand it, Rand found little to
add to Dr. Bruce Maccabee's exhaustive scientific investigations which go
back to 1974, so he basically confirmed Bruce's findings. I have worked with
Bruce since 1976 on the case studies and am also working with Rand (I began
my investigations in July 1972 as a result of exchanges with Phil Klass). An
entirely new generation of scientific studies of the Trent case is in the
works and promises to be a quantum leap above the preceding work.

Your suggestion of a control study photo of a hoax model is excellent. But
you should know that the Trent's camera was not even correctly identified
until I did so in April of this year. Thus the exact shutter speed, focal
length and other data was not precisely known or available until literally
just several weeks ago, as a result of my comprehensive reinvestigation and
re-analysis of the case. Hence, a proper control study would have been
difficult. Some control study photography of the lighting capabilities of
sunlit cumulus clouds to cast sunlike shadows have been done by Bruce and
David Rudiak. These refute Robert Sheaffer's and Klass' contention that
shadows on the east wall of the Trent garage could only have been caused by
the bright sun in the morning so supposedly disproving the evening time
reported by the Trents, who are then classified as liars by Sheaffer-Klass.
Weather records from east of the Trents prove the existence of altocumulus
clouds in the area at the exact time of the sighting, plus or minus several
minutes.

Fortunately, Bruce's figures for focal length etc. were not far off the mark
so the identification of the camera does not overturn previous findings but
lends support to them.

Regards,

Brad Sparks

The article Chris mentioned was called "Mystery of the Mystic", by Piotr
Butowski which appeared in the Aug 1994 issue of Air International.

As I recall, US Genetrix balloon recce flights across the Soviet Union
were supposed to have been halted in 1956 on the explicit orders of
Eisenhower following diplomatic protests.

However, according to Butrowski, some 793 (of more than 4000 observed)
balloons were shot down by Russian fighters between 1956 and 1977.

It seems that the "Mystic" was specifically developed for this purpose
and its design can be traced back to analysis of wreckage recovered from
the Gary Powers U-2 shootdown in 1960.

(There have been rumours that 4 copies of U-2s were secretly built by
Beriev)

Evidently, modern balloons are not easy things to shoot down with
conventional weapons, as the RCAF recently discovered.

very difficult to discern what a platform is. B-2 for instance,
if you're looking near co-altitude with it, it just seems to
disappear into the background.


NC: But again, these people are describing things that literally
hover over them sometimes, seemingly unmistakable sightings of
these things.

GM: Well, I'll tell you, if they can get me the name of the
contractor and whosoever operating, I'd love to put them under
contract to develop some of these things.


Which is the most extraordinary confirmation of the point I've
been emphasising during recent years and specifically highlighted
in the material posted to the UFO Research List in the past
weeks.

There is no evidence that the USAF has any triangular-shaped
aircraft capable of hovering, or travelling at 'walking pace',
yet also able to suddenly accelerate at 'phenomenal' speed.

Even if USAF had developed such technology, they would not be
operating these aircraft over densely populated areas at the
frequently reported 'tree-top' level and especially, would
refrain from harassing people as reported in the numerous,
comparable, 'highway encounters', which are the essence of this
'triangular UFO' enigma.


Far from verifying that 'man-made UFOs' (MMUFOs) are responsible
for a significant percentage of 'UFO' sightings, Nick Cook's
documentary has produced unprecedented evidence to the contrary.
Finally, someone was able to ask the simple question of a senior
USAF representative - should these reports of amazingly low-
altitude, hovering, triangular-shaped 'UFOs' be attributed to
covert USAF developments [nudge, nudge, just give us a 'say no
more' nod].

The answer - if only we did have that capability.

If the USAF doesn't have it now, then presumably we can conclude
they certainly didn't have it in the 1960s/70s/80s.


There is of course possibly, if not probably, a mundane
explanation for all of the reports which come into this category.

However, thanks to Jane's Defense, we can now 'officially'
proclaim UFOs ARE REAL!!!

OK, slightly 'tongue in cheek'. ;)

However, there are some 'curious' repercussions from this
development.


I wonder what Lt. Gen. Muellner would have said in answer to
'UFO' sightings of 'triangular' craft, accompanied by recognised
USAF aircraft, say... over the North Sea in 1989.

Or the Belgian 'triangular UFO' reports.

Pity Nick didn't ask about this.


James.

Dear List Members

To have someone of Nick Cook's calibre and standing take a look at the
subject of UFOs is a major step in the right direction. For a serious
journalist, having anything to do with the dreaded U** acronym is a real
poisoned chalice.

Without his credentials and professional standing, talking to people such
as Lt. Gen George Muellner, Jack Gordon and Boyd Bushman would have been
impossible. As it was, although they were less than forthcoming, it was
good to see the people who are involved in advanced aerospace development
on-camera and to be able to watch their reactions to his questions.

OK, so he didn't manage to get anyone to give us a heads-up on these MMUFOs
which clearly exist...but did anyone seriously expect that to happen ?

I'm surprised that no one has so far picked up on Bushman's admission to
working on charged devices that 'lose weight' - for me that was a real show
stopper. It was also good to see footage of John Hutchison's expts.

As Bill says, there were odd factual errors, but they were minor.

The fact that it went out on C5 - (which for non-UK members is a minority
channel) is an indication of how little interest there is in
non-sensationalist programmes about UFOs.

David Windle

Date: Tue, 06 Jul 1999 02:43:49 +0100
From: James Easton <voyager@ukonline.co.uk>
Subject: NUFORC 'Triangular UFO' ReportsMessage-id:
<001501bec750$ff69fdc0$94c628c3@cis.compuserve.com>

UFO Research List - http://web.ukonline.co.uk/voyager/

I've received permission from Peter Davenport, director of the
National UFO Reporting Center (NUFORC), to make available their
published 'triangular UFO' reports, which I've previously
mentioned and often cited extracts from.

Containing over 200 cases which feature 'triangles', 'deltas',
etc., it's a consummate source of raw data.

Coming with my disclaimer, 'sold as seen - you never bought it
'ere mate', these reports cover most, maybe all, of the elements
which encapsulate that twilight zone between UFOs/black
aircraft/contemporary mythology.


Some can be attributed to the satellite triplets previously
identified, others might be explained as commercial aircraft
appearing in an unfamiliar guise to the observer, a few could
conceivably be sightings of 'unusual' aircraft and there's the
expected, occasional 'total whacko' experience [easily spotted!].

There remains that core of cases which seem ostensibly credible -
and most of them probably are - yet are difficult to rationalise
at _face value_.

What distinguishes these and has always set the 'triangular UFO'
aspect aside, are the detailed descriptions, often of an object,
or objects, allegedly seen at close proximity. Mercifully, no
'hypnotic regression' involved either.

The case reports have been collated in one large text file which
can downloaded from my web site at:

http://web.ukonline.co.uk/voyager/nuforc.txt

The file is 383k in size.


All of these 'core' reports obviously have an explanation and I'm
sure a consensus can be agreed. My suggestions would include:

- commercial aircraft
- known military aircraft - 'stealth' in particular
- 'black' aircraft
- helicopters
- blimps
- stylised hot-air balloons
- hang gliders
- light aircraft
- ultralites
- misidentified stars
- balloons with lights attached, maybe as an intended hoax
- military flares
- RPVs
- "too much LDS in the sixties..".


Any others?

Can any of these can be identified as matching some of the case
profiles?


No comments on the 'Midway city' video highlighted?

The NUFORC data includes several reports where a 'beam' is
directed downwards from the perceived object (outwith the NUFORC
material there are other such claims) and emitted from a large,
central light.

Not exactly what we would expect from advanced alien technology,
it has to be said.


Col. Halt's, documented on tape, 'laser-like' beam of light from
an unidentified, overhead object comes to mind.

I have suggested that Halt's 'UFO' could have been a helicopter
and depending on which evidence you accept, it is claimed
helicopters had been scrambled at that time, although Halt
refutes this.

I've also corresponded with one of the helicopter's maintenance
support team who assures that no helicopters were airborne then.


How consistent is that 'Midway' footage with a helicopter's
focused, searchlight beam?


James.
E-mail: voyager@ukonline.co.uk

On Tue, 6 Jul 1999, James Easton wrote:

> All of these 'core' reports obviously have an explanation and I'm
> sure a consensus can be agreed. My suggestions would include:
>
> - commercial aircraft
> - known military aircraft - 'stealth' in particular
> - 'black' aircraft
> - helicopters
> - blimps
> - stylised hot-air balloons
> - hang gliders
> - light aircraft
> - ultralites
> - misidentified stars
> - balloons with lights attached, maybe as an intended hoax
> - military flares
> - RPVs
> - "too much LDS in the sixties..".
>
> Any others?
>
> Can any of these can be identified as matching some of the case
> profiles?

These are suggestions about *what* could be these flying
triangles. Another important question is: *who* are the
pilots ? (whether on board, or elsewhere if these
triangles are remotely piloted vehicles). Of course
this assumes that there is really an "unidentified
flying triangle" phenomenon, something I am quite sure
of after my inquiry about the Belgian events.

In see only three possibilities, which I will list in
a "more and more disturbing, less and less probable"
order:

1) Pranksters. It would be a little disturbing because
that would mean that any private group with enough
resources could ridicule during a long period the
most powerful military organisation in the world: US/NATO
(the disturbing element is not that US/NATO would have
been ridiculed, but that other "pranksters" could have
less inoffensive intentions...).

2) Military. More disturbing, because:

- if it's US/NATO military, that would mean that they are
crazy (that's why I said that it's less probable, but
since recent events I begin to think that US/NATO are
really crazy...);

- if it's Russian military, it would mean that they
can do what they want where they want (on the other
hand, it would mean that they have a good sense of
humour and are not really dangerous...).

3) Even more disturbing (and less probable): others...

Jean-Pierre Pharabod

>UFO Research List - http://web.ukonline.co.uk/voyager/
>
>Perhaps the programme dealt with the wind cannon and sound cannon the
>Germans worked on at the end of the second world war. They were developed
>as anti aircraft devices, but their range was insufficient. Perhaps the
>technology was further developed...


Although I have heard of the Nazi wind cannon (Vindenkannon;-) ), the first
reference to an infrasound device was when a French scientist lodged a
patent in Paris during the late 1950's / 60's. It was, believe it or not,
based on a scaled up version of the French police whistle!!. It used
compressed air to make it work. The problem was that it was not very
directional, but I would think that with the advances in electronics and
speaker technology it is possible to make quite light weight units. If
you want to try playing with infrasound get a frequency generator, switch
it to about 18 Hz, connect into some speakers. Below is a report about its
effects. Sounds a bit like the classic UFO close encounter to me.

                 "Research has previously proven that exposure to low frequency
        sound can cause a variety of physiological effects, many of them
        adverse ones, such as shivering, anxiety and breathlessness.
        These responses can lead a person to think that some unseen
        danger is imminent, or feel like he is being watched. Infrasound
        might even cause hallucinations. Tests at NASA have shown that
        the human eyeball has a resonant frequency of 18 cycles a
        second, and will vibrate in sympathy with infrasound waves that
        have a similar frequency. Under these conditions, there would be
        a "smearing of vision" that is capable of making someone see
        evanescent hallucinations in the periphery of their visual
field. This
        effect is reminiscent of the theories of neurologist Michael
        Persinger, who has suggested that electromagnetic waves can
        interfere with brain activity and lead people to think they see
        ghosts or aliens."

Cheers

John B

From: James Easton <voyager@ukonline.co.uk>
Subject: * URGENT * - Mail ArchivesMessage-id:
<008901bec7d1$19d60020$097151c2@acad80.scot.ac.uk>

UFO Research List - http://web.ukonline.co.uk/voyager/

Uh... Houston, we have a problem...

The ListBot software which allows us to operate a free mailing
list has undergone some changes.

Familiarising myself with these, it looks like the options to
make this list private or public are:

`Anyone may view the archive'
`No one may view the archive'

`Anyone' appears to mean everyone, subscribers or not.

`No one' also seems to be unrelenting and means exactly that, no-
one, including subscribers can view the archives. Suddenly, there
is just no archive mail to view.

Incredibly, there doesn't appear to be an option where `Members
may view the archive'.

This hasn't posed any difficulties previously, as there wasn't a
`List home page', now kindly set up by ListBot.

The difference is that before, to view any list archives you had
to log on via the `list members' screen and required a password.

Now, anyone can go straight to the UFORL`home page' and if
`Anyone may view the archive' has been enabled, there's an
automatic ListBot link to the mailing list postings.

I've sent a copy of this mail to ListBot with my suggestion there
has been something of an oversight here.

If you log in as a list member, then you're still able to alter
your own settings. One of the options is `View List Archives' and
I hoped that even though `No one may view the archive' was
enabled, it would still allow list members access. Alas, the
message reads, `The archive for this list is not available for
display'.

So, I've been forced to proceed as originally intended and make
the list archives public - otherwise nobody has access.
However, the archives are currently marked as unavailable and I'm
going through all the list mail, marking `private' the messages
which I definitely don't want to appear on the public list
display. At least it's still possible to do that.

This means you have to be very careful about `list only' mail.
Please send it directly to myself and I'll ensure it does not
appear publicly when it's distributed to the list members.

Alternatively, there is a ListBot option to make this a
`moderated list', where all mail is automatically held back until
the list owner approves it for distribution. Any 'list only'
postings can be caught at this point.

It's similar to how `UFO UpDates' operates and means there is no
list mail until the moderator releases it en masse.

I'm assuming that the normal flow of mail is preferable and
unless suggestions otherwise, will continue with the careful
selection of public list mail.

I'll let you know how this proceeds.


James.
E-mail: voyager@ukonline.co.uk

Date: Tue, 06 Jul 1999 20:22:55 +0100
From: Jenny Randles <nufon@currantbun.com>
Subject: Re: MUFON 99 David <win@writer.win-uk.net>
Cc: pharabod@in2p3.fr
UFO Research List - http://web.ukonline.co.uk/voyager/

For those not on UFO Updates, heres a message about my recent trip to
Washington DC that may be of interest to some of you.

Hi,

I have just returned from the enjoyable MUFON 99 conference in Washington
DC. Thanks to all who played a part in inviting me. My presentation was
rather different from the one included in the procedings since I thought
this gave better value to those attending and buying the book, so to speak.
But as I was on early Saturday some who missed the paper asked me later in
the weekend to put a summary on the net. Others who heard it asked for some
help in the absence of a version in the procedings. So here is my
contribution. No revelations, as someone said. But, I hope, salient points
that are worth considering whatever your perspective on the subject.

My paper focused on the conference theme of 'comfort zones' in UFOlogy. I
offered 12 problem areas within our field that serve as 'discomfort zones'
and challenge the preconceptions of UFOlogists, the media, skeptics and
science. For each we all should contemplate alternative scenarios and
reflect on whether we are just sitting in our own personal comfort zone
standing by a long held opinion.

It seems not many other speakers took the conference theme as literally as I
did. I thought the idea was to build a paper around the theme. So I did!

In deference to the requests and for those not at Washington here is a brief
account of my 12 points. I will happily elaborate if requested.

1: IFOs are not failures but success stories -
How and why solving cases is a task UFOlogists can do well to the benefit of
society and is an achievable goal as compared with the largely unachievable
ones such as proving that aliens are here that tend to dominate our
thinking.

2: There is not an answer to the UFO phenomenon, but answers to the UFO
phenomena
The quest for 'the truth' is misleading to all sides until we recognise
there are multiple phenomena reported under the catch all term UFO and each
requires a different form of answer. These phenomena may only be linked
together by social factors and not by any actual connections. Thus a search
for the unified field theory of UFOlogy can actually be counter productive.

3: We can show that UFOs are of benefit to mankind
Ignoring any hypothetical aliens, there are naturally occurring phenomena
reported as UFOs that will stretch scientific knowledge (eg types of plasma)
and may offer new energy sources, etc, for the 21st century. UFOlogy's task
is to persuade science of that. Science must escape its ignorance of what
lies beyond the tabloid imagery of UFOlogy.

4: UFOs are not academic they can be dangerous
Certain types of UAP, eg those involved in ongoing mid air encounters (over
40 above the UK alone post l992) are a potential threat. They are natural in
origin, not alien craft. But as modern aircraft fly by computers the EM
fields of these UAP are a clear danger. The media need to find more honest
and objective reporting. Science needs to pay heed to UFO data. UFOlogists
need to show restraint in presenting such sober evidence without talking all
the time about aliens.

5: Close Encounters do not just happen to anyone
I outlined the clues that we have uncovered that there is a 'close encounter
prone personality' - items cited included above average early life recall,
acute visual creativity, etc. There were six key factors here.

6: Abductions occur inside a UFO
This challenges a key comfort zone of UFOlogy that during missing time the
CE phase occurs inside a UFO. I showed why this is an assumption imposed
onto the story by investigators and is open to some doubt. If an abduction
does not occur inside a UFO then all bets are off as to the correct
interpretation. As such this is a critical area because if we mistakenly
jump to the conclusion that an incident occurs inside a UFO we are
fundamentally misperceiving the enigma.

7: Close Encounters occur during an altered state of consciousness
They are not real world physical events, even though they do have a reality.
I set out why we must accept this (to many) quite disturbing premise via
case evidence.

8: The ETH must be the answer
I outlined reasons why it may be - pro ET evidence such as the 'Star Trek'
effect I have uncovered within abduction cases. But I also showed the
contradictions, via case evidence, such as that perception creates at least
part of the CE experience and how the subconscious mind at work in the story
lines is evident (eg one alien contact where the witness was told by the
aliens that their Proxima Centauri home world translates as 'love and peace,
everywhere and forever' but in English is 'Afoni' - say it phonetically to
get my point here!! The ETH is an assumption and part of our comfort zone.

9: CE cases are a form of psychic experience
In the brodest definition of that term, a paranormally experienced
phenomenon, I showed why we have to conclude that it is. Rather than run
from the threads that weave abductions, NDEs etc together we need to seek
them out. I likened the result to a lucid dream - without arguing that it
was a dream, which it isnt as such.
10: We are the architects, not just the archivists of the UFO mystery
 - decisions taken by UFOlogists as to how to investigate and interpret a
case can push it down pathways and to adopt a format that may not be
entirely its true nature. We hone and shape the data without realising it
and can make an experience that under other circumstances would, for
instance, be a ghost or NDE into an alien contact. We dont just record we
actually influence the mystery.

11: Sometimes you just have to say you dont know
It is not a neccesity to come up with an answer all the time. There are
puzzling cases where it is wiser and safer not to jump to a conclusion in
any direction. To do so will have a negative effect on data gathering. We
need at times to be humble enough to admit an answer is beyond us - be we
skeptics or believers.

12: The cover up may not be what it seems
yes, there is a cover up, but need there be sinister motives for it? I
expressed arguments as to why such a thing is a natural consequence of what
UFOlogy represents and how, by pleading a massive conspiracy to hide an
alien plan on earth, we actually damage our credibility and deepen the cover
up as unpaid agents of the very conspiracy we deplore.

Hope this helps grasp what I was trying to say in DC.

Best wishes,

Jenny Randles

>Hi Jenny,
>
>You make some very valid points with your 12 problem areas, but could
>please clarify what you mean by Point #7, which says,"close encounters
>occur during an altered state of consciousness."
> Should "close encounter" be taken to mean alien abduction?
>
>Bill Rose


Hi,

Thanks and by all means I will try to help. In my view the evidence decrees
the following as a position statement. I say this to indicate it is not a
firm and fixed view. Evidence can and might change my perception of it but
its what my experience to date indicates.

There are two basic types of UFO. One is physically real and can be seen by
anyone in the right place at the right time. It can also be photographed,
tracked on radar, etc. It probably is not 'a' phenomemon in the singulat
sense but a range of phenomena (eg some types of UAP). There may, or may
not, be physically real craft of unknown (non terrestrial) origin in this
mix. I have an open mind on that.

The other UFO type is essentially the close encounter experience. It is an
experience as opposed to a sighting (which UFO type one is). It does not
occur to just anyone, but certain kinds of witness. It does not occur
anywhere, but in specific locations and at certain times. It is possible (as
real cases show) for person A to be near person B and for person A to have
the experience and person B not to do so. In that sense it is subjective.
The average number of witnesses per case for an objective UFO is 2.6. The
average number of witnesses for the close encounter experience is around
1.2, showing the fundamental difference. People have been seen during the
close encounter at a time when they believed they were having an alien
abduction. In fact they had physically gone nowhere and were variously
observed as being in a trance like state, or deep asleep, or some other
similar status. In other words the experience was occurring at the level of
an ASC rather than as a physically real event. This seems hard to deny from
much of the evidence.

What I mean by a close encounter is not the strict Hynek definition. In my
view his CE 1 case is not even a close encounter but a mundane sighting and
CE 2s with physical evidence are usually some form of UAP, but are certainly
objectively real events. So I am talking about CE 3 and CE 4 cases - alien
contacts and abductions. These are the episodes that appear to take place
during an altered state (as demarked by the onset of phenomena I call the Oz
factor where perception of time and space changes and sensory deprivation
occurs). NDEs and OOBEs also occur during altered states. I have had an OOBE
so can speak first hand about that, although in many respects it felt like a
real world event. Only research indicates my doubts about that.

Calling these things altered states, by the way, is not a method to
denigrate them. Nor is it a solution to the problem. They may well still
involve amazing, life changing phenomena and indeed may even still involve
real alien contact. It is simply a description of the method through which
these contacts appear to occur - not in the mundane everyday reality mode
that you and I share now as we write and read e mail messages (although
some e mails induce an altered state called sleep pretty fast in my
experience!) This is an insight we need to take on board because a
presumption of real world objectivity directs our search for answers and
misleads us if we are hunting for the wrong thing, as I believe we are.

Best wishes,

Jenny Randles

From: James Easton <voyager@ukonline.co.uk>

I've been looking at one of the unsolved `Blue Book' cases, where
the object was apparently described as a `semi-triangular grey
mass with large luminous cylinders at the end of each wing'.

The witnesses were "Deputy Sheriffs Bob Goode and Billy McCoy",
from, Damon, TX. Source:

http://www.temporaldoorway.com/ufo/report/650903a.htm

What would we expect this `triangular UFO' report to contain?

Well, the object would be a-hoverin', probably at `tree-top
level' and it might be an immense size, possibly `as large as a
football field', which has been mentioned on several occasions.

The alleged encounter would likely take place at night and the
object was almost certainly first seen as just a `light' or
`lights', which then began to come towards the car, revealing the
object itself.

There's a fair chance of it beaming down a light or `beam' at
some point.

It would depart at 'tremendous speed'.


Slightly selective, but not unreasonable, I would suggest.


The report, by comparison, reads:

"Returning from a night football game, the two officers were
passing through Damon when they noticed some lights to their
right. The lights moved upward. The officers tried to get close
to the lights, and lost sight of them until the lights approached
their vehicle across the prairie. There was a bright pulsating
purple light stationary above the horizon (which was several
miles away). A second light, blue, moved away from the first
light and hovered not far away. They saw no solid object until it
the lights [sic] approached. `It was about telephone pole high,
maybe 100 feet... it looked like a football field. I mean, the
shadow it threw was like a football field. I couldn't see any
windows or portholes or anything... The inside of our patrol car
was a brilliant light. We estimated the thing was 200 feet
wide... It was a dark grey-looking object.'

Deputy Goode's hand was outside the car window and he could feel
heat from the object. The object moved rapidly back to where they
first saw it, and then shot vertically into the sky".


This `returned to its original position' before leaving is an
odd feature which comes up in several reports.

Looks like it _could_ be another `highway encounter'.

Any further information on this case?


Dated 3 September, 1965, it's also now the earliest (probable)
`triangular UFO' sighting I've found that fits the established
hovering/low altitude, etc. pattern and is a detailed account.

Yet again, no obvious explanation and no apparent sense in the
actions of the presumed object's controllers.

[Shrug]

Up ahead in the distance
I saw a shimmering light...

If I might make a suggestion on the late-1950s Convair saucer that was
allegedly related to KINGFISH... this is from Aviation Week, August 15,
1960, p 27-8.

- J Carpenter
------------------------------------------

"Disk-Shaped Vehicles Are Studied For Potential as Orbital Aircraft

Washington -- Disk-shaped vehicles are attracting strong interest as
potential orbital aircraft, making the disk the first configuration to show
promise for applications at opposite ends of the flight spectrum.

Although the general impression has been that the disk was of primary
interest as a relatively low-performance aircraft -- with some promise for
high-performance applications well within the earth's atmosphere -- a number
of major aircraft companies and the National Aeronautics and Space
Administration have been investigating its potential as a re-entry vehicle
for quite some time.

The disk is among the half-dozen more promising approaches to solution of
the re-entry problem, out of a great number of different configurations that
have been explored in theoretical studies and by wind tunnel model tests.

Re-entry vehicle shapes will vary according to mission to an even greater
degree than conventional aircraft. The disk is competing with blunt,
high-drag capsules, blunt but flatter 'motorboat' shapes, and a number of
others, including several that have not been revealed publicly.

Army and Air Force have for several years financed study of the disk
planform VTOL built by Avro Aircraft, Ltd., of Canada. Army's interest has
centered on a vehicle that would fly subsonically and at low altitudes for a
variety of missions ranging from reconnaissance to the possibility of a
troop carrier if the basic aerodynamic approach proved feasible.

USAF's aim in investigating the disk has generally been assumed to be a
search for a supersonic aircraft to operate at high altitudes. Aviation Week
has learned, however, that USAF's interest in the Avro disk, almost from the
beginning of its support of the project some five years ago, has been in a
hypersonic vehicle that would operate up to and into the orbital velocity
range. Second in importance is use of a disk for flight just above Mach 1.0.

In addition to NASA's extensive research on hypersonic disks, most of the
major airframe companies have shown considerable interest, and a number of
them, including Convair, Boeing and Lockheed, have proposed hypersonic
disk-shaped vehicles to USAF.

Convair is studying a rocket-powered, disk-shaped craft and has company
approval for a major effort if USAF shows enough interest.

Both Army and USAF, but particularly Army, find the disk-shaped machine
attractive because it eliminates the weight and complexities involved in
landing gear....

Interest in the disk shape right now lies in these three segments of the
speed range:

* Up to high subsonic -- around Mach 0.7 or 0.8 -- for low-altitude Army
missions.
* Mach 1.2 to 1.5 for a high-speed, low-level Tactical Air Command attack
aircraft
* Hypersonic flight, including orbital speed.

Disk presently is not considered competitive with other shapes over most of
the subsonic or low hypersonic range.

Disk-shaped vehicle would be light, strong and compact and would have a
large area to handle the maximum heating load imposed on a re-entering
vehicle. It should have the good drag characteristics necessary to slow its
entry into the atmosphere and still have the high lift-to-drag ratio
necessary for some maneuverability within the atmosphere. Disks for
hypersonic applications probably would have sharp edges, rather than the
blunt edges of the Avro vehicle, although blunt edges might be preferable if
re-entry heating was a stronger consideration than flight within the
atmosphere..."

[6 more paragraphs-JC]

Adding to Joel's informative posting, from John Stone's aerospace
site at:

http://www.thepoint.net/~jstone/successortou2.html

[Begin]
This document was approved for release by the CIA in Oct 1994, it
is an expanded version of the history of the A-12.

[...]

By the late summer of 1959, both Convair and Lockheed had
completed new designs for a follow-on to the U-2. Convair's
entry, known as the KINGFISH, used much of the technology
developed for the F-102, F-106, and B-58, included stainless
steel honeycomb skin, planiform wing design, and crew capsule
system, which eliminated the need for the pilot to wear a
pressurized suit. The KINGFISH had two side-by-side J58 engines
inside the fuselage, which significantly reduced the radar cross
section. Two additional important design features that
contributed to a small radar return were fiberglass engine inlets
and wings whose leading edges were made of Pyroceram. Convair
Division, General Dymanics Corporation. "KINGFISH Summery Report"
1959 (S). Kelly Johnson was very skeptical of the Convair design,
noting in the Archangel project log on 1-20 August 1959: "Convair
have promised reduced radar cross section on an airplane the size
of A-12. They are doing this, in my view, with total disregard
for aerodynamics, inlet and afterburner performance"

Lockheed's new entry was much like it's first, but with several
modifications and a new designator, A-12. It too, would employ
two of the powerful J58 engines. Lockheed's major innovation in
reducing radar return was cesium additive in the fuel, which
decreased the radar cross section of the afterburner plume. This
improvement had been proposed by Edward Purcell of the Land
committee. Desiring to save weight, Kelly Johnson had decided not
to construct the A-12 out of steel. Traditional lightweight
metals such as aluminum were out of the question because they
could not stand the heat that would be generated as the A-12 flew
at Mach 3.2, so Johnson chose a titanium alloy.

On 20 August 1959, Lockheed and Convair submitted their proposals
to a joint Department of Defense, Air Force, and CIA selection
panel. As the table shows, the two aircraft were similar in
performance characteristics, although the Lockheed design's
specifications were slightly better in each category. The
Lockheed design was also preferable in terms of overall cost. In
the vital area of vulnerability to radar detection, however, the
Convair design was superior. It's smaller size and internally
mounted engines gave it a smaller radar cross section than the
Lockheed A-12. OSA History: chap 20. pp. 18-19.
[...]

[End]


The CIA document also has a comparison between the Lockheed and
(not quite so secret) Convair designs.

> designed disc, or lens shape would undoubtedly perform very well.
>

> The first photographs released of wind tunnel Kingfish (Fish) models

> article "In the Valley of Shadow," by Dr David Baker.
> The overall shape of this aircraft was probably influenced by the
> ventral air breathing engine layout and hypersonic studies conducted in
> the early 1980s by McDonnell Douglas seem to have used almost the same
> formula.

> Kingfish would have been powered by two Marquardt ramjet engines,

James-

This artist's impression reminds me of the cover sketches that can be found
on Popular Mechanics in the U.S., and I would suspect that it came from
that type of publication. I would, of course, be interested in the exact
provenance of this drawing (if that information is available). I should
add that this type of drawing may well have been part of a package of
information designed to help secure funding, but it reminds me of "Concept
Car" mock ups that used to be shown at car shows in the US (and perhaps
still are). They were little more than wishful thinking, and had little or
no chance of development, since the future development of automobile rarely
took the path outlined by "dreamers". It would also be interesting to know
exactly what the intake ports were for on the apparent "front" of the
saucer, since it doesn't appear to have any exaust ports (of course we
can't see the bottom from the angle shown).

Maybe I'm way off base, but I really hate to see one more "impression"
being used in support of an annecdotal theory.

Steve

Chris and all-

The Aviation Week article is somewhat misleading on this subject, I think.
What it actually seems to have been talking about was NASA's investigation
of "lenticular" reentry vehicle shapes. They were being considered as shapes
for ICBM warheads and manned spacecraft. The "rocket-boosted Convair disc"
would have been launched into orbit on a Titan or similar booster (as
proposed for the other manned lifting bodies and Dyna-Soar) inside a
cone-shaped fairing, like a satellite. Reentry would have been
blunt-face-forward, like the Apollo capsule, and as it slowed down to around
Mach 1 it would pitch down and transition to a glide (a little better glide
ratio than a brick, I would think). The NASA drawings show it using big
deployable flaps at the trailing edge for pitch trim. So in "normal" flight
it wouldn't really look like a disc. I was wondering if maybe the Convair
designer was actually describing the development work that Convair did on
these disc-shaped high-speed vehicles, and not something related to
KINGFISH. The AW article also mentions Boeing and Lockheed hypersonic disc
designs. I have seen some Boeing concepts but never anything from Lockheed
that would fit this hypersonic reentry vehicle description.

- J Carpenter

>What was this first USAF 'jet-powered vertical rising craft',
>being produced by the Ryan Aeronautical Company and which was
>about to be tested?
[edit]

Just re-read the articles James posted and realised no one had answered
his question.

The Ryan X-13 made its first flight in Dec '55, so going by the date of the
report, this is likely to be the a/c in question. It made its first
VTOL flight early some months later.

Like all X Planes, it was experimental - this particular vehicle was
designed to explore VTOL for the USN & USAF. It wasn't disc shaped - it
was a small delta winged a/c of a type known as a tail sitter - that is,
it sat on its rear end for both t/o and landing. Not what you might
consider ideal. The project was canned in '58 after two were built - one
may still be in the San Diego Aerospace Museum - the other was in USAF
storage - probably Wright- Pat.

That's my best guess - maybe Bill or Chris have some thoughts...
