Here is Easton's summary of Arnold's BD sighting:


"It was on the morning of July 29, 1947 that I took off from a
private cow pasture near my home.
(SNIP)
It was a perfect day to fly. The air was sharp, moist, clear as
crystal and smooth as silk. There is something of a real thrill
in flying on a day like that.
(SNIP)
Within an hour I was over Baker, Oregon.
SNIP
I began to let down over North Powder, Oregon in preparation to
land at La Grande when I noticed above me and about ten miles to
the right the Empire Airline's old Boeing, also coming in to land
at La Grande. There is something about having company in the air
that always seems pleasant and friendly. I rocked my wings at him
in a gesture of hello and continued my let down until I was
directly over Union, Oregon at 5,000 feet.

I recall looking at my instrument clock which read about five
minutes to seven. As I looked up from my instrument panel and
straight ahead over the La Grande valley, I saw a cluster of
about twenty to twenty- five brass coloured objects that looked
like ducks.

They were coming at me head on and at what seemed a terrific rate
of speed. I grabbed my camera and started rolling out film. Even
though I thought they were ducks when I first saw them, I wasn't
taking any chances.

The sun was at my back and to my right. These objects were coming
into the sun. I wasn't sighting through the viewfinder on my
camera but was sighting along the side of it. As the group of
objects came within 400 yards of me they veered sharply away from
me and to their right, gaining altitude as they did so and
fluttering and flashing a dull amber color.

I was a little shocked and excited when I realized they had the
same flight characteristics of the large objects that I had
observed on June 24. These appeared to be round, rather rough on
top, and to have a dark or a light spot on top of each one. I
couldn't be absolutely positive of this because it all happened
so suddenly. I attempted to make a turn and follow them but they
disappeared to the east at a speed far in excess of my airplane.
I knew they were not ducks because ducks don't fly that fast.

After a few minutes I gave up the chase and continued to let down
at La Grande. I phoned Dave Johnson from there and related my
experience but told him not to print it. I knew he had more than
a newsworthy interest now in flying disks. I questioned the whole
crew of the Empire Airlines ship to see if they had seen this
cluster of objects, too. If they had seen them, they would not
admit it, but there is a good possibility they did not see them.
They were on almost their final approach to the La Grande
airfield, their plane being much faster than mine, and this
cluster of objects at the time would have been seven to nine
hundred feet above them.

I heard later that several farmers in the vicinity of Union had
observed what they thought a peculiar cluster of birds that same
morning. I did not know of this until much later. Actually, they
flew in a cluster more like blackbirds than ducks but each one
was larger than a duck. I should judge some twenty-four to thirty
inches in diameter. They rather wheeled on edge, flipping as they
went as efficiently as when they were flat in reference to the
surface of the ground. That morning I was pretty disappointed
that no one around the airfield had seen them, to my knowledge.

I am fully familiar with the La Grande Valley, the reservoirs,
streams and lakes that are all over this area in the summer and
you can be sure, on the conservative side, that I felt positive
these things were not birds. I was curious as to what my movie
film had recorded. Later, after it was developed, I found that my
movie try was not very successful. Only one or two of these
objects could be found on my film and you could see them only
under a jeweller's glass".

Compliments of the Duke:

QUOTE----

AS A defence journalist working in Britain, you know when you're
getting dangerously close to something the Ministry of Defence
would really rather remained under wraps, because you'll almost
certainly get a call from the Ministry's D-Notice Committee
telling you so before you rush to print.

The D-Notice system is a fairly gentlemanly affair and relies on
a certain amount of goodwill on both sides.

Chances are, a retired rear admiral or air vice-marshal will
gently pull you aside and explain patiently how your story will
endanger national security, or the lives of serving British
military personnel, or both. The system is voluntary, but it
lets you know where you stand before things get heavy and
unpleasant under the Official Secrets Act.

The essential point is that you're in no doubt where the line
is -- and you step beyond it at your peril.

-----UNQUOTE

This is paranoid rubbish. How does the MoD know what every hack
is writing, that an old gent is hauled out of his Club to have a
word? It doesn't. And defence correspondents are extremely well
connected, and suitably discreet: this image of a "word in the
ear" from some old buffer comes from the fiction of John Buchan,
or worse.

The D-Notice system is indeed voluntary: generally speaking, only
if an editor feels queasy about the security implications of some
story does he contact MoD and ask if it's okay to print it.
D-Notices *may* be issued by the MoD giving guidelines about
what's patriotic to print, or not, in time of war or "limited
conflict", but the issues are usually technical, like not showing
Navy wives baring their breasts to HMSs departing from Plymouth
Sound on combat duty (an ancient tradition). The consequences of
ignoring the advice are no worse than an injunction against
publication, usually. No editor is going to be mad enough to
print details of the Chevaline warhead or Chobham armour, and the
OSA is hardly ever invoked as a consequence.

During the Falklands War there was some huffing and puffing in
military and MoD circles about the amount of expert speculation
that was going on, on TV news programmes & so on, some of which
undoubtedly gave some gratuitous hints to the Argentines as to
Brit intentions and options on the ground. No one was silenced,
no injunctions were issued, and no one was indicted, however.

That ought to give you a measure of how nervous the MoD really is
about those in the know giving real secrets away.

best wishes
Palmreader D. Milehighclub
Black Hand

about the CIA. The CIA did not "enourage " flying saucer reports.

What was actually said was this. The people running the U-2 project
CLAIMED (in top secret literature, so the general public was not aware of
it) that over half of the UFO sightings reported to Project Blue Book
after
August, 1955 when the U-2 started flying were caused by the U-2.. They
claimed that the Blue Book staff, knowing about the flights, were diligent
to explain the sightings as natural phenomena, thereby covering
up the U2 flights. That was "OK" as far as the CIA operators were

Actually, they were wrong on all counts.... see below:



CIA'S UFO EXPLANATION IS PREPOSTEROUS
by Bruce Maccabee
June 3, 1997

  The CIA recently (May, 1997) published an article that describes its
involvement in the history of UFO phenomena. (The article is published in
the unclassified version of "Studies in Intelligence," a twice-yearly CIA
journal.) According to historian and author Jerry Haines, the CIA believed
that when the U-2 high altitude spy plane began flying in early August,
1955,
     "commercial pilots and air traffic controllers began reporting a
large increase in UFO sightings."

  The U-2 is the high altitude spy plane made famous by the 1960
shootdown of Gary Powers as he flew over the Soviet Union and by photos of
Russian missile sites in Cuba during the "Cuban Missile Crisis."

  Mr. Haines has written,
    "According to later estimates from CIA officials who worked on the
U-2 project and the OXCART (SR-71 or Blackbird) project, over half of all
UFO reports from the late 1950's through the 1960's were accounted for by
manned reconnaissance flights (namely the U-2) over the United States.
This led the Air Force to make misleading and deceptive statements to the
public in order to allay public fears and to protect an extraordinarily
sensitive national security project. While perhaps justified, this
deception added fuel to the later conspiracy theories and the coverup
controversy of the 1970's. The percentage of what the Air force considered
unexplained UFO sightings fell to 5.9 percent in 1955 and to 4 percent in
1956."

   This explanation for many ("over half of all") UFO reports is new in
the sense that it has never before been publicized. It was not contained
within documents released by the CIA in December, 1978 after a lawsuit
filed under the Freedom of Information and Privacy Act (FOIPA) by Ground
Saucer Watch, a civilian UFO organization which closed in the early 1980's.

   According to Mr. Haines the U-2 was reported as a UFO because
     "the early U-2's were silver (they were later painted black) and
reflected the rays of the sun, especially at sunrise and sunset. They often
appeared as fiery objects to observers below. Air Force BLUE BOOK
investigators, aware of the secret U-2 flights, tried to explain away such
sghtings by linking them to natural phenomena such as ice crystals and
temperature inversions. By checking with the Agency's U-2 Project Staff in
Washington, BLUE BOOK investigators were able to attribute many UFO
sightings to U-2 flights. They were careful, however, not to reveal the
true cause of the sighting to the public."

    Project BLUE BOOK was the publicly known Air Force effort to collect
UFO sightings and explain, or at least categorize, them as explainable or
unexplainable. Project Blue Book ran from early 1951 through 1969. When
it closed Blue Book and its predecessors (Project Sign, 1948, and Project
Grudge, 1949-1951) had collected about 13,000 sightings, of which about 700
were left unexplained.

    The claim that the U-2 caused "over half of all UFO reports from the
late 1950's through the 1960's" is, to put it gently, preposterous. The
U-2, with its 80 ft long by 6 ft wide (front to back) wingspan flew at
60-70,000 feet and at that altitude was essentially invisible during the
day. It created no contrail because of the lack of moisture at that
altitude. It was, after all, intended to be invisible! During the hour
before sunrise and the hour following sunset it would be possible for an
unpainted aircraft to reflect the sun enough to be visible, perhaps with a
reddish glow resulting from the reddening of sunlight (caused by passage of
the sunlight through the atmosphere, which acts like a filter that removes
blue and green relative to red). High altitude balloons (e.g., Project
Skyhook) did cause some UFO reports during these times of day and were so
identified by the Air Force and civilian investigators. However, only a
small fraction of sightings occur during these times. The largest
fraction of sightings is at night when the U-2 can't be seen and the next
largest fraction is during the daytime.

   A check of the Project Blue Book sighting statistics, which includes
sightings by pilots and air traffic controllers as well as by military
personnel and civilians, shows the following: for July, 1955 there were 89
reports and for August there were 67. These numbers are the sum of
explained and unexplained sightings and so, presumably, include U-2
sightings, if any. These numbers show that the sighting rate
**diminished** just as the U-2 started flying. The Blue Book record shows
about 316 sightings in the 6 months before the U-2 and about 326 in the six
months afterward.

   Mr. Haines has pointed out that the percent unexplained fell from 5.9%
in 1955 to 4% in 1956, with the implication that this decrease was a result
of more explained U-2 sightings. If we assume that the increase in
sightings from 316 to 326, mentioned above, was caused by the U-2, then the
U-2 could acount for about 100 x (10/320) = 3% of the sightings in the 6
months following. Hence these statistics do not bear out the claim that
there was a large increase in sightings by any segment of the population,
pilots and air traffic controllers included, once the U-2 aircraft started
flying.

   Statistics based on a different set of data are contained within the "U
Database" of over 16,000 sightings by Larry Hatch (Larry Hatch Software,
142 Jeter St., Redwood City, CA 94025-1957). This excellent PC based
software provides statistics that are based on unexplained sightings
recorded by Project BLUE BOOK and by other organizations (civilian UFO
groups). If Project BLUE BOOK investigators explained some sightings as
the U-2, these sightings would not appear in the list of unexplained Blue
Book sightings and hence would not be included in this database. On the
other hand, the far larger collection of non-Blue Book sightings in this
database could include U-2 sightings, if the CIA is correct, that were not
identified by civilian investigators who were unaware of the U-2's
existence and hence a comparison of the sighting statistics before and
after U-2 flights started could provide evidence that the U-2 was being
reported as a UFO. In this database I find the following:

   As one can see from the above table, there is scant evidence of a jump
in sighting rate following the first flight of the U-2 on Aug. 4, 1955.
The surprising jump in November, 1957 is coincident with the "Sputnik flap"
which occurred just after Sputnik 2 was launched. (This flap is noted for
the large number of close-range car-stopping events. Most of the
sightings were not sightings of Sputnik itself.)

  An even more telling set of statistics uses the sightings which
occurred near sunrise or sunset when, according to Mr. Haines, the U-2
would have appeared as a shiny or fiery bright spot in the sky.

   Clearly there is no statistical support for a sudden increase in the
number of sightings at sunrise or sunset when the U-2 started flying. In
fact, the number of sightings in August 1955 was lower than during the
previous month.
  In the early 1960's many of the U-2s were painted black or other
camouflage colors thus reducing the number of U-2's that could potentially
be seen by glint reflection from the sun.
  Aside from the statistics it should be pointed out that many unexplained
sightings involved relatively nearby, structured objects, not nearly
invisible distant points of reflected light. These objects were reported
to move rapidly at speeds that would far exceed in apparent speed that of
the U-2, flying at about 500 mph at 70,000 ft (the U-2 would seem to move
slowly, if seen at all).

  The documented history of the agency involvement has been known to
ufologists since late 1978 when the CIA, after an FOIPA lawsuit. The
history has been published in "Clear Intent" by Larry Fawcett and Barry
Greenwood, in "Above Top Secret" by Timothy Good and most recently in "The
FBI-UFO Connection/the REAL X-files" by Bruce Maccabee (available from the
author). There is little not previously known in the new, official CIA
history.
   The CIA history is to be available on the web page of the Center for
the Study of Intelligence at www.odci.gov/csi (where odci = Office of
the Director of Central Intelligence.... shudder!)

Dear Nick,

In the July issue of 'NICK POPE'S WEIRD WORLD', you wrote:

"Over the past few months I'd been becoming more bullish in my
response to certain people within ufology who'd been sniping at
me over the years. Nobody likes criticism, and I'd been getting
a fair bit - little of it constructive in nature. If people were
criticising my views on, say, Roswell, then fine. I wasn't
there, and so my view probably counts no more or no less than
anybody else who's followed the case with a reasonable degree of
interest. But it rankled when outsiders who'd probably never
even visited MOD Main Building started casting doubts on my
knowledge about - and access to - government and military UFO
files. I've worked for the MOD for over fourteen years now, and
three of those were spent researching and investigating UFO
sightings, alien abductions, crop circles, animal mutilations and
any other weird and wonderful reports that came my way".


I trust I'm not one of the aforementioned 'critics' and perhaps
you can help clear up some of the confusion which surrounds a
number of claims.

To recap; your appointment with the Ministry of Defence (MoD) was
as an Executive Officer. To clarify for the 'uninitiated' (I'm a
former Civil Servant), the standard grading hierarchy is clerical
assistant - clerical officer - executive officer - higher
executive officer - and upwards.

Although your affirmation clearly gives the impression of being
HM Government's full-time investigator of "UFO sightings, alien
abductions, crop circles, animal mutilations", etc., I understand
that was not the situation.

Weren't your duties varied and 'UFO etc. reports' only one
aspect? In possibly the first 'promotional' interview you gave,
to 'UFO Magazine' (UK) on 5 May, 1996, it was stated:

UFO Magazine: When did you join this office, and indeed, were you
aware of its function?

Nick Pope: I've been in the Ministry of Defence since 1985. We
are just 'posted around' every two or three years to acquire
experience. I had just finished various duties associated with
the Gulf War and it just so happened that there was a vacancy
which cropped-up. Also in this office was a chap I had worked
with quite closely with Gulf War duties and he offered me the
job. I was aware that UFO research was one of its functions.

UFO: Was this the reason you switched departments?

Nick Pope: I was certainly interested, it sounded fascinating,
but I was quite keen to get out of my old job.
[End]

As you said, "UFO research was one of its functions".

Can you please clarify what the job title was and its other
functions?

What percentage of your appointment was actually spent on 'UFO
etc.' related matters?

Was it, for example, a situation where the 'UFO etc.' duties took
up, approximately, 75 percent of your time, 50 percent, or did
they only perhaps demand a few hours per week, maybe even, over a
period of three years, average a few hours each month?

It's obviously of interest to know how much emphasis our
government put on this and whether it continues to do so.


On the question of any 'cover-up', you helpfully confirmed and
have maintained this had no substance whatsoever. Typical of your
response was the one given to Michael Lindemann, editor of 'CNI
News', on November 17, 1996, during a 'UFO conference' at
Blackpool.

Lindemann asked, "This seemingly irrational denial of significant
UFO events could be interpreted as evidence of a deliberate
cover-up. What are your views on that?".

To which you replied, "I found no evidence to support a cover-up
in Britain. I think, without trying to sound too arrogant, that I
would have gotten a few hints in three years if there had been
someone doing my job but on a covert basis, not least because the
one thing they would have needed beyond anything else was access
to the raw data of the witnesses, and never once in three years
had any witness complained that I had sent someone around to the
house".

his fifth cup of tea of the day he picks up the phone and rings the US
Embassy in Grosvenor Square, London;

Pope; Er, hello. My name's Nick Pope, I'm at the MOD. I'm a very junior
civil servant but could you put me through to liaison. I want to ask about
one of your Top Secret aviation projects.

Operator; Thank you, I'm putting you on hold sir......(My God, we have a
wacko on the phone, want's to know about one of our Top Secret aircraft!).

DIA spook; Oh Christ, not again! Who is it this time? Pope, let me handle
this....

Hello, Mr. Pope, how can I help you? Bob Smith, Defence Intelligence, happy
smiling face of the New World Order here....

Pope; Er, well, Bob, we've had a few reports about these triangular
aircraft under escort by F-15s. I wondered if you could give me anything on
that?

Smith; Hell, yeah, sure. The US Government doesn't have anything like that
I'm afraid. Area 51? Never heard of it, it's not on any of my maps! Must
have been another F-15 at a strange angle.

Pope; I hear you Bob, but these witnesses were RAF personnel, some of them
trained observers.

Smith; OK, Pope, how can I put this, our government has a good relationship
with yours and it would be a shame to jeopardize this by asking too many
questions. UFOs, we don't have any, and none crashed at Roswell either. I'm
sorry that you've had to waste valuable time on this....Bye!

Pope; Oh well, the US would never lie to the MOD would they. Now where's my
kettle........

(And so the cover-up continues. Later that night, Sir Anthony Bollingers,
UK head of the DSTI is dining at his club when his old Berlin buddy Bob
Smith appears, grinning.)

Smith; Well, hey Bolls, how's it hangin'??. What a day! Can I have a quick
word with you?

Bollingers; Do sit down old chap. What's up?

Smith; Well, it's nothing really, just had a call from a Mr. Nick Pope at
something called Air Staff 2a this morning. Wanted to know about our joint
hyperjet projects!

Bollingers; Jesus Christ! His brief is to keep his head down and, in
future, to write books about UFOs, not to ask questions like that. God,
next thing he'll be doing is getting drunk and shouting our security
classifications across a crowded London pub after a UFO Conference!

Smith; So you'll sort it?

Bollingers; No problem, we've covered this little baby up for 25 years and
we've had no problems thus far!

I shouldn't worry about Pope. That department had it's balls cut off at
birth. As long as the idiot public believe these things are alien
spacecraft that's fine by me. Or natural phenomena. I don't want to see my
publishing shares in Ryman and Booster lose value after all! My brothers'
the MD you know.

Smith; Perfect, just perfect.

Date: Mon, 09 Aug 1999 13:26:54 +0100
From: Jenny Randles <nufon@currantbun.com>
Subject: Re: An Open Letter to Nick Pope - short sketch below...Message-id:
<000301bee262$944b7c80$528e01d4@default>

UFO Research List - http://web.ukonline.co.uk/voyager/
Date: 07 August 1999 08:09
Subject: Re: An Open Letter to Nick Pope - short sketch below...


>UFO Research List - http://web.ukonline.co.uk/voyager/
>
>Dear All,
>
>As one of the vocal and "aforementioned critics" I'd just like to say how
>welcome James' open letter is. It seems to me that several things are
>clear;
>
>1 - Nick Pope's work for Air Staff 2a was part-time. His successors have
>confirmed to me that the UFO work, if you can call it that, makes up but a
>minor part of the job.



JR: - I interviewed / was interviewed by one of Nick's predecessors in the
job when Brenda, Dot and I took the Halt memo unannounced to the MoD and
challenged her (Pam Titchmarsh). She insisted that her job devoted only a
few minutes per day or a couple of hours per week to UFO matters. The rest
of the time was spent on other matters interfacing the Air Force and public
(eg complaints about low flying aircraft). James suggests that Nick's first
interview was in UFO magazine May l996. It was not. I interviewed him (on
camera) for my BBC documentary in December l995. Only parts of the film I
secured were transmitted . I asked Nick then about the above issue. He told
me that the percentage of time spent had increased since Pam Titchmarsh's
day but was still only a proportion of his job. I got the impression Nick's
personal interest caused him to spend more time than others on the job.
Certainly no prior or subsequent Air Staff 2A occupant has communicated so
freely by letter and phone with UFO investigators during what at times were
almost joint investigations of cases. On several occasions,also, I commented
to other BUFORA investigators (and I think put in print in articles) how
strange it felt to be seeking to solve cases and concluding that an answer
had been found whilst the MoD office was encouraging us towards an unsolved
nature to a case. I recall specifically the 31 March l993 case where there
is little doubt in my mind that most - if not all - that was seen that night
was a Cosmos burn up. We reached that conclusion at BUFORA quickly but
Nick's letters were directing us towards parts of the case he regarded as
unsolved . It was an odd experience being the skeptic to the MoDs 'believer'
but it happened sometimes with Nick.

None of this is sinister, I should emphasise. I am not suggesting hidden
meaning. But I had no doubt from my dealings with Nick as far back as l993
whilst only mid way through his MoD tenure that he was sufficiently
interested/personally persuaded by the evidence to look beyond
misperceptions and seek UFOs amidst otherwise seemingly resolved stories -
something previously unthinkable activity for the MoD.
But the basic point that he was not a full time worker is correct. He never
left his office to investigate a case, so far as I know. But he was
liaiasing with UFO investigators in the field in a way the MoD has never
done before or since. Not because of the job, I suspect, but his own
interest in it. Every previous Air Staff 2A or DS 8 occupant I dealt with
over 20 years (and that was quite a few) treated the post as a sort of exile
where they had to do terminally boring work like answer letters from UFO
nutters accusing them of cover ups. Either this was bad luck and the MoD
just chanced to pick UFO skeptics for the job time after time or it was
design and Nick - vwith his personal interest - slipped the net. But at the
heart of it, as I found via Pam Titchmarsh when I interviewed her, was the
sincere belief by those who did the job that Air Staff 2A simply did not get
the calibre of case that UFOlogists were always telling her about. No radar
visuals. No car stops. No physiological effects. No abductions. Just
trivial, easily resolved, LITS. As such UFOlogists were arguing that the MoD
must be doing this or that about the data on the assumption that they were
receiving a similar cross section of evidence as say the Piddletown UFO
Group . As such PUFOG thought the MoD were covering up. But as Air Staff 2A
was getting no such thing they thought the UFOlogists who kept writing
making accusations were deluded cranks. That is absolutely what the position
was when I spoke to Pam - unless, of course, she was lying to me and I dont
think she was. This begs the question - was there a flow of better case
evidence going not to Air Staff 2A but to elsewhere? Or, did the input of
data change to become much better during Nick's day ?

As yet I have not seen Nick refer to close encounters, or car stops or other
such big cases that came into Air Staff 2A during his three years - at least
not ones that were not publicly known at the same time. Much of 'Open Skies'
is filled with already known cases. I am not suggesting Nick break witness
confidences or MoD rules. But could he maybe give us a breakdown of the 1000
(?) or so cases the MOD must have received during his tenure. It would be
useful to know, for instance, how many came from air bases, or pilots, how
many were car stops, physiological effects, abductions etc. So we can cross
refer to other sources of UFO data.

The only alien contacts he cites (anonymously) as submitted to the MoD in
'The Uninvited' are worrying because I can identify most of them. They too
are already investigated cases by UFOlogy. One is a famous story in UFOlogy
that is akin to Condons 'universe populated by bears' saga used by him as an
after dinner speach. It is not a case that would enlighten UFOlogists abiut
UFO reality as a five minute phone conversation with the witness (which Nick
cannot possibly have had) would easily demonstrate. If Nick had any real
knowledge on that case (as I do from first hand meetings with the witness )
he would never have risked the public ridicule he would have faced had I
chosen to enlighten his many media admirers to the full story of this case
that he had foolishly included uninvestigated into his book.

But thats an aside. My real point is that we dont need tall tales like this
one from Nick. We need usable data (l991 to l994) - even guesstimates from
Nick would allow us to compare with the data flowing into private UFO groups
during the same period. This will enable us to make a vital judgement. Had
the inflow of data to the MoD changed since Pam Titchmarsh's day? Was it now
more like what UFO groups are getting than Pam attested it was in her day?
Or, if not, why was it such a different sub set when you might have thought
close encounters stood at least an equal chance of being reported to the MoD
rather than BUFORA.

And if not, and the data coming into 2A is inferior to that reaching UFO
groups, then why is Nick so scornful of the possibility I hve to take very
seriously (that this better calibre data by passed Air Staff 2A and went
elsewhere in the MoD?) His argument that it could not be because such a unit
would need the data he had so would have to interact with him does not seem
watertight. Presumably he was supplying reports with basic data on them up
the chain in the MoD. These could be read by another department and would no
doubt be all they needed on inferior quality cases. But if, as I suspect,
the role of Air Staff 2A is a public aunt sally - a distraction to lure
public attention away from the real UFO data research - then it would have
no need to know about the higher classification data going elsewhere and the
recipient of all that better data would have little need to have to go cap
in hand to Air Staff 2A.

It all revolves around the - to me - pretty feasible argument that the
occupant of Air Staff 2A is made to feel like the only one doing this job by
intent and by believing he or she is the head of the MoD UFO desk they can
honestly respond to the public that nothing much is going on and all the
crackpot UFOlogists who say otherwise are misguided. As that PR headache is
taken away the real MoD research goes on way out of sight and at several
classification levels about Nick's admitted civil service ranking at the
time of Captain.

If not, then why did Ralph Noyes (ranking Air Commodore) tell me he saw gun
camera film but Nick told me in that Dec l995 interview he knew nothing of
such evidence? To me the most obvious answer is that a Captain was not
security cleared high enough to do so. But if it existed and was not at Air
Staff 2A (not just the film was missing but any written record of analysis
of same, which surely would survive even if, as Nick suggested to me, the
film itself had deteriorated over time) then does this not infer the better
data went somewhere else above and beyond Air Staff 2A.

So, to me, we should not be attacking Nick Pope as an individual but seeking
to get from him an insight into such reasonable questions and why he is
adamant no such other department can exist and that he cannot have been - in
effect - an MoD patsy, pretty much as I suspect Ed Ruppelt was.

>
>Kevin McClure, another researcher interested in Pope's claims, worked out
>that over three years he worked on "UFOs" for something less than 100 days.
JR: - Based on what Pam Titchmarsh told me (she cited fairly precise
figures) a three year tenure in her day involved no more than 30 days spent
in total on UFO matters. So if Kevin is correct there has been a three fold
stepping up of UFO time allocation between l983 (the day of Pam Titchmarsh)
and l993 (Nick Pope's day) - itself an interesting fact about changes in MoD
policy and about which we might want to ask questions.
>

>
>3 - He had an interest in UFOs BEFORE he took the Air Staff job. THIS IS
>VITAL because it destroys the image of the man who only became interested
>in the UFO issue after he saw the " massive evidence".
>
>I challenged him about his supposed 'Florida abduction' on a live TV debate
>and since then he's smeared me to the extent of my having to involve
>solicitors. I am hardly the only person to have been highly critical of his
>behaviour in this matter.
>
>We know for a fact that Pope's publishers, Simon and Schuster, amended the
>proofs of "Open Skies, Closed Minds" in order to cover this unfortunate
>fact up. Pope didn't even write all of it - a ghost writer from Sussex did
>alot of the work. Now that's spooky.....
>

JR:- I know the truth about this story but I have been asked to publicly
refrain from talking about it. As it is not my place to do so, I have
agreed.


>4 - He has made a great deal of money from Ufology on the false pretence of
>being an expert. I suggest that his conversion to Ufology was planned.
>After all, he was having dinner with well-known UFO personalities very
>early on in his tenure.....
>

JR:- All of which is true, but Nick is as entitled to be regarded as an
expert as any of the rest of us. And you should not hold making money out of
UFOlogy against someone. It is a distraction from what really matters -
which is not Nick, his money making or the publicity he has attained. It is
what is really going on at the MoD. I think rather than antagonise Nick with
accusations we should seek to get him to reveal useful data about his
experience at Air Staff 2A (which, sadly, Open Skies, did not provide) - the
kind of data requested above that might help us determine if indeed Air
Staff 2A is all that there is to the Mod UFO involvement.
Best wishes,

Jenny Randles

Upon request by Victor Kean, who has been collecting triangle-shaped UFOs
reports for some time now, I asked all Regional Catalogues coordinators
here in Italy to extract pertinent data of such Italian reports, and a
specific Italian database DELTACAT was initiated by Roberto Raffaelli
("http://www.ufodatanet.org/workgroups_e.htm"). Only a few have answered as
yet, but based upon those data and my own personal experience, I'd add a
specific source of triangular IFOs which - though more frequent in the '60s
- is still with us.

I mean the high-flying stratospheric balloons, usually sent up for special
interest studies. French CNES (Centre National d'Etudes Spatiales) has been
regularly sending them from the Atlantic base of Air-sur-Adour, as well as
Italian CNR (Consiglio Nazionale delle Ricerche) has been doing from
Trapani, in Sicily.

I am not meaning simple, small-sized weather balloons, but those huge
monsters more than 100 meters in diameter.

Our own reports include thousands of bewildered witnesses in large areas,
beginning in the mid-'60s, so much that a popular mysteries magazine in the
early '70s titled: "Triangle: the New Shape of the Motherships?". Air Force
planes were dispatched to intercept such UFOs, some times. A strong polemic
exchange was kept alive between true-ET-believers and
man-made-UFO-proponents, in 1971-72, as of their exact nature.

Similar objects were sighted (and photographed) in Spain (I can remember a
very spectacular case in 1968 over Madrid), and a whole triangular-UFO flap
developed over Yugoslavia in 1971 (NATO spy-balloons this time). Am I wrong
to also recall some 1967 UK reports and the following discussion in FSR
about "deltavolants" and the like?

Similar sightings have been recorded over Italy since at least 1954, but
the most recent Italian flap of the triangular kind was in 1985, when
national TV news gave front page treatment to one such objects seen by
thousands, photographed by dozens and even filmed by one of their crew who
tried to chase it with a small plane over Aosta. My colleagues and I took
the trouble of passing a few weekends chasing some dozens witnesses from
widely scattered places in order to be able to get precise azimut and zenit
data, so to triangulate (oops!) its position, altitude and real dimensions.
'twas precisely one of those giant balloons, a French one.

I can also remember some very graphic reconstructions of a fast-flying
triangle who crossed the Italian skies at dawn on September 14, 1978, but
it was just a bolide, i.e. a very large meteor. But that's another story.

Though I can easily agree that the greater part of presently reported
"triangular UFOs" in our own country is nothing more than three lights in
the night sky (most often planes, plus that well-known "airship effect"
making separate dots of light looks like a structured dark object).
I mean: we don't even need to call for some terrestrial man-made high
technology, in most reports we get. Old-fashioned, classical IFOs often
suffice (blame on me).

That was my two-pence contribute, folks, but I'd like to get some other
experiences from other countries, too (that's why I'm also crossposting to
EuroUfoList).

Regards

"Oct 23 1978 - Corby, Leicestershire.

Investigators Mark Brown and Graham Hall produced an eighty-three

Here is a typical description by a man from Corby: 'I noticed
three white lights travelling towards me. I thought at first it
was an aeroplane going to land at Castle Donnington with landing
lights on. As it got nearer the lights got very bright and formed
a triangle. This in itself seemed an unusual formation. I slowed
down to view it more safely and realised there were no other
lights as on a normal aircraft . . . as it got closer . . . I
could see the shape as a black silhouette. It was like a Vulcan
Bomber, triangular with a light on each point. The other strange
thing was I heard no noise at all. After it passed the lights
were no longer visible . . . ' (Source: The Unknown - Nov 1996 /
Peter Hough)"

...with a link to:

http://www.farshore.force9.co.uk/ft102378.htm

`Close FT Encounters'

"Steven Spielberg's film "Close Encounters of the Third Kind" was
released on an unsuspecting public in 1977. With the release of
the film, sightings increased dramatically - no doubt it made us
much more aware of the possibility of visitors from outer space.
I must admit that the film fired my imagination and I hoped that
one day I would see a UFO, although I did not really believe it
would happen. Well happen it did.

It was the evening of Monday 23rd October 1978, and at that time
I lived on Hinckley's Hollycroft estate. On Monday evenings I
drove my wife to an evening class at Hinckley College, and on
this particular Monday I was driving up Hollycroft Hill at about
6.35pm when my wife suddenly said: "what's that strange object in
the sky"? I glanced in the direction of the Gas Works in Covenrty
Road and saw it for myself.

The object appeared to be delta-shaped and had lights dotted
around it. By the time I reached the junction of Lower and Upper
Bond Street, the object was high in the sky above The Borough. I
drove along Lower Bond Street into Holliers Walk and then into
Stockwell Head. All the time my wife was saying the object was
overhead, and my curiosity got the better of me. I pulled into
the Concordia Theatre car park and noticed that two or three
other cars were doing the same thing.

We got out of the car - as did other people - and looked up. The
object was immediately above us. It was now perfectly still. How
high I could not say. There was no sound coming from it. There
appeared to be some form of observation cabin below the main
structure, which seemed to have numerous windows from which
lights flashed on and off. We all held our breath, not knowing
what was going to happen next, when all of a sudden there was a
loud "whoosh" and the object vanished.

Those of us who had been watching in silence suddenly began to
discuss what we had seen, but nobody seemed to be too sure.
Recently I discussed the incident with someone who is very
knowledgeable about astronomy and he contended that it could not
possibly have come from outer space.
Well, I can only tell you what I saw. It was certainly no
hallucination as a number of other people saw it as well. So what
did we see on that night? Whatever it was, it was an unnerving
and thrilling experience".
[End]


This October 1978 account is personally of interest, in view of
the March 1978 report I documented in detail. It featured a
`massive' triangular object viewed at close range near Ulceby
Cross - see:

http://web.ukonline.co.uk/voyager/paul_h.txt


An above description notes, "I could see the shape as a black
silhouette. It was like a Vulcan Bomber"; the witness I
interviewed, commented, "The craft was shaped like a delta, very
similar to the Vulcan bombers based in Lincolnshire at the time".

He also emphasised, "However, it was about four times the size of
a Vulcan, flew extremely slowly and was absolutely silent!".

Do any of our UK subscribers have a copy of that eighty-three
page report? I think it could be very interesting to reconsider
this some 20 years later and in light [white at each corner and a
big red one in the middle] of the `silent vulcan' enigma.


Interesting to be reminded of current `hovering' technology in
the following news story:

''Heliplanes' race to take off'

"A vision of the future: Artist's impression of the Eurotilt.

A consortium of European engineering companies is reported to be
developing a vertical take-off passenger plane".

Full details at:

http://news.bbc.co.uk/hi/english/business/the_economy/newsid_3960
00/396241.stm

[this URL will `wrap around' at 65 characters]

Accompanying this article is the sketch of a `futuristic' twin-
rotor, heli-plane. If there was a reality and advanced technology
behind the reported silent, hovering, etc. `mega-vulcan' of
twenty years ago, there's no evidence of it in this `latest' VTOL
aircraft!

which I have enabled.

subscribers and all archive mail can be viewed.

A reminder how to do so, especially for some recent subscribers:

Archives of messages posted to the list can be viewed on the
ListBot server, at URL:

http://www.listbot.com/

Log in as a list member under:

contents - log in - list member

You will require the password provided by the list server when
you subscribed.

If that's been mislaid, use the 'Lost yours?' link above the
password field.

You can also use the member log-in to:
- unsubscribe
- change your password
- change the e-mail address where you wish mail to be sent (very
useful and this can be done regularly)
- add e-mail aliases, i.e., provide additional addresses you
might send mail from
- update your member profile, i.e., any information you may have
provided when you joined the list.

From: joel carpenter <ufx@mindspring.com>
Subject: :)Message-id: <003a01bee33f$71cb0d50$0100a8c0@mindspring.com>

UFO Research List - http://web.ukonline.co.uk/voyager/

http://www.cs.hmc.edu/~hodas/courses/cs5/week_02/lecture/foo.html

The New Hacker's Dictionary contains the following entry under Foo:

foo /foo/

1. /interj./ Term of disgust. 2. Used very generally as a sample name for
absolutely anything, esp. programs and files (esp. scratch files). 3. First
on the standard list of metasyntactic variables used in syntax examples. See
also bar, baz, qux, quux, corge, grault, garply, waldo, fred, plugh, xyzzy,
thud.

The etymology of hackish `foo' is obscure. When used in connection with
`bar' it is generally traced to the WWII-era Army slang acronym FUBAR
(`Fucked Up Beyond All Repair'), later bowdlerized to foobar. (See also
FUBAR.)

However, the use of the word `foo' itself has more complicated antecedents,
including a long history in comic strips and cartoons. The old "Smokey
Stover" comic strips by Bill Holman often included the word `FOO', in
particular on license plates of cars; allegedly, `FOO' and `BAR' also
occurred in Walt Kelly's "Pogo" strips. In the 1938 cartoon "The Daffy Doc",
a very early version of Daffy Duck holds up a sign saying "SILENCE IS FOO!";
oddly, this seems to refer to some approving or positive affirmative use of
foo. It has been suggested that this might be related to the Chinese word
`fu' (sometimes transliterated `foo'), which can mean "happiness" when
spoken with the proper tone (the lion-dog guardians flanking the steps of
many Chinese restaurants are properly called "fu dogs").

Paul Dickson's excellent book "Words" (Dell, 1982, ISBN 0-440-52260-7)
traces Foo to an unspecified British naval magazine in 1946, quoting as
follows: "Mr. Foo is a mysterious Second World War product, gifted with
bitter omniscience and sarcasm."


Other sources confirm that `FOO' was a semi-legendary subject of WWII
British-army graffiti more-or-less equivalent to the American Kilroy. Where
British troops went, the graffito "FOO was here" or something similar showed
up. Several slang dictionaries aver that FOO probably came from Forward
Observation Officer. In this connection, the later American military slang
`foo fighters' is interesting; at least as far back as the 1950s, radar
operators used it for the kind of mysterious or spurious trace that would
later be called a UFO (the older term resurfaced in popular American usage
in 1995 via the name of one of the better grunge-rock bands).
Earlier versions of this entry suggested the possibility that hacker usage
actually sprang from "FOO, Lampoons and Parody", the title of a comic book
first issued in September 1958, a joint project of Charles and Robert Crumb.
Though Robert Crumb (then in his mid-teens) later became one of the most
important and influential artists in underground comics, this venture was
hardly a success; indeed, the brothers later burned most of the existing
copies in disgust. The title FOO was featured in large letters on the front
cover. However, very few copies of this comic actually circulated, and
students of Crumb's `oeuvre' have established that this title was a
reference to the earlier Smokey Stover comics.

An old-time member reports that in the 1959 "Dictionary of the TMRC
Language", compiled at TMRC, there was an entry that went something like
this:


FOO: The first syllable of the sacred chant phrase "FOO MANE PADME HUM." Our
first obligation is to keep the foo counters turning.
For more about the legendary foo counters, see TMRC. Almost the entire staff
of what later became the MIT AI Lab was involved with TMRC, and probably
picked the word up there.

Very probably, hackish `foo' had no single origin and derives through all
these channels from Yiddish `feh' and/or English `fooey'.

and the specularity of birds per se:

[...]

"They looked like metallic mirrors, and they were oscillating or
flipflopping with a regular seesaw motion. Once again, I could
not guess their size or distance.; they were so bright and tiny
against the darkening sky that it was almost impossible to
decide their shape, but they gave the impression of being
ellipses. I don't mind admitting that in the few minutes before
they came closer I felt myself wondering if the Martian invasion
had started; this was the only time I have ever seen a fleet of
textbook flying saucers.

[...]

The lights I saw flipping across Brisbane were nothing more than
sea gulls, the undersurfaces of their wings acting as mirrors.

Though I have lived beside the sea for a quarter of my life and
am doing so now, this is the only time I have ever witnessed
this phenomenon, and I would never have credited it without the
evidence of my own eyes.

The effect of oscillating metallic disks was absolutely
realistic; it would have fooled anyone".

COMMENT:

James, there is no missing text. The very sentence you quote from Arnold, "I
trimmed out my airplane in the direction of Yakima," is his statement of
ending the 300-degree turn by leveling out and heading straight. If he had
been flying roughly southeast across the southwestern slopes of Mt. Rainier
looking for the crashed Marine plane then a 300-degree turn would take him on
an approximately EAST heading towards Yakima.

Sincerely,

Brad Sparks

Date: Sun, 15 Aug 1999 02:30:32 +0100
From: James Easton <voyager@ukonline.co.uk>
Subject: The Socorro 1964 'UFO' CaseMessage-id:
<003101bee6bd$c51a5fc0$88ce28c3@cis.compuserve.com>

UFO Research List - http://web.ukonline.co.uk/voyager/

During recent discussions on the 'Project-1947' mailing list, I
brought up the 'classic' 1964 Socorro incident, specifically that
there was a conceivable, yet maybe little known, explanation for
the 'UFO' which local Police Officer Lonnie Zamora encountered.

Initially, I wrote to Brad Sparks:

Socorro, on the other hand, is a case which can conceivably be
resolved with proof.

If the object encountered was the hot-air balloon which Larry
Robinson claims he saw evidence of, it can be traced and enough
information exists to do that.

I'm not sure how well known Robinson's published material is
known and perhaps surprisingly, or maybe not, I've only ever seen
it mentioned once, briefly, on any 'UFO' related forum. He
states:

"I believe I have solved the 1964 Socorro NM UFO case. I not
only think I know what it was, but who owned it. I have seen the
same thing here, and identified it. Once, it flew so low over my
house that I could hear the occupants talking. The intermittant
roar scared my dog. I have seen it land and take off, and the
effects and sounds were identical to the descriptions in
Sanderson's and Hynek's books. I even saw the tilting of the
elliptical shape, and heard the rise in pitch when the roar
ceased.

What was it? A manned hot air balloon. I didn't tumble to this
fully until I heard the rising pitch of the burner as the pilot
shut it down after a burn. I have seen them start it up, and I
have witnessed a touch-and-go landing, as well as several end of
flight landings. The only difference is the color. Our local
balloon is green, with white advertizing for the owner's local
winery on the side.

I then remembered seeing an ad published in 1962 or 1963, showing
the development of this wonderful vehicle by the St. Regis Paper
Company. My hobby at the time was aviation and model airplanes.
The ad was in a magazine in my social studies classroom (so I do
not know what magazine it was, but it had to do with business).
There was a beautiful picture of the balloon flying over the
northwest forests. The company logo was on the side of the white
balloon. The blurb said the balloon was going to fly an
exploratory mission around the western U.S. in 1963-64. Get
this: The company logo is A CIRCLE WITH AN ARROW IN IT, POINTING
UP. Very similar to what Zamora reported.

Here's what I think happened. Either the dump flap on the
balloon (for collapsing it after landing) accidentally opened
partway, or some other problem forced a landing. The crew made
it right, and seeing a policeman approaching (with a possible
trespass arrest), set up the stand, turned the fans and burner
on, refilled the bag, and took off. With a warm bag, this can be
done in one to three minutes. The bag tilts from a horizontal
ellipse to a vertical one as it fills with hot air. A man stands
near the bag to keep the mouth open with the stand and a pole.

Notice the flame blasts up from the basket into the balloon, just
as Zamora described. The fan sounds like a gasoline engine
(which runs it), and the burner roars much louder. The platform,
crew, and stand leave marks -at one end of the landing site! The
bag probably did not.

This early balloon had a platform with a railing rather than a
solid basket, so Zamora didn't see the platform easily without
his glasses. Note that this may have been the only one of these
in the world at the time. The sport developed from the St. Regis
balloon--the ad said they developed the burner.

The only discrepancies seem to be the size reported (Zamora
thought it was a car at first), and the speed of disappearance.
We know how hard it is to determine the size, speed, or distance
to an unfamiliar object without knowing at least one of them
accurately. I have seen our local balloon go from hovering to
disappearing in the distance in under five minutes by rising into
moving air. Add to that the loss of Zamora's glasses and the
balloon could easily have been lost to sight quickly".


Quit significant claims for the Zamora case and having read Ray
Stanford's 'Socorro Saucer' earlier this year, I didn't see
anything in the evidence which argued against the hot air balloon
suggestion and plenty that supported it.

In a summary of his investigations, Robinson notes:

"1) 1963-1964: I saw an advertizement in a magazine showing a
balloon belonging to, or sponsored by, the International Paper
Corporation. The logo is a circle containing an arrow, made of
the letters I and P, pointing up. They were going to go on a
cross country exploration with it".
and also makes another striking claim:

"2) 1965-Feb 1967: I saw an article or ad showing the results of
a multi-state series of hot-air balloon flights. A map was
included, showing the landing points of the balloon and some
amusing anecdotes of things that happened to the balloonists. One
of these was an encounter with a lawman who they thought was
going to shoot it out with them. The balloon freaked him out. The
article said, "We later found out that he thought he was seeing a
space ship." IF ANYONE CAN POINT ME TO THIS ARTICLE, IT MIGHT
COMPLETE THE PROOF".


The (current) 'International Paper' logo is indeed practically
identical to Zamora's sketched 'insignia' and a copy can be seen
on their web site at:

www.internationalpaper.com


Although Robinson says that 'International Paper' never answered
his e-mail - so far as I know, this all dates from 1996 - they
have responded to my enquiries (some months ago now) and I'll say
more about that in due course.

I did locate an article in the National Geographic magazine,
entitled, 'Hot Air Balloons Ride on Silent Winds', published in
the March 1966 issue.

Although this isn't the article Robinson recollects, it has
provided important clues and I currently have some follow up
enquiries awaiting replies.

So far, many of the points Robinson makes have been verified by
archive material I've found. Some of these are significant facts
and were not at all easy to find information about.

As such, no reason to question the sincerity of Robinson's
recollections and if he's correct, it odds-on that's the
explanation.
[End]

James,

Re: 1964 Socorro Incident

I'm always in favour of looking at rational explanations for UFO
incidents.
 However, if you want to pursue the balloon idea as an answer to the
Socorro Incident, I believe you must accept that Sgt Zamora is either an
exceptionally poor witness or he decided to alter specific parts of his
story.
 I regularly see all manner of hot air balloons in my part of the world
and I cannot imagine any observer would be so mistaken, even at
twilight.
 Its also my understanding that Zamora had studied the object carefully
before his prescription glasses dropped off and he ran for cover.
 The close proximity to White Sands has always struck me as the most
significant detail of this incident and as I recall, Blue Book dismissed
the balloon idea and privately concluded that it might have been a
prototype vehicle for NASA's Surveyor Moon landing project which had
gone astray during a test flight on the range.
 Surveyor landing trials were certainly taking place at White Sands on
the same day as the Socorro incident, but this explanation can easily be
dismissed on technical grounds.
 Okay, so balloons manufactured by the St. Regis Paper Company carry a
company logo that has a red arrow and circle on it, but I find it odd
that Zamora might be expected to note this detail, while apparently not
being able to tell he was looking at a hot air balloon.
 Douglas Aviation also used a company logo which was not totally
dissimilar to one described and during the 1960s, they produced many
studies of re-usable rocket vehicles for NASA/USAF.
 These Douglas concepts were more advanced than anything else being
considered at that time and NASA believed they might lead to an SSTO
(single stage to orbit) spacecraft using advanced aerospike engine.
 But the work quietly faded away, only to be resurrected relatively
recently as McDonnell Douglas DC-XA VTOL rocket demonstrator. (Which was
destroyed during a test flight!)
 Sgt Zamora's description of the craft bears a striking resemblance to
some of the early Douglas proposals and I would suggest that if we
accept that he provided a solid account of what happened, (please excuse
me if I don't repeat all the details) everything points towards it being
a black budget, manned, chemically fuelled rocket vehicle undergoing
trials within the massive White Sands Range that ran into trouble.
 Furthermore, it wouldn't be the first or last time that something
launched within the site came down in the wrong place causing a great
deal of official embarrassment.

Bill Rose

Bill, it's an interesting point and lord knows I often suspected the same
type of thing, but there are two issues that are hard to reconcile with this
approach. First, if it were a rocket-powered vehicle, its weight could be
estimated within a reasonable range based on the ground prints. This would
give a ballpark engine thrust range for the observed departure speeds. If
you think about the effects on the ground, there doesn't seem to be anything
like the blast footprint that engines of that level of thrust would produce.
Didn't the DCX operate off a special pad for this reason? I think that the
Zamora object would have produced a tremendous mushroom cloud of dust and
debris that would dwarf helicopter rotor downwash effects and would have
been visible for a considerable distance, and would have continued as the
object flew off. Imagine what the DCX would do if flying "nap of the earth"
over open terrain. Not very inconspicuous...

Although it does seem rocketlike in some respects, it's almost as though it
was weightless, which is a point in favor of James' theory.

Second, say it was a "black" test vehicle that somehow came down off-range.
Would the crewmen _really_ have jumped back in their ailing craft and
blasted off in the _opposite_ direction to the range when they saw a car
approaching? If they were in distress, wouldn't they have welcomed an
approaching officer who could call for assistance, help secure the area and
potentially prevent intruders from coming too close?

- J Carpenter

From: engima9 <ENGIMA9@compuserve.com>
Subject: Re: Socorro Incident

UFO Research List - http://web.ukonline.co.uk/voyager/

I ALSO can see MANY problems with the "Socorro UFO was a rocket-based
device" theory;

1: Endurance; would it have been POSSIBLE to build a rocket-powered craft
with sufficient fuel to fly some distance, land and then take off again (to
fly back to it's "hanger" (or whatever). In regards to the Socorro "UFO",
we seem to be talking about an object the size (and weight) of a car,
moving under Earth's gravity, with no wings/fins to generate any extra
lift/stability and - given that it WAS an early experimental rocket-powered
device - built in the early 1960's!!! Remember, too, that IF this craft
was a "rocket", it would HAVE to have been a "Vertol" device (ie an
aircraft kept airborne totally by it's own thrust, without NO generated
lift from any wing surfaces). This would add - dramatically - to the
craft's fuel consumption rate.

Rocket powered aircraft are very fast, but very fuel-hungry, with
fuel/flight durations often measured only in minutes (ie the WW2 Me-163 had
a powered flight duration of 10 minutes (and a very bad safety record to
boot). Many Rocket aircraft had to be designed as gliders, as all of their
fuel was used during flight. Hence, the pilots had to land "deadstick" (ie
glide down, like the space shuttle has to even in the 1990's). Of course,
ICBM's and rockets (unfortunately!) have much longer ranges, but only
because 90%+ of their mass is rocket fuel; i.e the V2 rocket = Take-Off
mass 12,900 kgs, Payload mass 1000 kg!
(Range 320 Kms).

2: Power/weight factor. If the Socorro "UFO" was a rocket-powered flying
machine, it would have to be powered by a sufficiently powerful - and
elaborate - rocket engine to give it lift and, by all description, a quite
flexible (vertol?) flight capability. This device, in addition to the fuel,
engine and body-mass would also have to lift the weight of two men. Note
also that TWO "men" were seen
If it *was* an experimental rocket-system, why not aim to initially liff
the mass (and carry the volume) of only ONE man, which would have been MUCH
easier!). A two-man vehicle would equate to quite a heavy craft, having to
carry quite a heavy payload (and hence much less fuel) in regards to most
other rocket-powered devices.

- Little wonder, then, they were described as being "small men or large
kids"; they would have needed to be!

And yet, the physical evidence for the Socorro was that - whatever it was -
it didn't generate all THAT much thrust; the upward take-off force for the
"object" only very lightly - in rocket terms, anyhow - toasting a
greasebush. Surely, an rocket-powered device would badly toast the ground
about it and create notable down-blast traces?

3: The "Rocket" that could (seemingly) fly - without any thrust!
Appart from the other problems listed above, it has to be explained - if it
WAS a rocket - HOW the "UFO" was seen by Zamora
to be airborne WITHOUT a flame or "roar", a factor that was noticed several
times during the sighting!

...."It had no flame whatsoever as it was travelling over the ground and
made no smoke or noise....".
Lonnie Zamora (HYNEK UFO Report p 228. Sphere 1981).

That was SOME rocket! Rocket propulsion that doesn't require any thrust.

Truely amazing; an't science grand!.....


Now, in regards to the balloon theory.....

In regards to Zamora's testimony, he DID , at one point in his statement,
compare the "UFO" to a "balloon".

 ......"He asked, "What it is?" I [Zamora] answered , "It looks like a
balloon....."
THE HYNEK UFO REPORT ( pg 228).

In regards to his closeness to the UFO and the clarity of his
observation.... Although it seems he got several (fairly) good looks at the
"UFO" when he initally approached it, they were from some distance
initially (an estimated 150-200 yards; it seems the closest he came to it
was 75-100 ft or so). Not only that, when he WAS fairly close to it. he
heard a "roar" from the UFO, and ran away from it, hitting his leg on the
fender of his policecar and fell over, knocking his glasses off. After
doing this, he then got up and continued running (fearing that the object
was going to explode) - "glanc(ing) back" a couple of times at it while
doing so.

Yes, he was able to see "two figures" associated with the "UFO", at one
point, but not clearly enough to make out their features.

So, the clarity of Zamora's view of the "UFO" is - based on his own
testimony alone - a little questionable. But it doesn't make him a fool, or
a bad witness, only someone who saw something at a distance, tried to
approach and then quickly removed himself from the site of something he
feared was going to explode.

So what could have Zamora have seen? I feel there are three options:

1: A highly advanced wingless vertol aircraft, running on conventional
aviation gas, using experimental turbofan/turbojet engines
(a system which probably has a better "endurance" than a rocket-based
system). The "flame" could have been the device in "afterburner" mode -
they were, after all, seen during take-off (the "UFO" was also most noiser
at this phase in the sighting, as well). Maybe once it was airborne it then
flew off (in a quiter "turbofan" mode).

However, such a device would require quite a highly developed vertol
technology to construct, even today.

2: The device WAS a balloon. The sighting IS consistent with this idea. A
flame was seen on take-off (along with a roar), then the UFO (balloon?)
floated up into the air (ie the "gasbag" being heated by a burner?). Being
an aerostatic body it would be capable of flight without requiring thrust;
hence NO flame and NO roar when it was airborne. Furthermore, most
balloons carry about two people (and can do so quite easily). The "UFO"
itself was even compared to a "balloon" by the witness himself......

Lastly, the striking similarity the Socorro "UFO" insignia shares with the
International Paper logo (even down to it having a red colour!) is uncanny,
to say the very least. For those interested in seeing this, I have a Jpeg
showing both logo's (ie the "UFO" and the International Paper one )
side-by-side; just email me and I'll be pleased to send it on).

However, some will find it difficult to accept that the Zamora "UFO" could
have been as something as proasic
as a balloon!

3: The UFO was an extra-terrestrial craft. It was a "contragravity"
device, able to become virtually massless in flight and hence only require
a small degree of thrust to "lift" it (ie an advanced form of "rocket"
motor?). Hence, it generated no destructive backblast effects with it's
propulsion system on take-off. Once airborne it was able to "coast" on
it's previously generated thrust (remember, we are talking about a
hypothetical , very highly advanced device able to "screen" itself from our
planet's gravity), and hence didn't need to generate any further thrust,
for a while, at least. Hence the noise and flame stopped as it "sailed"
away!!

- Or another form of ultratech exotic propulsion that doesn't generate
dangerous levels of heat and backblast effects (ie devices akin to the
"gravitational thrusters" featured in Larry Niven's "known space" Si-Fi
works?).

Obviously, this last theory is highly controversial and would be rejected
by many due to lack of proof for "alien" UFOs, the lack
of evidence for any advanced extra-solar culture(s), and the lack of any
scientific research that supports the possibility that such exotic
propulsion systems could be developed outside the pages of a science
fiction book!
Robert Moore.

Friday, July 9, 1999

Something (Probably) Is Out There

Space: Most everybody thinks they're wacky, but next millennium
might prove the prescience of the MUFONeers.

By JAMES P. PINKERTON

***

At the end of a century, at the dawn of a millennium, American
presidential politics has boiled down to a choice between
Republican middle-of-the-roadism and Democratic
split-the-difference-ism--a battle between the bland and the
blanched. Yet just 30 years ago this month, on July 20, 1969,
Americans did something truly bold: They put men on the moon.

Then the U.S. stepped back from greatness; the space program was
mothballed, an innocent victim, perhaps, of the Vietnam War. In
the minds of many, the Right Stuff rocket jocks were too close
to Phantom-flying baby-napalmers. The first Earth Day, in 1970,
signaled an anti-technology backlash; meanwhile,
counterculturalist historians were redefining discoverers and
explorers as despoilers and exploiters. And short-termist
politicians expanded domestic spending programs that crowded out
funding for space. Even now, with the deficit days over,
Washington is transfixed by such weighty questions as whether
Medicare should pay for Viagra. Manifest Destiny will just have
to wait.

But if NASA isn't doing much, there's MUFON. That's the Mutual
UFO Network, based in Seguin, Texas; some 700 "X-Files" types
gathered in Washington last weekend for their annual convention.
MUFON is an outsider vigilante space organization; if Uncle Sam
won't own up to looking outward and upward, then it will. And
while one can easily make fun of flying saucer followers, and
while all of them are likely misguided in their particulars,
they're probably right in general: Something is out there. And
whether It becomes known to us in the next year or the next
thousand years, all those who watched and waited by the sky
horizon will have earned their vindication.

Unfortunately, most MUFONeers are to serious space research what
astrology is to astronomy. Typical is Budd Hopkins, a New Yorker
who has been writing about alien abductions for a
quarter-century. In a speech to a rapt audience, he recounted
the tale of a man who claimed he had been kidnapped and
physically probed by space aliens in 1961. Of course, there is
no physical evidence to support his story; his account emerged
when he was under hypnosis. But to UFO true believers, the more
incredible the claim, the more credible it is. As Hopkins said,
even survivors of the Holocaust have a hard time believing it
happened to them, even though it did. So, by that
sleight-of-logic, Hopkins argued, if it's hard to believe in
alien abduction, then it's easier, maybe, to believe it actually
happened.

Philip Klass, a veteran writer for Aviation Week & Space
Technology magazine, also attended the conference. He has
studied UFOs for three decades, written four debunking books and
publishes a skeptical newsletter. He has seen zero evidence, he
says, for anything extraterrestrial. Then why does he stay on
the case? Because if ET does exist, he wants the story, he says,
still eyeing the future at age 79: "I'd win a Pulitzer Prize and
every other prize there is."

The search for the truth out there also animates the newest star
in UFO firmament, Joe Firmage, a Silicon Valley mogul who was
pushed out of the company when his interest shifted from
cyberspace to outer space. Firmage is a believer; he has written
in the past of an encounter with "a remarkable being, clothed in
brilliant white light."

But in an hour-long presentation to MUFON, he made a more modest
argument: the more scientists learn, the more they learn about
what has yet to be learned. And so, given the enormity of the
universe, isn't possible that others have learned more than us?
Now all of 28, he has both a fortune and a mission to last a
lifetime; he will shortly unveil the International Space
Sciences Organization, which will attempt to bring scientific
rigor to UFO research.

Many, maybe most, will regard Firmage as a crackpot, but
Christopher Columbus was lightly regarded until he discovered
America; today he is justly remembered as a man for the
millennium.

But now another millennium is coming, and a new set of heroes
will emerge. Since the current crop of vision-thing-less
politicians have so little to offer, someone such as Firmage has
a chance to step into immortality. The next thousand years will
quite possibly be remembered as the era when They find us--or we
find Them. - - -


James P. Pinkerton Is a Lecturer at the Graduate School of
Political Management at George Washington University. E-mail:
Pinkerto@ix.netcom.com

Date: Mon, 16 Aug 1999 19:31:49 -0400 (EDT)
From: RB47Expert@aol.com
Subject: Re: Re: Socorro IncidentMessage-id: <6d1eedfb.24e9f965@aol.com>

UFO Research List - http://web.ukonline.co.uk/voyager/

James & List,

I find it highly ironic that UFOlogists who have never before regarded
Project Blue Book's investigations as competent and thorough are now reciting
Blue Book's investigation of the Socorro case as if it was. There is no
indication that Blue Book ever even thought of a manned hot-air balloon as a
possible explanation for the case so Blue Book could not possibly have
investigated an explanation it didn't know about it -- it had trouble enough
investigating matters it did know about!!

If manned hot-air balloons were a relative rarity in April 1964 it makes it
all the less likely that Zamora, Blue Book, Hynek, White Sands Missile Range,
APRO, et al., would ever have thought of it, much less investigated it and if
they had it would be in their investigative reports. That should be a
straightforward matter to check their reports for mentions of manned hot-air
balloons.

TIME DURATION: I haven't found any reports of a TIMED reenactment and the
most quantitative data comes from Zamora's original raw police report which
mentions just seconds of observation interspersed with periods of distracted
driving, walking, running -- there seems to be even LESS quantitative time
data in subsequent investigations. In Jerry Clark's revised UFO Encyclopedia
(vol. 2, p. 861b) I find excerpts from Hynek's memo of May 20, 1964,
mentioning that he and Zamora (and Chavez) "reenacted it at the spot." But
there is no mention of a TIMED reenactment in what is quoted, and there is no
quantitative time data from such a reenactment. Maybe such data are
unpublished still if the timings were ever actually done at all.

Zamora's original police report suddenly drops out on quantitative time data
at the very end when he states "The object seemed to lift up SLOWLY, and to
'get small' in the distance VERY FAST. It seemed to JUST CLEAR Box Canyon or
Six Mile Canyon mountain. It disappeared at it went over the mountains. It
had no flame whatsoever as it was travelling over the ground..." (my
emphasis). It would be very important to get a quantitative time estimate
for this "very fast" receding to the distance and a quantitative angular size
change as to how "small" it got. But note that Zamora DID NOT say it
DISAPPEARED that way only that it "got small." He kept saying it was
"travelling" low "over the ground," that it just "cleared" the dynamite shack
by three feet, it only "just clear[ed]" the canyons or "mountains" (how far
away, how high?) This sounds like a balloon with lift problems.

WIND DIRECTION: This seems like such an important refutation of the hot-air
balloon theory. Yet where is the documentation for it? Who reported that
the wind was from the SSW and at WHAT TIME? A weather station several miles
away in Socorro at the local airport? Or from many miles away at White
Sands? Wind directions are notorious for varying over very short distances
and very small changes in height, and they CHANGE WITH TIME -- a report from
the morning would not be valid for the evening, for instance, and winds often
change at sundown due to the drop in solar heating. Surface wind is not
necessarily the same as the winds aloft. The SSW direction sounds
suspiciously like it may have come from Zamora himself instead of a
professional weather observer since it was the approximate direction of the
UFO and he said there was wind from that direction. What if Zamora was wrong
about the wind direction? What WAS the direction of "Box Canyon" and "Six
Mile Canyon mountain" that Zamora mentioned the object just cleared? What if
there was a channeling or wind tunnel effect in the arroyos that sent wind in
his direction at his location but channeled it in another direction for the
object?

We need the surface weather and winds aloft reports from ALL the weather
stations in that region of New Mexico for the afternoon and evening of April
24, 1964. If there was one consistent wind direction everywhere and aloft,
then we might have some confidence in it as applying to the site of Zamora's
encounter, though that would still leave the possibility of a local
wind-tunnel effect with channeling along the gullies.

LANDING MARKS: Speaking of Hynek's report, he states that from his firsthand
observations on April 29, 1964 -- contrary to various sources such as Ray
Stanford who claimed the landing prints were "impressions" caused by "great
weight" -- that in fact they were "4 rectangular SCRAPINGS as if a
rectangular object had SCRAPED along DIGGING into the ground.... The
GOUGING
was done away from the center in every case."

A very sharp photo of one of the Socorro "pad prints" appears in The UFO
Encyclopedia, p. 859, which shows the heavy rocks Army Capt. Holder placed
around it to protect it. The print shows several small rocks protruding IN
SITU from the crater as if they belonged there but now are exposed -- so they
could not simply have been accidentally kicked in by investigators from the
surrounding soil outside of the landing print.. These small rocks have
obviously NOT been pressed down into the bowl shape of the crater by any
"great weight." A "great weight" would have pushed the small rocks down into
the soil so that their tops would have been flush or almost flush with the
contour of the crater, and they most likely would have been crushed or broken
-- but they are not pushed down or broken. The imprints look like they have
been dug or gouged out exactly as Hynek said, NOT pressed down by a massive
object.

"BALLOONISTS" REACTIONS: The Larry Robinson story is that he saw an ad for
manned hot-air ballooning that mentioned a landing incident with a "lawman"
whom the crew thought was going to "shoot it out" with them thinking the
balloon was a "space ship." Zamora did say that one of the two white-cloaked
figures noticed him approaching and seemed startled. Some have pooh-poohed
this saying that balloonists in trouble would have approached a law
enforcement officer seeking help, and that that is the only possible
response. But even besides the "shoot out" fear there are several other
possibilities, not all mutually exclusive either: The balloonists may have
feared arrest for trespass and endangering the public with the balloon and
its fire hazard -- especially if they did in fact set a fire (smoldering
bushes were found by the initial officers on the scene). The balloonists
might have had a problem with the balloon such that they could not leave it
untended even for one second to go approach the officer for help and when the
problem was rectified at least partially that they could not stop what they
were doing but had to proceed with their ascent or risk losing control of the
balloon. Some might object that the balloonists could have waved at Zamora
without leaving the balloon, but Zamora said he only saw the "figures" for
about "two seconds" as he drove towards them but lost sight of them as his
car dipped down into the gully.

Obviously we need a lot more data on this case. Once again, as with other
classic UFO cases such as the Kenneth Arnold sighting, the public record does
not have all of the important investigative data collected together in one
easily accessible place, or the data are missing or were never collected in
the first place. THOUSANDS of UFO books have been published over the past
half century, yet not one book that collects all of the available
documentation on the Arnold case, not one that documents everything available
on the Socorro case (Ray Stanford's book certainly doesn't qualify), etc.
Yet many books are published with complete reprints of the fraudulent MJ-12
