This is from the National Security Archive website. Please note the fourth
paragraph. The "sources and methods" issue as always is the probable driver
for any residual secrecy surrounding Socorro, if it involved a secret
balloon. If you read the complete document referred to by the link below,
you can see the Agency's Oct 1962 obsession with providing plausible
deniability for a propaganda balloon operation against Cuba. There were to
be only two people, it says, who were "witting" as to the US Government's
sponsorship of the operation -- the Cuban asset and the CIA officer funding
the project. This document was considered more sensitive in 1993 than even
Kennedy-Khrushchev communications from the Missile Crisis period. Was it
because of the description of the process of creating a front for an
operation, or because of the discussion of the use of balloons for
propaganda purposes?

Also, the issue of the Agency's "extensive tests" during the 1950s
concerning balloon/aircraft attacks has a direct bearing on many UFO cases
which were apparently balloons (Mantell, Gorman, etc.) This documentation
should be obtained if it's still available. It's rare data.

- J Carpenter


"27 August 1993

Echoing Earl Long's famous taunt to arch-segregationist Leander Perez
("Whatcha gonna do now, Leander? The feds got the H-bomb!"), book reviewers
have challenged thriller-writers ("Whatcha gonna do now, le Carre?") with
the end of the Cold War. John le Carre of course simply retired Smiley to
the British equivalent of the Declassification Branch and rang for The Night
Manager. But judging by some of the truth-is- stranger-than-fiction items
which have emerged in recent months from archives on all sides of the Cold
War, spy novelists won't have to come in from the cold for lack of material.

August's Document of the Month, for example, reads like a movie treatment:
"High Winds Over Havana," featuring Ricardo Montalban as The Sponsor (p. 1)
and Arnold Schwarzenegger as the brave Balloon Technician. See Arnold battle
tropical depression and protect Cuban schoolchildren from being thumped on
the head with four-pound propaganda drops (p. 8).

A casual reader might think this memo is completely serious, but it contains
several dead giveaways which illustrate the dry wit and sense of delicious
irony with which the CIA approached its Operation Mongoose mission to
undermine Fidel Castro. For example, the balloon drops were not only to
include written propaganda, but also "novelty items such as 'gusano libre'
pins, toy balloons... decals, stickers, etc." (p. 6). Also, on the issue of
risk to aviation, the memo notes that "during the extensive tests conducted
by CIA during the 1950's, it proved to be impossible to fly a
propeller-driven aircraft into an unmoored balloon" (p. 8). (Imagine Tom
Cruise as "Top Pop.")

Only in the final round of settlement negotiations this summer, which
brought our Freedom of Information Act lawsuit for Cuban Missile
Crisis-related documents to a successful conclusion, did the State
Department release this document. Why was this the very last document
produced, the most secret of all 3,500, more sensitive even than the
Kennedy-Khrushchev letters? Because, said State in 1992, "Disclosure of this
document could vitiate the potential usefulness of this and similar
proposals in the future," and "intelligence sources and methods" must be
protected under the National Security Act of 1947.

This legal limitation suggests that the review of the secrecy system ordered
this year by President Clinton will not succeed in reducing secrecy and
cutting costs just by executive order; some legal relics of the Cold War
also need to move from the U.S. Code to the realm of novels and screenplays.
Enjoy your reading. "

[Cross-posted from 'UFO UpDates']

I didn't bring up the 'Socorro' incident on the 'public' UpDates
list and currently wouldn't have, in view of certain ongoing
enquiries.

However, as it's a controversial topic and comments are being
made without any appreciation of recent breakthroughs in research
(not only my own, I would add), I will respond.

It may be prudent to keep in mind the following, from an article
entitled `Don Piccard - 50 Years of Ballooning Memories', at:

http://www.balloonlife.com/9707/piccard.htm

"During his years at Raven, between 1962 and 1964, Piccard
devoted his energy to marketing the Vulcoon, one-man thermal
balloons. Stressing his lack of security clearance at the time,
Piccard says he worked strictly on sport balloons and had no
contact with any of Raven's military contracts. Be that as it
may, following a 1987 interview in Balloon Life with Don Piccard,
where he described his civilian work with Raven, the CIA library
in Langley, Virginia, began to subscribe to the magazine".

[...]

"Reflecting back to those days at Raven, Piccard thinks the
company's sport balloon division was a cover-up for the military
applications of ballooning. `The sport balloon program, which was
not believed in by the Raven Industry management, was strictly
getting this crazy guy who liked to fly in balloons and make
cover. So, when one of these other balloons went down, it would
just look like a sport balloonist'. When the Navy terminated its
contract with Raven, the sport balloon program died too. That was
in December of 1964".
[End]


Although generally realised that the reconnaissance possibilities
offered by hot-air balloons were overtaken by the successful
deployment of spy satellites, this is a significant 'cover up'
claim by Piccard, one of the central figures in the development
of hot-air ballooning.
If the "military applications" program was terminated at the end
of 1964, then all work must have taken place before then.

Which means that there were a number of publicly undocumented,
hot-air balloon flights prior to December 1964 and these must
have taken place somewhere.

It's now known exactly where.


Some 'impossibilities' have been cited in opposition to the
suggestion (which was Larry Robinson's, not mine) that Zamora
possibly encountered a hot-air balloon.

Recent, unpublished, developments have proven that some
'impossibilities' are not based on a full understanding of the
overall situation at that time.

This has nothing to do with Zamora and everything to do with what
none of us realised about the work Don Piccard alludes to.

Until some further enquiries are resolved, it's not really
possible to say more and whether there might be a connection to
the Zamora sighting


The rumoured 'International Paper' balloon may be a misnomer.
Larry Robinson's recollections seem to involve elements of
different articles he read and which have become jumbled over
time.

It still requires some sorting out, however, the probabilities
are much clearer now.

As previously highlighted, Robinson claimed:

"1965-Feb 1967: I saw an article or ad showing the results of a
multi-state series of hot-air balloon flights. A map was
included, showing the landing points of the balloon and some
amusing anecdotes of things that happened to the balloonists. One
of these was an encounter with a lawman who they thought was
going to shoot it out with them. The balloon freaked him out. The
article said, "We later found out that he thought he was seeing a
space ship." IF ANYONE CAN POINT ME TO THIS ARTICLE, IT MIGHT
COMPLETE THE PROOF".

This 'multi-state series' was almost certainly a transcontinental
crossing of the U.S. by Tracy Barnes from April to September
1966.
As such, this could not have involved the Zamora case.

These flights were featured in a number of magazines and one
source - which hasn't yet been located - is the 'Popular
Science', July 1966 issue.

Interestingly, Robinson refers to 'Popular Science' as a magazine
he read:

3) Mar 1967: I bought the LOOK special on flying saucers.(2) I
first saw the account of the Socorro sighting here. For some
reason, the name Socorro NM was very familiar at the time,
because I had just seen it on a map. I thought of a map I saw in
Popular Science involving a performance run of a car, but Socorro
was not on it. I did not see the drawings Zamora made until June
1968, in NICAP's "The UFO Evidence." I immediately thought of the
logo I had seen earlier, but I discounted a balloon, because I
did not know balloons could be noisy.
[End]


As the July 1966 'Popular Science' article was written whilst the
transcontinental flights were ongoing, it couldn't have featured
a map of all the locations visited. It might have shown the
intended landing points.

If it did refer to a humorous incident, when a 'local cop thought
a hot-air balloon was a space-ship', it could still be a
knowledgeable reference to the Zamora incident from 1964.

That article is obviously important to see.

Does anyone have access to a copy?

Its contents and the possible significance of some other matters,
can hopefully be clarified before too long.


James.
E-mail: voyager@ukonline.co.uk
[End]


UFO Research List Only:

Jim Winker, former Vice President of Raven Industries has
confirmed that circa 1964, a hot-air balloon would conceivably
have had "a platform with a sort of railing, rather than a
basket".
He now has a copy of Zamora's statement and has been asked if he
can reconcile the 'trace evidence' and 'thumps' reported by
Zamora.

It could be that in these early flights, as Larry Robinson
suggested, "The burner blasts sideways during refilling until the
envelope lifts".

At 03:51 PM 8/17/1999 EDT, Karl wrote:

[snip]

>Finally, I would caution against putting too much emphasis on reading

I would also caution against making too many generalized statements . . . .
<g>

Let us not forget that English was a second language to Lonnie Zamora, who
primarily spoke spanish. A lot was made of his various interviews and how
he came across as someone who was (as you put it) a "tad slow on the
uptake". However, much of that can probably be attributed to language
difficulties, rather than his expertise. You are probably correct in that
we need to be careful in taking his statements too literally, but perhaps
not entirely for the reason you state. I would also agree that he was not
a highly educated person and would have generated his descriptions in terms
that he was familiar with.

Since you have looked into this far more than I, as it happens to be near
your back yard (so to speak), do you know if there were any interviews in
spanish that would have perhaps generated a more clear picture of his
experience? As I understand it, Zamora became quite upset with his
treatment by the press and others after the incident and eventually left
Socorro for a time and really didn't want to discuss the incident further.
But I've seen him on more recent programs, so that apparently isn't the
case any longer.

I suppose it would also be interesting to have Zamora's reaction to the
theory that he had witnessed an early version of the common Hot Air Balloon.

Another question that comes to mind is that of the burning, or smouldering,
brush that was left behind. I don't know the specifics of this prototype
Hot Air Balloon, but if it is similar to more modern versions, the balloon
(or canopy) is inflated while the burner if being operated with the flames
(and heat) being directed along the ground and into the opening. As the
camopy fills with hot air, the balloon lifts up and the basket (or Gondola)
is tilted upright. This action could indeed cause brush to become charred
and burn the ground around the take-off point. However, this would only
occur in one direction from the point of take-off, usually downwind. Do
the records incidate that the charred or burned brush was only on one side
of the depressions in the ground left by the "craft"? If brush on all
sides, or at least two opposite sides, became charred, then it sould seem
to rule out this scenerio and we still need to come up with an explanation
for the charred brush.

Steve

BRAD SPARKS & FELLOW LIST COLLEAGUES--

Brad, quoted ("xxx") material from your post--

"But the weather data looks even more confused and
uncertain now. The current USGS Geographic Names Information System lists a
separate "Socorro Weather Station" that is NOT at the Airport but located
downtown. This is 1999 info so I can't tell if that was the arrangement in
1964. If it was, the distance to the Zamora site was greater than the
approximately 2 miles to the airport terminal / weather station. Furthermore
someone else posted that there supposedly was NO weather station at Socorro
in 1964 and that the weather data came from White Sands scores of miles away."

Re the location of the local weather station: You're right about the current
location, of course, and Charlie Moore seems to think there was no weather
station at the airport in '64, but we don't know this for certain yet. This
DOES make life difficult.

"And we still don't have the TIME recorded for the weather observation."

We need that info, of course. The way you phrased this suggests you have
winds data from 24 April '64. Is this so? If so, what does it show?

"And I'm very disturbed at the discovery that the Socorro Airport runway was
just a mile from the Zamora landing site and in approximately the direction
of the UFO's departure (to the South to SSW). I had never remembered ever
reading this before. I had thought it was a completely isolated and almost
deserted area outside of town. It raises all sorts of questions: Why didn't
someone at the Socorro Airport see the UFO -- especially when it departed
almost directly over the runway -- but even before it landed? Could the
object have been part of some military activity using the airport as a
staging area?"

Referring to the map in Olsen, "The Reference for Outstanding UFO Sighting
Reports" (p. 3-93), the UFO landing site was ~3800 feet DUE NORTH of the
north end of the airport's (roughly) N-S runway--i.e., the north end of the
airport is DUE SOUTH of the landing site. The UFO departed on a SSW track,
flying very low and never approaching the airport boundary more closely than
~3000 feet. As for its approach to landing, if Opal Grinder's account of
what he was told by the motorist who pulled into his gas station as Zamora's
sighting was underway, then the thing came in VERY low from the east, passing
over U.S. 85 well north of the airport. Both inbound and outbound flight
paths make it entirely plausible that the UFO might not have been seen from
the airport. Moreover, Soccoro Municipal is a very sleepy operation even
today; don't think it even has a tower...
Maybe (MAYBE) Z did see some sort of earthly experimental vehicle (NOT, I
think, a balloon), but if he did, it doesn't seem likely it was staging from
the Socorro airport (if it were, wouldn't the pilot flown there after
"wrenching" his ship?), nor from White Sands, as it departed and kept going
in the wrong direction to return to base there (SSE would have been right),
unless it made a wide swing around well south of where Z lost sight of it.

Unless you're willing to buy into the Klassian view that Zamora's a liar who
helped to perpetrate a hoax--and I don't, not by a long shot--seems to me
about the only thing we can be safely sure of at this point is that he sure
as heck saw some kind of very strange vehicle with some very interesting
capabilities... A UFO. -- Cheers, KARL

BRAD & LIST --

A few comments in haste...

I don't see why you find the airport issue so disturbing. Moreover, I'm
surprised you've only just tipped to the field's close proximity to the
Zamora site. Further, please note that in '64 the Socorro airport wasn't
exactly Denver International, still isn't. As I noted, it's a very sleepy
place. And why do you assume the terminal is located near the runway
centerpoint--or even that there's a terminal at all? I don't think there's
one today and doubt there's one now. Socorro doesn't have any sort of
scheduled airline service. Your comments seem to assume ground flight
operations personnel observing and guiding traffic, etc., when this was (and,
I believe, is) a field at which pilots make a pass over the field to check
the windsock to determine which way to approach for landing. No ground to
air radio, etc. Like I said, sleepy...

True, line of sight from the airport doesn't end with the fence. My point
was the thing was reported to have been flying very low and so could well
have been missed, especially from a quiet field without a tower, etc.

Concerning the "mysterious" New Mexico Tech activities: The national
institute for explosives research (don't recall formal name offhand) has been
there "forever." They do all sorts of work for various and sundry U.S.
gov't. agencies, among them DoD, CIA, FBI, ATF (ugh). In addition, there's a
good amount of gov't. contract and grant work, some classified, done in the
Tech labs, among them the Langmuir lab on a peak above the city. However,
nothing at Tech then and now suggests activities involving mysterious
vehicles with unusual capabilities.

Concerning departure paths and such, I measured the distance from the Z site
to the end of the runway. I merely eyeballed the closest approach distance.
Further, and I haven't time to check this precisely, the departure track is
closer to WSW than SSW, which does make a difference.

The Olsen is well worth digging out, and not just for info on this case. I'm
indebted to Herb Taylor for loaning me his copy (which I'll copy and get back
to you soonest, Herb! Honest Injun), as this was one I missed when it was
new and have never succeeded in finding to buy since. The map on the Zamora
case is excellent, with the data taken from the USAF file and plotted on a
large-scale USCGS chart. The one in Ray Stanford's book is also helpful and
squares with Olsen's. -- Cheers, KARL

Date: Thu, 19 Aug 1999 19:48:25 -0400 (EDT)
From: RB47Expert@aol.com

UFO Research List - http://web.ukonline.co.uk/voyager/

Karl & List,

We'll just have to see specific data on the nature and operations of the
Socorro Airport in 1964, as well as specific meteorological data by date,
time, and location.

Karl can you point to me ANY major account of the Socorro case that mentions
the AIRPORT and the PROXIMITY of the Airport to the UFO landing site? Maybe
I missed something or have faulty memory. (And I don't mean a map either but
an actual textual discussion.) That's my point. The existence and closeness
of the Socorro Airport to Zamora's UFO landing site is a gigantic surprise to
me -- and I shouldn't even have to justify its relevance to an investigation
of the Zamora case. I can recall a number of published accounts of the
Zamora case that discuss the possibility that some activity at White Sands
might have strayed off site and mention that checks were made at White Sands.
 I do not recall any such similar point being made about the much much closer
Socorro Airport. Nor do I recall anyone ever writing something like the
following to dispose of the possibility of additional witnesses at the
airport, "Socorro Airport was nearby but it doesn't have permanent operations
personnel manning a tower or a terminal and no one could find records of
pilots or crew who might have been eyewitnesses of Zamora's UFO." For all we
know in 1964 there WERE airport personnel who might have seen or known
something. Today's "sleepy" condition, here in 1999, is not a reliable
indication of its status in 1964. You can't assume linear progress and
project back in time an even more "sleepy" state for 1964. Activities may
have been up and down. Airports can experience decreasing activity for
various reasons (economy of the region, loss of an air carrier's route, etc.)
rather than only increasing activity.

If the Socorro Airport was checked and disposed of back in 1964 then every
major account should say so, even if just in a laundry list of something to
the effect of "We checked the FAA, White Sands, SOCORRO AIRPORT, Holloman
AFB, NASA" and we should see that kind of list all over the place. But I've
never seen Socorro Airport ever mentioned that way or mentioned AT ALL.
Maybe I just don't remember and it is there in someone's published account.
Maybe it's in Blue Book's investigative report.

You may be even more right than you thought on the UFO's departure path. The
two site maps from the Blue Book file (see Steiger book) show the landed
object taking off towards the dynamite shack almost due W of it.
Interestingly, the object was in a E-W gully so if there were wind channeling
effects it is possible the wind -- at least initially as a balloon rose --
might have blown to the W, the same direction of the UFO's initial ascent.
Crosswinds of course are quite hazardous to aviation even for powered
aircraft so imagine a balloon totally at the mercy of air currents and sudden
turbulence (CAT) and crosswinds. However there are further landmarks for the
UFO's final disappearance which are mentioned in Zamora's police report (Box
Canyon and Six Mile Canyon Mtn.) and in Hynek's final trip report of March
1965 (a "pearlite mill"), whose direction and distance need to be
established.

Hynek's trip reports inconsistently mention either a SW or a S wind, but
doesn't cite the source for the info. I was bothered to note that Hynek's
March 12-13, 1965, trip report says that Zamora was denying having ever said
to him that he had seen a flame BEFORE the landing that he'd "only" seen the
flame "at the time when he saw it [the UFO] rise from the ground." Hynek
agreed with Menzel on this one point only that "Zamora's evidence is very
mixed up and suggests some embroidery of the original sighting either by
Zamora or by Captain Holder." But the flame and the roar are in all the
early reports of Zamora's sighting and so the "mixup" must only have come a
year or so later when recollections were dimming and getting contaminated by
press attention and public controversy.

Another point that is ambiguous or conflicting in the reports I have is
Zamora's exact position when he heard the roar and saw the "flame" to the SW.
 In the more rough-appearing site map from Blue Book files (Steiger p. 108)
this Point A is located BEFORE a branched-off road turn and the distance to
the eventual UFO landing site looks like roughly 1,700 feet. Whereas in the
more refined map (Steiger p. 117) there is no mention of seeing the "flame"
pre-landing only hearing the roar and that Point "A" is positioned AFTER the
road turnoff, at roughly 1,400 feet from the eventual landing spot.

In either case Zamora was roughly 1/3 mile or less (1400-1700 feet) from the
eventual landing site which was off to his west or WSW when he first saw the
"flame" to the SW, which was roughly the same direction of both the WIND and
the landing site. But at that moment Zamora's distance estimate was 1/2 to 1
mile to the "flame," or well beyond the landing spot. If that was correct,
then the UFO "flame" was not sighted as it was vertically descending but as
it was flying FROM the S or SW in the direction of the reported WIND (if we
can ever verify this further) and coming from the direction of the Socorro
Airport.

Although Hynek mentions in his Sept 29, 1964, letter to Menzel that he had
"reenacted the crime with him [Zamora], along with STOPWATCH, etc." on site
on Hynek's second trip to Socorro, Aug 15, 1964, there is no mention of any
timings recorded in his actual trip report and I don't know if they are
available elsewhere. Zamora's original police report estimates about 10
seconds for the initial flame-roar, an unknown gap as he turned west, tried
to get up the steep hill, and got to the top, then he drove 10-15 seconds
westward on gravel road (leading to the dynamite shack) before first sighting
the landed UFO, then about 2 seconds observing the landed object and two
"figures," then drove further down the gravel road for an unknown interval
before stopping and radioing, then "possibly 20 seconds--just a guess" of
close encounter as the object lifted off until it disappeared. Thus by
Zamora's own original estimates when summed up, the total UFO observation
time was something like 32 seconds interrupted with intervals of unknown
length. The final period before disappearance may be subject to much greater
estimation error since it was influenced by the extreme stress of Zamora
running for cover from the loud flaming UFO taking off.

Keep me posted. I will look forward to what you find.

Brad

James and All,

I begin to think the first hurdle is still to try and establish if
Zamora was a credible witness. Despite everything that's been said, I
cannot believe he was unable to recognise a hot-air balloon, however
unusual its appearance might have been, even if it was carrying a fully
enclosed pressurised gondola.
 If some kind of a balloon was responsible, does this mean that Zamora
quickly decided to embark on a major enhancement of the story or was it
in reality just a pre-planned hoax?
 Certainly, Zamora continued to adjust (or he agreed to the adjustment
of) details in pseudo documentaries and "Dark Skies" which pictured the
landing of a disc shaped flying saucer. (Okay, I know this was fiction,
but...)

Then there is the question of Blue Book, who were little more than a PR
operation. If you accept that the Pentagon has covered up the truth
about Roswell and numerous other UFO incidents, it seems quite
reasonable to suggest that Blue Book participated in covering up this
incident.
 Saying they checked with all the local military facilities and possible
aerospace contractors really means nothing at all.

My Rand-McNally road map of NM shows Highway 85 as some way above
Socorro. Does anyone know if this road originally formed part of the 25
and where exactly did the car chase take place?

Nobody has mentioned the footprints around the landing site, said to
have been left by the occupants of the craft and there has been no
recent reference to the two hatch doors (?) being slammed shut or the
"girderlike" landing legs.

It seems to me that the only thing which can be confidently dismissed is
the idea that a vehicle operated by extraterrestrials might have been
involved and I am unaware of anything which even suggests this.


Bill

<<UFO Research List - http://web.ukonline.co.uk/voyager/

* LIST ONLY *

James and All,

I begin to think the first hurdle is still to try and establish if
Zamora was a credible witness. Despite everything that's been said, I
cannot believe he was unable to recognise a hot-air balloon, however
unusual its appearance might have been,

COMMENT: Zamora's first radio report of the object said "It looks like a
balloon."


even if it was carrying a fully
enclosed pressurised gondola.

COMMENT: I don't think anyone has suggested that the hot-air balloon carried
a pressurized gondola.

However, Zamora's failure to describe or see ANY gondola at all is a major
problem for the manned hot-air balloon theory. I think I've seen it
suggested that one of the early manned hot-air balloons had only a "platform"
for the crew rather than a gondola or basket, and a flat platform on the
ground with air and cords in between might have been missed by Zamora because
of the rough terrain (the stick-like "legs" he saw may have been the cords
attaching the platform below which was out of view due to the terrain
obstructions). If not a platform, the only explanations for the failure to
see a gondola beneath the round balloon envelope that I can think of are that
the rough terrain obscured the lower part of the object, the envelope was
partially collapsed over or in front of the gondola from Zamora's viewpoint
during the 2 seconds he saw "figures," and the remainder of the sighting was
also too brief in duration and influenced by fear.

Bill,

It's almost certain Zamora wouldn't personally have seen and
heard a hot-air balloon in the US before April 1964. It appears
there were only around a dozen or so hot-air balloons in the
entire country then, maybe not that many.

The first crossing of the US by hot-air balloon didn't take place
until 1966 and even that was a news story which may not have been
a hot topic in Socorro.

Zamora might have been familiar with hydrogen and helium filled
balloons, certainly, but most unlikely a balloon whose ascent and
descent was controlled by the intermittent release of a roaring
flame.

What would Zamora's frame of reference have been if it "looks
like a balloon", yet balloons don't have rocket-like propulsion.

It's crucial to realise that Zamora rarely got a good look at the
object at all.

As his affidavit confirms:

"...heard a roar and saw a flame in the sky to southwest some
distance away--possibly a 1/2 mile or a mile. Came to mind that a
dynamite shack in that area had blown up, decided to leave chased
car go.

Flame was bluish and sort of orange too. Could not tell size of
flame. Sort of motionless flame, slowly descending. Was still
driving car and could not pay too much attention to the flame. It
was a narrow type of flame. It was like a "stream down"--a funnel
type--narrower at top than at bottom. Flame possibly 3 degrees or
so in width--not wide.

Flame about twice as wide at bottom as top, and about four times
as high as top was wide. Did not notice any object at top, did
not note if top of flame was level. Sun was to west and did not
help vision. Had green sun glasses over prescription glasses

Could not see bottom of flame because it was behind the hill. no
smoke noted. Noted some "commotion" at bottom--dust? Possibly
from windy day--wind was blowing hard. Clear sunny sky otherwise-
-just a few clouds scattered over area.

Noise was a roar, not a blast. Not like a jet. Changed from high
frequency to low frequency and then stopped. Roar lasted possibly
10 seconds-was going toward it at that time on the rough gravel
road. Saw flame about as long as heard the sound. Flame same
color as best as recall. Sound distinctly from high to low until
it disappeared.

After the roar and flame, did not note anything...".


It's the tale of an overhead, roaring flame.

As for the source - Zamora could see absolutely nothing.

He did later confirm to Ray Stanford that the flame/object
descended slowly.

That was part one.

Part two I've detailed from 'Socorro Saucer', which adds further
insight. Zamora's official report tells the story thus:

"After the roar and flame, did not note anything, while going up
the somewhat steep rough hill--had to back up and try again, two
more times. Got up about halfway first time, wheels started
skidding, roar still going on, had to back down and try twice and
rock. While beginning third time, noise and flame not noted.

After got to top, traveled slowly on the gravel road westwardly.
Noted nothing for awhile. . .for possibly 10 or 15 seconds, went
slow, looking around for the shack--did not recall exactly where
the dynamite shack was.

Suddenly noted a shiny type object to south about 150 to 200
yards. It was off the road. At first glance, stopped. It looked,
at first, like a car turned upside down. Thought some kids might
have turned over. Saw two people in white coveralls very close to
the object. One of these persons seemed to turn and look straight
at my car and seemed startled--seemed to jump quickly somewhat.

At this time I started moving my car towards them quickly, with
idea to help. Had stopped about only a couple seconds. Object was
like aluminum-it was whitish against the mesa background, but not
chrome. Seemed like O in shape and I at first glance took it to
be overturned white car. Car appeared to be up on radiator or on
trunk, this first glance.

The only time I saw these two persons was when I had stopped, for
possibly two seconds or so, to glance at the object. I don't
recall noting any particular shape or possibly any hats, or
headgear. These persons appeared normal in shape--but possibly
they were small adults or large kids.

Then paid attention to road while drove towards scene. Radioed to
sheriff's office "Socorro 2 to Socorro, possible 10-44
(accident), I'll be 10-6 (busy) out of the car, checking the car
down in the arroyo."

Stopped car, was still talking on radio, started to get out, mike
fell down, reached back to put up mike, then replaced radio mike
in slot, got out of car and started to go down to where I knew
the object (car) was".


No matter what it actually was, I've never been able to
understand why an overturned white car was his first impression
of an oval-shaped object. The fact that Zamora reported over the
radio that he was 'checking the car down in the arrayo', might
question his [then] eyesight when viewing distant objects.

Let's take a time-out here and further realise that Zamora had
only, by his own account, seen the actual object for a couple of
seconds at this point.

What happened next:

"...got out of car and started to go down to where I knew the
object (car) was.

Hardly turned around from car, when heard roar (was not exactly a
blast), very loud roar--at that close was real loud. Not like a
jet-knows what jets sound like. Started low frequency quickly,
then roar rose in frequency (higher tone) and in loudness--from
loud to very loud. At same time as roar saw flame. Flame was
under the object. Object was starting to go straight up--slowly
up. Object slowly rose straight up. Flame was light blue and at
bottom was sort of orange color

>- [maybe briefly searches for them]

>- runs a further twenty-five feet
>- jumps over the hill's edge
>- turns towards the object, shielding his eyes
>- the roar stops, leaving a short whining, which also stops>

>- Zamora runs back to his car, whilst keeping watch on the object
>(per his affidavit)
>- finds his glasses
>- gets into the car
>- calls the station and speaks to Nep Lopez.>


>Stanford also writes:

>[Start]
>He [Zamora] later commented: "I couldn't tell what might have
>kept the thing up or going; it was now completely silent. It kept
>>and never did get much higher until it got over near the perlite
>mill on the west side of US 60, maybe a mile away. Then it angled
>up at a steep climb and got small in the distance, over the
>canyon or mountain that way, very fast".
>

I am struck by the short duration of th flame and roar. Ten seconds,maybe?
The point ciomes in a question: If it is true that there was no flame/roar
after 10 seconds while within ear/eyeshot of Zamorra, then:
how much time must a flame be introduced into a balloon to
take it from a "lying on the ground state" (flame horizontal to
burn some bushes) to an upright state and a lift of the basket and then
maintain and altitude while allowing itself to be blown in th wind?

To phrase it differently, it seems to me that the flame would operate
rather continuously or perhaps in a series of bursts to maintain the
altitude. I have heard such balloons and they periodically eject
hot air/gas into th balloon just to maintain altitude.

IF it was a balloon that landed for some reason,. why would they allow
the gas to get so col that the balloon itself and not just the basket
would lie on the ground?"

Bottom line: THIS IS TESTABLE. Get the best approximateion to
a 1964 vintage gas-jet supported hot air balloon and time how long
it takes for the balloon to lie on the ground after landing (The balloon
MUST be above the basket at the time the basket touches the ground...
else the basket crashed!) and then how long does it take for the balloon
to be "re-erected" from a "on te ground" position. And then how long
does it take for the balloon to lift a basket or frame with two men in it?

(Note: Odd that Zamorra did not report the men's heads being visible
over the railing of the basket or over th side of the framework.,.\
Did any such balloons carry completely enclosed gondolas such that
an external observer couldn't see inside?)

Brad, when light aircraft pilots calculate weight and balance charts, they
usually use 200 lb per passenger as a standard weight figure (allows for
some baggage, etc.) So let's say that the two occupants weighed 400 lb. The
1966 Popular Science article on Tracy Barnes' transcontinental hot air
balloon trip gives weight figures for his smaller 21,000 cubic-foot
balloon - 40 lb for the balloon envelope and "even less than that" for its
wicker basket. Let's say that the entire loaded balloon weighed around
500-550 lb., since the occupants probably weighed less than 200 lb each and
the burners and tanks have substantial weight. It appears to be between 20
and 30 feet tall.

I have seen data on some balloons as small as 10,000 cubic feet.

J Carpenter

Reprise on Tim's unqualified claim that witnesses are unreliable.

>
They ARE unreliable and it's the job of this forum to fight its' way around
the problem. The "trained observer" is largely a myth - although Chris's
1989 sighting can be taken rather more seriously, but how many ROC people
witness UFOs for that matter - especially when it comes to Policemen!!!

IF you're interested I think we've got to the point where UFO sightings
without any other corroboration (photo, video, other independent witnesses
and so on) are worthless and that includes close encounters of the whatever
kind.
<

OK. So they are unreliable. What level of unreliability, nis the question.
Witnesses often mix "raw observation" with "interpretation." The result of
this mix
can be VERY unreliable. It is the job of the interviewer/investigator to
separated,
as much as possible, the raw observation from the interpretation. ONce
the
details of the raw observation the investigator can then try to compare
these
with "candidate explanatory hypotheses" or with Klassic "prosaic
explanations."
In most cases one or more prosaic explanations will be consistent with PART
OF
the raw observation data. The investigator is then left with a choice:
reject the
explanations or reject the conflicting "raw data." Granted that there is
some
"modification of raw data" possible since there still could be a "modicum
of
interpretation " buried within the raw data, one must still be careful not
to
go to a reductio ad absurdum aka "pelicanization" and conclude that because
it is impossible to prove the observation could not be explained, that,
therefore
one may as well accept some explanation. (Maccabee's First Rule for
Debunking:
ANy explanation is better than none.)

Regarding Tim's point about only multiple witness, photo and "hard
evidence" cases being worthy of
analysis from now on is well taken. It is much easier to pelicanize a
single witness case. There are multiple witness cases, even some
supported by visual imagery, which form the truely hard core of th ufol
mystery. These are cases in which the pelicanizer must assume that two or
more people "went wacko" temporarily, perhaps in concert with a camera or a
radar set, and that everything reverted to nnormalcy immediately afterward.

Pardon yet another post by me on this today -- (and my last was a little
garbled too Karl) --

One of the hot air balloon (HAB from now on in my posts) manufacturers -- I
think it's Cloud9 -- in a comment on their website concerning balloon
envelope durability, points out that the entire useful life of a nylon
balloon could be used up in one day if it was heated to 350 degrees. This is
an interesting comment. Assume that there was such a thing as an agent HAB,
inherently disposable and just barely capable of lifting two occupants and a
box of nasty items. The big tourist-type HABs we're used to today are
conservatively designed for durability and long lifetime. An agent HAB might
be smaller than would be considered ideal and would have to be kept aloft by
"overburning" the propane, since there would be little concern for envelope
life. It would be interesting to plug 350 degrees into Rudiak's equations.
Of course there would be a range penalty.

Note that Yost's balloon, according to James' info, WAS smaller than a
modern typical HAB and was MYLAR, not cloth-like nylon, and was white,
smooth, seamless, shiny and not ribbed like the ones you typically see
today. Very flattened-egg-shaped.

I still am hung up on the wind direction. This is priority one for even
giving the balloon theory a chance.

J Carpenter

Why Socorro?

Why would any aerial vehicle (AV) have landed in that exact spot?

The evidence doesn't imply an emergency landing. If that were the
reason, how could the AV have taken off again, with so little
time to repair what had forced it down.

Maybe it was only a two-minute repair, or a `maintenance stop'
which was aborted?


Alternatively, we know Zamora saw two figures in what resembled
white coveralls. As there's no evidence that either were in the
AV when it landed, what about the possibility that one, or both,
were already waiting and the landing was a pick-up at this pre-
arranged rendezvous.

It may be a wrong assumption that the occupants departed again so
quickly because they realised someone had observed them. The AV's
landing and quick get-away, might always have been the intention.


It's this type of `agent(s) extraction' training exercise which
was being/had been conducted as part of the New Mexico project,
even if the Socorro incident is completely unrelated.

Should it have been an alien spaceship, there's also of course no
reason why the `agent extraction' scenario couldn't equally
apply. Perhaps `Our Humanoid in Socorro', was due for a spell of
home planet leave.


I'm curious about the proximity of the `dynamite shack', which
according to `Socorro Saucer', was "owned by the Mayor".

Do Mayors in New Mexico normally keep stores of explosives?

Is this because the locals can be such lawless rednecks, or an
incentive to make sure you _do_ vote for the Mayor next time.

JOEL, KARL & LIST,

A 9,000 cubic foot balloon would be 25.8 feet in diameter as a sphere. I
think I've seen UFO size estimates attributed to Zamora that were 12-15 feet
or 15-20 feet, but I'd like to see the documentation (I can't readily find
it). But 50% or even factor 2x witness errors are common in UFO
investigations especially when there is only a SINGLE WITNESS to provide data
so there is no cross-check, no averaging.

I do vaguely recall reading somewhere that someone worked with Zamora to
obtain exact terrain/vegetation reference points in the gully where the UFO
landed in order to precisely determine the UFO's dimensions. This would be
extremely useful info to have and to have documented as it could settle the
whole question of a hot-air balloon. Such data could narrow down error
margins well below 50% or 100%.

As for wind directions, we still have no documentation, no source references,
no time/location/altitude data, except Hynek's inconsistent statements in his
trip reports referring to a S or SW wind (still unsourced though,
undocumented). Plus the site maps (see Steiger pp. 108, 117) show the UFO in
a gully oriented E-W, with a N-S gap between hills on the east end where
Zamora had trouble getting the car to climb over. This could make a
wind-tunnel effect channel for the wind to go E to W, which was very roughly
the initial direction of the object as it lifted off, even if the wind was
otherwise from the south. But the direction of movement still needs to be
better documented. The second site map shows the landed UFO and the dynamite
shack that Zamora said the object barely cleared, and they are on a line
about 10 degs S of W. However, I have no data on how the west line on the
map was determined (by magnetic compass? was declination corrected? by
eyeballing the road and referring to street maps?).

As I've pointed out, Zamora's distance estimate of 0.5 to 1 mile for the
initial "flame" in the SW when combined with the fact the eventual UFO
landing site also to his SW was only about 0.3 mile away suggests the object
was a further 0.2 to 0.7 mile away to the SW of the landing spot when Zamora
first sighted it as the "flame."

This indicates the UFO came in from the SW -- the same approximate direction
as the reported though undocumented wind direction -- before it landed. But
this inference depends on Zamora's initial distance estimate for a highly
unfamiliar "flame" seen in the sky with no reference marks to determine
distance. Thus Zamora's distance estimate like any other observational
estimate could be off by a large factor.

So the main problems with the manned hot-air balloon theory are:

1. AVAILABILITY OF BALLOON (was such a balloon ACTUALLY there?)
2. SIZE TOO SMALL (needs more documentation)
3. WIND DIRECTION vs. UFO MOVEMENT (needs documentation)
4. APPARENT LACK OF GONDOLA (was it a platform instead of gondola/basket,
which was hidden below terrain? why didn't Zamora see crew below balloon
right in plain sight at 103 feet distance BEFORE he ran and dropped his
glasses? how was that distance determined anyway?)
5. LANDING MARKS (what part of a hot-air balloon would create the four marks
in the ground or did the crew dig them and why? could the hot-air burner or
crew attempts to relight have caused burned brush?)

Other potential problems with the hot-air balloon theory will require
QUANTITATIVE DATA or better documentation before they can be considered
serious objections as witness observational accuracy may not be sufficient:

6. UFO LIFT RATE & DISAPPEARANCE (what was the lift rate in feet/sec? how
reliable is that? what was the duration of Zamora's encounter at different
segments? how was it determined? what was the distance to disappearance?
was Zamora wearing his glasses when it disappeared? Zamora says "I picked up
my glasses" which he had earlier dropped in his panic but says NOTHING ABOUT
PUTTING THEM BACK ON again. was Zamora nearsighted or farsighted?)
7. FLAME APPEARANCE/COLOR/ORIENTATION (how reliable can this be?)
8. SOUND/NOISE (quantitative data on Zamora's observations? on balloons?)

POSSIBLE points in favor of manned hot-air balloon theory depending on how
well each holds up on further scrutiny:

1. GENERAL SHAPE & SIZE (Zamora himself initially radioed to dispatch "It
looks like a BALLOON")
2. TWO-MAN CREW (don't they pick balloonists to be SMALL like jockeys
because of weight considerations?)
3. INSIGNIA
4. FLAME
5. ROARING SOUND
6. SLOW LIFTOFF
7. POSSIBLE CLASSIFIED PROJECT UNKNOWN TO BLUE BOOK
8. LANDING MARKS?? BURNED BRUSH??

Those are the facts but we need a lot more. The possibility of a manned
hot-air balloon never occurred to anyone until the 90's so it was never
investigated at all by Blue Book, Hynek, McDonald, APRO, NICAP or anyone else
in the 60's (if it WAS investigated let's see the investigative reports
saying so). At this point, I'm not rendering an opinion one way or another
on this possible explanation for the famous Socorro case.

Brad Sparks

Well, I've been reading all the versions of the story I can find, and they
all repeat the mantra that the wind was blowing strongly from the SW, or
WSW. It _appears_ that the object flew straight into the wind. Hynek used
this as an argument as to why the people in the nearby house (apparently)
downwind didn't hear the object's roar.

possible that it was Zamora's own estimate. Although since they were a half
mile or so from the airport, they should have been able to check the
windsock or wind T pretty easily.

department kept records?

James,

The proximity of the allegedly "sleepy" Socorro Airport less than a mile away
may be a factor to consider, too. "Sleepy" airports were a favorite of CIA
special ops in the 50's and 60's and probably up to the present. It
facilitated the transport of personnel and equipment for ops, training,
tests, etc., with reduced chance of observation (though of course people did
from time to time see the Tibetans at Camp Hale, Colo., etc.).

JOEL & JAMES,

I think Hynek meant to say UPwind NOT "down wind" in his Aug 64 trip report
as a down wind location actually helps carry sound. The nearby Felix
Phillips home was apparently E of the Zamora landing site and according to
Hynek was actually in the gully or in the direction of the gully that the UFO
landed in (according to Klass it was only 1,000 feet away; it's Klass' map
that shows the Phillips to the E). If there was a wind-tunnel channeling
effect in the gully, then the wind might have come down the gully E-W even
though overall the wind might have been from the south or southwest or
whatever (we still don't know that). That would have made the Phillips house
upwind but it might account for a balloon initially rising from the gully and
going off to the West. Hynek in his report claimed it was a strong SW wind
blowing, which would have been a crosswind to the Phillips rather than up or
down wind.

In Hynek's Mar 65 trip report, he argues against a kids' prank balloon
because "the fact of the matter is that the wind was from the SOUTH, and the
object went WEST. A balloon released at that time would have gone directly
over town."

Brad

JOEL,

You don't mention whether the 350-degree temperature for nylon balloons was
350 F or K or C. I'm assuming it was 350 F which equals 450 K. So if
plugged into Rudiak's assumptions, the balloon volume would be about 333
cubic meters or about 11,600 cubic feet. However, a mylar balloon could have
been heated more perhaps, which would have given greater lift from a smaller
volume. And what about exotic materials for balloon envelopes? Given a
"black project" budget and availability of exotic materials, high-performance
burners, frame, etc., a classified agent infil/exfil balloon might have been
smaller still. Reducing the visibility of a balloon for agent infiltration
ops would be an important consideration. Testing the visibility in a
sparsely populated but not completely unpopulated area might have been part
of the testing and training.

Brad

Pardon yet another post by me on this today -- (and my last was a little
garbled too Karl) --

One of the hot air balloon (HAB from now on in my posts) manufacturers -- I
think it's Cloud9 -- in a comment on their website concerning balloon
envelope durability, points out that the entire useful life of a nylon
balloon could be used up in one day if it was heated to 350 degrees. This is
an interesting comment. Assume that there was such a thing as an agent HAB,
inherently disposable and just barely capable of lifting two occupants and a
box of nasty items. The big tourist-type HABs we're used to today are
conservatively designed for durability and long lifetime. An agent HAB might
be smaller than would be considered ideal and would have to be kept aloft by
"overburning" the propane, since there would be little concern for envelope
life. It would be interesting to plug 350 degrees into Rudiak's equations.
Of course there would be a range penalty.

Note that Yost's balloon, according to James' info, WAS smaller than a
modern typical HAB and was MYLAR, not cloth-like nylon, and was white,
smooth, seamless, shiny and not ribbed like the ones you typically see
today. Very flattened-egg-shaped.

I still am hung up on the wind direction. This is priority one for even
giving the balloon theory a chance.

J Carpenter

Ok, so how about this then:

Kirsten and I were travelling south on the A46 Narborough Road in South
Leicester, date hazy, but spring 97, I do remember the time as I was
picking Kirsten up from work, so 2010hrs local. Clear skies, twilight,
brightest stars just becoming visible. We approached the traffic lights
at the Rex Williams snooker hall. We have the sun roof (what the
British get instead of air conditioning) open.

I notice two white lights moving north at about 11 o'clock, high.
Aircraft methinks, but I see no nav lights or strobes. I comment on
this to Kirsten who sees the pair of lights as well. We stop at the
traffic lights. Kirsten lowers the passenger window (on the left, over
here) for a better view. I'm thinking satellites.

By this time the lights are to our left, but are clearly visible to me
through the sun roof and to Kirsten through the open window. The lights
stop dead, then rotate about a common centre at a mid point between
them.

I say "Did you see that?" Kirsten says "Yes". I say "What did you see?"
Kirsten describes exactly what I saw.

The traffic lights change and I take a left turn and pull over for a
better view. When I stop the car and get out, the lights have gone.

I have no explanation for this, but two of us saw this.

Has this ever been seen before?

Why didn't I report this? The usual reason why most people don't report
this stuff. You are labelled a "nutter" and some chap turns up at the
door telling you that this was obviously the Ordivician Mothership. Who
do you report this stuff to?

So, a UFO sighting from an ROC chap. There are more, I'm sure, but they
tended to keep quiet about them. After all, we were supposed to be
experts in what was flying about. Admitting that you didn't know what
you saw was asking for having the piss taken. Pete Edwards (as
qualified as myself in the recognition field) saw a light moving across
the sky in a "stepped" motion in the mid 1960s. Although I've known Pete for 20
years he only admitted to this about 5 years ago.

I think the ROC was asked to report UFO sightings back in the 60s, but
I have no hard evidence on that (might be in the PRO) and don't intend
looking as it isn't my field. As Tim says, UFO aren't really my
interest.

A delta in a field is, however. I would ask this chap some questions
relevant to what it probably was rather than being an answer to
everything.

Chris

Dear Oh Dear!

Sheltering witnesses - rubbish. This sounds curiously conspiratorial.

In an email sent to me some months ago Chris noted, amongst other things,
that - in what he termed - the "post - Lazar" age nothing was provable
anymore. Well, that may be the case.

The facts are clear as far as I'm concerned. Sightings by themselves are
useless and that's Ufology's central weakness and one we can't get around.

In my book, which is obviously a matter of some concern to Chris, I tried
not to rely just on sightings. If, for instance, at a point 3/4 years ago
when sightings of a small triangular aircraft were at their peak in and
around the NW coast, we hadn't known about Warton and been told by various
employees with the requisite clearances etc. that something was going on at
the Special Projects Site, then, by themselves, the sightings would have
been pretty useless.

Then of course these things were being reported under escort by RAF
Tornados - AND BEING PICKED UP BY LOCAL MIL SPOTTERS - on 264.4
MHz.....

Steve Douglass band of Interceptors, military monitors, have been far more
successful in indicating the true nature and extent of the cover-up
relating to black aircraft projects - through just a few radio intercepts.
He's also got some intriguing, but by no means 100% solid, video footage to
accompany his monitoring activities.

In the book I also tried to bring in other information including recently
released documents and so forth. As I pointed out in relation to the
pathetic and much-criticised Fortean Times review/hatchet job this month -
a book review undertaken by somebody who had not read "UFO Revelation" -
there was no attempt to rely upon documents either. I ensured that I asked
the right people, including Chris, non-Ufologists in the main, for their
views and opinions on the subjects I was covering. Apart from Chris,
they're pretty happy - as are the dozens of people who have sent supporting
emails to me since publication. They're not Ufologists either.......

Sightings prove that SOMETHING has been seen and no amount of evasion can
alter the fact that witnesses are terribly unreliable. Effective skeptical
UFO research proves this time and time again whether it be related to the
increasing number of holes being fired into the body of the Roswell alien
craft myth (numerous crash sites, different numbers of bodies, different
shaped craft, different people involved at different times, Glen Dennis 10
years out etc. etc.), the supposed "aliens" at Rendlesham (the lighthouse
and....) or the supposed "UFO crash retrieval" in Wales in the 1970s.

Venus is, of course, actually an 'alien mother craft' according to many a
local UFO witness in England's North West....In Tony Dodd's book "Alien
Investigator" he even claims a UFO picture exclusive and shows a photograph
of a planet! He's a former Policeman, and therefore a "trained observer".

I was looking at the hundred of pages of released FBI FOIA material on
UFOs/Flying Saucers in my files today (again) and what became clear was
that terminology used in the press/media encouraged a certain kind of
reporting by witnesses. Any anomaly was described as a "flying saucer" and
soon anomalous objects (anomalous to the viewer, that is) became flying
saucers.

Moving on, good evidence for this comes in the shape of the October 23rd
1978 'UFO wave' over Leicestershire. Having re-evaluated my position on
this somewhat - by having had another look at the detailed UFOIN report
completed two years later - it is clear that many people's descriptions of
what they saw were coloured by what they THOUGHT they should see; in other
words whilst a majority drew pictures of triangles and diamonds, a
significant number drew pictures of the 'classic' flying saucer even though
it is clear that the one "UFO" seen by all, at the same time of night, was
on the same flightpath as their sightings....

I note also the powerful imagery of the "Close Encounters" film that was no
doubt in many peoples' minds at the time......

Perhaps from the point of view of a suggestion that witnesses are (very)
reliable comes a report in the 23rd October document where people in the
same area reported the same object at the same time and drew entirely
different pictures of it.......

Lets just hope that around the UK this week the "trained" military and
Police observers of Ufology's legend are not out chasing stars, reporting
UFOs, making "credible reports" to Air Staff 2a and building more myths in
the process.

Tim M.

So far as I'm aware, the only referenced source about the wind
direction is in fact Zamora. The following comes from 'Socorro
Saucer':

"...I couldn't see bottom of that flame. It was behind a hill
from my view. Didn't notice any smoke, but some dust seemed
moving over the land in that general direction. The wind was
blowing hard. Possible it came from the windy day. But the sky
was mostly clear - just a few clouds scattered around. Wind was
blowin' against me, from the south-southwest or maybe the
southwest, 'cause I could tell the way the dust [from spinning
tyres] flew off when I was trying to put the car up that first
hill to where I had a view of the ravine and the object down in
it".

As he struggled to climb that hill, presumably focusing on
controlling the car and with his first two attempts being
failures, it seems uncommon that Zamora would consciously have
noted which direction the dust was blowing.
Could this possibly have been a retrospective recollection, when
a question arose of how the object was travelling in relation to
the wind?

>
One of the hot air balloon (HAB from now on in my posts) manufacturers -- I
think it's Cloud9 -- in a comment on their website concerning balloon
envelope durability, points out that the entire useful life of a nylon
balloon could be used up in one day if it was heated to 350 degrees. This
is
<

We better find out "which degrees."

350 C or 350 F?

Rudiak assumed 102C = 375 K ("absolute" scale). that is T = 375.

350 C would be 350+273 = 613 K,. Compared to the previous value, this
temperature is
1.6 times the previous value, so the density of the gas inside would be
1/1.6 = 0.6
of that used before. Hence the volume would be 0.6 of the previous
volume.
Since the volume is proportional to the radius
cubed, the radius is proportional to the 1/3 power of th volume. Note
that the volume
RATIO is here estimated as 0.6, so the radius ratio is estimate as
(0.6)^0.333 = 0.84.
So the radius at this high temperature would be about 80% of the previously
estimated value
Not a big change.

If the 350 refers to F degrees, convert to C and get (5/9)(F - 32) = 176 C,
which is lower
than the350 C used in the above calculation and so there will be even less
reduction
in the radius.

Bruce.

Not that I'm convinced by the balloon hypothesis, but in the interest of
fair play: Why does this have to be an either / or choice ?

A Rozier type balloon uses a lifting gas such as Helium in conjuction with
an secondary internal hot air balloon inside the same envelope. The idea
is to use the hot air to control trim, thus conserving the main lifting
gas.

It was developed some time in the 1780s and is still such a good principle
that just about all the round-the-world balloon attempts used a Rozier
design. They have burners like a hot air balloon, so they look like one,
but they have far more lift

I don't know what time of day the sighting took place - it's important
in that it would affect the ambient temp. As you know hot air balloons
generate less lift in hot weather than in cold - the same is true of any
LTA craft. I always imagine NM to be hot, so the lift from a pure hot air
craft wouldn't be very inspiring.

As for the flames underneath, well that's a tough one. I've never heard of
RATO being used in LTA, but I suppose it's a long shot possibility.

Dave W

Since this was investigated almost immediately after it occured (and there
is a lot of information about it in the Project Blue Book files), we don't
need to reach back into our memories to determine many of the specifics of
this case. While we can come up with gaps in the investigative process,
looking back on it some 35 years after the fact, we shouldn't ignore (or
forget) that there are many known facts about this case.

James has raised an interesting issue, which needs to be investigated
fully. But let's keep in mind that the Socorro sighting is primarily built
on annecdotal testimony. If we begin to diverge from that testimony we can
only build an arguement based on speculation and inuendo. If we choose to
discount part of the testimony, then why should we bother with any of it?
I should point out that the U.S. Air Force took this case very seriously,
and it remains an Unknown in their eyes to this day.

I would also suggest that while Zamora might not have recognized an
experimental Hot Air Balloon (and I''m not convinced of that), I can't
imagine that Air Force investigators wouldn't have recognized it from his
description shortly after the fact. Certainly with all of the military
sites in that part of the U.S., which were carefully monitored for unwanted
intrusions from both the land and air, any experimental craft would have
quickly become discovered.

I believe there were also other witnesses to an unusual craft that day and
thought by some to be the same one. I would have to dig up the details,
but it is my understanding that their description isn't very balloon-like.
On the other hand, Zamora's descripton doesn't seem to fit that of a "space
craft", so it remains (at least in my mind) an Unknown.

well as the geometry of the other sightlines, so none of these important
issues rely on witness estimates. The location of first sighting (or
"hearing"), speed of disappearance, etc., depend more on estimates by
Zamora, but they can at least be ballparked.

Exactly. Correct me if I'm wrong, but I believe this is the only occupant
case on the Blue Book "unidentified" list. It's a distinctive case from a
number of points of view.

> I would also suggest that while Zamora might not have recognized an

This is a strange case of the "dog that didn't bark," isn't it? Why _wasn't_
the balloon issue ever raised by Blue Book, if only to cover all the bases?
The case file mentions all sorts of other theories, like helicopters
(there's a sketch of a chopper with the strange insignia on its side,
setting the bushes on fire with its exhaust), and Quintanilla seems to have
really been into the idea that it was a lunar test vehicle. He contacted
NASA and several aerospace contractors about that. But no mention of
balloons...it's a rare instance where the AF _didn't_ trot out the balloon
"cover story" <g>.

I'm really torn over this balloon idea. There are many things that recommend
it and some that I just can't easily accept. I do have a hard time with the
size issue. It's just a fact that it takes a HAB of around 20,000 cubic feet
to lift two men, according to the balloon books I have, unless there are
some special techniques that I don't know about. This means that his size
estimates were radically wrong. Of course that's possible.

I keep thinking of a classic example of this effect in a non-UFO case. R V
Jones' book on his WWII technical intelligence work goes into detail on the
type of judgment he had to develop to pull the reliable details out of
eyewitness accounts of new German weapons systems. In one case, he requested
the French underground to provide him with details of a giant German radar
installation. The antenna of this thing was huge, literally the size and
shape of a bridge, and was mounted firmly in a fixed location. Several
agents got a look at it and forwarded sketches to Jones. In the book, Jones
has a photo of the actual antenna compared with the sketches, and _not one_
of them is accurate. Most of them are so cartoonish that they're laughable,
and completely useless for purposes of estimating anything technical about
the antenna. Granted, the witnesses couldn't just walk up to the antenna and
measure it, but it was immobile, at a fixed distance, etc. It's exactly the
type of thing that Alan Hendry pointed out about UFO testimony. I don't want
to dump on witnesses, but it's just a fact that you can't take their
estimates literally.

J Carpenter

JOEL & LIST,

I was surprised, Joel, when you turned up HEATED HYDROGEN as used in some
hot-air ballooning (e.g., Don Cameron's first Atlantic crossing attempt)
despite the dangers. Previously you found one model of sport hot-air balloon
with 9,000 cubic feet volume and one-man crew. If hot hydrogen was
substituted the volume could be reduced by a factor of 13 (the difference in
density between hydrogen and air) to 700 cu-ft per person OR LESS because we
keep forgetting that Zamora said the crew looked like "SMALL ADULTS" or
LARGE
CHILDREN. It stands to reason that experimental balloon test pilots might be
chosen for small size like jockeys, so instead of 170 lbs maybe 120 lbs, but
let's ignore this size reduction for now.

Using these scaling factors, a 1400 cu-ft HOT HYDROGEN balloon could carry a
normal-sized two-man crew and the balloon envelope diameter would be 13.8
feet -- exactly within the size range reported by Zamora. A HOT HELIUM
balloon of a volume 2800 cu-ft with two-man crew would be 17.4 feet in
diameter, still within Zamora's size estimate range (if I recall correctly a
15-20-foot figure for one estimate).

One can imagine intelligence agencies testing the limits of safety and
endurance (e.g., the U-2) to see if an extremely small heated hydrogen
balloon could be used for clandestine agent ops.

Brad

Let's put some numbers to this. This is from "Ballooning: The Complete Guide
to Riding the Winds" by Dick Wirth and Jerry Young (Random House, 1991). I
hope my formatting doesn't get garbled like the wind data I posted the other
day.

J Carpenter

------------------------------------------------------

Hot-air balloons are bigger than gas balloons because even heated air is
much denser than hydrogen or helium, so more of it is needed to lift off.
Typically a gas balloon (hydrogen) will derive about 60 lb of lift per 1,000
cu ft whereas a hot-air model will develop only 17-20 lb per 1,000 cu ft (at
100-120 deg C). Thus a 77,000 cu ft balloon will lift: 77 X 17 = 1,309 lb
gross lift.

Assuming the weights are:
Envelope - 160 lb
Basket and burner - 150 lb
4 gas tanks - 290 lb
total - 600 lb
Net lift: 1309-600= 709 lb

The average person weighs 170 lb and therefore a standard '77' operating in
standard atmospheric conditions will lift 709/170= 4.17 people -- or three
passengers, one pilot and equipment.

Type Max size (cu ft) crew

AX2     12,000           1
AX3      20,000          1
AX4      31,000          1
AX5       42,000         2
AX6      56,000          2/3
AX7      77,000          3/4
AX8       105,000        5/6

Brad, as Mr Piccard explained it to me, they had used conventional hydrogen
balloons for agent operations, but the advantage that HABs have is that they
confuse the adversary. His explanation is that gas balloons have well known
flight characteristics that allow their point of origin to be backtracked
with some accuracy. Say an agent landed in East Germany and stepped out of
the balloon, which would then obviously fly away and land somewhere. It
could be recovered by the East German authorities, weighed and measured, and
if the winds aloft were known, its point of origin could be backtracked with
accuracy.

Since a hot air balloon has great maneuverability by comparison, its point
of origin could -not- be determined by an adversary with the same accuracy,
confusing the issue. That's half the game.

Since the balloons were supposed to be disposable, I don't know if they
would have made them as exotic as this hybrid system, knowing they would
fall into the enemy's hands.

As far as the heated gas issue, if you read histories of the rigid airships,
such as the Zeppelins and the USN Akron and Macon of the 1930s, they often
deliberately let them heat up in the sun to gain a good deal of extra lift.
It was called "superheat". According to one history of the Hindenburg, the
Zeppelin company planned to install electric resistance heating elements in
the helium gas cells of the ship they were designing to replace the
Hindenburg. This would give the ship a substantially increased payload
capacity at launch. Pretty advanced stuff.

If I had to bet on the builder of a classified advanced lighter-than-air
vehicle that could possibly be responsible for Socorro, I'd bet on Goodyear.
They did build inflatable planes for agent operations. See Marchetti's "CIA
and the Cult of Intelligence." (reliable? I don't know...) There are
pictures of these things, they did fly them -- the "Inflatoplane"... they
were tight with the Navy...

J Carpenter

JOEL & LIST,

Joel thanks also for correcting my calculations in your E-mail. The actual
lifting capacity of hydrogen, depending on ambient temperature etc., is about
65 lbs per 1,000 cu-ft. So two men of small size, with balloon envelope,
burner, fuel, gondola or platform, would probably need 4,000 cu-ft (diameter
20 ft) of hydrogen at least.

Good points on the greater maneuverability of a hot-air or hot-gas balloon
over a simple gas balloon. However, disposability was not necessarily always
a requirement as in the border crossing example I gave previously.

Brad

COMMENT: In the days of sailing before powered ships, sailors could go from
A to B then back to A again using the wind. Wind directions change
especially near sunrise and sunset when solar heating changes drastically and
thus the convection patterns of air masses. The Zamora incident took place
close to sundown. Wind directions also change depending on the terrain --
I've suggested that the E-W gully the UFO landed in could have channeled a
south wind into an E-W direction. But again, the provenance and/or
reliability of our wind data is highly uncertain at present.

Moreover, when facing desperate situations against formidable opponents and
there is no other way out, a solution to the wind problem could no doubt be
devised, based on shrewd understanding of meteorology.

The CIA has had to extract defectors from within the then Soviet Union over
heavily fortified borders. I recall one high-level KGB defector
(Gordievsky?) traveled from Moscow over thousands of miles to a southern
border and it was remarked that the interior travel was easier than the last
few miles of border crossing. The manner of the border crossing remains
secret.

One can easily imagine a CIA operative in a balloon crossing over a remote
Soviet border to drop off equipment for another balloon, and waiting for the
wind to reverse in order to return. Then the agent (maybe a defector)
arrives at the drop site, assembles the balloon, waits for the right wind
then sails over the border to freedom. Highly dangerous, extremely risky,
but what if there was no other way? Perhaps the border is remote and
unmanned but consists of miles and miles of booby traps, land mines and
barbed wire, so that a balloon with a 10-20 or 50-mile range is all that is
needed to sail right over it.

From: joel carpenter <ufx@mindspring.com>

Listmembers, particularly James-

On the topic of balloon maneuverability, here are some more details from the
excellent book "Ballooning: The Complete Guide to Riding the Winds":

"How can you race balloons? They are virtually unsteerable, and they travel
at the pace of the wind. But, the competitive urge being as strong as it is,
balloonists have devised a range of close-quarter contests as tests of
flying skill...To understand how balloonists compete with each other one
must discard the notion of the winner always being the first past the post.
Since balloons are at the mercy of the atmosphere, all traveling in the same
airstream at more or less the same speed, balloon racers have to be accurate
rather than fast. The winner is the balloonist who comes closest to a
target -- either by landing on it or by dropping a marker to fix his
notional landing point....

In the northern hemisphere the wind generally veers to the right with
height. And the words 'Right with height' are drummed into every learner
pilot's head. Race theory, then, is simple. A target is chosen downwind of
the launch site and the balloon pilot gains altitude to turn right and flies
low to regain left, zig-zagging through the sky while aiming for the
target."

Then some examples of competitions are given:

"Hare and Hounds. In this race the hounds try to land or drop a marker as
close as possible to the landing position of the hare...

Judge Declared Goal. The pilot flies to a goal downwind and drops his
marker. The winner is closest to the goal. In the early days of racing only
one goal was set but the one-target version has been superseded by the
multiple-target version...The pilot chooses the most appropriate goal when
actually in the air. The result of this variant has been to produce some
amazingly accurate flying. Pilots as good as world champion Paul Woessner
have achieved zero ft -- putting the marker in the center of the target
cross.

Big Bender or Elbow. This race involves changing course as acutely as
possible. Balloons fly out for a specified minimum distance, for example 5
miles; the pilot drops a marker to indicate his position and then flies the
second leg, attempting to change course as much as possible...on a typical
day they may climb to between 10-15,000 ft in an effort to find 'Right with
height.'"
...Target smoke and target approach.
Good balloon pilots are capable of steering their craft with a reasonable
degree of accuracy through a narrow band of wind about the main flow and
most competitive pilots can land within 200 yds of a goal. Most problems
occur in the final approach to the target because the wind is fickle; either
smooth flowing or turbulent, it runs like a river over trees, houses and
hills....The wind is capricious below 250 ft, and many pilots plan their
approach to arrive at 250 ft over target and 'drop like a brick'...
Last-minute wind indicators, such as chimney smoke, help and the ground crew
may set off a smoke bomb to show the local turbulence."

Comment: One could speculate that in the Socorro case a person on the ground
was burning a smoke bomb or flare to indicate the wind direction, and this
is what burned the bushes.

J Carpenter
