Date: Wed, 25 Aug 1999 11:48:56 -0500 (EST)
From: Larry Robinson S/AP/EIS Kinesiology <lrobins@indiana.edu>
Subject: Landing at Socorro

UFO Research List - http://web.ukonline.co.uk/voyager/




First, I suggest that you read my web page on the subject.
Since it is not robot-searchable (due to decisions beyond
my control), I am not sure if all of you have found it.

It is at:

http://php.indiana.edu/~lrobins/howisoco.htm

For the same reason, I cannot paste from other emails, email
through web page forms, or control the line length.

Addressing the comments of all who have posted (part of this
is an edited copy of a message I sent to UFOmind):

1. The burner used in modern hot-air balloons was invented
  in 1962. The balloons were very rare in 1964, but several
  races had already occurred. I can get documentation of
  this if necessary.

2. The metal triangular platform was used until 1965, when
  a suitable basket became available. I have photos of
  them, including some copied from a Time magazine article
  published before the sighting. Zamora's "legs" would
  have been the A-frame over the platform (which explains
  why only two legs were seen).

3. Newer burners are quieter and more efficient than the
  original ones.

4. A zinc-iron alloy (described in the analysis of the
  scrape mark) is found on the surface of galvanized iron.

5. At the first sighting of the flame, the roof of the car
  may have hidden the envelope of the balloon, or the
  sunglasses may have made it match the sky.

6. My work here at Kinesiology has borne out this relevant
  fact:

  NO human can correctly estimate the size, distance,
 speed, or altitude of an object, unless one of these
 happens:

 a. The witness knows what the object really is, and thus
   has a valid size estimate.
 b. The object comes within 20 feet (6 m) of the witness,
   where binocular vision can find distance accurately.
 c. The object passes in front of AND behind known
   objects.
 d. The object casts a shadow from a known light source,
   or leaves marks in a known location (Zamora's visual
   estimate differs remarkably from the actual measured
   distance to the marks).
 e. Other measuring techniques or instruments are used.

 If the witness makes an incorrect guess of the identity of
 the object, ALL size, distance, speed, and altitude
 estimates are distorted by the guess.

 Pilots and air support personnel can routinely make good
 estimates of the distance, speed, or altitude of airplanes.
 But they have one advantage the UFO witness does not have:
 They KNOW the objects they are looking at are airplanes,
 and so have a pretty good size estimate. A UFO can be the
 size of a bug, a building, or a planet. Attempts to
 estimate distance, speed, and altitude fail when the
 unknown object is assumed to be the size of an airplane
 (or in this case, a car).

 It is amazing that UFOlogists habitually ignore these
 facts. They routinely take an estimate of size, distance,
 speed, or altitude given by a witness to be an ironclad
 fact, instead of a very rough guess based on the sizes of
 known vehicles.

 Even trained observers cannot find out this information
 without the aids listed above. Many guesses are off by
 factors of 100, and quite a few are off by factors of
 100,000 to 1,000,000. Many air traffic controllers made
 this last mistake before the invention of RADAR, radioing
 landing instructions to bright planets (especially Venus)
 that were suddenly uncovered by clouds.

7. Using USGS maps of the area, I determined that Zamora
  underestimated the distance to the landing site by a
  factor of 3 (first sighting) and 2 (last sighting).
  Scaling up the distance also scales up the men and the
  balloon envelope to normal size. In addition, since the
  wind was at his back at the last observation site, the
  envelope of the balloon was farther away from him than
 the landing marks were.

8. Likewise, if Zamora ran as he said he did, he BROKE the
  world record for sprinting. Zamora's time-sense seems to
  be off here. This is a common phenomenon of human
  perception in emergency situations.

9. Likewise, the other witnesses' estimates were no better
  due to the same types of perception error.

10. Zamora could not identify the balloon because he never
  heard of a noisy balloon. Neither had the Air Force
  officers (the original project was for the Navy).

11. The logo was for purposes of sport balloon racing, not
  advertising. Most balloons in such sports still carry
  a symbolic ID inside a circle. They are used to identify
  the balloons for scoring purposes, like numbers on race
  cars and football jerseys.

12. The triangular platform was made of a pipe or welded
  metal frame, with a mesh metal grid (similar to those
  found on fire escapes) on top. It could very well have
  made the marks, especially if the landing was hard
  (kinetic energy, not just weight).

13. The bottom of the object (if it was indeed a balloon) was
  never seen clearly by Zamora. First it was hidden by
  terrain (from both viewpoints), then he lost his glasses.

14. The wind and the rough terrain should cause a rough
  landing. This could cause the deep marks, and probably
  the burnt brush. The platform might even have turned over.

15. The takeoff happens in these stages (I have seen this many
  times):

  a. The envelope is inflated on the ground (from the
    account, it never deflated; it just lost lift).
  b. The burner is fired SIDEWAYS to lift the envelope.
    The fire have been started by a sideways blast.
  c. As the envelope lifts, the burner is angled up (the
    initial hovering). This takes 10 to 20 seconds. This
    explains the tilting of the oval shape given by one
    account.
  d. Another blast of the burner is used to lift the craft
    off of the ground (the horizontal motion starts as
    the wind takes over once the craft is off the ground).

16. The object did NOT disappear in the distance, but went
  behind terrain. As I recall, the balloonists (in their
  article) said they flew a few miles and set down again.

17. The object stayed low enough on takeoff that Zamora
  probably never saw the (edge-on) platform -- if only he
  hadn't lost his glasses.

18. Three of the marks coincide almost exactly with the
  dimensions of the platforms. The fourth could have been
  from an early strike, from the platform turning over,
  from the mouth ring of the envelope, or from accessory
  equipment.

19. Zamora stated that "the wind was at my back" during the
  sighting from the location where he parked. Other
  accounts (by investigators) of wind direction were
  probably reversed by the false assumption (shared by many
  UFOlogists) that a south wind blows toward the south (a
  south wind is defined by the National Weather Service
  [and its predecessor, the US Weather Bureau] as coming
  FROM the south). Even Hynek gets this reversed, not just
  here but in other UFO cases.

20. If the wind speed had been brisk, the chase car might
  have been left behind (as they also are where roads are
  sparse). Also (unless you knew what you were looking for)
  would you recognize a chase car or grasp its
  significance? The first time I saw one, I had no idea
  what it was for. The trailer looked like it had a small
  airboat (for swamps) on it.

21. The ground does not look that hard in the original photos
  of the landing site. The soil seems almost sandy around
  each mark. Was the hardness tested at the time of the
  landing, or after some time (and weather) had passed?
  Also, did the estimate of "several tons" assume only
  vertical force? The corners of the platform could exert
  several tons per square foot each if the platform
  bounced from one corner to another as it hit.

22. The first Vulcoon had a thirty foot (diameter) envelope,
  and a parachute-style harness to hold one man. Later
  models were bigger (40, 50, and 65 ft) and used platforms.

23. The roar is much louder if you are in the cone below the
  mouth of the envelope, where you can hear the resonant
  echo from inside the envelope. In the modern balloon,
  the basket blocks much of this, but the open mesh
  platform would not be able to do that.
24. I have the July 1966 Popular Science article. The 65 ft.
  balloon had an enclosed triangular gondola painted orange.
  The envelope of this balloon had orange and white stripes.
  It is NOT the article I am looking for.

25. Unfortunately, I was not yet interested in UFOs when I
  read the article by the balloonists mentioned in my web
  page. I found out about the Socorro case later, after the
  magazine had been returned to its owner. I do have a
  drawing I had made of the balloon at the time I read the
  article (I had wanted to make a flying model of it at the
  time). It has the International Paper logo on it.

  Other items found in the spiral notebook the drawing is
  in date the contents to a period encompassing February
  1965 to January 1967. I first learned of the Socorro case
  in March 1967.

  If and when I find the article again, the contents will
  conclusively determine whether my solution is correct.

26. I wish someone had performed this simple experiment at
  the time: Have two men stand at the landing marks while
  Zamora drives his squad car over the route he originally
  took. Then ask Zamora to compare the two events.


Let's not assume that unusual or exotic technology is
needed where a simple misperception will suffice to explain
a sighting.


If we can't even agree on the first year of the 3rd
millennium (it's really 2001, since there was no year
numbered 0), how can we ever solve any UFO case?

By the way, if someone ever does catch an extraterrestrial
space ship, it can't be called a UFO anymore, because it
is no longer an Unidentified Flying Object.


Larry Robinson

myself, because I didn't know how LOUD those things can get
at close range.

aviation theme (it was very possibly an industry trade mag),
but I did not save the details at the time (the magazine
was borrowed). When I read the article, I was interested in
making a tissue-paper flying model of the balloon, not
solving a UFO case (I was a teenager at the time).

the article were the 1963 Fairfield IL case (which made the
local paper), the 1965 Exeter NH case, and the 1966 Michigan
"swamp gas" sightings.

Another thought just occurred to me: Zamora was in the
cone where the resonant sound is loudest during the part
of his last sighting before the balloon lifted. If the
envelope were on the far side of the platform, then the
mouth would have been pointed toward him. (And if the mouth
were pointed away from him, the flame would not have been
visible until the bag rose.)

One-man (agent) in aboard one-time-use balloon. For extraction, air-drop a
balloon kit. Even if prevailing winds not favorable (e.g., blowing
westward), it's possible in certain places that a lift to the ESE would make
a relatively safe pick up possible. Or, how about this: Agent goes up in

hook/loop/net (as, e.g., the early photosat film packages were recovered).

lifting the harness line high enough for a low flying plane to snatch. A
free balloon with dangling agent might be better in certain situations.

directly privy to much nuttier/dicier ops. -- Cheers, KARL

Addressing the comments of all who have posted (part of this
is an edited copy of a message I sent to UFOmind):

1. The burner used in modern hot-air balloons was invented
  in 1962. The balloons were very rare in 1964, but several
  races had already occurred. I can get documentation of
  this if necessary.

2. The metal triangular platform was used until 1965, when
  a suitable basket became available. I have photos of
  them, including some copied from a Time magazine article
  published before the sighting. Zamora's "legs" would
  have been the A-frame over the platform (which explains
  why only two legs were seen).

3. Newer burners are quieter and more efficient than the
  original ones.

4. A zinc-iron alloy (described in the analysis of the
  scrape mark) is found on the surface of galvanized iron.

5. At the first sighting of the flame, the roof of the car
  may have hidden the envelope of the balloon,

COMMENT: The top edge of Zamora's windshield might have been at something
like 30 to 45 degrees elevation. If the balloon was a half mile to a mile
away it would have been at an altitude of perhaps 2,000 to 5,000 feet
roughly. Granted that the time interval data between the "flame" and the
landed sighting of "figures" is unavailable or unknown, it was presumably
less than a few minutes. That might make for a dangerous or impossible
descent rate of a hot-air balloon.


or the
  sunglasses may have made it match the sky.

6. My work here at Kinesiology has borne out this relevant
  fact:

  NO human can correctly estimate the size, distance,
  speed, or altitude of an object, unless one of these
  happens:

  a. The witness knows what the object really is, and thus
    has a valid size estimate.
  b. The object comes within 20 feet (6 m) of the witness,
    where binocular vision can find distance accurately.
  c. The object passes in front of AND behind known
    objects.

COMMENT: Granted that Zamora's non-close-encounter observations may fall
prey to the previous objections. Still, his sighting of the LANDED object
against background and foreground terrain and vegetation of measurable
distance is quite a different situation than the typical nebulous witness
estimation without visual distance cues. I recall but cannot place where I
read that investigators worked with Zamora to exactly frame the landed UFO
against measurements of terrain and vegetation that bracketed the UFO to come
up with upper and limits on the UFO's dimensions.
 d. The object casts a shadow from a known light source,
   or leaves marks in a known location (Zamora's visual
   estimate differs remarkably from the actual measured
   distance to the marks).
 e. Other measuring techniques or instruments are used.

 If the witness makes an incorrect guess of the identity of
 the object, ALL size, distance, speed, and altitude
 estimates are distorted by the guess.

 Pilots and air support personnel can routinely make good
 estimates of the distance, speed, or altitude of airplanes.
 But they have one advantage the UFO witness does not have:
 They KNOW the objects they are looking at are airplanes,
 and so have a pretty good size estimate. A UFO can be the
 size of a bug, a building, or a planet. Attempts to
 estimate distance, speed, and altitude fail when the
 unknown object is assumed to be the size of an airplane
 (or in this case, a car).

 It is amazing that UFOlogists habitually ignore these
 facts. They routinely take an estimate of size, distance,
 speed, or altitude given by a witness to be an ironclad
 fact, instead of a very rough guess based on the sizes of
 known vehicles.

 Even trained observers cannot find out this information
 without the aids listed above. Many guesses are off by
 factors of 100, and quite a few are off by factors of
 100,000 to 1,000,000. Many air traffic controllers made
 this last mistake before the invention of RADAR, radioing
 landing instructions to bright planets (especially Venus)
 that were suddenly uncovered by clouds.

7. Using USGS maps of the area, I determined that Zamora
  underestimated the distance to the landing site by a
  factor of 3 (first sighting) and 2 (last sighting).

COMMENT: What are your distance figures and Zamora's? You don't mention.
Zamora's first sighting of the LANDED object was at an estimated distance of
150 to 200 yards (450-600 feet), according to Zamora's account written within
seven hours of the incident (according to Hynek, Hynek UFO Report, pp. 224,
226). The site maps (Steiger pp. 108, 117) show that distance to be 800
feet, presumably as measured by the on-site investigators (there may be
investigative reports I don't have that say so explicitly and explain how it
was measured, by whom, when, etc.). Zamora labeled his drawing of the object
at that point as at a distance of "APPROXIMATELY .15 MILES" (about 792 feet)
presumably using the investigators' more accurate measurement.

That is NOT a factor 3 error. In fairness to Zamora, 600 feet should be
taken as his visual estimate and the error to 800 feet is only 33% or so,
about a factor 1.3.

So are you saying that on USGS topo maps you can prove that the 800-foot
distance evidently measured by investigators on-site was actually more like
2,000 feet or more? How can a USGS topo map have enough contour detail to
enable anyone to do that?


 Scaling up the distance also scales up the men and the
 balloon envelope to normal size.

COMMENT: Apparently a distance of 103 feet was measured by investigators
with Zamora at the point of closest encounter (Steiger p. 110), the distance
between Zamora's car and the landing marks. Presumably Zamora's car was
easily located as it had not been moved anywhere before the first
investigators arrived and it's location could easily be redetermined from
tire tracks after it was moved.

Are you saying this 103-foot figure also was in error by a factor of 2 or 3?
If you're not saying this then how could any scaling up of OTHER
size/distance estimates be relevant?


In addition, since the
  wind was at his back at the last observation site, the
  envelope of the balloon was farther away from him than
  the landing marks were.

COMMENT: According to Hynek the wind was blowing towards Zamora and the
City
of Socorro, not on Zamora's back. However, I've pointed out the winds might
have been different down in the E-W gully due to channeling.


8. Likewise, if Zamora ran as he said he did, he BROKE the
  world record for sprinting. Zamora's time-sense seems to
  be off here. This is a common phenomenon of human
  perception in emergency situations.

COMMENT: How so? Zamora said he had run about 25 feet in what he guessed
was about 6 seconds when he "glanced back" at the rising UFO. That's about 4
ft/sec or 3 mph, a very SLOW running speed on smooth ground, a fast WALK in
fact, but on rough terrain it might have as fast as was possible. But
certainly NOT a world record for sprinting (which is closer to 26 mph I
believe). In another place in his original report Zamora suggests he covered
the fifty feet away from his car and back, total about 100 feet, in possibly
20 seconds. That's again a very reasonable 5 ft/sec or almost 4 mph.

9. Likewise, the other witnesses' estimates were no better
 due to the same types of perception error.

10. Zamora could not identify the balloon because he never
  heard of a noisy balloon. Neither had the Air Force
  officers (the original project was for the Navy).

COMMENT: True. But he did tell the dispatcher "It looks like a balloon."


11. The logo was for purposes of sport balloon racing, not
  advertising. Most balloons in such sports still carry
  a symbolic ID inside a circle. They are used to identify
  the balloons for scoring purposes, like numbers on race
  cars and football jerseys.

12. The triangular platform was made of a pipe or welded
  metal frame, with a mesh metal grid (similar to those
  found on fire escapes) on top. It could very well have
  made the marks, especially if the landing was hard
  (kinetic energy, not just weight).

COMMENT: This is widely ignored by UFOlogists, starting with Ray Stanford,
who kept insisting the marks were done by weight of the object. Whereas
Hynek says they were "scooped" or "gouged" which is done by force.


13. The bottom of the object (if it was indeed a balloon) was
  never seen clearly by Zamora. First it was hidden by
  terrain (from both viewpoints), then he lost his glasses.

COMMENT: True enough. But how could he miss seeing the two-man crew from
103 feet BEFORE he dropped his glasses due to backing up into his car?
Zamora gives a very detailed account of the appearance of the flame and the
changing noise at this point, all BEFORE bumping his leg on his car, so he
seemingly had a good view.


14. The wind and the rough terrain should cause a rough
  landing. This could cause the deep marks, and probably
  the burnt brush. The platform might even have turned over.

15. The takeoff happens in these stages (I have seen this many
  times):

  a. The envelope is inflated on the ground (from the
    account, it never deflated; it just lost lift).

COMMENT: If it was a hybrid Rozier-type balloon with sealed envelope of
hydrogen or helium or other gas, then it would never completely deflate.
  b. The burner is fired SIDEWAYS to lift the envelope.
    The fire have been started by a sideways blast.
  c. As the envelope lifts, the burner is angled up (the
    initial hovering). This takes 10 to 20 seconds. This
    explains the tilting of the oval shape given by one
    account.
  d. Another blast of the burner is used to lift the craft
    off of the ground (the horizontal motion starts as
    the wind takes over once the craft is off the ground).

16. The object did NOT disappear in the distance, but went
  behind terrain. As I recall, the balloonists (in their
  article) said they flew a few miles and set down again.

COMMENT: Where is this reported? More importantly though, Zamora says he
picked up his glasses again but NEVER SAYS HE PUT THEM BACK ON. He was
content with just leaving his sunglasses where he dropped them, so he was
apparently rattled enough to not be doing things logically at this stage
after his panic run from the UFO. We don't know if Zamora was nearsighted or
farsighted.


17. The object stayed low enough on takeoff that Zamora
  probably never saw the (edge-on) platform -- if only he
  hadn't lost his glasses.

COMMENT: As I mentioned before, that may explain not seeing the platform
below the two-man crew, but it doesn't explain not seeing the two men at this
point!


18. Three of the marks coincide almost exactly with the
  dimensions of the platforms.

COMMENT: What ARE the "dimensions of the platforms"? Let's see those
numbers and compare them with the exact measurements at Zamora's site.


The fourth could have been
  from an early strike, from the platform turning over,
  from the mouth ring of the envelope, or from accessory
  equipment.

COMMENT: Which one was this "fourth"?


19. Zamora stated that "the wind was at my back" during the
  sighting from the location where he parked.
COMMENT: This is such a crucially important point we need to have the exact
source referencing for this. All I can find in Zamora's original report was
"wind was blowing hard" (Steiger pp. 116-7, Hynek UFO Report p. 225).


Other
  accounts (by investigators) of wind direction were
  probably reversed by the false assumption (shared by many
  UFOlogists) that a south wind blows toward the south (a
  south wind is defined by the National Weather Service
  [and its predecessor, the US Weather Bureau] as coming
  FROM the south). Even Hynek gets this reversed, not just
  here but in other UFO cases.

COMMENT: Quite possible. I didn't make that mistake though. What are these
"other UFO cases" where Hynek got the meteorologists' definition of wind
direction wrong?


20. If the wind speed had been brisk, the chase car might
  have been left behind (as they also are where roads are
  sparse). Also (unless you knew what you were looking for)
  would you recognize a chase car or grasp its
  significance? The first time I saw one, I had no idea
  what it was for. The trailer looked like it had a small
  airboat (for swamps) on it.

21. The ground does not look that hard in the original photos
  of the landing site. The soil seems almost sandy around
  each mark. Was the hardness tested at the time of the
  landing, or after some time (and weather) had passed?
  Also, did the estimate of "several tons" assume only
  vertical force?

COMMENT: I don't know where this estimate of "several tons" comes from, do
you? If it wasn't determined by a competent soils engineer and fully
documented I wouldn't take it seriously. Someone digging with a shovel can
exert "several tons" of force along the thin blade edge, loosely speaking.

(More precisely taking "several tons" to be 3 tons, spread over 2 to 3 sq ft
of area covered by all four marks, is about 21 to 31 lb/sq in pressure. A
170 lb person bearing full weight on the edge of a shovel one foot wide by
1/4 inch thick exerts a pressure of about 57 lb/sq in.)



The corners of the platform could exert
  several tons per square foot each if the platform
  bounced from one corner to another as it hit.
22. The first Vulcoon had a thirty foot (diameter) envelope,
  and a parachute-style harness to hold one man. Later
  models were bigger (40, 50, and 65 ft) and used platforms.

COMMENT: Are you saying Zamora's UFO was 30 or 40 feet in diameter? Are you
discounting hydrogen Rozier balloons?



23. The roar is much louder if you are in the cone below the
  mouth of the envelope, where you can hear the resonant
  echo from inside the envelope. In the modern balloon,
  the basket blocks much of this, but the open mesh
  platform would not be able to do that.

24. I have the July 1966 Popular Science article. The 65 ft.
  balloon had an enclosed triangular gondola painted orange.
  The envelope of this balloon had orange and white stripes.
  It is NOT the article I am looking for.

I just wish there was much less confusion about technical details of radar,
AF reporting formats, etc., on your web site based on incomplete or obsolete
sources, as with the 1956 Bentwaters-Lakenheath case. You don't seem to have
Condon Committee radar physicist Gordon Thayer's 1971 AIAA article on the
Lakenheath-Bentwaters case or Thayer's 1980 Encyclopedia of UFO's article,
which I edited since I was actively involved in investigating the case at
that time in conjunction with Thayer, Peter Sturrock and Phil Klass. Thayer
clearly explains that the Bentwaters MPN-11A radar's sweep rate was 2
seconds, not 6.4 or 10.66 seconds. You may be confusing this with the
six-second sweep rate of the Lakenheath CPS-5 radar. And the "golf ball"
comparison is part of a standard Air Force Regulation 200-2 UFO report form
format that specifically asks for the size compared to a "known object" at
ARM'S LENGTH.

The bad news for the meteor explanation scheme for Bentwaters is that in
early 1998 I discovered a previously overlooked HEIGHT-FINDING EFFECT in the
data on the "streaking light" incident. This was when visual observers in
the C-47 at 4,000 feet overhead and in the Bentwaters tower and on the ground
saw a brilliant light streak under the plane from east to west at the same
time the Bentwaters radar tracked the E-W unidentified object at tremendous
speed. As you put it, "This is the only sighting combining ground RADAR,
ground visual, and air visual in the entire episode."

The height-finding effect I discovered comes from the UFO's disappearance or
skipping over the radar "blind zone" above Bentwaters. The radar operator
reported one blip 2 miles E of the radar station followed "immediately" by
the next blip 3 miles W of station. Since the MPN-11A radar beam was only
about 9 degrees in vertical height, it is flatly impossible for an object
higher than about 2,500 feet to be tracked closer than about 2-1/2 miles from
the radar otherwise it will vanish in the "blind zone." It's simple
trigonometry, and elementary radar principles, but was completely overlooked
by generations of investigators.

This fact stunningly and unexpectedly PROVES that the object was at a very
low altitude, below the 4,000 foot height of the observers in the C-47 who
saw the light fly below their aircraft. And it strikingly confirms the
ground observers' estimate of a 2,500 foot height for this "streaking light."
 It is very difficult to explain a meteor maintaining horizontal flight at
2,500 feet.

(BTW, a hypothetical "skip-range" error in the radar -- so it displays a
distant meteor as if closer in range -- could not possibly position a series
of a dozen or more evenly spaced blips on a linear path RADIALLY across the
radar screen on OPPOSITE SIDES on a continuous path.)
The Trent case should not be discredited on the basis of someone else's
hoaxes of color photos made to resemble the Trents' B&W shots. Nor should it
be dismissed on the basis that the Trents understandably sighted IFO's over
the years and had no technical ability to distinguish them from UFO's.

You are missing Bruce Maccabee's technical physical optics work on the Trent
case published by CUFOS in 1976 and 1988 which represent the most complete
and exhaustive treatments of the case published to date. I have worked on
this case since 1972 and am working on new findings which will take the case
a quantum leap further.

Bruce has experimentally refuted the "sun shadows from the east" theory and
proven that a large cumulus cloud in the east reflected sunlight at sunset --
he measured the angular size of the light source as approximately 3 degrees
wide by 8+ degrees high (much larger than the sun's 1/2 deg). Weather
records from a station east of the Trents prove there were altocumulus clouds
present at 7:28 PM on May 11, 1950, the exact time of the sighting plus or
minus several minutes.

And as for Top Unexplained UFO cases you overlooked one of the most important
lists of all, the Condon Committee's "Sightings, unexplained" list (Condon
Report p. 961). And you missed Vallee's 1966 survey of UFO groups. Despite
the many years separating these lists you would find more overlap among these
higher-quality efforts than with "Strange Universe" magazine. The Trent or
McMinnville photo case appears on most of these lists.

You should also look into the RB-47 case which baffled the Condon Committee.
I have now published an exhaustive refutation of Klass' explanation, and
which culminates investigations of mine going back to 1971 (see AIAA
Astronautics & Aeronautics, Dec 1971). See my 30-page preliminary report in
Jerome Clark's The UFO Encyclopedia, 2nd Edition, 1998.

As I've very briefly summarised in a private e-mail, the search
for the evidence you highlighted has taken a few twists and turns
and resulted in some interesting and previously unknown
information coming to light, even if it is not directly to
Zamora's sighting.


Going back to the beginning, this 'International Paper' balloon
is a real mystery. It's such a specific recollection, with the
distinctive logo closely resembling Zamora's 'insignia', that it
seemed this must have a basis.

Yet, as you well know, the evidence has proved illusive.

I'd like to take a look at this again.

The first point is why a company such as 'International Paper'
would have any interest in hot-air balloons. You referred to an
advertisement circa 1963/64, which showed a balloon with their
logo and mentioned a planned 'cross-country exploration'.

This is very early in the development of hot-air ballooning and
any form of sponsorship.

How certain are you that the 1963/64 advertisement related to
'International Papers'?

There was research carried out by 'Raven Industries' into the use
of hot-air balloons to carry logs from mountain slopes. However,
these were helium-filled, cable driven balloons and that research
didn't commence until 1967. I don't know of any proven connection
to 'International Papers', though I might have located a
photograph of these balloons in use (I'm awaiting a copy from one
of the balloon museums).

Could this have been something you saw mentioned in a much later
article, and in due course thought was retrospectively connected
with earlier material you had seen?

Although this seems unlikely - what about the possibility that
the 1963/64 article you remembered was in fact about a
significant balloon flight across the English Channel. This I now
know took place in April of 1963 and was sponsored by a new
French travel magazine called 'VIA'.

The 'Raven' balloon used was piloted by Ed Yost and Don Piccard
and the flight was intended to publicise Raven's new 'sporting'
hot-air balloons.


In 1996, you stated:

"1965-Feb 1967: I saw an article or ad showing the results of a
multi-state series of hot-air balloon flights. A map was
included, showing the landing points of the balloon and some
amusing anecdotes of things that happened to the balloonists. One
of these was an encounter with a lawman who they thought was
going to shoot it out with them. The balloon freaked him out. The
article said, 'We later found out that he thought he was seeing a
space ship'."

As you know, the first 'multi-state' flight was undertaken by
Tracy Barnes' during April-September 1966. This was sponsored by
Lennox Industries, of Columbas, Ohio, manufacturers of heating
and air-conditioning equipment.

The article you saw must surely have been about these balloon
flights.

Were you ever able to contact Tracy Barnes?

He could be the key and with this in mind, I recently asked Don
Piccard if he could assist with contact details for Barnes. I
have these now and this needs to be followed up if it hasn't
already been.

It sounds like Tracy Barnes could be a prime candidate for any
involvement with 'Socorro'. Presumably in the article, he must
have noted a humorous incident from a pre-1966 balloon flight,
or, the incident Barnes referred to happened during the 1966
cross-country flights and has nothing to do with Zamora at all!

The aerostat had not deflated, but had lost lift enough to
lean over and touch the ground The only way it could have
done this without rotating the insignia is to have leaned
away from Zamora.

Zamora could not see the platform or the men at this point,

position (similar to the first drawing) The bottom of the
aerostat was now visible, but the platform and men were still
hidden behind the terrain. As the aerostat tilted, the cone
of resonant reflected sounds from inside it tilted away from
Zamora, changing the tonal quality of the roar.

Once the aerostat was able to lift the platform, the wind
took charge of it, causing horizontal motion. At about the
same time, the balloonists shut down the burner because
they had sufficient lift. Any further burns took place well
away from Zamora, and probably would not have been heard.

I calculated the sweep rates backwards from the calculated
object speed and the number of blips. If the sweep rate was
really 2 seconds, then either the calculated speed or the
number of blips is wrong.

I can think of nothing that is a golfball at arms length except
a very close airplane. That's six times the angular size of
the moon. Something the angular size of a golfball at arm's
length at a real altitude of 2500 feet would the size of a
quarter block lot. That's why I asked the question. Many times,
people have confused the meaning of that question, and
reported a size comparable to an object hit in the air instead.

An example is Venus, which has been repeatedly reported to be
the size of a baseball at arm's length on the form. I suggest
you take a baseball and hold it at arm's length against the
sky. In one case, the observer pointed out Venus as the UFO
the next night. Yet, he wrote "baseball" on the AFR 200-2 form.
Another case had "basketball" written on the form.

Another witness misunderstood the form as asking what common
object would hide the UFO if the UFO itself was an arm's length
away. He wrote "boxcar." How much of the sky would be covered
by a boxcar (UK: train van) at arm's length.

@The bad news for the meteor explanation scheme for Bentwaters is that in
@early 1998 I discovered a previously overlooked HEIGHT-FINDING EFFECT in
the
@data on the "streaking light" incident. This was when visual observers in
@the C-47 at 4,000 feet overhead and in the Bentwaters tower and on the ground
@saw a brilliant light streak under the plane from east to west at the same
@time the Bentwaters radar tracked the E-W unidentified object at tremendous
@speed. As you put it, "This is the only sighting combining ground RADAR,
@ground visual, and air visual in the entire episode."

@The height-finding effect I discovered comes from the UFO's disappearance or
@skipping over the radar "blind zone" above Bentwaters. The radar operator
@reported one blip 2 miles E of the radar station followed "immediately" by
@the next blip 3 miles W of station.

Was this 1/2 sweep later, or 3/2 sweeps later?

@Since the MPN-11A radar beam was only about 9 degrees in vertical height,
@it is flatly impossible for an object higher than about 2,500 feet to be
@tracked closer than about 2-1/2 miles from the radar otherwise it will
@vanish in the "blind zone." It's simple trigonometry, and elementary
@radar principles, but was completely overlooked by generations of
@investigators.

But with a third-trip echo, the meteor would not be two miles
from the station, but two miles PLUS two complete pulse trips
(186272, times twice the time between pulses) away at the time.
Same angle, different actual range.

Do you know the pulse frequency (not the transmitter frequency,
but the rate at which it was gated)?

@This fact stunningly and unexpectedly PROVES that the object was at a very
@low altitude, below the 4,000 foot height of the observers in the C-47 who
@saw the light fly below their aircraft. And it strikingly confirms the
@ground observers' estimate of a 2,500 foot height for this "streaking light."
@ It is very difficult to explain a meteor maintaining horizontal flight at
@2,500 feet.

Third trip echo can still do this. The meteor is real, but it
is farther away. The RADAR design assumed that there could
not be anything that far from the set.

I thought of the meteor explanation primarily because:

1. All of the high speed UFOs were westbound

2. The date coincides with an annual meteor display.
The C-47 crew could have seen its reflection in the ocean.

BTW, that was ONE of my hypotheses. The other was that a missile
was accidentally launched from a naval vessel or was launched by
an amateur "rocketeer."

I have an account of one of these amateur launches, where a
ten foot length of 6 inch sewer pipe buried itself in a real
estate agent's backyard in Albuquerque NM. Someone had hammered
the front to a point, filled the pipe with black powder, and set
it off. It flew remarkably straight according to witnesses.

@(BTW, a hypothetical "skip-range" error in the radar -- so it displays a
@distant meteor as if closer in range -- could not possibly position a series
@of a dozen or more evenly spaced blips on a linear path RADIALLY across the
@radar screen on OPPOSITE SIDES on a continuous path.)

If it's really two dozen blips, then third trip echos are not
very probable (the range would be nonlinear). Also, a meteor
would probably not persist that long, and there weren't any
satellites to re-enter then. I had thought the number of sweeps
was far fewer.

I was referring mainly to the UFO that appeared for only
three sweeps.

@The Trent case should not be discredited on the basis of someone else's

But that does not refute a solar column, which I have seen many

Also, the object is suspiciously very similar to a pressure
cooker lid my grandmother used to have. Unfortunately, the lid

to lock down the lid went from the center through a groove in the
lid to one edge when it was locked, and raised to about an 80
degree angle to unlock it.

So why did all of the sources travel exactly up-scope? Were
the UFOnauts daring the RB-47 to race them? :)

Question: did the UFOs fly at exactly twice the speed of the
plane? If so, then Klass was right. Aha! A testable
hypothesis.
Since I am an electronics engineer (well versed in how
things go wrong), I tend to agree with Klass on this one,
although some of his other explanations are a bit off
(especially Exeter NH).


Also possible:

1. maintenance tech wired the search dish servo wrong,
and covered up his mistake later to avoid reprimand.

2. A short (say a loose solder ball) in the servo system
caused a temporary change in one axis.

3. A loose connector pin kept the relay current from
reaching one of the relays. I use some of those military
connectors, and sometimes a pin dislodges from the
connector shell. Push it back in and it clicks into place,
with no evidence that it had ever come out.


There are many relay failure modes:

1. Insufficient current to pull in the relay.

2. Leakage current holds the relay in when it should
drop out.

3. A surge magnetized the core, holding the relay in.

4. Weak return spring.

5. Foreign matter in the hinge.

6. Foreign matter between contacts (the first computer
bug was a cockroach wedged between relay contacts, hence
the term).

7. Welded contacts.

8. Oxidized or blued contacts (won't make contact).

9. Stray magnetic fields from other equipment. (I once
had a sensitive relay pull in every time a telephone
next to it rang.)

10. Failed filter capacitor in the power supply.

11. Iron particles between electromagnet core and
armature.
12. Solder bridge between terminals.

13. Coil burned out.

14. Shorted turn in coil.

15. Loose wire.

16. Circuit fault away from the relay.

17. Bad solder joint.

18. Armature knocked off its hinge (can snap back in
place later after a few actuations).

19. Vibration.

20. Buzzing (AC relay with insufficient current).

21. Damaged armature.

22. Gravity sensitivity (won't work upside down).

23 Bad relay socket.

and many more.

One really sneaky problem is when one source activates
two relays. If one relay develops a short in its coil,
it will always pull in, but it may deprive the other
one of enough current to operate.

@"black hole" with a fire in it? Also, what altitude is the
@opening of the balloon when the balloon is on its side? If the
@balloon is 25 ft from edge to center when inflated, how wide (in
@this case, high) is it when lying on its side?

Since the opening is tied to the A-frame, it should be below the
top of the "legs." It is not black, but just a little darker than
the rest of the aerostat, since the fabric is translucent (the
other end shows through).

The aerostat would be somewhat flattened at this point, reducing
the height and increasing the width (giving the horizontal
elliptical shape).

The aerostat in flight is usually somewhat taller than it is
wide. Some of them are pear shaped, with the neck at the bottom,
others are egg shaped with the small end down.


@>Zamora could not see the platform or the men at this point,but
@>he could see the flames and the top of the A-frame that
@>supports the burner.

@Is that so. How much higher than the heads of the men is the
@opening of the balloon when it is lying on its side, deflated?

About even with their heads, if they were standing.


@And, if the opening is so much higher than the basket when deflated, and
@the burner is turned sideways to blow into the hole, the burner must be
@considerably above the ground. so, how did it manage to burn brush on the
@ground?

There were no baskets on hot-air balloons in 1964. The more I look
at this, the more I am convinced the platform turned over when it
landed. The impact may have caused the cord to be pulled, or the
burner may have been firing to slow the descent.

The footprints are under the final location of the platform (the
isosceles triangle), just where a man would need to stand to pull it
upright. The mark with the 9 and 13 foot distances would have been
where the A-frame hit the ground.
@Yes, and up to the point of tilting up Zamora was seeing a
@flame and hearing no roar? Or a faint roar?

Depends on how much the "throttle" was open. When heating the
aerostat, the throttle is only partway open. To take off, it is
opened all the way and kept there until the platform is clear of
the ground and all obstacles.

@And he didn't just happen to notice that this big round thing
@was "fattening up" and then he didn't notice it float upward
@(into the stiff breeze!)?

He reported that!!! It lifted into the air and hovered. Remember
that he was in "panic mode" by this time.


@Incidentally, if there was a stiff wind, regardless of direction,
@it might have dragged the "basket" over the ground some
@distance before actually taking off..... unless they had
@ballast. But then, did they throw out ballast (rocks,
@presumably).

Since they have a power source, they don't carry ballast. Gas
balloons use ballast and a gas dump valve for control, but
hot-air balloons use the burner and a hot-air dump valve.

@>Once the aerostat was able to lift the platform, the wind
@>took charge of it, causing horizontal motion. At about the
@>same time, the balloonists shut down the burner because
@t>hey had sufficient lift. Any further burns took place well
@>away from Zamora, and probably would not have been heard.

@If there was a stiff wind, as Zamora said, I should think there
@would have been some tilt to the balloon, the top tilting away
@from Zamora (since, obviously, the wind was blowing the balloon
@away from him). This should make the undercarriage even more
@obvious.

The (flat) platform was still behind the terrain. At this point,
Zamora lost his glasses. According to the balloonist account I
read (assuming my, recollection is factual), the balloonists
flattened out to avoid gunfire from a crazed cop.

As the aerostat heats up, it becomes more vertical rather
suddenly. When it has almost enough lift to lift the platform,
it will be vertical regardless of the wind, considering the
weight attached.

At this point, they open the "throttle" all the way, so the
aerostat quickly lifts them off, rather than dragging along the
ground. LOUD roar! This is standard takeoff procedure.

in conjunction with Ed Yost.

and had researched your claims when they first came to his

was unaware of. The issues set in context, he then wrote:

would have been with different balloons at a different time.
Experiments were made (and eventually routine operations
conducted) using helium balloons to lift logs off of mountain
slopes. These were cable-driven, not free flying. This work
started in the summer of 1967 and we were actively involved in
providing and testing new models for at least a decade (such
balloons may still be in use today). At least one of those
balloons had a logo consisting of a stylized evergreen tree in a
circle; again not the IP logo, but with similarities. This could
not have been before the 1970s.
You can be positive that neither St. Regis, International Paper
nor anyone else but Raven spawned the hot air balloon as we know
it."

is a man wearing a dark shirt standing at the location of the landing
traces and a jeep (with canvas cover; not an open jeep) parked on th
hillock where Zamorra's car was. I made measurements using a 1/60 "
scale on this photo which is abou 6" long by about 3 1/4 inches high.

I found the vertical image of th man was abou 1.5/60 and the width of the
jeep was abou 4.5/60. "Printers dots" which make up the picture limit the
accuracy to about 0.5/60 inch. At the same time th distance from the
center of the jeep image to the center of the man image is 144/60.
Now assume the jeep was 6 ft wide and the vertical dimension of the visible
man is 2 ft (waiste to top of shoulders). The ratio is 3. At the same
time the ratio 4.5/1.5 is three. In other words, there is some consistency
between image size and known (estimated) object size here.
BUT: if I now use this scaling to calculate the distance from the car/jeep
to the man/landing area, I get 144/4.5 = 32 and so the distance is 32 x 6
ft = 192 ft, not 103 ft! (I had this all nicely spelled out in detail
before, Now you guys are going to have to understand this by yourselves!

Klass says 100 to 200 ft , and in Steiger's Blue book pon page 107 it says
150 ft. The maps read 103 ft. Don't know how they measured this, I bet
my calculation is the first from photo scaling.

perpendiocular to Zamorra's line of view. Funny he said it looked like a

Date: Sat, 28 Aug 1999 00:30:02 -0400
From: joel carpenter <ufx@mindspring.com>
Subject: Glowing parachutesMessage-id:
<002801bef10d$ff7689a0$0100a8c0@mindspring.com>

UFO Research List - http://web.ukonline.co.uk/voyager/

Listmembers-

Another oddity I ran across while surfing the C-130s sites, at

http://www.spectrumwd.com/c130/articles/fallings.htm


How many people would ever believe something like this existed circa 1961-2?
Imagine the other strange and wonderful things that have flown around in the
last few decades...

- J Carpenter
-------------------------

Government engineers and aerospace contractors devised a unique method for
getting that vital data down to intelligence experts, and this is where our
Hercules transport comes into the picture. Tracking ground stations
signalled the satellite to fire its retro-rockets. That slowed the satellite
causing it to fall into the atmosphere. At about 30,000 feet automatically a
parachute opened and a radio transmitter permitted airplanes to home-in
towards the descending payload. Airplanes would have to catch the payload
before it splashed into the ocean or crashed onto the rocks. The payload
data must not be lost or destroyed.

Two problems had to be overcome to effect recovery. The point of re-entry
must be controlled to make sure that recovery airplanes rendezvous with the
parachute in time. It would not be helpful if the payload landed where the
Soviets could get to it first. The second problem was helping the recovery
airplanes to locate the payload during descent before splashdown.

The pilot of our particular JC-130 transport was about to make a test
recovery of a satellite payload. What made the flight unique was that this
recovery was to be made at night, the very first attempt to catch a payload
in darkness. It is difficult enough to make airborne retrievals in daylight,
but a catch in the dark is a real challenge. The pilot must be able to see
the parachute and maneuver his airplane to be slightly above it while
attempting to snare the quarry.

...

The pilot and copilot anxiously scanned the starlit sky for a first glimpse
of the parachute. Could they even see that thirty foot hemisphere of nylon
with its suspended payload? It was really black out there. And where should
they look? .. to the south? .. or westward towards the Sierra Nevadas?

Fortunately, the payload's radio signal was being received by the special
direction finding equipment mounted atop the customized Hercules. The
instrument panel needle pointed to the payload indicating the radio source
was to the southwest. Additionally, this particular payload was fitted with
upward pointing spotlights that illuminated the parachute canopy.

At about six miles out the pilot saw the dimly glowing hemisphere of the
parachute canopy. It appeared to be hanging motionless, slightly above them,
at first. But, indeed, the payload was descending at about fifteen hundred
feet per minute towards the desert below. The Hercules was at nearly 18,000
feet as it approached to within a mile or two of the glowing target. That
meant the pilot had about ten minutes to effect a retrieval before they ran
out of altitude....

I can think of nothing that is a golfball at arms length except
a very close airplane. That's six times the angular size of
the moon. Something the angular size of a golfball at arm's
length at a real altitude of 2500 feet would the size of a
quarter block lot. That's why I asked the question. Many times,
people have confused the meaning of that question, and
reported a size comparable to an object hit in the air instead.

2. A short (say a loose solder ball) in the servo system
caused a temporary change in one axis.

3. A loose connector pin kept the relay current from
reaching one of the relays. I use some of those military
connectors, and sometimes a pin dislodges from the
connector shell. Push it back in and it clicks into place,
with no evidence that it had ever come out.


There are many relay failure modes:

1. Insufficient current to pull in the relay.

2. Leakage current holds the relay in when it should
drop out.

3. A surge magnetized the core, holding the relay in.

4. Weak return spring.

5. Foreign matter in the hinge.

6. Foreign matter between contacts (the first computer
bug was a cockroach wedged between relay contacts, hence
the term).
7. Welded contacts.

8. Oxidized or blued contacts (won't make contact).

9. Stray magnetic fields from other equipment. (I once
had a sensitive relay pull in every time a telephone
next to it rang.)

10. Failed filter capacitor in the power supply.

11. Iron particles between electromagnet core and
armature.

12. Solder bridge between terminals.

13. Coil burned out.

14. Shorted turn in coil.

15. Loose wire.

16. Circuit fault away from the relay.

17. Bad solder joint.

18. Armature knocked off its hinge (can snap back in
place later after a few actuations).

19. Vibration.

20. Buzzing (AC relay with insufficient current).

21. Damaged armature.

22. Gravity sensitivity (won't work upside down).

23 Bad relay socket.

and many more.

One really sneaky problem is when one source activates
two relays. If one relay develops a short in its coil,
it will always pull in, but it may deprive the other
one of enough current to operate.

COMMENT: All of these other sources of electrical failure are themselves
failures -- of the FACTS of the case. As I pointed out above the ELINT
equipment on the RB-47 was functioning perfectly before, during and after the
UFO incident.

quite in the realm of probability. It seems just about right.

Paul,

It certainly is.

I was also interested to see a reference to an Ed Yost/Raven
balloon flight - I think from 1961 - which took place from an
aircraft carrier.

There are clearly a number of indications that the
military/intelligence applications of hot-air balloons were of
considerable interest in the period between 1960-1964, especially
to the Office of Naval Research (ONR).

There's an 'on-line' biography of Ed Yost which notes:

"Leaving General Mills, Yost and 3 others moved to Sioux Falls,
South Dakota and formed Raven Industries. One of Raven's first
projects was a commission from the U.S. Navy's Office of Naval
Research to create an aircraft that would carry one man and
enough fuel to fly for three hours, carry a load to 10,000 feet,
and be reusable. Additionally, the system was required to be of
small size and weight and have a fast inflation and launching
system that required a minimum of personnel.

In October 1955 Yost made the first moored flight of a modern
hot-air balloon. The envelope was plastic film, and heat was
provided by plumbers pots burning kerosene.

On October 22, 1960, Yost made the first free flight of a modern
hot-air balloon from Bruning, Nebraska. By then Yost had switched
to nylon for the envelope, and had created a propane heater. The
gross weight of the balloon, including Yost and fuel, was 404
pounds. He was in the air 25 minutes and landed 3 miles from his
takeoff point.

The next flight was made November 12, 1960 from the Stratobowl,
situated at 4500' MSL. Yost had increased the burner power,
reinforced the envelope at the equator to add handling lines, and
increased the opening at the top from 9 to 13 feet, doubling the
deflation port size. The inflation took 6 minutes and he lifted
off at 8:40 a.m. with a gross weight of 465 pounds. At 9:12 a.m.
he made an ascent at 300 feet per minute to 9000', then made a
600 feet per minute descent which he successfully halted with the
new burner. He landed at 10:30 after a flight of 1 hour and 50
minutes covering 39 miles.

In October 1961 Yost concluded his report to the ONR as follows:

"At the completion of this program in October 1961, all of the
basic requirements had been met. A low-weight, manned flight
system capable of safely carrying one man for three hours, at
altitudes of up to 10,000 feet had been repeatedly flown.

"Inflations and launchings in winds of more than 10 mph and
temperatures as low as +5 degrees F had been successfully
accomplished. Operations at altitudes of 4,500 feet MSL (above
mean sea level) had been demonstrated. Ground support equipment
had been developed so that inflation, under light wind
conditions, could be carried out in less than ten minutes.
Controls, burners and instrumentation adequate to operate the
system had been developed.

"As a result of the work done under this contract, the
feasibility of using hot air balloons for sustained flight was
demonstrated. By the application of modern materials, design
techniques and instrumentation, an aerostat which had been known
for more than 175 years was resurrected and shown to have
substantial value in modern research and operations. The limits
of duration and lifting capacity appear to far exceed that
developed under this contract; the low cost, simplicity of
operation, and logistic advantage which hot air balloons provide,
when compared with light-gas balloons, are most impressive.
Within the altitude limits where hot air balloons may be used,
these modern Montgolfier systems may become an important tool for
atmospheric and low-level lifting and transport tasks."
[End]


In a further brief history, 'Raven Industries', now encompassed
within 'Aerostar', acknowledge:

"Early hot air balloon sales were made exclusively to the
government for military and research applications. But by the mid
1960s some adventuresome folks outside of the ranks of Raven
Industries employees began buying the balloons for recreation and
sport".


Don Piccard, in the previously referenced and revealing article,
reinforces:

"Raven Industries hired Don Piccard to manage their nascent sport
balloon program. 'They had no idea of what to do with a sport
balloon,' he says emphatically. 'They had no knowledge of what to
do with it.' But, 'I had design responsibilities,' he recalls,
and after flying their Mittlestadt balloon, 'I set about
designing a version that would be closer to the balloon Yost had
built for the government.' At the helm of Raven, Yost was being
financed by the Office of Navel Research on top-secret hush-hush
projects".


Apart from any connection between a hot-air balloon and
'Socorro', it might be something of an aside so far as UFO
related research is concerned, however, it's one of those often
intriguing, diverse facets.

It's also arguably not unrelated at all, the more we understand
about any aerial objects which could have resulted in UFO
reports, it enhances our perspective of what was possibly 'out
there' at the time.


Also much appreciated is the overall response to my query about
the practical use of hot-air balloons for intelligence operations
- where ufology apparently meets James Bond...

COMMENT: I do not follow the reasoning here at all. Zamora did not run
TOWARDS the landed UFO down in the gully so the distance to the UFO is not
relevant here. Zamora said he RAN AWAY from the object and backwards away
from his patrol car an estimated 25 feet in 6 seconds before glancing back,
to a point 50 feet back, then came back the same 50 feet to his car, all in a
total of "possibly" 20 seconds he figured. Either way the speed is not even
sprinting but a fast walk, about 4 - 5 ft/sec. So there is no discrepancy
here in Zamora's account and he did not have to break a world's record, as
had been previously suggested.

I am much more disturbed by Bruce Maccabee's photographic scaling of the
distance from Zamora's car to UFO landing site. Assuming the car and landing
site positions are correctly indicated in Klass' photo, there is a serious
error in the original on-site investigators' supposedly measured distance of
103 feet versus Bruce's 192 feet. This is almost a factor 2x error. If it
is valid to apply this error factor to Zamora's SIZE estimate, possibly the
UFO size would have to be doubled as Larry has suggested IF AND ONLY IF
Zamora's size estimate comes from angular size with distance. However,
Zamora's size estimate must still be researched as I recall that it was
determined by bracketing the appearance of the UFO with specific mesquite
bushes and terrain features then measured to get upper and lower limits, so
that it was NOT dependent on Zamora estimating angular size and distance but
was directly linearly measured on site.

Another consequence of this distance error is that it decreases the
depression angle of the UFO landing site from Zamora's vantage point about 20
feet higher on top of the ridge. At 103 feet this angle is only about 11
degrees but from 192 feet it is only about 6 degrees. This is hardly enough
for the shape and position of the hypothetical balloon to hide much of
anything as it is virtually side-on. However, at this shallower angle any
intervening terrain between the UFO landing site and Zamora's position could
pose a greater obstruction to viewing the lower part of the object.

For information, re the landing traces, this is from Stanford's
book and describes the evidence of 'burning':

Chavez and others noticed no odour whatever that would indicate
that combustion of any conventional fuel had caused the burn
damage. In fact, there was no odour detectable by those present,
excepting the familiar aroma of creosote or greasewood bushes,
made stronger by the recent burning of foliage. Some of the
bushes were still expelling steam when State Patrolman Jordan and
Undersherrif Luckie arrived.

Jordan said that what most impressed him at the landing site was
the way the 'flame' had evidently 'sliced' a large greasewood
bush, located almost centrally in the landing gear quadrangle,
without leaving any signs of strong turbulence, as the exhaust of
a powerful rocket thrust unit or even the whirling of helicopter
blades would have done.

'They'll never explain that thing Lonnie saw as any 'pogo' [VTOL
aircraft], helicopter, or anything I know about,' Jordan said
firmly. 'The flame from that damn thing just sliced that
greasewood bush in half, just burned it off clean like a blade of
fire had cut right through it.'

[...]

Examining the region southwest along the ravine where the papers
had been burned [old paper scraps - James], I could not help but
deduce that the 'fiery finger' from beneath the craft had
extended itself from northeast to southwest, reaching out for
some yards from where the mysterious object had elevated above
the ravine, probably during its landing approach and manoeuvre,
prior to orienting the exhaust directly downwards for the final
descent".

These indications seem to confirm that the 'flame' was emitted in
one direction along the ground.

Stanford's diagram of the landing site, with his measurements,
has been uploaded to:

http://web.ukonline.co.uk/voyager/landing.jpg

800 ft. The does raise the question of why he didn't see it before 800 ft.
 The answer to this
question involved the LRH assumption of just how high the top of the
balloon above the ground at the landing point, and just what the terrain
was BEFORE Zamorra got to the 800 ft point.
Would it be "safe" to assume that if the platform framework were, say,. 6
ft high, and the balloon itself from opening at the bottom to the top was
25 ft high (lower bound?) that the top of the balloon would have been atbou
30 ft from the ground?

Also: LRH (Larry Robinson Hypothesis)
assumes this was nearly a "crash" landing, with the platform skidding
(to explain gouges in the ground) and then the burner tipping over (to
explain burned
bushes). This all happened, one presumes, in the minute or so that it took
Zamorra to get to the hillock. By the time he arrived there the crash had
occurred and the
balloon was lying, pointed away from Zamorra. Quick as a wink the
balloonists, managed to
point the burner into the balloon and begin reheating. THey knew a police
car was coming.
When Zamorra got to the top of the hill he couldn't seem them or the
structure holding the balloon...which suggests that they may not have been
able to see him either. In any case, it would have been obvious to them
that he did not drive to their location from the point 800 ft away, but
instead went to another loation (hillock) over 100 ft away. Shortly after
he stopped and got out of the car (seconds) they gave the burner the goose
and a big swoosh occurred, dumping a lot of hot air into the balloon as
Zamorra turned to run. The balloon was still lying on the ground as
Zamorra turned so he didn't see it vertical. He wouldn't have seen "legs"
under the balloon, either. 'cause he couldn't see the framework.
One has to assume, I suppose, that any changes in the balloon surface, like
waves moving across the surface were not noticed by Zamorra. One may
imagine that there were such waves since, as we are told, therewas a brisk
wind (from the east in the LRH).

be vertical. The aerostat had lifted, but the entire vehicle had
not yet lifted. The cables are now taut between the aerostat and
the platform. Buoyancy is now completely supporting the aerostat

I have only twice by chance seen a hot-air balloon close enough
to hear the loud roar, once in 1976, and the other in 1998. The
other times I have seen hot-air balloons, they were:

- too far away to hear anything but a soft whoosh
- not firing at full power, or
- times I purposely attended a launch or landing (including the
  time when I put the whole Socorro thing together)

We have hot-air balloon activity here weekly during good weather.

The newer burners seem to be quieter than those used in the 60s
and 70s.

It is quite possible that Zamora has never been in such a
position to hear one close again.

While Bloomington has nearly weekly of hot-air balloon activity
(with three companies having active balloon teams), there is
almost no activity in Spencer, only 15 miles away. The
availability of places to take off and land influences the
activity level, as does the local interest.

Let's look at that time sequence again:

1. Zamora sees the flame out the right side window. The car roof
hides the aerostat.

2. Zamora turns onto the side road. Intervening terrain hides the
balloon from his view. He takes some time to get to a vantage
point, because his car needs three tries to make it up a hill.

3. The platform hits the ground and turns over. The aerostat
remains buoyant, but the burner goes off and sets fire to things
on the ground.

4. The balloonists turn the platform right side up. This makes
dust.

5. Zamora arrives at the first vantage point. He sees the balloon
from 800 ft, with the crew standing up, and the dust. The A-frame
struts appear to him as "legs."

6. Zamora decides to drive on, and leaves sight of the balloon.
While radioing headquarters of a possible auto accident, he heads
for a closer point on the road. Intervening terrain hides the
balloon from his view.

7. The aerostat loses some lift and touches the ground.

8. Zamora arrives. He sees the aerostat and the top of the
A-frame, sits and watches, starts to get out, then ducks behind
the car door after getting out (the radio mic fell). He puts the
mic back.

9. The balloonists (mostly hidden down in the arroyo) see Zamora
"hide" behind the car door (not knowing he dropped his mic), and
fear the worst. They relight the pilot light, and fire up to try
to lift off again. The two thumps might have been the pilot light
rekindling, or the wind making the aerostat move.

10. Zamora (still thinking vehicle wreck) sees the flame, hears
the roar, expects an explosion, and immediately runs to hide
behind the car. He bumps the fender and loses his glasses. Then
he runs to hide behind the hillock.

11. The aerostat lifts up to support its own weight (but not the
platform). The balloonists open the throttle wide.

12. Zamora glances back about 25 feet from the car to see the
object hovering as he runs. He sees the aerostat (now vertical)
hovering at about 20 ft from the ground (at the end of the
stays). He keeps running.

13. The platform now lifts off the ground and the balloon starts
traveling horizontally. The balloonists shut off the burner.

14. Zamora ducks behind the hillock. He intends to keep going
down the hill, but the roar stops. He then looks and sees the
object departing horizontally.

15. The balloon barely clears the dynamite shack from Zamora's
view (meaning that the aerostat seems to just miss it -- but
actually it is farther away). The platform may be still hidden
behind terrain (possibly on purpose, to keep the balloonists out
of the line of fire).

16. Zamora runs back to the car, picks up his glasses, and radios
in. He asks that Chavez (of the state police) be sent. At this
point, the platform is insignificant in size compared to the
aerostat.

17. The object disappears behind the nearby 6-Mile Canyon
Mountain.

18. Zamora makes sketches.

19. Zamora goes down in the arroyo to investigate. He finds the
burning bush.

20. Chavez arrives and Zamora returns to the car.

21. Both go down into the arroyo.

>@And I still don't understand why he wouldn't see the platform
>@structure hanging off the balloon after he returned to his car

To which LRH responded:

>The object was much farther away by the time he got his glasses
>back.

>He was looking into the sun.

>The platform is small compared to the aerostat, and he might not

<

Let's see just how small the platform and two men would appear:

Unfortunately I don't have exact size for the platform except 8 - 12 ft
high.
If there were no walls on the platform, then the largest "objects" would be
the
men and the burner would be next largest. To give this idea its best
chance
of working assume that the men were standing one behind the other and in
front ot
the burner from Zamorra's
point of view so he could see only one man. Any other objects on the
platform would
ADD to the visual detactability of the platform. So this calculation
provides the minimum
"optical area" that would be silhouetted against the background sky and or
mountains,
depending upon how high the platform was. If we assume the balloon was
rising
continually, then the platform woudl eventually have been silhouetted
against the sky.

At any rate, we assume Zamorra could see well enough, with his glasses on,
to
detect a man at 800 ft, since he reported seeing the assumed men at 800 ft.
The visual detectability depends upon contrast with the background and
angular
size. One could make an assumption that the men wore "sky colored" clothes
in which
case they might be barely detectable at a great distance, but it seems to
me that
except in the case of extreme use of camouflage, whatever was hanging below
the balloon
would have been detectable at least as a "dot" when the balloon was far
enough way so that the
angular size of this "dot" was comparable to the visual resolution of the
eye. Those of you
who have been through the "pelicanization" of Arnold may recall that 3
minutes of arc
(Hynek's number for the minimum detectable angular size) was an
overestimate that was
refuted by Arnold himself (who stated that he could see the spacing between
the engines of a C-47 at 15 miles north of him, which corresponds to an
angle of about 0.75 milliradians = 0.43 degrees = 2.6 minutes of arc).
However, to be safe, let's use 1 milliradian = 3.4 min of arc as an
overestimate of the angular size at which a man could be detected. Apply
this to a man's height. Use 5 ft as an estimate of height of legs and
torso (ignoroe head) and get
5 ft/0.001 rad = 5000 ft. In other words, if there were NOTHING but a man
hanging by a thread under a balloon one would expect to be able to detect
that man, at least as a dot, at about 1 mile (unless his clothing matched
the background). (Yes, I know the width of the man is less than his
height. However, the eye effectively integrates along a length. That's
why distant power wires are detectable to the eye even though piece of the
same size wire only a foot long or less could be totally undetectable.)

The question now, is, how long would it take for the balloon to get to be a
mile away, as compared to the time it takes for Zamorra to get up from
lying on the ground, run to his car and put his glasses on?
Perhaps it took 2 minutes (overestimate?) for Zamorra to get his glasses
on. Here time zero is when the balloon lifts off because after liftoff it
is at the "mercy" of the wind..

Under optimum conditions for the balloon "escape" the wind was steady (or
gusting) continually from the time of lift off. To go 1 mile would take 1
hour in a 1 mile/hour wind. But we are told there was a stiff breeze
(from the southwest.... oh, well, this detail has been modified by 180
degrees). Try 10 mph. THen it takes 6 minutes. To get 1 miles in 2
minutes requires 30 mph wind. That's stiff.

In other words, if we assume that over a 2 minute time period from liftoff
the wind speed averages 30 mph FROM the northeast, then the balloon might
travel to 1 mile from Zamorra in the 2 minutes it takes for Zamorra to put
his glasses on.
ERROR BARS:
   the above calculation assumes the balloon accelerates instantaneously to
the full wind speed.
BUT, I bet there is a lot of "slippage" of the air past the balloon which
results in (a) non-instantaneous acceleration (thereby increasing the time
to go 1 mile) and (b) a "speed factor" less than unity which says that even
after acceleration there is some lag behind the wind (the balloon does not
travel in th wind as would an object completely encompassed in an
incompressible fluid). I don't know what this speed factor would be, but
it, to would increase the time to go 1 mile.

The 2 minutes could well be an overestimate of the time from "lift-off" to
"glasses-on."

This leaves no time for "hovering." On the other hand, perhaps what was
interpreted by Zamorra as "hover" was actually the moment of liftoff and
before the balloon started to pick up speed. If so, Zamorra's observation
of "hovering" should be the start of the 2 minute clock. According to
Zamorra he was running away and looking back when he saw the object
"hovering." How many minutes from that point to when he put on his
glasses...?

Regarding the visual acuity or ability to detect at a distance, consider
that LRH wrote:


>He probably assumed it was part of the legs he saw earlier,
>since they were attached to it.

The framework is made of pipes. I don't know the diameter of the pipes so
I'll use 1.5"
(sounds like a strong pipes to me). According to LRH, then,Zamorra could
easily see
0.125 ft ft pipes at 103 ft (or 200 ft if the photo scaling is correct).
the angular width of these
pipes is about 1.2 mr from 100 ft (and half that if the distance was 200
ft). Hence the use of 1 mr
as minimum detectable size is reasonable. (Zamorra might have been able
to detect the
pipes as thin lines at 1 mile (2" wide by 8 ft high) (0.03 mr angular
width by 1.5 mr high).

At any rate, the above calculated distance of 1 mile
 was based on seeing 1 man. The probability that the
two men would align perfectly and also block the view of the burner is low.
 More likely that the
men were nearly side by side (and watching Zamorra to see if he was going
to chase them or lob a little lead in their direction... after all, he
appeared crazy to them).
 This would increase the "optically effective area" of the
platform/men below the balloon. In other words, it would increase the
distance at which
the platform could be seen. That would increase the required speed of the
balloon/wind.
This might not double the distance at which the platform could be seen as a
dot below the
balloon, but it would increase it somewhat.

Having a 30 mph wind blowing could have an impact on other aspects of this
sighting.

Bruce.

From: James Easton <voyager@ukonline.co.uk>
Subject: 'Skyhook'Message-id:

UFO Research List - http://web.ukonline.co.uk/voyager/

Re previous references -

There's an insightful, now declassified article on the 'Skyhook'
project entitled, `Robert Fulton's Skyhook and Operation
Coldfeet', published in the CIA's `Studies in Intelligence', 1995
Edition -- Volume 38, Number 5.

It's on-line at:

http://www.odci.gov/csi/studies/95unclas/lea.html

This material reaffirms the Office of Naval Research and CIA's
interest in agent insertion and extraction techniques, with
`Operation Coldfeet' being one successful `skyhook' mission.

The article closes by noting that, "While the Skyhook system
provided an important asset for all manner of intelligence
operations, its utility as a long-range pickup system was
somewhat undermined during the 1960s by the development of an
aerial refueling capability for helicopters. Still, it appears
likely that Fulton's Skyhook did find employment in a number of
specialized clandestine operations following Coldfeet, although
its subsequent use by CIA and the military services remains
shrouded in secrecy".

It's understandable why the parallel 1960s development of hot-air
balloons was potentially of great interest as a short to medium
range `pick-up' system. `Skyhook' was pretty crude! -

"Conditions for the pickup were marginal at best. The ice had a
grey hue, and it was difficult to make out an horizon. The
surface wind was blowing at 30 knots, nearing the limits of
Skyhook's capability. After inflating the balloon attached to 150
pounds of exposed film, documents, and equipment samples, Smith
and LeSchack had to keep a tight hold on the canvas bag
containing the cargo lest it be blown away.

As Seigrist lined up for the pickup, the horizon disappeared. "I
was instantly in a situation," he recalled, "what could be
imagined as flying in a void." The pickup line and its bright
orange mylar marker, however, provided sufficient visual clues to
enable Seigrist to keep his wings level. He flew into the line,
made a good contact, then immediately went over to instrument
flying to avoid vertigo. Winch-operator Daniels brought the cargo
on board without difficulty.

As prearranged, Price, a former Navy pilot, now took over the
left seat to make the pickup of LeSchack. The wind was blowing
stronger, and Smith had to struggle to hold LeSchack from being
blown away. As the rising balloon caught the wind, LeSchack tore
away from Smith's grasp, pitched forward on his stomach, and
began to drag across the ice. After 300 feet, his progress was
stopped by an ice block. As he lay on the ice and tried to catch
his breath, Price hooked into the line.

Smith watched as LeSchack rose slowly into the air, then
disappeared throughout the overcast. Although LeSchack rode
through the air facing forward, he managed to turn around and
assume the correct position before being hauled on board the
B-17".


Trivia: In that 1956 classic, `Earth vs the Flying Saucers', the
rocket launch site/project where our hero scientist and his wife
worked was called `Operation Skyhook'.


James.
