From: Larry Robinson S/AP/EIS Kinesiology <lrobins@indiana.edu>
Subject: Re: Landing at Socorro

UFO Research List - http://web.ukonline.co.uk/voyager/



On Wed, 1 Sep 1999, bruce maccabee wrote:

@UFO Research List - http://web.ukonline.co.uk/voyager/
@
@
@I wrote:
@>@And I still don't understand why he wouldn't see the platform
@>@structure hanging off the balloon after he returned to his car
@>@and got his glasses again. Do you think that perhaps he was
@>@still afraid and decided not to put his glasses on to look at
@>.@it?
@
@To which LRH responded:
@
@>The object was much farther away by the time he got his glasses
@>back.
@
@>He was looking into the sun.
@
@>The platform is small compared to the aerostat, and he might not
@>have noticed it.
@<
@
@Let's see just how small the platform and two men would appear:

@Unfortunately I don't have exact size for the platform except 8
@- 12 ft high. If there were no walls on the platform, then the
@largest "objects" would be the men and the burner would be next
@largest. To give this idea its best chance of working assume
@that the men were standing one behind the other and in front of
@the burner from Zamora's point of view so he could see only one
@man.

Hold it! In flight, the burner is held up by the aerostat by
cables, and is at or above the top of the A-frame. It consists of
one or two cylinders about two to three feet long. When the
balloon is landed, another cable attached to the A-frame supports
the burner.

@Any other objects on the platform would ADD to the visual
@detectability of the platform. So this calculation provides the
@minimum "optical area" that would be silhouetted against the
@background sky and or mountains, depending upon how high the
@platform was. If we assume the balloon was rising continually,
@then the platform would eventually have been silhouetted against
@the sky.

@At any rate, we assume Zamora could see well enough, with his
@glasses on, to detect a man at 800 ft, since he reported seeing
@the assumed men at 800 ft.

@The visual detectability depends upon contrast with the
@background and angular size. One could make an assumption that
@the men wore "sky colored" clothes in which case they might be
@barely detectable at a great distance, but it seems to me that
@except in the case of extreme use of camouflage, whatever was
@hanging below the balloon would have been detectable at least as
@a "dot" when the balloon was far enough way so that the angular
@size of this "dot" was comparable to the visual resolution of
@the eye. Those of you who have been through the
@"pelicanization" of Arnold may recall that 3 minutes of arc
@(Hynek's number for the minimum detectable angular size) was an
@overestimate that was refuted by Arnold himself (who stated that
@he could see the spacing between the engines of a C-47 at 15
@miles north of him, which corresponds to an angle of about 0.75
@milliradians = 0.43 degrees = 2.6 minutes of arc). However, to
@be safe, let's use 1 milliradian = 3.4 min of arc as an
@overestimate of the angular size at which a man could be
@detected. Apply this to a man's height. Use 5 ft as an
@estimate of height of legs and torso (ignore head) and get 5
@ft/0.001 rad = 5000 ft. In other words, if there were NOTHING
@but a man hanging by a thread under a balloon one would expect
@to be able to detect that man, at least as a dot, at about 1
@mile (unless his clothing matched the background). (Yes, I know
@the width of the man is less than his height. However, the eye
@effectively integrates along a length. That's why distant power
@wires are detectable to the eye even though piece of the same
@size wire only a foot long or less could be totally
@undetectable.)

According to Zamora, the clothing was white. The sky near the sun
is usually nearly white.

Remember that it was already more than 100 away from him.

@The question now, is, how long would it take for the balloon to
@get to be a mile away, as compared to the time it takes for
@Zamora to get up from lying on the ground, run to his car and
@put his glasses on? Perhaps it took 2 minutes (overestimate?)
@for Zamora to get his glasses on. Here time zero is when the
@balloon lifts off because after liftoff it is at the "mercy" of
@the wind.
@Under optimum conditions for the balloon "escape" the wind was
@steady (or gusting) continually from the time of lift off. To
@go 1 mile would take 1 hour in a 1 mile/hour wind. But we are
@told there was a stiff breeze (from the southwest.... oh, well,
@this detail has been modified by 180 degrees). Try 10 mph.
@Then it takes 6 minutes. To get 1 miles in 2 minutes requires
@30 mph wind. That's stiff.

Zamora: "The wind was blowing hard."

@In other words, if we assume that over a 2 minute time period
@from liftoff the wind speed averages 30 mph FROM the northeast,
@then the balloon might travel to 1 mile from Zamora in the 2
@minutes it takes for Zamora to put his glasses on.

@ERROR BARS:

@the above calculation assumes the balloon accelerates
@instantaneously to the full wind speed. BUT, I bet there is a
@lot of "slippage" of the air past the balloon which results in
@(a) non-instantaneous acceleration (thereby increasing the time
@to go 1 mile) and (b) a "speed factor" less than unity which
@says that even after acceleration there is some lag behind the
@wind (the balloon does not travel in the wind as would an object
@completely encompassed in an incompressible fluid). I don't
@know what this speed factor would be, but it, to would increase
@the time to go 1 mile.

Oh! What factor (other than the initial inertia) would be slowing
it down? A sailboat has the drag of the water, but any buoyant
airborne object has NO other factor other than the air to act on
it. The only difference between balloon speed and wind speed
should be caused by the inertia of the mass of the balloon when
the wind changes speed or direction.

@The 2 minutes could well be an overestimate of the time from
@"lift-off" to "glasses-on."

@This leaves no time for "hovering." On the other hand, perhaps what was
@interpreted by Zamora as "hover" was actually the moment of liftoff and
@before the balloon started to pick up speed.

I repeat for the third time, the "hovering" occurred while the
aerostat was lifted up to the ends of its cables, but the
platform was still on the ground. This is a NORMAL phase in the
start-up sequence, and occurs in EVERY hot-air balloon launch.


@If so, Zamora's observation of "hovering" should be the start
@of the 2 minute clock. According to Zamora he was running
@away and looking back when he saw the object "hovering." How
@many minutes from that point to when he put on his glasses...?

The "in-flight clock" should start one or two seconds before the
roar stopped. If the burner had continued to run at full
throttle, the balloon would have shot up fast instead of moving
almost horizontally.

When he got over the top of the hill, he intended to keep
running, but the noise stopped. When he turned around and looked,
the object was already in horizontal motion away from him.


Zamora states in his original account that it took 20 seconds
from when he left the car to when he got back to it. I find it
quite difficult to comprehend how someone can do all of these
things in the time given:

- run to the back end of your car

- fall down

-get up

- run uphill the distance of going to the back door of the second
car parked behind you on the street (that's the shorter estimate
of 50 feet, not the measured 100 ft)

- turn around

- get down on the ground

- watch the object long enough to determine that it was going
away from him

- get up again

- run two parking space lengths lengths back to the car

This is the "record breaking run" I referred to earlier. I think
his time-sense was altered by the emergency nature of the
situation. This is a commonly reported phenomenon.


@Regarding the visual acuity or ability to detect at a distance,
@consider that LRH wrote:

@>He probably assumed it was part of the legs he saw earlier,
@>since they were attached to it.
@The framework is made of pipes. I don't know the diameter of
@the pipes so I'll use 1.5" (sounds like a strong pipes to me).
@According to LRH, then,Zamora could easily see 0.125 ft ft
@pipes at 103 ft (or 200 ft if the photo scaling is correct). the
@angular width of these pipes is about 1.2 mr from 100 ft (and
@half that if the distance was 200 ft). Hence the use of 1 mr as
@minimum detectable size is reasonable. (Zamora might have been
@able to detect the pipes as thin lines at 1 mile (2" wide by 8
@ft high) (0.03 mr angular width by 1.5 mr high).


The platform is about 2 " thick, with pipe underneath. The
modern A-frame uses 2" aluminum tubing. The old ones used a
lattice girder structure. See photos in the Newsweek article
"Death on the Wind" (Feb 3, 1964) to see examples of the
equipment in use then, including the triangular platform. A
balloon being started (and still lying down) is also depicted.


@At any rate, the above calculated distance of 1 mile was based
@on seeing 1 man. The probability that the two men would align
@perfectly and also block the view of the burner is low. More
@likely that the men were nearly side by side (and watching
@Zamora to see if he was going to chase them or lob a little
@lead in their direction... after all, he appeared crazy to
@them). This would increase the "optically effective area" of the
@platform/men below the balloon. In other words, it would
@increase the distance at which the platform could be seen. That
@would increase the required speed of the balloon/wind. This
@might not double the distance at which the platform could be
@seen as a dot below the balloon, but it would increase it
@somewhat.

Of course, this is the best possible case, which is the one that
must be used if the factors are unknown. Zamora still could have
subconsciously attributed everything below the aerostat to the
"legs" he saw earlier.

Notice that it was at this point that he first conceived of the
object as some kind of flying machine. Before this, he was
thinking "auto accident."

The burner is above the men, not on the platform (you really need
to familiarize yourself with these aircraft -- go to a carnival
where they are giving tethered balloon rides and watch). Remember
that the first one (the Vulcoon) had no platform at all, just a
parachute-style harness, and the burner was held up by the cables
(Popular Mechanics, Apr 1963). The throttle is opened by pulling
a rope.
The men, if they were really worried about gunfire, would have
been lying down on the platform.


@Having a 30 mph wind blowing could have an impact on other aspects of this
@sighting.


BTW, Zamora later denied seeing the flame at any time before he
parked the car. See "Project Blue Book" Steiger, p133.

BRIAN & LIST,

I don't have info on Zamora's vision, as I pointed posted before. But the
fact Zamora never says he put his glasses back on in the short time between
picking them up from the ground and when the UFO disappeared, and he was
distracted enough by his panic response to the UFO to just leave his
sunglasses on the ground, suggests to me he wasn't wearing his glasses when
the UFO disappeared. Maybe he was farsighted (hyperopic) and it wouldn't
matter. But it calls into question the utility of calculating disappearance
velocities which assume normal vision.

I think the answer is : Word processing.

When I wrote my first book, that was in 1983-1984, and
I had only an old typewriter. It was a popularization of
quantum mechanics (probably more difficult than a novel).
I had six months to write it. While typing a chapter, I
had to start again several times from the last dissatisfying
sentence/paragraph/page. Every chapter had to be typed
again entirely when the publisher was dissatisfied; some
chapters have been typed again two times. I worked every
evening up to midnight, every Saturday, every Sunday,
the whole Xmas and Easter holidays (by the way, I don't know
how to type correctly, I use only one or two fingers...).

Now I use computers and/or word processing machines, and
it's three times faster (maybe four).

Jean-Pierre Pharabod

Chris,

With few people having perfect eyesight and the majority of
UFO cases seeming to take place at night, plus different
perceptions of what's actually being observed, it sure ain't
easy.

We can only be grateful so many accounts are documented at the
time and not compounded by later recollections. Many cases
reported on-line, e.g., to the National UFO Reporting Centre, are
old sightings.

I experienced first-hand the problems with this a few years ago.
Someone in the US - a reasonably well known ufologist - said he
would try and document for me the daylight sighting of a large
`triangular UFO' which had been seen by his mother, father and
sister.

@1983ish.

@Where we lived was a semi-rural area south of Greensboro, North

@idea what it could be.

@have no idea exactly how long they witnessed the object. Then,

I had a similar experience once. The object was a black triangle,
moving erratically in the sky (this is different from above),
seemingly as big as a low airplane. Suddenly, it was just gone.
A minute later, it rose up again from behind a stand of trees. I
went closer and discovered two kids flying a large (5 ft span)
black triangular kite. It apparently had turned edge-on to me.
Did anyone think of something like this?

Another thought is that someone tried to make a small hot-air
balloon out of a trash bag and it burned up or melted.

Hi Jean Pierre,

Re: Your comments on writing.

As a coincidence, I wrote my first 50,000 word sci-fi novel in the early
80s. I stored various ideas in a couple of exercise books and the
manuscript was produced with a small portable typewriter. It was
incredibly tedious and I almost gave up on the project - more than once.
 I couldn't agree more that computers have revolutionized writing and I
now produce non-fiction articles which are never printed out (by me) and
usually go straight to publishers via the Net.
 But the sheer creative effort required to put a half decent novel
together takes a major committment in terms of mental involvement with
the storyline and I certainly couldn't consider turning out a book in
the space of say 12-18 months while running a small business at the same
time.

From: Larry Robinson S/AP/EIS Kinesiology <lrobins@indiana.edu>
Subject: Socorro

UFO Research List - http://web.ukonline.co.uk/voyager/



In Kevin Randle's "UFO Casebook" Dr Hynek is quoted:

"The wind was blowing down the gully, and the Phillips house is
in the opposite direction."

Using the map in Klass's "UFOs Explained" (which locates the
Phillips house) it makes the wind direction toward the southwest,
thus it is a northeast wind (by the meteorologist's definition).

This makes the wind direction favorable for the balloon theory.


The standard meteorological definition of wind direction is to
report the direction the wind comes FROM. This is the direction
most important to those who use the wind: sailors and farmers.
Many books on the subject of UFOs somehow get this reversed,
(including all of the ones from APRO, which used this faulty
assumption to "disprove" many balloon sightings).


Dr Hynek's other statement on wind direction could be caused by
one or more of the following sources of error:

1. All of the site maps made by Zamora have south at the top of
the map.

2. He confused the definition of wind direction himself.

3. Someone else confused the definition of wind direction and
then told him the wrong information. This is likely, especially
if the information came through several people.

4. The information was wrong at the airport.

5. The weather data at another time and place was different from
that at the site of the sighting.

Voyager Newsletter - Issue No. 7


* Socorro `64: Shaken but not Stirred *


In the last newsletter, I wrote:

"When the `UFO Research List' (UFORL) was set up earlier this
year, my intention was to provide a discussion forum which
addressed scientific evidence, including the interface between
UFOs and `black projects'


During recent discussions on the list, I brought up the subject
of `The Socorro 1964 UFO Case'.

My reason for doing so was a belief that this unexplained
`classic' could still be resolved and to highlight a conceivable,
yet maybe little known, rationale for the `UFO' which local
Police Officer Lonnie Zamora encountered.

To briefly recap; on the 24 April 1964, Zamora was chasing a
speeding car when he was distracted by a loud `roar' overhead. He
witnessed a corresponding intermittent flame, although its source
wasn't visible because of the bright light from the directly
opposed sun.

Zamora broke off his chase and instead followed the aerial
object, which had descended and seemed about to land in an
arroyo, just behind a nearby, small hill.

Eventually, he came upon a white, upright, oval-shaped object on
the ground and briefly, only for a couple of seconds, noticed two
figures wearing what resembled white coveralls.

When he reached a closer vantage point, Zamora was startled and
admittedly scared when the deafening flame recurred and the
object slowly rose up from the ground. It took several seconds to
reach a height of around twenty feet, then the `propulsion
system' stopped and the object silently travelled parallel to the
ground for a while, before slowly rising upwards again,
disappearing out of sight. As the object departed in the
distance, Zamora radioed to the police station, "it looks like a
balloon".

The reliability of Zamora's report was never in doubt; the object
had left trace evidence, including still smouldering bushes.


The rationale originated from claims published in 1996 by Larry
Robinson, a Systems/Applications Programmer at Indiana
University.

The Socorro `UFO' was, he believed, a hot-air balloon.

Larry's reasoning seemed sound - he had personally experienced
the surprisingly loud roar made by a hot-air balloon's burner
[which would apparently have been even louder circa 1964
ballooning technology] and considered that overall "the effects
and sounds were identical to the descriptions" which Zamora
reported.

Added to this was the potential significance of two articles
Larry recalled seeing:

"1963-1964: I saw an advertizement in a magazine showing a
balloon belonging to, or sponsored by, the International Paper
Corporation. The logo is a circle containing an arrow, made of
the letters I and P, pointing up. They were going to go on a
cross country exploration with it.

1965-Feb 1967: I saw an article or ad showing the results of a
multi-state series of hot-air balloon flights. A map was
included, showing the landing points of the balloon and some
amusing anecdotes of things that happened to the balloonists. One
of these was an encounter with a lawman who they thought was
going to shoot it out with them. The balloon freaked him out. The
article said, `We later found out that he thought he was seeing a
space ship'."


The distinctive International Paper logo does look practically
identical to the `insignia' which Zamora noticed on the object
and later sketched.

Furthermore, if there was a balloonists' anecdote of a lawman who
had been spooked by a hot-air balloon around that time, it seemed
a reasonable assumption this referred to the Socorro incident.

However, as no evidence had ever been located to prove any hot-
air balloon connection, I thought it worthwhile following up the
leads Larry had provided. Surely, some clarification of the
issues had to be attainable.


Initially, I obtained an article from `National Geographic'
magazine, entitled, `Hot Air Balloons Ride on Silent Winds',
published in the March 1966 issue. Although this wasn't the
article Larry mentioned, it did provide important clues to
investigate further.

What subsequently became clear was an understanding of how
development of the hot-air balloon corresponded with the history
of helium and hydrogen balloon technologies during the 1950s and
1960s. It's potential applications had not gone unnoticed by the
military and intelligence communities...


Setting this in some context was an article published by `Balloon
Life' magazine, as extracted from the July 1997 issue [Volume 12,
Number 7]:

`Don Piccard - 50 Years of Ballooning Memories'
by Peter Stekel.

[...]

"During his years at Raven, between 1962 and 1964, Piccard
devoted his energy to marketing the Vulcoon, one-man thermal
balloons. Stressing his lack of security clearance at the time,
Piccard says he worked strictly on sport balloons and had no
contact with any of Raven's military contracts. Be that as it
may, following a 1987 interview in Balloon Life with Don Piccard,
where he described his civilian work with Raven, the CIA library
in Langley, Virginia, began to subscribe to the magazine".

[...]

"Reflecting back to those days at Raven, Piccard thinks the
company's sport balloon division was a cover-up for the military
applications of ballooning. `The sport balloon program, which was
not believed in by the Raven Industry management, was strictly
getting this crazy guy who liked to fly in balloons and make
cover. So, when one of these other balloons went down, it would
just look like a sport balloonist'. When the Navy terminated its
contract with Raven, the sport balloon program died too. That was
in December of 1964".
[End]


Piccard was one of the central figures in the development of hot-
air ballooning.

If the "military applications" program was terminated at the end
of 1964, then all work must have taken place before then.

Which means that there were a number of publicly undocumented,
hot-air balloon flights prior to December 1964.

During 1962 Piccard organised the world's first hot-air balloon
race in Paris. According to that `Balloon Life' article, the
nascent sport attracted four entrants:

"Don Piccard flew in a civilian balloon, Dick Keuser had an old
brown silicon hot-air balloon that had been built for a research
program. Yost flew a Mylar-nylon CIA balloon, and Tracy Barnes
had a homemade balloon made out of parachutes".

The Ed Yost `CIA' balloon was interesting to read about. In 1956,
Yost was one of Raven Industries' founders. It's common knowledge
that an early commission came from the Office of Naval Research
(ONR) and this funding seems to have continued through to 1964.

The company's work for the CIA also apparently ceased that year,
the aforementioned article noting, "In the autumn of 1964, the
CIA had canceled their contract with Raven".


During that 1962-1964 period, whilst Piccard was looking after
the development of Raven Industries' new sporting hot-air
balloons, Ed Yost continued to be was pivotal in the company's
government/military research contracts.

Some background regarding Ed Yost, from a brief, authorised
biography:

"Leaving General Mills, Yost and 3 others moved to Sioux Falls,
South Dakota and formed Raven Industries. One of Raven's first
projects was a commission from the U.S. Navy's Office of Naval
Research (ONR) to create an aircraft that would carry one man and
enough fuel to fly for three hours, carry a load to 10,000 feet,
and be reusable. Additionally, the system was required to be of
small size and weight and have a fast inflation and launching
system that required a minimum of personnel.

In October 1955 Yost made the first moored flight of a modern
hot-air balloon. The envelope was plastic film, and heat was
provided by plumbers pots burning kerosene.

On October 22, 1960, Yost made the first free flight of a modern
hot-air balloon from Bruning, Nebraska. By then Yost had switched
to nylon for the envelope, and had created a propane heater. The
gross weight of the balloon, including Yost and fuel, was 404
pounds. He was in the air 25 minutes and landed 3 miles from his
takeoff point.

The next flight was made November 12, 1960 from the Stratobowl,
situated at 4500' MSL. Yost had increased the burner power,
reinforced the envelope at the equator to add handling lines, and
increased the opening at the top from 9 to 13 feet, doubling the
deflation port size. The inflation took 6 minutes and he lifted
off at 8:40 a.m. with a gross weight of 465 pounds. At 9:12 a.m.
he made an ascent at 300 feet per minute to 9000', then made a
600 feet per minute descent which he successfully halted with the
new burner. He landed at 10:30 after a flight of 1 hour and 50
minutes covering 39 miles.

In October 1961 Yost concluded his report to the ONR as follows:

`At the completion of this program in October 1961, all of the
basic requirements had been met. A low-weight, manned flight
system capable of safely carrying one man for three hours, at
altitudes of up to 10,000 feet had been repeatedly flown'.

`Inflations and launchings in winds of more than 10 mph and
temperatures as low as +5øF had been successfully accomplished.
Operations at altitudes of 4,500 feet MSL (above mean sea level)
had been demonstrated. Ground support equipment had been
developed so that inflation, under light wind conditions, could
be carried out in less than ten minutes. Controls, burners and
instrumentation adequate to operate the system had been
developed'.

`As a result of the work done under this contract, the
feasibility of using hot air balloons for sustained flight was
demonstrated. By the application of modern materials, design
techniques and instrumentation, an aerostat which had been known
for more than 175 years was resurrected and shown to have
substantial value in modern research and operations. The limits
of duration and lifting capacity appear to far exceed that
developed under this contract; the low cost, simplicity of
operation, and logistic advantage which hot air balloons provide,
when compared with light-gas balloons, are most impressive.
Within the altitude limits where hot air balloons may be used,
these modern Montgolfier systems may become an important tool for
atmospheric and low-level lifting and transport tasks'.

Raven Industries sold their first sport balloon in November 1961
and the new sport of hot-air ballooning was born.

In 1963, Ed Yost made the first hot-air balloon crossing of the
English Channel. With crew member Don Piccard, he made the flight
from Rye, Sussex, England to Gravelines Nord, France, in 3 hours
and 17 minutes in a 56,000 cubic foot Raven balloon named
`Channel Champ'."


A photograph of Ed Yost's inaugural hot-air balloon flight can be
seen at:

http://www.nott.com/favorite_balloon_flights.htm


In my correspondence with Don Piccard, he confirmed that the
`Channel Champ' adventure took place on Easter Monday, 1963.

A separate source, who was also directly associated with Raven
Industries at that time, explained, "This exhibition [flight] was
sponsored by a new French travel magazine called `VIA'. There was
a logo on the side of the balloon with the magazine name in
large, bold letters".

"The VIA emblem had white letters on a black background. It was
attached to the balloon envelope (actually, draped) just below a
permanent insignia showing origin of the balloon -- which was in
red. That inscription included: RAVEN (possibly 2 to 3 ft tall),
followed by an American flag. Then U S A vertically; SIOUX FALLS
in half the height and SOUTH DAKOTA just below it. Finally, there
was the registration number N-xxxx".

Although ostensibly to promote Raven's hot-air balloons as a
sporting pastime, this exhibition flight had another agenda, as
we shall see.

The `Balloon Life' article recalls:

"An Air Force tanker flew Piccard and Yost from Milwaukee to
England, `Loaded everything on board and away we did go!' The two
balloonists were designated, `Majors in the Wisconsin National
Guard: uniforms, I.D. cards; everything.' He pauses and chuckles
softly. `All in the national interest, of course'."
The `Channel Champ' balloon was a model `S 50' and its back-up an
`S 45'. Both balloons were brought back to America, returning by
airplane to General Mitchell Field in Milwaukee.

Incredibly, there may be a connection between this promotional
flight, Raven's work for the government and Lonnie Zamora's April
1964 `UFO' sighting.


During my research, the most profound discovery was evidence of
`classified' hot-air balloon flights which took place in the New
Mexico area during 1963 and 1964. Publicly, their existence was
previously unknown and full details are disclosed here for the
first time.

As would be expected, these test flights involved Raven balloons.

US researcher Karl Pflock contacted Ed Yost, who acknowledged
having flown in the tests which took place. However, Yost was
adamant that none of the balloons were ever within some 50 miles
of Socorro. He didn't say whether any activities took place on
the 26 April, 1964, only that they did extend into 1964.

Thanks to Karl, it's also known exactly where they were launched
and if anyone claims to have first-hand evidence, they should be
able to confirm that location.

What were these tests possibly concerned with?

Both Karl and fellow researcher Joel Carpenter noted that in
addition to the reconnaissance benefits offered by manned, hot-
air balloons, there were clear indications of the CIA's specific
interest in agent insertion and extraction operations.


It was my understanding, from an informed source, that two hot-
air balloons involved in the New Mexico tests were the `Channel
Champ' model `S 45' and its back-up balloon, the `S 50'.

Independently, another informed source suggested this was more
than likely, as these balloons were effectively owned by the
government.

I can now confirm this was not only correct, it seems the
`Channel Champ' flight was, extraordinarily, something of a US
government/military public relations and marketing exercise.

It can also now be substantiated that even before the advent of
hot-air balloons, gas filled balloons were being used for covert
agent insertion operations during the `cold war', in Eastern
Europe.

The source of these confirmations is Ed Yost.

The July 1999 issue of `Balloon Life' [this magazine should be
compulsive reading for all researchers!] published a feature
entitled, `Ed Yost honored by the Aero Club of New England',
written by Jim Ellis.

Reporting on a formal presentation to Yost of the prestigious
Godfrey L. Cabot Award, Ellis wrote:

"Over 200 aviation enthusiasts and dignitaries were in attendance
for the presentation of the award. Yost chose to save his most
interesting stories for an informal get-together in a room at The
Harvard Club following the formal presentation of the Cabot
Award.

About two dozen aviation enthusiasts, primarily New England
balloonists, got to hear the father of hot air ballooning give
his bluntly honest answers to a range of questions. It was a rare
look at the start of hot air ballooning as we know it from the
man who literally started it all".

"Yost said that throughout the 1950s he was involved with
military and other classified government programs using balloons
to carry leaflets and even men across the Iron Curtain from three
launch sites in West Germany. Using different sized balloons,
most of Eastern Europe could be covered, carrying anywhere from 4
pounds to over 750 pounds of leaflets.

Yost said that the leaflets were actually small newspapers that
would give inhabitants of Communist dominated countries news of
the West they couldn't get any other way. He said `the thing
worked too damn good and we got the Hungarian Revolution.
Eisenhower stopped the program. We should have been dropping
45s.'

It is apparent that the Communist bloc countries were in the
habit of looking for and shooting down the gas balloons. Yost
said that `we were launching big balloons in the daytime. Some
days there would be a trail of balloons across the sky. Fighter
planes were blowing them out of the sky, so they changed to
launching at night.'

The modern hot air balloon evolved from experiments in the mid-
1950s which Yost was conducting aimed at using hot air as a
lifting gas. Yost was well aware of early smoke balloon flights,
and began experiments to quantify the lifting properties of hot
air compared to helium and hydrogen. Beginning with plumbers pots
fueled by white gas used to heat air in plastic balloons indoors,
he determined that 64 cubic feet of hot air would be required to
lift one pound compared to 16 cubic feet of helium. Possibly
throwing out a challenge to today's balloon experimenters (Brian
Boland was among the balloonists in the room), Yost pointed out
that steam would require only 32 cubic feet to lift one pound.
One of the balloons was photographed holding a man on a harness
under the tethered balloon, and Yost used the photo to negotiate
a 47,000 dollar contract from the Office of Naval Research".

"By the time he and his team had met all of the Navy requirements
for a one-man balloon and the final report was written, Yost had
developed and flown hot air balloons incorporating all of the
major characteristics of today's modern hot air balloons
including non porous coated synthetic fabrics, liquid propane
fueled burners with preheater tubes and fast acting valves, and
maneuvering and deflation vents for control of the aircraft
during flight and landing".

"Perhaps the most fascinating story Yost told was of his flight
across the English Channel. He said that the flight was not a
sport balloon flight but rather the idea of his government
sponsor, who wanted to demonstrate the range and endurance
capabilities of the balloon. When told by European air traffic
control officials that there was too much traffic at the shortest
point near Calais, he said that was no problem because he had 12
hours of fuel on board and wanted to go where the Channel was
wider. The balloon was flown to England on an Air Force KC-97
tanker/cargo aircraft which left from Minnesota".

Copyright 1999 Balloon Life. All rights reserved.
[End]


Additional and insightful information on related CIA operations
can be found in the declassified document, `Operation Mongoose-
Propaganda Balloon Operations Plan, 10 Oct., 1962'. See:

http://www.gwu.edu/~nsarchiv/nsa/DOCUMENT/930827.htm


I'm still looking for a photograph of the 1963 `Channel Champ'
and one of the balloon museums indicate they may be able to
assist. Meantime, I have been able to locate a photograph of the
balloon's platform, which carried Yost and Piccard on what, as
Yost acknowledges in the full article, was a seriously hazardous
flight.

The platform, on display at the `Musee des Balloons', Chateau de
Balleroy, France, can be seen in an earlier `Balloon Life'
article, at:

http://www.balloonlife.com/publications/balloon_life/9512/history
.htm

[This URL will wrap around]


Yet, despite these previously undocumented, `classified' New
Mexico flights taking place at around the same time as Zamora's
encounter, there's perhaps no relationship at all. It may simply
be coincidental.

However, what I can add is I know, for a fact, that the balloons
involved in those New Mexico tests were white and the crew were
carried on a platform much like the one used on the `Channel
Champ'. These balloons were large though and I suspect too big
for the object Zamora described, which seems to have been much
smaller. If it was a hot-air balloon `test' he witnessed, it
could have been a model which was specifically designed to be
unobtrusive, with clandestine operations in mind. The attire worn
by crew members could well have been white coveralls, which was
common.


There is another candidate for a hot-air balloon having
responsible for Zamora's encounter and it takes us back to Larry
Robinson's recollections.

I was able to ascertain that almost certainly no `International
Paper' hot-air balloon had been built by 1964. If one ever
existed, it may have been a helium-filled, cable driven balloon
used for carrying logs from mountain slopes, a development in
later years. According to a Raven Industries source: "Experiments
were made and eventually routine operations conducted using
helium balloons to lift logs off of mountain slopes. These were
cable-driven, not free flying. This work started in the summer of
1967 and we were actively involved in providing and testing new
models for at least a decade. Such balloons may still be in use
today".

I have suggested to Larry that the article he saw in 1963 or 1964
may have included an artist's impression of a balloon with the
company's logo. He agrees that is a possibility.


The 1965-Feb 1967 article about a "multi-state series of hot-air
balloon flights" would most likely have been a feature on the
first transcontinental crossing of the U.S. by balloon. This
endeavour was undertaken by a known balloonist between April to
September 1966, a story which appeared in a number of magazines.

As it seems the article Larry remembers must have been written
after the successful crossing, it narrows the publication date to
September 1966-February 1967. Of course, if it was the tale of a
lawman who was startled by a balloon during the 1966 flights, it
couldn't relate to Zamora's 1964 experience. It would have to be
the account of an earlier incident.

Of more consequence now is having identified the 1966 pilot and
obtaining contact details, he should be able to clear up all of
these points first-hand. Someone will hopefully be speaking to
him presently, or will have done by the time this newsletter is
published.

In the meantime, it's not the intent of this newsletter to debate
the merits of any views on whether Zamora may have observed an
early hot-air balloon, which in 1964 he was most unlikely to ever
have seen or heard previously. Also perhaps now best wait to see
what ongoing enquiries might reveal.


In 1964, the US Air Force's `Project Blue Book' was the official
channel for investigating UFO reports.

Two years later, Blue Book's chief, Major Quintanilla, confided
in a then classified CIA publication, "He [Zamora] is puzzled by
what he saw, and frankly, so are we. This is the best-documented
case on record, and still we have been unable, in spite of
thorough investigation, to find the vehicle or other stimulus
that scared Zamora to the point of panic".

Even if immaterial, it does look as though the existence of those
`classified' New Mexico hot-air balloon flights had not been
considered, investigated and eliminated by `Project Blue Book'
before reaching that conclusion. It seems there's no firm
evidence they had considered a private hot-air balloon flight
either.


Looking to establish the overall context of balloons being used
for such intelligence operations, I asked some questions of an
acquaintance in the US who is an `Intelligence' historian.

He advised, "The Office of Naval Research did a lot of balloon
work and they were involved in inflatable aircraft work with
Goodyear Rubber Co. CIA was also interested in both of these
areas. The Navy's Strato-Lab program ran, at least, into the
early 1960s because, on May 4, 1961, the Strato-Lab V balloon
carried two Navy flight surgeons to an altitude of almost 115,000
feet. The General Mills Company in Minneapolis, Minnesota, also
did early (late 40s, early 50s) balloon work.

CIA, and others, have been interested in clandestine methods for
agent infiltration and exfiltration since the `Iron Curtain'
descended across Europe. While balloons have some potential for
agent infiltration (moving from west to east), there are obvious
problems in using them for exfiltration (prevailing wind
direction).

I know there was some work done by CIA, including some manned
`flight testing' of a one-man balloon. I have done some checking
and I find no indication that this information has been
released".

Which implies this newsletter may be the first public disclosure
of specific details about these `one-man balloon' test flights. I
can reveal that a knowledgeable source indicates the project

being referred to was carried out in Minnesota during the early
1960s and definitely before 1964.

Although the Don Piccard `Balloon Life' article reports that
equipment for the 1963 `Channel Champ' flight was flown to
England from Milwaukee, the July 1999 Ed Yost article claims,
"The balloon was flown to England on an Air Force KC-97
tanker/cargo aircraft which left from Minnesota".

I'm sure this can be clarified.


So, what started out as an exercise in search of the `UFO'
evidence Larry Robinson cited, became an adventure into the world
of James Bond.

There's still some way to go before reaching a conclusion about
recent developments and any relationship to Zamora's sighting,
Karl Pflock expressing his conviction that the object was not a
hot-air balloon. Although I'm not so sure, there are grounds to
be optimistic that the new evidence can be augmented and will
eventually become self-determining.

One point which should be emphasised is that no matter what the
outcome, Lonnie Zamora was an exemplary witness. He simply
reported and then documented exactly what had been observed,
leaving others with more `expertise' to come up with an
explanation.


Considerable appreciation is expressed to the various unnamed
sources -they would prefer to remain anonymous - who have helped
to unravel a fresh perspective. Also to Karl, Brad Sparks, Larry
Robinson and all others who have provided input during recent
discussions.

Date: Mon, 13 Sep 1999 17:24:41 -0400 (EDT)
From: RB47Expert@aol.com
Subject: Re: Voyager Newsletter - Issue No. 7Message-id:
<1e1d78ca.250ec599@aol.com>

UFO Research List - http://web.ukonline.co.uk/voyager/

Bruce & List.

Thanks Bruce for putting in a plug for me. Barry Greenwood and I have
independently advanced the tangential or escaping meteor hypothesis for the
C. B. Moore et al. sighting of April 24, 1949. The main problem with the
explanation has been Moore's statement that the object was picked up to the
south-southwest directly above the balloon they were tracking, at about 210
degs azimuth heading east, it got lost in the sun, then was seen heading
north where it disappeared at about 25 degs azimuth. A meteor ordinarily
cannot cover more than 180 degs of arc and that would have to be from horizon
to horizon passing directly overhead, which didn't seem to be the case here
(the 185 degs of azimuth change suggests a turn). I suggested the remote
possibility that midway through the sighting (when lost in the glare of the
sun) the meteor broke up with the main piece going off in a more northerly
direction, or perhaps it aerodynamically skidded to the north due to
irregularities in the meteor's shape.

However, I recently located Moore's crew statements which are significantly
at odds with his account in a number of respects. William Akers stated in
his very detailed report (it even includes Moore's drawing that is missing
from Moore's reports) that the balloon was at about 173 degs azimuth NOT 210
degs when the UFO was sighted. That would mean only about 148 degs of
azimuth covered, making it possible that it was a linear meteor trajectory.
Still, Akers himself reported that at 80 degs azimuth (nearly due east) the
UFO "swerved" to the north, i.e., the object made a TURN.

The Artesia, NM, sighting by balloon observers on Jan 16, 1951, sounds pretty
inexplicable as the two objects circled the balloon then left.

The Kaliszewski sightings of Oct 10-11, 1951, seem dubious though and the
time estimates seriously overestimated. In the second incident, the object
crossed the observers' aircraft windshield "rapidly" or at a "high rate" of
about 50 degs/sec from east to west which could not have taken more than
about 3 SECONDS total. Then it "slowed down" and climbed in "lazy circles"
or "gyrations" or a "falling oak leaf inverted" for "a couple minutes" before
a "very rapid acceleration" and disappearance to the east. But the total
observation time is given as about 5 MINUTES, which is about DOUBLE the
"couple minutes" just mentioned. Since Kaliszewski and Reilly were flying in
an airplane eastward they would have traveled about 10+ miles AWAY from the
UFO in five minutes if that was how long they had it in sight, and they would
have had to strain their heads to LOOK BEHIND THEM virtually the entire time,
which seems unlikely. Most likely the sighting duration was well under a
minute.
The pre-Arnold Minczewski sighting of April 1947 sounds like a meteor since
the observer could hardly get a good view of the object's shape in the brief
interval he saw it in the theodolite, with total duration estimated at 5-6
seconds (part of that time he tried to see it with his naked eye but
couldn't), and it made no turns or other maneuvers.

Brad Sparks

Hi Larry,

Good points re the Arrey sighting by Moore et al. But it would be nice to
have a known precedent of a meteor path deflection such as you or I have
theorized. Using William Akers' more exact data the azimuth covered from
beginning to end of the sighting was apparently about 148 degs. It could
have been less because these are estimates, since they could not keep the
theodolite on the object throughout the sighting. Error bars of at least +/-
5 degs are reasonable for beginning and ending points or at least +/- 10 degs
for the 148-degree total azimuth range. Splitting the azimuth range evenly
puts the midpoint or presumed closest approach a bit south of due east -- not
too far from the sun -- at roughly 100 degs azimuth with half of azimuth
range to the north and half to the south. Moore said the UFO was at about 45
degs elevation when first sighted to the south. If it was a meteor in
horizontal flight at say about 40 miles altitude then at midpoint or closest
approach it would have been about 11 miles away in ground range and about 75
degs in elevation above the horizon (or less if it also dropped to minimum
height around this time, lower than 40 miles). Just seconds prior when
passing close to the sun at about 125 degs azimuth (almost SE) it would have
been a little lower in elevation angle, at about 73 degs with error margin at
least +/- 5 degs if not +/- 10 degs -- or lower if the meteor was reaching
its lowest height before bouncing back. Given witness error in angular
estimates, this was close to the sun or the sun's glare.

To illustrate this effect of increasing then decreasing elevation angle, if
it was a meteor in nearly horizontal flight and it passed directly overhead
the elevation angle would of course increase to 90 degs (zenith overhead)
before decreasing again. If the flight path was off to one side the
elevation angle would increase to a maximum at the point of closest approach
to the observers and the decrease again until it disappeared. And in fact
Moore in a later account states the object passed through the sun (or near it
presumably) which he calculated was at 60 degs elevation, or an INCREASE in
elevation angle from the initial 45 degs, followed by a DECREASE till it
disappeared at about 29 degs elevation (it reached a minimum of about 25 degs
at the end then zoomed up about 4 degs which may have been the escape bounce
or ascent of a tangential meteor).

Correction: Ruppelt misdated the Artesia case, it's Jan 16, 1952, NOT 1951.
See Hynek's The UFO Experience and Blue Book Status Report No. 6. I do not
have copies of the sighting reports. There were 6 witnesses, 2 were General
Mills aeronautical personnel and 4 were pilots.

Brad

Brad wrote:
>disappeared at about 29 degs elevation (it reached a minimum of about 25
degs
at the end then zoomed up about 4 degs which may have been the escape
bounce
or ascent of a tangential meteor).
<

I don't buy the "bouncing meteor" explanation of the increase in angular
elevation.

There is nothing to "bounce against" near the end of the meteor's path of
visibility. If there is any "bounce" it is at or before the time/location
of
maximum penetration into the atmosphere.
Also, the 60 seconds is long for meteor visibility, even if seen from
horizon to horizon (the maximum estimated horizon to horizon visible time
would be about 86 seconds... see attached report).

I have attached a report which I did initially over 20 years ago based on
my
analysis of the "Remarkable Meteor" sighting that was discussed recently by
Barry Greenwood. Because of his recent discussion I updated my report.
Although that report is directed toward that particular sighting that
occurred
in 1904 (seen by crew on the USS Supply), there are comment and analysis
that
apply to the CB Moore et al sighting.
If we ASSUME that the track was actually straight or at most slightly
curved in
a "horizontal" direction then we still have to show that the time duration
and the apparent final increase in angular elevation could be consistent
with a
meteor.

There is no justification I am aware of for a curved track that would curve
AWAY from the surface of the earth. All real meteor tracks bend by some
amount
around the center of the earth. (If gravity were repulsive they would bend
away from
the earth, as for example, the trajectory of an electron on a "grazing
path"
toward a large negatively charged sphere.)

TIME: Moore said it was first seen at angular elevation 45 degrees and
last
seen at 29 degrees. Now get yourself a piece of paper and draw a big arc
on it
and label it 4000 miles (earth radius; 6328 km if you are metric). Now
draw a straight line
above the arc with a small spacing that corresponds to 40 miles (64 km).
(Don't try to
draw to scale.) The earth's curvature is going to be difficult to detect on
a scale
that makes 40 miles visible on your drawing.
Anyway, place CB and the boys under the point of closest approach. Assume
the
straight track passes right over their heads at H = 40 mi up. Now mark
to the right
(southwest) an elevation of 45 degrees. Now mark to the left (northeast)
an
 angular elevation of 29 degrees (elevations above earth surface, or a
horizontal
plane tangent to the earth's surface of course.)
  Now calculate the length of the straight trajectory:

40 tan (90-45) + 40 tan (90-29) = 40 + 72 = 112 mi.

If this was traversed in 1 minute the speed was about 6700 mph.
IF Moore's last elevation was WRONG, and it was only 25 degrees the
distance was 40 + 86 = 126 which gives a speed of 7500 mph.
IF 60 seconds is an overestimate and it was only 50 seconds the speed
could have been 7500 x 60/50 = 9000 mph.
IF THE time estimate were horribly wrong and it was only 30 seconds, the
speed would be at most 15,000 mph.

Orbital speed at 100 mi altitude is about 17,000 mph (higher at lower
altitudes, but no one does it because of air). (90 minute satellite
orbit at 100 mi)

POINT: anything coming to "graze" the earth at only 9000 mph is going to
be
grabbed. Even 15,000 mph would be grabbed.

AHA!!! you say. The actual path is curved. Therefore the distance is
greater
from 45 degrees elevation on one side to 29 (or 25) degrees on the other
side.

BUT, say I, the largest amount of curvature allowed without crashing is
that of
a track parallel to the earth's surface at altitude 40 mi. Any greater
curvature and the
object will crash. So let's assume a track parallel to the surface by 40
mi high.
Let's use the 25 degree final elevation so that the straight line path 126
mi long calculated
above is the chord of a circle of radius 4040 miles (40 miles above 4000 mi
approximate
radius of the earth). The angle (at the earth's center) created by the
126 mi straight line
is 2 arcsin[(126/2)/4040] = 1.78702 degrees = 0.0311894 radians. The
distance along a curved
arc of radius 4040 miles is S = R (theta) = 4040 x 0.0311894 = 126.005 mi
In other words, the radius
of curvature is so large that the arc distance cannot be distinguished from
the straight line
distance.
QED.

As for the change in angular elevation near the end of the visible track,
assume again a
straight line meteor path over the earth's surface. Start a CLOCK at the
time the meteor
is directly overhead at 40 mi elevation. Then the distance from overhead
is vt, where
t is the time after overhead and v is the velocity. The angular elevation
in this straight
line approximation is E = arctan(H/vt) where H is the overhead elevation (H
= 40 mi).
One sees immediately that E decreases as t increases. Thus the angular
elevation
should drop at all times after the meteor passes overhead. A curved track
for the
meteor would create an even faster drop.

Thus an observation that the object increased angular elevation in the last
seconds
must be interpreted as an actual increase in elevation above the "flat"
(approximation)
earth. This definitely contradicts the normal meteor hypothesis and
throws it into
the category of "remarkable meteors."

Bruce.........

observations generally but I have no info about theodolite operators being
asked to be on the lookout for aerial phenomena until Feb 1950, when the
Holloman AFB base commander issued just such a request. The world's first
UFO observation network was set up on May 4, 1949, at Killeen Base nuclear
weapons storage site, Camp Hood, Texas, but it involved artillery observation
equipment. By May 17, 1949, AFOSI had set up the first 24-hour UFO
observation post northeast of Albuquerque, as a result of suggestions from
Dr. Joseph Kaplan of AFSAB who visited on a secret AF Intelligence/AFSAB
mission regarding GF's on April 27-28 -- but this was days AFTER the Moore
sighting at Arrey. And the AFOSI observation post used cameras and
spectrographic cameras but not theodolites.

Brad, this is what I was referring to:

Basic Ltr, CG, AMC, to CO, CFS, Subject: Project "Grudge"

1st Ind ... 18 May 1949
Base, Dayton, Ohio, ATTN: MCIAXS

.... 2. Several months ago, Mr. C. B. Moore, now of General Mills, Inc.,
but formerly associated with the balloon project at New York University,
discussed with Dr. Peoples of this station the problems encountered with
obtaining reliable information when observing unidentified objects. Mr.
Moore sent to Dr. Peoples an information copy of his observations near
Arrey, New Mexico on April 24, 1949. It is felt that although the theodolite
and stop-watch were of great assistance in making estimates, the principle
factor responsible for the unusually specific information contained in this
report, is that Mr. Moore was made aware in advance of what factors should
be observed in case such an object were sighted. Therefore, it is urged that
your office issue detailed advance observation instructions to people who
might be in a position to make observations and turn in reports....

Joseph O. Fletcher
Major, USAF
Director, Base Directorate for Geophysical Research

-------------

Moore's report immediately after the incident contains this:

" The object was not a balloon and was some distance away. Assuming escape
velocity, a track was figured which put the elevation about [sic] the
station of about 300,000 feet over the observed period. If this is true, the
flight would have probably gone over the White Sands Proving Ground,
Holloman Air Force Base and Los Alamos.

INFORMATION IS DESIRED IF THIS WAS SOME NEW OR EXPERIMENTAL
AIRCRAFT or for
any explanation whatsoever [my emphasis]."

Now why would he have said that? This is my point -- he had talked to
Peoples from the Cambridge Research Center about UFO sightings "months"
before the sighting, had obviously been keeping an eye peeled for some
time -- and even considering the tremendous performance of the object, he
still wondered if it was an "X-vehicle" of some
kind...

It clearly didn't _look_ like a meteor to him. He wasn't thinking in terms
of natural phenomena.

J Carpenter

Bruce & List,

The Rocky Mountain Fireball of Aug 10, 1972, was the first conclusive proof
of the existence of escaping tangential meteors. U.S. DSP infrared missile
warning satellite data proved the meteor "bounced." There was a paper in
Nature that gave the exact latitude, longitude, and altitude coordinates and
velocity for beginning, low point (perigee), and end points -- I can't find
my copy. I have notes that the declassified satellite data shows the
fireball was hot enough to be tracked for 101.2 seconds from central Utah to
Edmonton, Alberta, over about a 1,000-mile track (classified data may contain
a longer tracking) and the descent and ascent angles were about 2 degrees to
the minimum height of 58 km (if I recall right). Interestingly, the meteor
followed the curvature of the earth over about 14 degrees of arc, except for
the descent/ascent angle. At least one ground observer, in Montana, saw the
fireball nearly horizon-to-horizon over about 150 degs of arc, for roughly 60
seconds.

In the Arrey case, I can't accept the time estimates or angular elevations
and azimuths as anything but guesstimates because they were apparently NOT
measured by the theodolite. According to Richard G. Davidson, "I took over
the open sight on the Theodolite to try to put Moore on the object. We got
on the object for ABOUT A SECOND about North-East, and LOST IT again, and
could NEVER GET ON IT AGAIN because when it got almost North, we ran into a
whirlwind of dust, but right before I lost it, the object was rising plenty
fast. I lost it about 35 [degrees]."

Notice that there isn't even an elevation or azimuth reading for the one time
they DID have the UFO in the theodolite. And notice that Davidson's figure
of 35 degs from the object's disappearance elevation is quite a ways off from
Moore's 29-deg figure -- if it was an exact theodolite reading they could
have had it down to 10 seconds of arc, so it evidently was not a theodolite
reading.

As for time estimates no one but Moore had an estimate and he said it was
"about" or "around" 60 seconds. William Akers did report an angular velocity
-- and it disagrees with Moore's by a factor of 2x. Moore said 5 degs/sec
but Akers said "about 5 [degrees] in 2 seconds."

As I pointed out before, the total azimuth range of the object's travel was
about 148 degs +/-10 degs or more. Because of the "latitude" effect the
actual arc length must be multiplied by the cosine of the effective
"latitude" or elevation angle, say, 45 degs, hence an arc length of roughly
100 degs.
Using Moore's angular velocity, this would imply a duration of about 20
seconds. Using Akers' angular velocity, the duration would be about 40
seconds -- in either case much less than the 60-second guesstimate.

As you pointed out, Bruce, the path length of the object during the sighting,
if it was a roughly horizontal meteor at 40 miles altitude and assuming the
initial and terminal elevation angles above the horizon, would be:

  (40 mi /tan 45 degs) + (40 mi /tan 29 degs) = 40 + 72 = 112 miles

Of course, the elevation angles are very approximate and the meteor height
might have been say 60 miles, yielding a path length of about 168 miles.
With a duration of 20 seconds, the velocity would be about 20,000 mph to
30,000 mph -- meteor speeds.

Brad

I don't buy the "bouncing meteor" explanation of the increase in angular
elevation.

There is nothing to "bounce against" near the end of the meteor's path of
visibility. If there is any "bounce" it is at or before the time/location
of
maximum penetration into the atmosphere.
Also, the 60 seconds is long for meteor visibility, even if seen from
horizon to horizon (the maximum estimated horizon to horizon visible time
would be about 86 seconds... see attached report).

I have attached a report which I did initially over 20 years ago based on
my
analysis of the "Remarkable Meteor" sighting that was discussed recently by
Barry Greenwood. Because of his recent discussion I updated my report.
Although that report is directed toward that particular sighting that
occurred
in 1904 (seen by crew on the USS Supply), there are comment and analysis
that
apply to the CB Moore et al sighting.
If we ASSUME that the track was actually straight or at most slightly
curved in
a "horizontal" direction then we still have to show that the time duration
and the apparent final increase in angular elevation could be consistent
with a
meteor.

There is no justification I am aware of for a curved track that would curve
AWAY from the surface of the earth. All real meteor tracks bend by some
amount
around the center of the earth. (If gravity were repulsive they would bend
away from
the earth, as for example, the trajectory of an electron on a "grazing
path"
toward a large negatively charged sphere.)

TIME: Moore said it was first seen at angular elevation 45 degrees and
last
seen at 29 degrees. Now get yourself a piece of paper and draw a big arc
on it
and label it 4000 miles (earth radius; 6328 km if you are metric). Now
draw a straight line
above the arc with a small spacing that corresponds to 40 miles (64 km).
(Don't try to
draw to scale.) The earth's curvature is going to be difficult to detect on
a scale
that makes 40 miles visible on your drawing.
Anyway, place CB and the boys under the point of closest approach. Assume
the
straight track passes right over their heads at H = 40 mi up. Now mark
to the right
(southwest) an elevation of 45 degrees. Now mark to the left (northeast)
  Now mark
to the right
(southwest) an elevation of 45 degrees. Now mark to the left (northeast)
an
 angular elevation of 29 degrees (elevations above earth surface, or a
horizontal
plane tangent to the earth's surface of course.)
  Now calculate the length of the straight trajectory:

40 tan (90-45) + 40 tan (90-29) = 40 + 72 = 112 mi.

If this was traversed in 1 minute the speed was about 6700 mph.
IF Moore's last elevation was WRONG, and it was only 25 degrees the
distance was 40 + 86 = 126 which gives a speed of 7500 mph.
IF 60 seconds is an overestimate and it was only 50 seconds the speed
could have been 7500 x 60/50 = 9000 mph.
IF THE time estimate were horribly wrong and it was only 30 seconds, the
speed would be at most 15,000 mph.

Orbital speed at 100 mi altitude is about 17,000 mph (higher at lower
altitudes, but no one does it because of air). (90 minute satellite
orbit at 100 mi)

POINT: anything coming to "graze" the earth at only 9000 mph is going to
be
grabbed. Even 15,000 mph would be grabbed.

AHA!!! you say. The actual path is curved. Therefore the distance is
greater
from 45 degrees elevation on one side to 29 (or 25) degrees on the other
side.

BUT, say I, the largest amount of curvature allowed without crashing is
that of
a track parallel to the earth's surface at altitude 40 mi. Any greater
curvature and the
object will crash. So let's assume a track parallel to the surface by 40
mi high.
Let's use the 25 degree final elevation so that the straight line path 126
mi long calculated
above is the chord of a circle of radius 4040 miles (40 miles above 4000 mi
approximate
radius of the earth). The angle (at the earth's center) created by the
126 mi straight line
is 2 arcsin[(126/2)/4040] = 1.78702 degrees = 0.0311894 radians. The
distance along a curved
 a curved
arc of radius 4040 miles is S = R (theta) = 4040 x 0.0311894 = 126.005 mi
In other words, the radius
of curvature is so large that the arc distance cannot be distinguished from
the straight line
distance.
QED.

As for the change in angular elevation near the end of the visible track,
assume again a
straight line meteor path over the earth's surface. Start a CLOCK at the
time the meteor
is directly overhead at 40 mi elevation. Then the distance from overhead
is vt, where
t is the time after overhead and v is the velocity. The angular elevation
in this straight
line approximation is E = arctan(H/vt) where H is the overhead elevation (H
= 40 mi).
One sees immediately that E decreases as t increases. Thus the angular
elevation
should drop at all times after the meteor passes overhead. A curved track
for the
meteor would create an even faster drop.

Thus an observation that the object increased angular elevation in the last
seconds
must be interpreted as an actual increase in elevation above the "flat"
(approximation)
earth. This definitely contradicts the normal meteor hypothesis and
throws it into
the category of

<

There is a summary of Moore's report in my paper "STILL IN DEFAULT"
available at
www.stardrive.org/maccabee.shtml. Look about 3/8 of the way into the
paper,
after Kenneth Arnold (pelican man!) and before Project Twinkle.
According to Sparks
Moore had the initial azimuth wrong.

The only data are angles and times. No data on distance.

Clearly the speed estimate depends upon the distance assumed given the
angular velocity estimates.
Fortunately th meteor hypothesis comes with a range of "built in "
distances.
That is, any meteor which grazes the earth's atmosphere or "bounces/skips"
off the
atmosphere is going to be 30 or more miles up. The lower it is the slower
it was going
(because the path between end points shrinks as the altitude shrinks).
Alternatively the
higher it is the faster it was going, BUT..... the higher it is the dimmer
it is and the shorter is
the time of visibility because the atmospheric density decreases rapidly
with height.
Thus, for example, inmy previous calculation I could assume a minimum
height of 100 miles
and get the calculated speed to be comparable to meteoric speed. HOwever,
the meteor wouldn't glow brighty enough (or, more correctly, there wouldn't
be enough atmospheric density to make
a bright glow from heated atmosphere) for it to be seen. Hence, as I
said already, there is an
acceptable distance (height) range for the meteor hypothesis. If it were
within that range, then it
was gopng to slowly to be a meteor. Obviously, if it were a lot lower,
say at the altitude of the balloon,
then it was going a lot slower...but still very fast (several thousand mph
if at 20 miles altitude)

articles in various in-house UFO magazines and also general news stand
publications around the world. As we hope to encourage and include many
contributions from outside the UFO community, we could broaden our scope for
publications to other specialist areas and publications. This should include
universities, colleges and schools where we could package the specific projects
as they are rolling, into a small booklet form for information purposes . </P>
<P align=justify></P><B>
<P align=justify>BUFORA</P></B>
<P align=justify>These projects will be maintained throughout their life under
the banner of BUFORA, specifically the Research and Investigations Departments.
John Spencer and Gloria Dixon will jointly collate the input from others and
jointly edit the publication of material together with all those in the Research
and Investigations Departments, who will be involved in the project and an
overall examination of the material.</P>
<P align=justify></P>
<P align=justify>During the last few years BUFORA has conducted research into a
number of highly important projects, but behind the scenes rather than on the
main stage. This has resulted in a lack of visibility for others to assist and
become involved with these projects. We believe that expanding the boundaries of
these projects is paramount to the aims of BUFORA as a viable research
organisation. It is vital to Ufology that research and investigation conducted
by BUFORA becomes highly visible to all those who support the study of UFOs and
related phenomena and to those in specialist fields, who could support and
contribute to these &lsquo;rolling projects&rsquo;.</P>
<P align=justify></P>
<P align=justify>Because of the increase in personal invective and general
non-ufological debate as well as the vociferous character assassination, which
is now rife in many areas of ufology, we believe it is time BUFORA took a lead
in addressing these issues, in conjunction with other such initiatives around
the world, in bringing ufology back to itself and sanity.</P>

<P align=justify>It is these four projects that are central to Ufology as it
stands today and therefore these will be treated as our primary objective in
circulating requests for input. Each project is outlined below</P>
<P align=justify></P><B>
<P align=justify>Memory Retrieval Project</P>
<DIR>
<DIR></B>
<P align=justify>This is the most compelling project we envisage, as there are
some critical and fundamental issues which must be looked at very closely here,
specifically as they relate to aspects of close encounter cases and UFO
research, and because these experiences are becoming more prevalent in cases
being reported to BUFORA and other UFO organisations across the world. We need
to determine whether close encounter experiences have any connection with the
UFO subject at all and whether hypnosis and other memory retrieval methods have
played a major part in creating the abduction mythology. </P>
<P align=justify></P>
<P align=justify>There is a great and very controversial debate about the safety
and value factors of the use of regression hypnosis for eliciting an objective
and accurate truth about the close encounter experience. BUFORA holds a
moratorium on the use of hypnosis by any investigator or BUFORA member, which
has been in effect for many years. If this moratorium is to stay in place and we
demand that investigators do not use this technique, we need to give them the
opportunity to examine the data, because there are investigators who played no
part in the original debates and we feel they will feel more committed to the
moratorium if they are given the chance to examine the evidence and recent
developments into medical and non-medical research into hypnosis and memory
retrieval in general. </P>
<P align=justify></P>
<P align=justify>We want to broaden this debate to include all those within the
subject and the medical professions, advocates and dissenters of the
technique.</P>
<P align=justify></P>
<P align=justify>This project should examine all forms of memory retrieval as
well as hypnosis and what alternatives, if any, may be valid, </P>
<P align=justify></P>
<P align=justify>What is the value of even conscious memory recall? Medical and
non-medical viewpoints sought here also.</P><B>
<P align=justify>This debate should have as its aims:</P></DIR></DIR>
<UL></B>
   <P align=justify>
   <LI>To reinforce or remove the BUFORA moratorium.
   <P></P>
   <P align=justify></P>
   <LI>To set out the best possible evidence for and against the use of
   hypnosis.
   <P></P>
   <P align=justify></P>
   <LI>To set out the evidence of experience.
   <P></P>
   <P align=justify></P>
   <LI>To suggest alternatives to hypnosis with similarly examined pros and
   cons and experiencial data.
   <P></P></LI></UL>
<P align=justify></P>
<DIR>
<DIR>
<P align=justify>We expect this to be a rolling project of several years with
many interim stages.</P>
<P align=justify></P></DIR></DIR><B>
<P align=justify>Alternative to ETH guide Project</P>
<DIR>
<DIR></B>
<P align=justify>Many close encounter experiencers approach BUFORA
investigators
and researchers seeking an explanation for their extraordinary experience, often
a confirmation of their belief that they have undergone an encounter with UFOs
and aliens. These reports have increased dramatically in the last few years and
because they are reported to BUFORA and many other UFO organisations we must
extensively address the issues that surround them as soon as possible. </P>
<P align=justify></P>
<P align=justify>We believe that a well-structured and coherent document/leaflet
must be produced by a wide spectrum of ufologists and the scientific
disciplines, which should be drawn from documented experiences and research from
around the world. The goal of this document should be to offer the close
encounter witness reasoned alternatives to the extraterrestrial hypothesis,
which has been very media-driven and consequently, has become integrated into
the belief system of many, by the image makers. This will not be designed to
refute the ETH, but to deny its prominence as only one possibility.</P>
<P align=justify></P>
<P align=justify>What should such a leaflet contain?</P>
<P align=justify></P><B>
<P align=justify>Censorship Project</P></B>
<P align=justify>BUFORA has recently been forced to debate the questions of
censorship in ufology. This has been a great dividing point within the UFO
community and has raised heated and valid questions as to what constitutes
&lsquo;censorship&rsquo;. In fact in many ways it has split the community in
half and therefore it is imperative that this issue should be debated in a
rational and logical manner with an understanding that all aspects of this
complex debate should be highlighted.</P>
<P align=justify></P>
<P align=justify>The broad question is a debate between, on the one hand freedom
of speech and the responsibility of BUFORA to give its members the widest choice
of ideas for debate: </P>
<P align=justify>On the other hand, should we have a duty to provide serious and
well -informed research which adheres to the strict code of practice that BUFORA
holds?: This would present future problems and how do we police this? It must be
remembered that speakers are &lsquo;invited&rsquo; by BUFORA to present lectures
at our conferences and London lecture programme? Does this mean that we should
be selective about who we invite and what does this mean in terms of giving the
widest choice of ideas for debate? Should we ensure that speakers from both
sides of controversial UFO issues are asked to speak at the same time in order
to give BUFORA members and the public the widest possible framework for making
up their own minds? </P>
<P align=justify></P>
<P align=justify>Do we entertain the public OR inform the public in the most
responsible way possible and where does the responsibility of BUFORA and UFO
organisations stand on this issue? Surely there must be an integrity to the
public in the subject matter we are promoting and will be seen to promote when
using a BUFORA platform, even though we emphasise that BUFORA does not
necessarily share the views of the speakers, etc. etc.</P>
<P align=justify></P>
<P align=justify>How can a balance be achieved that addresses these important
issues and at the same time shows respect and courtesy to all those involved in
this subject as well as the subject at large.</P>
<P align=justify></P><B>
<P align=justify>Close Encounter Study Project</P></B>
<P align=justify>There is a great deal of controversy about the problems arising
with close encounter research and there are many researchers who feel, very
strongly, that UFO study should not be involved in close encounter research, as
it is promoting experiences that may sometimes be due to possible mental
illness, and, therefore, by promoting these experiences in any form, can only
reinforce and exacerbate the problem. There is also the idea that these
experiences are due to re-interpretation and redefining of extraordinary
experiences, as alien and UFO encounters, within the mythology of today, due to
the powerful imagery emerging on a daily basis about ET.</P>
<P align=justify></P>
<P align=justify>However, the alternative argument is that the subject exists
NOW and that it is too powerful to ignore. Consequently organisations like
BUFORA should take a lead in dealing with it constructively and with
determination in examining all ideas, theories and particularly the beliefs
rampant within the abduction scenario both by the researchers and the witnesses.
We believe this project MUST encompass views, research and evidence from within
the relevant scientific disciplines particularly consciousness studies.</P>

Dear John and Gloria,

I am interested in the Instrumented Detection and Electromagnetic
Anomalies projects. However, I should point out that I tried to contact
BUFORA a couple of years ago with a view to helping in the electrical
hypersensitivity project and despite sending in a CV to indicate my
qualifications for that project, I never received a reply. When I
e-mailed BUFORA, my message returned with an error that the address
doesn't exist. When I telephoned BUFORA I got a message on the
answerphone which stated that this is no longer the telephone number for
BUFORA, that the new number was not known and not to leave a message for
BUFORA at that number.

If you are undertaking such a large initiative, you must ensure that you
have the communications infra-structure so that contributers can
acutually contribute. I know that sounds obvious, but it has been one
of BUROARA's failings in the past so it needed to be said. I would
suggest that project co-ordinators e-mail addresses and if possible
telephone numbers should be made available to everyone involved in the
projects.

Yours sincerely,

Bill Bimson.

>BUFORA has recently been forced to debate the questions of censorship in ufology.
This has been a great dividing point within the UFO community and has raised heated
and valid questions as to what constitutes ‘censorship’. In fact in many ways it has
split the community in half and therefore it is imperative that this issue should be
debated in a rational and logical manner with an understanding that all aspects of this
complex debate should be highlighted.
>
>
>The broad question is a debate between, on the one hand freedom of speech and the
responsibility of BUFORA to give its members the widest choice of ideas for debate:
>
>On the other hand, should we have a duty to provide serious and well -informed
research which adheres to the strict code of practice that BUFORA holds?: This
would present future problems and how do we police this? It must be remembered
that speakers are ‘invited’ by BUFORA to present lectures at our conferences and
London lecture programme? Does this mean that we should be selective about who
we invite and what does this mean in terms of giving the widest choice of ideas for
debate? Should we ensure that speakers from both sides of controversial UFO issues
are asked to speak at the same time in order to give BUFORA members and the public
the widest possible framework for making up their own minds?
>
>
>Do we entertain the public OR inform the public in the most responsible way
possible and where does the responsibility of BUFORA and UFO organisations stand
on this issue? Surely there must be an integrity to the public in the subject matter we
are promoting and will be seen to promote when using a BUFORA platform, even
though we emphasise that BUFORA does not necessarily share the views of the
speakers, etc. etc.
>
>
>How can a balance be achieved that addresses these important issues and at the same
time shows respect and courtesy to all those involved in this subject as well as the
subject at large.
>
>
>Close Encounter Study Project
>
>There is a great deal of controversy about the problems arising with close encounter
research and there are many researchers who feel, very strongly, that UFO study
should not be involved in close encounter research, as it is promoting experiences that
may sometimes be due to possible mental illness, and, therefore, by promoting these
experiences in any form, can only reinforce and exacerbate the problem. There is also
the idea that these experiences are due to re-interpretation and redefining of
extraordinary experiences, as alien and UFO encounters, within the mythology of
today, due to the powerful imagery emerging on a daily basis about ET.
>
>
>However, the alternative argument is that the subject exists NOW and that it is too
powerful to ignore. Consequently organisations like BUFORA should take a lead in
dealing with it constructively and with determination in examining all ideas, theories
and particularly the beliefs rampant within the abduction scenario both by the
researchers and the witnesses. We believe this project MUST encompass views,
research and evidence from within the relevant scientific disciplines particularly
consciousness studies.
>
>
>Viewpoints Please.
>
