Bruce,

It's always pleasing to be in agreement that objective research
is one of the most expedient ways forward.

Somewhat ironic that the only person who has expressed objections
to our recent sceptical appraisals, is your very good friend
Philip Klass.

He writes:

"Reference your recent file on Socorro, and its statement that
`the reliability of Zamora's report was never in doubt...'

If you read Hynek's report on his 2nd visit to Socorro, you'll
learn that Felix Phillips, who lived only 1,000 ft. from the
`landing site' and was working outside in his garden, reported
hearing NONE of the noises that Zamora reported and Phillips who
promptly visited the site told Hynek that he suspected the
incident was a hoax.

Hynek chose to ignore same on the grounds that Zamora was NOT
bright enough to think up such a hoax. Hynek failed to consider
that the hoax might have been conceived by someone else--such as
Mayor Holm Bursom--and that Zamora might simply have been his
agent.

When I visited Socorro in late 1966, my investigation included a
chat with Phillips, and expression of doubt voiced by a physics
professor at the NM Institute of Technology. My investigation
concluded that the incident WAS a hoax, inspired by Mayor Bursom,
to provide the then economically depressed town with a tourist
attraction. Details in Chapt. 12 of my book "UFOs Explained".


In my response, I pointed out that Ray Stanford had
addressed these claims long ago in `Socorro Saucer' and as there
appears to be no actual evidence supporting the hoax hypotheses,
plus considerable evidence to the contrary, this could explain
why there seems to have been almost universal scepticism about
Phil's suggestion.

I also mentioned that Ian Ridpath (formerly a supporter of the
hoax contention) has noted he is now less sceptical about the
hot-air balloon rationale.


Phil makes one further comment about this case which I personally
found astonishing, however I'll say no more until that until
Tracy Barnes has clarified if either himself, or anyone he knows
of, had any connection with Zamora's sighting.

Barnes wasn't identified in the newsletter as I don't want his
name appearing all over the Internet in relation to `Socorro',
when no there's no proven association and current speculation may
shortly be refuted.

Unfortunately, due to his business commitments it's difficult (as
anticipated) to speak with him at present, however it should be
possible within the next week or so.


Phil's `blind faith' in his own conclusions, as with other
prominent CSICOP members and their `solutions' to UFO cases,
often seems to be borne out of anxiety that they are obliged and
expected to provide an `ordinary' explanation.

Does it really matter if it's evidentially sound? Or is the
inherent judgement that a mundane cause must be responsible
anyway, even if the explanation on offer isn't really `right'.

Some might conclude that Phil's prime concern isn't about the true
origins of the Socorro incident being revealed, it's that his
`hoax' allegation could be embarrassingly proven so wrong.

One thing that might affect this is the bending of light near the
horizon. This is the effect that keeps the stars visible longer
than they otherwise should be when they set. Since this effect is
variable (depending on the temperatures of the different masses
of air the light passes through), it could cause the path of a
meteor to appear to curve from the viewpoint of the observers.


One test: did anyone else report sighting a meteor (or UFO) at
the same time, and if so, where?

* A search of newspapers in the southwest might prove fruitful.

* If nobody else noticed it, it might indicate that the object
was a lot closer and slower.

Larry, Bruce & List,

Standard atmospheric refraction is approximately 0.6 deg at the geometric
horizon and it rapidly diminishes at larger grazing angles, so that it is
essentially zero at elevations of 25-60 degs such as in the Arrey case
(refraction actually 0.03 to 0.01 deg approx. which is negligible). See
graph in Condon Report p. 623.

Seeming absence of other reports is not a very good indicator of visibility,
it's like trying to prove a negative. Southwestern and south-central New
Mexico was in 1949 and is today a lightly populated region -- one reason why
the first nuclear test and rocket range was set up there (White Sands).
Daytime meteors do not attract as much attention as nighttime meteors because
of sunlight.

It also seems that the only reason even C. B. Moore's crew spotted the object
was because they were already looking in that direction to follow the pilot
balloon they were tracking.

Brad

UFO Research List - http://web.ukonline.co.uk/voyager/

The on-line `Search the UK Parliament' facility is maybe worth a
mention, especially for HM's subscribers.

It's a comprehensive record of parliamentary debates, questions
and answers etc.

A couple of tips: if the search criteria produces one or more
documents, go down to the bottom of the search results and you
should find the search input screen now lists suggested
`keywords', generated by your enquiry.

Clicking on the `check box' underneath any search result, then
selecting `expand' from the search menu, will also produce a list
of suggested `keywords'.

The database features some items on the `UFO' front [more hits on
`unidentified flying object' than `UFO'], including a few I
hadn't seen before - mainly questions from Lord Hill-Norton re
Larry Warren's claims in `Left at East Gate' [search on
`bentwaters'].

For information - this is some of the main `UFO' database
content:

in running the group. The group they want YOU to work yourself into the
ground for! And I know; I was editor of the Bulletin for 8 months of hell,
where my life was not my own. Where my life was effectively dominated by
meeting their unrealistic publishing deadlines. Once I did "take my time"
with getting the Bulletin ready; only to find that all the work I did was
"bumped" by another issue of the BULLETIN which Steven Gamble did behind my
back. He oh-so-kindly said I could incorporate my work with the next
issue; but that was only said so the "inner" council could censor what I
had to say about the Max Burn's fiasco!

- A fiasco that NO member of council has had the guts to explain to the
members of the association within the BULLETIN.
For that you have MY total undying shame and contempt.

Rather than pay court to such mealy-mouthed attitudes I ripped up my work
and threw it away; better for it to die in honor than live
in dishonor!

The only future the BUFORA "Inner council" clique offers British Ufology
is one where THEY dominate. One where THEY remain in power, but where WE
- the workers in the subject - can removed from what little crumbs of
authority they offer us whenever THEY decide!

BUFORA is a group controlled by a self-interested clique who's only
interest is to stay in power,at all costs. A group of people which did
all it could to keep Andy Roberts - one of Britiain's leading Ufologists -
out of any position of authority. A group of people which virtually
performed a UFO-political assassination on Jenny Randles, to have her
removed as BUFORA's Director Of Investigations. A group of people who
pushed through the Max Burn's lecture at all costs, regardless of the
concerns of it's more rationally-oreintated members.

But then, with the current council, scientific Ufology always comes last;
as we saw that with their handling of the Max Burn's lecture affair. With
most of them dabbling in R.V courses can one expect anything else?

We have forgotten NONE of this, BUFORA council!

Lastly, I am disgusted with Gloria's Dixon's support of these bunch of
people. If you really cared about this subject YOU would resign from
BUFORA and help the struggle for freedom and a new, more hopeful future for
British Ufology. Why waste your time with these people when you can do
something like "Strange Daze? " The logic behind that is beyond my
comprehension!

So, Andy Robert's and John Rimmer WAS right; Lionel Beer KNEW they could
woo you back with a box of chocolates, flowers
and empty promises, and he was right!

They win, but British Ufology loses, yet again........

And because of that we will see another generation of Ufologists eaten up
by the vile power games that consumes this association. Another wasted
generation of talented reseachers and investigators will leave this
subject, sickened by what they find.
What a total waste!

I say to you all; show your concern for British Ufology and boycott
BUFORA; or a least demand the resignation of Steven Gamble. John Spencer
and Robert Digby; an entrenched clique who's only response to ANY situation
is to shuffle positions of authority between themselves!

Never send me ANY more emails about your stupid "rolling projects", ever
again. I'm not interested in you or your works, and I'm tired of wasting
my life and energy on keeping you all important.
You have used me for the LAST time.

Let the future of Ufology - if it has one - be in the hands of the British
UFO community alone!
Robert Moore.

Whilst I share Robert's opinion of the losers and weak-minded careerist
nobodies within BUFORA - an organisation less relevant than Brechin City
Football Club - I can't see why attacking Gloria is in any way useful.

I count her as one of my friends within Ufology and not just a "colleague"
- the latter term being one we use when we're trying to be nice about
people we can't stand. She is NOT to blame for the current mess within UK
Ufology and is, in fact, one of the few people whose input has moved some
of us in the right direction.

It is true that BUFORA has killed off Ufology over the years and, in the
latest pathetic development, I understand that Lionel Beer has been
smearing me to book publishers and others in a recent campaign reminiscent
of the SHADOW saga of 18 months ago. (Why anybody would want to work with
these idiots is beyond me!)

Their value in terms of actual UFO research - which is largely undertaken
by a tiny group of about 20 people in the UK - is nil.

The way to move forward is not to whinge about Gloria - whose 'Strange
Daze' is excellent and her work on close encounters second to none - but to
remove yourself from the loop and continue to carry our effective research
and "scientific Ufology" (I'm not entirely sure what this is).

There are many mysteries of earth, mind and body still to be solved and the
longer we fuss about a failed and "has been" organisation with a few
hundred members the longer the problems will continue.
In the North West groups like NARO and MARA have pretty much given up the
ghost leaving researchers like myself and Eric Morris to do alot of the
work. We relish the task and, much to the chagrin of the Beers and Gambles
of the world, do it rather well.

Perhaps most important is our ability to talk sense about Ufology on TV,
radio and in the media. This week has been a particularly good example of
how little progress Ufology has made in terms of presenting itself as a
credible research effort - largely because the clique at the top refuse to
move forward or to admit that they have nothing to offer beyond a few
badly-attended London lectures.

As to Max Burns, he's been in court this week facing serious drugs
charges.....

That is certainly no hoax.

Get it together people......read BEYOND. The best paranormal magazine in
the Universe......

See you in Leeds if you're going...

Tim Matthews - MI5.

Let's just get this "chocolates and flowers" thing out of the way. This
was my interpretation of a typically patronising remark from Lionel Beer
outside the Fortean UnConvention earlier this year.

The former BUFORA spinmeister was suggesting that Ms. Dixon might have
been led from the strait and narrow path by the "Andy Roberts Crowd",
but that with a little gentle persuasion the scales would fall from her
eyes and she would be welcomed back into the bosom of BUFORAdom. Whether
this has happened or not is, as so much in ufology, a matter of
interpretation.

I did not imagine that my flight of metaphorical fancy would be taken so
literally, but in the world of ufology I should have known better...

I shall defend Ms Dixon's honour by publicly stating that to my
knowledge not a single BUFORA coffee cream or fudge fondant has ever
passed her lips!

On Thu, 16 Sep 1999 RB47Expert@aol.com wrote:

@Larry, Bruce & List,

@Standard atmospheric refraction is approximately 0.6 deg at the
@geometric horizon and it rapidly diminishes at larger grazing
@angles, so that it is essentially zero at elevations of 25-60
@degs such as in the Arrey case (refraction actually 0.03 to 0.01
@deg approx. which is negligible). See graph in Condon Report p.
@623.

Those are normal conditions. At the junction of air masses of
differing temperatures, the refraction can be more pronounced,
and vary with azimuth. This is not quite a mirage, but just
enough to make the path of a meteor seem to bend.


@Seeming absence of other reports is not a very good indicator of
@visibility, it's like trying to prove a negative. Southwestern
@and south-central New Mexico was in 1949 and is today a lightly
@populated region -- one reason why the first nuclear test and
@rocket range was set up there (White Sands). Daytime meteors do
@not attract as much attention as nighttime meteors because of
@sunlight.

I just thought that if any independent accounts were found, they
might be used to triangulate. If they weren't, it might indicate
that the object was lower and slower (emphasis on the might).

Denver, Santa Fe, and Phoenix might have sightings. The 3/3/68
satellite re-entry was seen over an area ranging from Tennessee
to Ontario, and several day meteors were seen over an area just
as large.

Larry & List,

The problem with normal vs. unusual atmospheric conditions is that at high
grazing angles the refractive index must be absurdly high, requiring
temperatures in the 100,000's of degrees or millions of degrees (which would
make the air a plasma and therefore opaque, thus obviating the entire
refractive effect). Do you have any numbers to suggest?

No one has so far found any independent sightings. As you say, the object
may not have been bright enough to attract attention. Also, if the visible
track was only 110-170 miles long (roughly half south of Moore's crew and
half to the north) that would not reach Albuquerque let alone Santa Fe or
Denver.

Brad

In a message dated 9/16/99 2:51:12 PM, lrobins@indiana.edu wrote:

<<

On Thu, 16 Sep 1999 RB47Expert@aol.com wrote:

@Larry, Bruce & List,

@Standard atmospheric refraction is approximately 0.6 deg at the
@geometric horizon and it rapidly diminishes at larger grazing
@angles, so that it is essentially zero at elevations of 25-60
@degs such as in the Arrey case (refraction actually 0.03 to 0.01
@deg approx. which is negligible). See graph in Condon Report p.
@623.

Those are normal conditions. At the junction of air masses of
differing temperatures, the refraction can be more pronounced,
and vary with azimuth. This is not quite a mirage, but just
enough to make the path of a meteor seem to bend.


@Seeming absence of other reports is not a very good indicator of
@visibility, it's like trying to prove a negative. Southwestern
@and south-central New Mexico was in 1949 and is today a lightly
@populated region -- one reason why the first nuclear test and
@rocket range was set up there (White Sands). Daytime meteors do
@not attract as much attention as nighttime meteors because of
@sunlight.
I just thought that if any independent accounts were found, they
might be used to triangulate. If they weren't, it might indicate
that the object was lower and slower (emphasis on the might).

If it truly was a meteor, and it was bright enough to be noticed,
Denver, Santa Fe, and Phoenix might have sightings. The 3/3/68
satellite re-entry was seen over an area ranging from Tennessee
to Ontario, and several day meteors were seen over an area just
as large.


@It also seems that the only reason even C. B. Moore's crew
@spotted the object was because they were already looking in that
@direction to follow the pilot balloon they were tracking.

That might indicate that it was not very bright.

Brad wrote:
>@angles, so that it is essentially zero at elevations of 25-60
@degs such as in the Arrey case (refraction actually 0.03 to 0.01
@deg approx. which is negligible). See graph in Condon Report p.
@623.
Larry wrote:
Those are normal conditions. At the junction of air masses of
differing temperatures, the refraction can be more pronounced,
and vary with azimuth. This is not quite a mirage, but just
enough to make the path of a meteor seem to bend.

<

Bruce writes:
Don't buy it. The refraction of air is low and it decreases with
altitude.
Differences in density at the "junction of air masses" causes very slight
variations in the already small refraction. the "large angle bend" (less
than a
degree) of light near the horizon (star/sun refraction) is largely a result
of the
long path I(several hundred miles) through the "sensible" atmosphere, with
most bending in the portion of the path that is lower than 5 miles. In
other words,
the integrated bending effect over a long distance.

When you go to larger elevation angles,, light paths do not travel
hundreds of miles through
the atmosphere. Moreover, since atmospheric layers tend to be
"horizontal" (follow the curvature of the earth, light rays at elevation
angles of 10 degrees or more are more likely to pass through the layer
boundary than travel parallel to it for many miles.

Lateral bending of rays in the atmosphere is limited to a small fraction of
a degree.

1: BUFORA could not afford to lose her and I hoped she would stay on as D of
I. She has done a terrific job in a post I still care deeply about (after
holding it for 12 years how could I not?). Nobody could be doing what is a
vital role better than she is doing and it would be a tragedy not just for
BUFORA but British UFOlogy if she left.

2: That she should accept John Spencer's offer to co host the discussion
forums and that I would publicly endorse her decision to do so. This does
not mean I support BUFORA council - as my other reply makes very clear. But
it does mean that I regard these rolling discussions as sensible and to the
benefit of UFOlogy and frankly that is all that matters. Everything else is
an emotive response fostered by the fact that they are BUFORA suggestions.

Gloria took her decision not because of any inducement and if Lionel really
is crowing as someone on this list suggested he wants to beware because such
an attitude is the surest way to cause Gloria to reconsider. I know it was
far from an easy decision for her this time. I know - like me - she has
enormous loyalty towards BUFORA and thats a trait we should commend rather
than attack. I know she believes that what she has done is in the best
interests of UFOlogy and was not some emotional reaction. Even if you
disagree with her move then you should applaud the reasons she made it
rather than find ways to criticise a brave step.

As for this having anything to do with Gloria being a woman. I will say
this. It probably does, in the sense that in my experience the most
sensible, intelligent and hard working UFOlogists are. Lynda, for example,
being no exception. Any nonsense about flowers and chocolates should be
dismissed immediately. Gloria was not flattered back to the job. She did it
after much soul searching and because she considered it was right for
British UFOlogy and I understand and can only support that decision.

Unfortunately, unless things change in the male dominated BUFORA power
struggle world of UFO politics this may not be a decision that is
irreversible. Since BUFORA needs Gloria a heck of a lot more than she needs
them I do trust that they understand just how close they came to losing her
and how next time, in my view, the decision would go differently. So, for
what it is worth, I can only suggest, that some appraisal of tactics is
carried out to make sure there is no next time.

Best wishes,

Jenny Randles

Subject: Re: Rolling Projects.........
This is a copy of a reply I posted onto Eurolist, for your information...
Jenny
Hi,

Let me comment on this BUFORA situation. It is, as you might imagine, a
complex one, but sadly an awful lot of what Andy and Robert have reported on
this list is true. It pains me enormously to say this as I remain vigorously
loyal to this association. The criticism of Gloria Dixon is also misplaced
and
can probably now be levelled at me, because I continue to do work for
BUFORA (I write and record a weekly news and information service available
to
all UK telephone subscribers from which BUFORA gets all proceeds). I am also
a life member.

This support is despite - to be blunt - BUFORA having treated me and
numerous other serious UFOlogists whom they could not afford to alienate and
in fact needed in key positions not as donkeys, as Andy puts it (donkeys are
cared for and respected by their owners) - I dont think there is an
appropriately awful word.

However, Gloria and I have not dragged ourselves away from BUFORA
basically out of loyalty. I know this is how Gloria feels, because we have
discussed it and we both knew how people would react when the BUFORA plans
that she and John announced were made public. Gloria asked my advice on
these matters three months ago and Andy will, I know, be shocked to hear
that I supported Gloria's decision to become involved and promised to openly
endorse it - as I now here do. Let me try to explain why.

I have been a member of BUFORA since l969 when I was at school. I was on
council from l975 to l994, when I was forced out by the stupid, petty
politics that is every bit as terrible as Andy paints it. BUFORA is a deeply
flawed association and will never change under present management. I am sad
to admit that but the evidence is overwhelming. I dont expect the management
to change either. So we are at an impasse, but lack of support for those in
command (which I certainly feel and I suspect Gloria has to some degree as
well) is not the same as lack of support for the association they represent.
For they are, after all, just 10 elected representatives of an association
of 400 (?) people (I dont know as members dont usually know basic facts like
this). Whatever the case it would be unreasonanble to reject the good things
BUFORA have done - and there are certainly some (eg the code of practice,
the
regression hypnosis ban, the postal training course, etc) simply because
some of us dislike the methods of the ruling few. You need to see the bigger
picture. Gloria and I are attempting to do that fully aware of how we will
be attacked as stupid for taking such a stance.

Also, you do not just dump 30 years of loyalty to a group overnight. They
dont want me - that much is obvious. Despite my long association across the
years they have operated projects into British MIB cases and are posting a
book length study of Rendlesham - two subjects I have been intimately
involved with, researched deeply and written a great deal about. Nobody in
BUFORA has approached to ask for advice or info.
I certainly will not go running to them, because I do not think they have
earned that level of one way support. Had they come to me, of course, I
would have assisted without question.

But dont you find it curious that they have utterly shunned me as a life
member and their longest serving director of investigations . Sadly the
answer is obvious. I am personna non grata because I have dared to publicly
question some of their policies from outside the council. This is regarded
as heresy and treason rather than - as I see it - a deep concern to improve
the association which needs to be told when it is making terrible mistakes.

In particular I took great issue and offence at their horrific handling of
the Santilli autopsy affair . They have also not taken kindly to my
suggestion that the extra money, brand new to UFOlogy, that UFO Call (the
news and info service I operate) should be used for the good of UFOlogy. I
only write, present and coordinate this scheme. I dont have a clue how many
callers it gets or money it makes because, not being on council I have no
'need to know' . However, rumours tell me it has made a lot
of money (several thousand pounds per annum at one stage - and thus over 10
years surely a tidy sum of money UFOlogy would never have otherwise had).
This money was virtually all profit and should have been used by BUFORA to
further UFOlogy in new directions. I dont know how it was used (again no
need to know) but I dont see anything BUFORA has done in the past decade
different from what it would have done without this income.

So I recommended a summit where all UK groups were invited by BUFORA to
suggest ways to invest this new money for the good of UFOlogy. I thought
this would be a great way to boost BUFORAs image as a means to show it
wanted to be part of the UFO community not apart from it. The idea was
rejected as being anti BUFORA - amazing as it seems - so I just gave up
trying! A year or so later BUFORA called a summit (although not for this
purpose) . I dont know who turned up. But I received my invite to the
meeting on the same weekend the event was held 200 miles away, making it
obviously impossible to attend. Others told me the same thing happened to
them.

I do not regard these issues as petty and I am not being politically
provocative. Indeed not being political is what BUFORA have preyed on when I
was sacked (for make no mistake - although technically I resigned - the
truth is that I was deliberately fired by BUFORA council in a deeply
depressing fiasco that I will not bore you with discussing here). I could
have fought back and forced the issue through the membership. I could have
stood independently for council and secured votes from the members who were
never even told how or why I left. I was like a chararacter in a soap opera
not killed off but who walks off set and is never mentioned again by some
petty scriptwriter and producer determined to 'show them who is boss'. I
could - as I was urged - lead a rebellion and create a new anti BUFORA
group. I did none of these things and just went quietly, as I suspect many
there hoped I would.

Why did I do this? Two reasons. One is the same one that keeps me a member
now and keeps me doing UFO Call - just as it keeps Gloria in the BUFORA
fold. We can see the potential of this group. It is basically a good idea
being mismanaged. It is the only sober national group in the UK. We need it.
I totally support the aims and ethos of BUFORA as a consequence - so does
Gloria. I just do not support (all) the team that presently runs it. This
puts me
in a tough spot. Indeed even saying this to you here will risk great wrath,
I suspect. But I am only reporting the honest truth as I see it and if that
is deemed heresy and leads to me getting into hot water surely it merely
proves the point. For any good organisation should accept criticism honestly
made and not destructively aimed at wrecking the association (as I certainly
am not). Sadly BUFORA seems to respond to such comments as if you have just
stolen its favourite rattle.

The other reason I still back BUFORA (but as BUFORA not as its council) is
that there is no credible UK alternative. To form one would be perceived as
treason - through my terminal loyalty to some degree even by me. It would
create a battle royal that might split UFOlogy (who would thus needlessly
suffer) . It is just too hard to think of doing it. As such BUFORA stands as
our one
real hope in terms of national UFO groups. Which is not to say there are not
other - probably better - ways of doing UFOlogy for the new millennium. I
suspect there are and I think all traditional groups like BUFORA have just a
short term future anyhow.

New ideas to revolutionise British UFOlogy are being planned now. I suggest
list members watch this space for an announcement in the next few weeks.

As such I backed Gloria's decision to take part in the BUFORA projects for
the above reasons, but fundamentally because regardless of who had suggested
them these discussion forums do make sense. UFOlogy in general benefits and
it would be petty not to recognise that and use disdain as a weapon. It
would just be a sign of anti BUFORA-ism merely because of where the plans
originate. I dont see these ideas changing my views on BUFORA management. I
am no less disapointed by the way the only national UFO group I have ever
belonged to has progressed (if not regressed). I am still of the belief that
a totally new direction for British UFOlogy is needed. But these discussions
forums - such as they are - can only be good for UFOlogy and really thats
all that matters here. So I do support them - with the rather large caveat
that it is the ideas themselves I support .

What Gloria does is her decision. Like Andy I rather suspect before long she
will find life on BUFORA council intolerable. A dozen others whom BUFORA
desperately needed to have on side and not as bitter enemies cannot all be
wrong. BUFORA need Gloria infinitely more than she needs them and when the
day comes that this realisation outweighs her commendable loyalty then
council could be in trouble. Or, maybe, they will learn lessons and fight to
retain her services. Who knows. For Gloria's sake I hope so as loyalty to
BUFORA should be (but hardly ever is) rewarded with mutual trust in return.

So in my view it is wrong to criticise her for making an honest judgement to
back these plans because in her position I would have done exactly the same.

As such, what you decide to do with regards to supporting these 'rolling
projects' should be a personal decision. By all means support those you feel
are in UFOlogy's interests. It is a pity that politics have to enter UFOlogy
in such an overt way as here because they should not be a deciding factor in
whether we support good initiatives. Unfortunately, as I am sure Andy will
say, this is the real world and politics are all too relevant. As such the
unfortunately those concerns over the direction BUFORA council has
taken cannot just be ignored.

I can only tell you what I have decided. I am not going to denounce the
projects. I am going to say, as I have said here, that they are good ideas
worth supporting and that I applaud Gloria's move to front them. Her doing
so will
help ensure their success and as to say anything different would be
petty. I will respect anyone who chooses to back
them.If anyone asks me direct questions regarding these projects where I can
offer data to assist then I will respond as best I can. But
personally,however, I will not myself become directly involved with them.
This is partly
due to my belief that there are other things of more fundamental importance
to the future of UK UFOlogy right now that I intend to devote my time
towards. It is partly in protest at what I regard as the desperate levels of
BUFORA leadership .

But that is my silent protest and not, as you can see, a denial of the value
of the projects or an outright refusal to assist. It is a carefully weighted
judgement call that I
dont expect to win me many friends either inside BUFORA (who will not like
my less than total support) nor outside it (who will regard this statement
as weak fence-sitting and not the call for revolution some may seek).

However, all I can do is be true to my own conscience and this statement
best expresses how I feel. I just hope people out
there - most of whom feel far more strongly in a political sense about
BUFORA (either for or against its place in British UFOlogy) - can appreciate
it is not an easy thing to balance.

Frankly I am sick and tired of UFO politics. I am interested in UFO research
and seeing a better future for the serious nature of the phenomenon to which
I have devoted so much of my life . I had always hoped to do this via
BUFORA, contributing as much as I could to UFOlogy in that way. I was proud
to serve as a BUFORA officer for many years with a UFO group that I truly
believed in as one of the best in the world and It was in no way my choice
to give that up, even
though getting the boot has done me a huge favour.

Now free of the petty bureaucracy, money making needs, and to be honest
total trivia that dominates the command structure of any UFO group I can get
on with investigation, research and writing. In the five years since leaving
BUFORA I have published eight books. I would never have been able to do that
whilst working on council to the huge extent I previously did because so
much of my time would have been spent, as it was , voluntarily
cluttering up my day doing work for BUFORA like coordinating investigations,
running the postal training course, writing UFO call, and compiling at least
one or two UFO publications for BUFORA to sell and make money from each
year. Not having to do such things has allowed me to inflict more UFO books
on the world - in a far more selfish manner - something you may or may not
regard as a blessing. However, personally, I would gladly have swopped that
opportunity for continuing to work within BUFORA council to produce the kind
of case histories I was planning when I was unceremoniously dumped.

But BUFORA chose this path for me. Not the other way around and its history
now and largely irrelevant. I dont let it dictate how I think or act. What
matters is the future.

So - I repeat - my gripe is with the BUFORA rulers not with BUFORA, per
se, who have many good members and whose ethos I support 100%. Nor is it
with these ideas for discussion forums here proposed, which largely I regard
as well worth doing. I wish I could separate BUFORAs ideas totally from
BUFORAs rulers and thus back these plans all the way. Sadly, as noted, this
is the real
world and BUFORA council has done nothing to earn my trust or respect
(although I do still live in perpetual optimism that tomorrow it may all be
different).

To summarise, the discussion forums have my support. They may well benefit
UFOlogy. BUFORA is to be commended for running them. Gloria should be
applauded for her decision to act in the best interest of the subject
regardless of political pressures. My support for these plans and for
BUFORA's priciples should not be in any doubt. That is why, to the apparent
surprise of many, I still do UFO Call and remain basically loyal to the
association. What I cannot pretend to have any support for is the management
council of the association - or, that is, certain members of it (not by any
means all of them as I do respect quite a few). But I can treat that as a
separate issue from endorsing good ideas that can potentially benefit
UFOlogy. As such I do not see any appropriate reason not to publicly support
Gloria's efforts to get these forums up and running.

Best wishes,

Jenny Randles

On Fri, 17 Sep 1999, bruce maccabee wrote:

@Bruce writes:

@Don't buy it. The refraction of air is low and it decreases
@with altitude. Differences in density at the "junction of air
@masses" causes very slight variations in the already small
@refraction. the "large angle bend" (less than a degree) of
@light near the horizon (star/sun refraction) is largely a result
@of the long path I(several hundred miles) through the "sensible"
@atmosphere, with most bending in the portion of the path that is
@lower than 5 miles. In other words, the integrated bending
@effect over a long distance.

So what is a mirage?

Sometimes it is a reflection off of a horizontal junction of two
layers of air with a high gradient in refraction index. In
this case, the image is upside down.

But in other cases, it is the bending of light due to an oblique
junction of two air masses with a high gradient of refraction
index. In this case, the image is right side up.

I have seen several mirages. I know they were bent light because
I later came upon the objects that were imaged. One year I saw
three mirages in the same place - while I was driving on a newly
paved highway in northern Indiana on cool evenings after very hot
days. They were images of vehicles that were much farther away.


@When you go to larger elevation angles,, light paths do not
@travel hundreds of miles through the atmosphere. Moreover,
@since atmospheric layers tend to be "horizontal" (follow the
@curvature of the earth, light rays at elevation angles of 10
@degrees or more are more likely to pass through the layer
@boundary than travel parallel to it for many miles.

Except when a dry front passes through or a stagnant bubble of
hot air develops over an area. Then the junctions are at oblique
angles.

Bruce, Larry & List,

You're right, Bruce, "bubbles of hot air" is straight out of Menzel.
McDonald retorted that most such oblique angle situations far off near-90
grazing angles would require temperature inversions in the 100,000's of
degrees F or C or K (it doesn't matter which scale). Of course he was being
sarcastic because at that temperature you really have a plasma which is
opaque. Alternatively you'd need refractive indices like that of liquid or
solid water, hardly the case here with the clear desert skies in the Arrey
case, moreover the fast-moving object could hardly stay within any refractive
water or ice layer long enough to smoothly appear to ascend.

Brad

Dear All,


In recent days (as I'm sure you've all noticed!) I have been one of the
most vocal critics of BUFORA's "rolling research" scheme

So, you all might say, what alternatives do YOU have to offer, Mr. Moore;
or are you merely one of Lionel Beer's "destructive" personalities, after
all?

To that metaphorical question I offer the following (all too corporal)
answer.

The biggest flaw with the BUFORA "roving research" projects scheme is that
it is research conducted totally on the terms of BUFORA's council of
management, rather than those of the British UFO community. Which sadly
WILL include - if current form is anything to go by - ALL the corporate
and UFO-political small-mindedness which dogs that organisation like a
thick, noxious cloud.

It also strikes me as quite a "feudal" way of conducting things, given that
we are almost citizens of the 21st century.

So, what DO I suggest?

 I suggest - and in fact KNOW - that important research CAN be conducted on
an individual basis. Unfortunately, the "hive-mind" mentality of BUFORA
(and in particular John Spencer, due to his love for corporate culture)
dismisses that possibility totally - for what reasons I leave to your
imagination and insight.

For example, on my own, I managed to collate a listing of 871 possible
British "Unknowns" (the PRIMEBASE) project. This I did with NO corporate
"master-plan" and NO assistance from BUFORA's research department
whatsoever. So, yes, major projects CAN be done by one person. In fact, in
MY view they can ONLY be done by one person. Research by committee only
results in "UFO politics". Working on one's own (or with a small group of
like-minded associates, if you like) can produce all kinds of wonderful
things.

Another example is Dr. David Clarke's recent (and excellent) summary of
the 1909 British "scareship" wave. Here's another point to mention. The
high-quality work upon which our most reliable knowledge of this affair was
- and is - all NON BUFORA conducted. If it were not for the sterling - and
independent - work of David Clarke, Granville Oldroyd and Nigel Watson we
would be far more ignorant of the various pre-1947 "phantom" airship and
aircraft scares than we are today.

In comparison, much of BUFORA's research work (including that conducted by
myself, I admit) is insipid in comparison. Why do I say this, you may ask?
Because (in the past at least) BUFORA "packages" work to specific
researchers - often those who are neither the most informed in that
particular field or are the most enthusiastic concerning the topic at hand.
A lot of it is also conducted (and determined by) UFO-political motives.
For example, I was given "Bolide" merely because others on the research
committee didn't really want it (well, after they milked it's contents to
fill a book or two). I took it on, not because I had a burning interest in
this topic, but because I wasn't given anything (or rather trusted with
anything) else to do.

Bolide as it stands now, is not (and never will be) a definitive collation
of source-material for "Ball of light" phenomena. It is -and always WILL be
- way too patchy and far, far too wide in scope to be any meaningful use. I
have called time on this effort - in regards to myself, anyhow - for these
very reasons.

It is far better to construct catalogues of specific data relating to one
topic, rather than a general grouping of totally separate data coming from
totally separate sources. Which could lead to one spuriously "linking"
these topics when there is NO real link. Where there IS a link that
connection is obvious (to those with the insight to see) in the first
place. And that is the flaws with BOLIDE. So, I have now called time on
this effort, spilt the data up and "junked" the more worthless elements of
it. Such as a newspaper clipping relating the tale of someone's television
being blown up by lightning! Yes, quite a lot of the data in BOLIDE was
THAT bad and spurious!

I will be sending the more valuable data to researchers interested in that
topic, to aid their far more important and meaningful research. For example
I will be forwarding the Will-o'-the-wisp data I have to David Clarke, who
can make far better use of it than I (or can pass it to those who will). I
am retaining the "earthlights" related data myself, as I am keen to start a
local project aimed at studying possible local examples of this effort
(provisionally termed "Project Mendip"), and it will be useful as a
resource for that. Earthlights data that I am willing (and have willingly
shared) with other SERIOUS researchers; none of which is "earthshaking"
however (if you will excuse the pun!).

There is also the work of Andy Roberts, relating to the 1973 Welsh mountain
crash. Again, an effort largely conducted by one person (assisted by
others such as Tony Eccles), comes up with excellent and high quality
results.

All this exhibits another important point - it's the ability of the person
that causes good research to come into being. If someone is subjective,
distorts her or his sources the end product will be valueless - regardless
of the infrastructure that supports such work.

And in ALL the independent work I have mentioned there were NO hidden
motives! Just people who were interested in a topic, did the work and came
out with results at the end of it. Work that got finished because it was
NOT bogged down in committees and politics. Work that was also unhindered
by negative reputations or exclusionist policies.

I know this approach works because I have seen it myself, time and time
again, work, and found that it has also worked for me.

So, you conduct your research and finish it; but what do you do with it
afterwards? In the pre-Internet days you could privately distribute it -
but the expense involved in this was prohibitive. Such pressures (among
other things) brought about the existence of UFO groups. Today, you can
e-mail copies of your final reports to every researcher in the world; and
with computer printers (and photocopiers) you can send the data to the rest
of those who haven't!
All for a fraction of the cost of doing things the "old fashioned way".

You can now also get your data pasted onto a website. Yes, websites can be
expensive, but if a (small) collective of people get together they can
become quite affordable. And there are pre-existing websites interested in
pasting-up your work, anyhow. For example, I am sure the IUN (or Magonia)
website would be more than interested in such work.

By giving a project such a wide circulation it allows for the option of
independent "peer review" and comment; the flow and tone of which will be
unhindered by the political control of a large organisation with it's own
interests, biases and agendas to fulfil.

Those critical of your work can then do either of three things:

1: Write a commentary on your work - the points of which are addressed via
an e-mail debate.
2: Conduct research of their own, which demonstrates the shortfalls of the
other study.
3: Jointly review each other's data and comment on the sum of it, on a
researcher to researcher basis.

The third does sound a little bit like the BUFORA rolling projects scheme,
but there are stark differences. For example, the flow of data between
researchers is unhindered by "UFO politics". And the interactions are
conducted on an equal researcher-to-researcher" basis. The BIG problem with
the BUFORA "rolling projects" concept is that this relationship is likely
to be on the terms of "Head of a big UFO concern" vrs (and I use "vrs"
with all due forethought) a "small insignificant non-group researcher!. I
do not consider such a relationship either healthy, productive or conducive
to "fair play" or generating good research efforts.

To end with (or hopefully, to start with), I would like to state for the
record that the IUN website has space available for YOU to post your
research on, or an internet "link" to your own research webpage. The IUN
already has the text of David Clarke's Howden Moors Incident enquiry. Other
items will be "going up" in due course, including the most recent version
of my PRIMEBASE project (which is still - and always be - ongoing, and
always looking for new "entries" to incorporate within it!).

With that hopeful note I will end. I wish you all the best with your
ufological projects and research and hope this little item will encourage
you that the best way to do YOUR UFO projects is on YOU own terms.
Following such an ethos can only strengthen your reputation as a UFO
researcher and will ensure your interest in this subject will not be
consumed by the petty corporate back-stabbing and ego-politics that has
plagued the UFO-group based approach of doing things since the
establishment of (so-called) "organised Ufology".


Robert Moore.

researcher and will ensure your interest in this subject will not be
consumed by the petty corporate back-stabbing and ego-politics that has
plagued the UFO-group based approach of doing things since the
establishment of (so-called) "organised Ufology".


Robert Moore.

I think the whole point is that most people are unable to think for
themselves as far as any kind of research is involved; that's why they need
organisations.

The only way to make any progress is to work with those researchers we
choose to.

I also feel that there needs to be an 'instant response team' to deal with
the many and dangerous myths being promoted by the few 'best-known'
Ufologists; these relate to the myths of alien abduction, crash retrievals
of alien craft and NASA cover-ups (of dust particles and space junk!).

See my comments on the NASA footage on Updates.

If you'd been at the awful UFO Magazine (UK) affair yesterday you'd realise
how vital challenging these prevailing myths is. I suspect that one of the
biggest problems is that all too many of the people attracted to Ufology
are looking for some sort of alternative religion. On the evidence I've
seen so far most are not able to critically evaluate evidence and ask
difficult questions relating to checkable facts and proof.....

After all, certain people at Max Burn's London Lecture congratulated him on
his excellent "research".

National organisations are dead; long live Ufological disorganisation.

Tim M.

> Subject: "THIRD WAY" RESEARCH.
> Date: 19 September 1999 12:46
>
> UFO Research List - http://web.ukonline.co.uk/voyager/
>
> Dear All,
>
>
> In recent days (as I'm sure you've all noticed!) I have been one of the
> most vocal critics of BUFORA's "rolling research" scheme
>
> So, you all might say, what alternatives do YOU have to offer, Mr. Moore;
> or are you merely one of Lionel Beer's "destructive" personalities, after
> all?
>
> To that metaphorical question I offer the following (all too corporal)
> answer.
>
> The biggest flaw with the BUFORA "roving research" projects scheme is
that
> it is research conducted totally on the terms of BUFORA's council of
> management, rather than those of the British UFO community. Which sadly
> WILL include - if current form is anything to go by - ALL the corporate
> and UFO-political small-mindedness which dogs that organisation like a
> thick, noxious cloud.
>
> It also strikes me as quite a "feudal" way of conducting things, given
that
> we are almost citizens of the 21st century.
>
> So, what DO I suggest?
>
> I suggest - and in fact KNOW - that important research CAN be conducted
on
> an individual basis. Unfortunately, the "hive-mind" mentality of BUFORA
> (and in particular John Spencer, due to his love for corporate culture)
> dismisses that possibility totally - for what reasons I leave to your
> imagination and insight.
>
> For example, on my own, I managed to collate a listing of 871 possible
> British "Unknowns" (the PRIMEBASE) project. This I did with NO corporate
> "master-plan" and NO assistance from BUFORA's research department
> whatsoever. So, yes, major projects CAN be done by one person. In fact,
in
> MY view they can ONLY be done by one person. Research by committee only
> results in "UFO politics". Working on one's own (or with a small group of
> like-minded associates, if you like) can produce all kinds of wonderful
> things.
>
> Another example is Dr. David Clarke's recent (and excellent) summary of
> the 1909 British "scareship" wave. Here's another point to mention. The
> high-quality work upon which our most reliable knowledge of this affair
was
> - and is - all NON BUFORA conducted. If it were not for the sterling -
and
> independent - work of David Clarke, Granville Oldroyd and Nigel Watson we
> would be far more ignorant of the various pre-1947 "phantom" airship and
> aircraft scares than we are today.
>
> In comparison, much of BUFORA's research work (including that conducted
by
> myself, I admit) is insipid in comparison. Why do I say this, you may
ask?
> Because (in the past at least) BUFORA "packages" work to specific
> researchers - often those who are neither the most informed in that
> particular field or are the most enthusiastic concerning the topic at
hand.
> A lot of it is also conducted (and determined by) UFO-political motives.
> For example, I was given "Bolide" merely because others on the research
> committee didn't really want it (well, after they milked it's contents
to
> fill a book or two). I took it on, not because I had a burning interest
in
> this topic, but because I wasn't given anything (or rather trusted with
> anything) else to do.
>
> Bolide as it stands now, is not (and never will be) a definitive
collation
> of source-material for "Ball of light" phenomena. It is -and always WILL
be
> - way too patchy and far, far too wide in scope to be any meaningful use.
I
> have called time on this effort - in regards to myself, anyhow - for
these
> very reasons.
>
> It is far better to construct catalogues of specific data relating to one
> topic, rather than a general grouping of totally separate data coming
from
> totally separate sources. Which could lead to one spuriously "linking"
> these topics when there is NO real link. Where there IS a link that
> connection is obvious (to those with the insight to see) in the first
> place. And that is the flaws with BOLIDE. So, I have now called time on
> this effort, spilt the data up and "junked" the more worthless elements
of
> it. Such as a newspaper clipping relating the tale of someone's
television
> being blown up by lightning! Yes, quite a lot of the data in BOLIDE was
> THAT bad and spurious!
>
> I will be sending the more valuable data to researchers interested in
that
> topic, to aid their far more important and meaningful research. For
example
> I will be forwarding the Will-o'-the-wisp data I have to David Clarke,
who
> can make far better use of it than I (or can pass it to those who will).
I
> am retaining the "earthlights" related data myself, as I am keen to start
a
> local project aimed at studying possible local examples of this effort
> (provisionally termed "Project Mendip"), and it will be useful as a
> resource for that. Earthlights data that I am willing (and have
willingly
> shared) with other SERIOUS researchers; none of which is "earthshaking"
> however (if you will excuse the pun!).
>
> There is also the work of Andy Roberts, relating to the 1973 Welsh
mountain
> crash. Again, an effort largely conducted by one person (assisted by
> others such as Tony Eccles), comes up with excellent and high quality
> results.
>
> All this exhibits another important point - it's the ability of the
person
> that causes good research to come into being. If someone is subjective,
> distorts her or his sources the end product will be valueless -
regardless
> of the infrastructure that supports such work.
>
> And in ALL the independent work I have mentioned there were NO hidden
> motives! Just people who were interested in a topic, did the work and
came
> out with results at the end of it. Work that got finished because it was
> NOT bogged down in committees and politics. Work that was also unhindered
> by negative reputations or exclusionist policies.
>
> I know this approach works because I have seen it myself, time and time
> again, work, and found that it has also worked for me.
>
> So, you conduct your research and finish it; but what do you do with it
> afterwards? In the pre-Internet days you could privately distribute it -
> but the expense involved in this was prohibitive. Such pressures (among
> other things) brought about the existence of UFO groups. Today, you can
> e-mail copies of your final reports to every researcher in the world; and
> with computer printers (and photocopiers) you can send the data to the
rest
> of those who haven't!
> All for a fraction of the cost of doing things the "old fashioned way".
>
> You can now also get your data pasted onto a website. Yes, websites can
be
> expensive, but if a (small) collective of people get together they can
> become quite affordable. And there are pre-existing websites interested
in
> pasting-up your work, anyhow. For example, I am sure the IUN (or
Magonia)
> website would be more than interested in such work.
>
> By giving a project such a wide circulation it allows for the option of
> independent "peer review" and comment; the flow and tone of which will be
> unhindered by the political control of a large organisation with it's own
> interests, biases and agendas to fulfil.
>
> Those critical of your work can then do either of three things:
>
> 1: Write a commentary on your work - the points of which are addressed
via
> an e-mail debate.
> 2: Conduct research of their own, which demonstrates the shortfalls of
the
> other study.
> 3: Jointly review each other's data and comment on the sum of it, on a
> researcher to researcher basis.
>
> The third does sound a little bit like the BUFORA rolling projects
scheme,
> but there are stark differences. For example, the flow of data between
> researchers is unhindered by "UFO politics". And the interactions are
> conducted on an equal researcher-to-researcher" basis. The BIG problem
with
> the BUFORA "rolling projects" concept is that this relationship is
likely
> to be on the terms of "Head of a big UFO concern" vrs (and I use "vrs"
> with all due forethought) a "small insignificant non-group researcher!.
I
> do not consider such a relationship either healthy, productive or
conducive
> to "fair play" or generating good research efforts.
>
> To end with (or hopefully, to start with), I would like to state for the
> record that the IUN website has space available for YOU to post your
> research on, or an internet "link" to your own research webpage. The IUN
> already has the text of David Clarke's Howden Moors Incident enquiry.
Other
> items will be "going up" in due course, including the most recent version
> of my PRIMEBASE project (which is still - and always be - ongoing, and
> always looking for new "entries" to incorporate within it!).
>
> With that hopeful note I will end. I wish you all the best with your
> ufological projects and research and hope this little item will encourage
> you that the best way to do YOUR UFO projects is on YOU own terms.
> Following such an ethos can only strengthen your reputation as a UFO
> researcher and will ensure your interest in this subject will not be
> consumed by the petty corporate back-stabbing and ego-politics that has
> plagued the UFO-group based approach of doing things since the
> establishment of (so-called) "organised Ufology".
>
>
> Robert Moore.

conducive

The hunt for evidence of a genuine crashed UFO of ET origin
has generated a great deal of controversy since 1947.

To date the UK has held little of interest for the crashed saucer
buff, with The Rendlesham Forest case being the only possible
contender. However this case has failed to develop into
anything other than a confused mish-mash of claim and counter
-claim.

The collapse of Rendlesham as a crashed UFO case has left
the post X-Files generation of UK ufologists desparate for a
credible 'British Roswell' and to that end various stories and
rumours have been rehabilitated, the most prominent of which
is the so-called 'Berwyn Mountain UFO Crash'.

The details of this case are too long to post here for those who
have little or no knowledge of the case but briefly:

* An enormous explosion was heard and felt on the Welsh
  Mountain of Cader Berwyn at approx 8.30pm on 23rd January
  1974

* Several local witnesses had seen unusual lights in the sky
  throughout the evening of the 24 Jan, both before and after
  the explosion

* A local nurse drove up on the mountain road and claimed she
 saw a large red/orange light with other lights moving above
  and below it on the hillside

* A search team from RAF Valley scoured the hillside but
 reported finding nothing

* The incident was widely reported in the media with no firm
  conclusions being reached

This is a very basic account of the event. However, there was no
mention of crashed UFOs/alien bodies/cover-ups etc
until the early 1990s when the case was dragged out of the closet
and re-interpreted. Despite the majority of elements within the
case being satisfactorily explained the Berwyn Mountain Incident
is slowly being nudged forward into the position of a 'British
Roswell'. The following elements are now embedded in the case
and people believe any permutations of the following took place:

* Nothing, it was all a complicated misperception

* It was a military crash

* The mountain was cordoned off and witnesses were turned
  away

* There was a huge military presence in the area for a week

* An alien craft was found/bodies were removed

* Radiation fall out in the area was high - leading to a leukemia
  cluster

* There has been a massive military/police/media cover-up of
  information

* Several crash retrieval team members have contacted leading
  ufologists with information about the event

and so on

None of the second series of statements have been proven, yet
are rapidly becoming part of ufolore.

What can be done?

The aim of Berwyn Watch is to chart a case-in-progress. If, as I
believe, there is a concerted effort to make this case something
it isn't then we have a chance here to get in 'on the ground floor'
and chart the development of a myth. Alternatively, if on-going
research by myself or anyone else throws up new information it
can be aired in public before it becomes set in stone.

Berwyn Watch can also act as a forum to discuss queries anyone
may have about the case, discuss source material and so on.
Additionally any new articles, book references, mentions in
lectures or in ufological gossip can be acknowledged and dated
so that the orgins of any new motif can be discovered and tracked.
If you know of any such information please forward it to me.

Several of the UKs prominent and active ufologists have spent
time on the case and have become players in the game, these
include:

Paul Devereux (neutral)

Wrote about the case in 'Earthlights' and 'Places of Power'.
Originally believed Earthlight phenomnena was responsible.

Jenny Randles (still thinks there is some mystery)

Has covered the case extensively in 'UFO Reality', 'UFO
Retrievals' and in IUR, Northern UFO News, Sightings etc.
Lectured about the case at conferences.

Tony Dodd (pro crashed ET craft)

Has written about the case in UFO (UK) magazine. Also in his
book 'Alien Investigator'. Has lectured about it at UFO conferences.
Refuses to reveal many sources of information.

Margaret Fry (pro crashed ET craft)

One of the original investigators in the case. Has published one
or two articles. Refuses to share information or source material.

Nick Redfern (pro crashed ET craft)
Redfern has devoted several pages to the case in each of his
three books (Covert Agenda, FBI Files, Cosmic Crashes). Redfern
has changed his mind about several aspects of the case but still
believes an ET craft crashed on Cader Berwyn. The case
frequently features in his lectures.

Russel Kellett

Very little know about this person's views, but said to be a believer
in the ET craft explanation.

Andy Roberts

Has done a great deal of investigation into this case. Brief
summaries written for Fortean Times. Article on the case due in
IUR in 2000. Full details of investigation in forthcoming book 'The
UFOs That Never Were' (with Jenny Randles & Dr David Clarke),
London House, Feb. 2000

There may be others who I am unaware of, working at a more
local level. Again, please let me know if you know of someone
with a specific interest in this case.

If you wish to know more about the case please consult any of
the source materials given above. If anyone wants a more
detailed bibliography of material on the case I will be pleased to
supply one.

Please feel free to forward this message to any lists, discussion
or news groups or individuals who you think may be interested.
Comments/criticisms welcomed.
If you wish to be removed from this list please send me a message
with 'remove' in the subject area and I will do so.

Happy Trails

Andy

On Sat, 18 Sep 1999, bruce maccabee wrote:

@Larry wrote:
@>So what is a mirage?
@
@>Sometimes it is a reflection off of a horizontal junction of two
@l>ayers of air with a high gradient in refraction index. In
@t>his case, the image is upside down. >
@
@Refraction... BENDING not reflection.... of light over a long path. But
@the path is within 1 degree of
@horizontal (generally within a few tenths of a degree of horizontal).
@CHeck on the Condon Report which is an excellent source for
@atmospheric effects on light and radar . Actual reflection even from
@sizeable density gradients (temperature gradients) that might occur over
@several centimeters (very rare situation) are not strong enough to be
@detected.
@The most one coul hope for would be to detect a reflection of a light
@source
@at night. ... and the amplitude of reflected light would be MANY orders of
@magnitude lower than the intensity of the directly viewed light.

The mirages of headlights over a hot road at night are reflection
mirages, not refraction ones. They are due to the total internal
reflection case of refraction physics, where refraction through
the junction would require a speed of light faster than that in a
vacuum. The image is inverted.

@>But in other cases, it is the bending of light due to an oblique
@>junction of two air masses with a high gradient of refraction
@>index. In this case, the image is right side up.
@
@Depends upon wether the temperature gradient has T increasing
@wth height (density decreasing with height... the normal case) of
@T decreasing with height (inversion). Lateral bending of light is
@so slight as to be virtually undetectable without optical aids such as
@a telescope (the image of a planet or star can be shifted a small fraction
@of
@a degree left or right).
@
@>@When you go to larger elevation angles,, light paths do not
@>@travel hundreds of miles through the atmosphere. Moreover,
@>@since atmospheric layers tend to be "horizontal" (follow the
@>@curvature of the earth, light rays at elevation angles of 10
@>@degrees or more are more likely to pass through the layer
@>@boundary than travel parallel to it for many miles. >
@
@>Except when a dry front passes through or a stagnant bubble of
@>hot air develops over an area. Then the junctions are at oblique
@>angles.

@Even in this case the refraction of air is so low that only
@light paths that are nearly horizontal and travel over
@considerable distances can be noticeably bent.



@You are sounding truly "Menzelian" in these mirage arguments.
@Have you read Menzel's treatment of the C.B Moore sighting
@(which Menzel calls the best sighting of the period 1947-1952)?

I seem to recall it, but I read it about twenty five years ago.

I did not offer mirage as the answer to the sighting, but only to
the curved path of the object. It was just a thought. I have seen
one high (30 deg) elevation mirage, so it's not impossible.

An aside:

It's amazing how ignorant of the sky the general population is. I
have seen more than fifteen sundogs (which are NOT mirages, but
ice crystal phenomena). I saw three this year (it helps to know
when and where to look). Yet I still come across people who think
that sundogs are figments of peoples immaginations.

So when they see one, they report it as a UFO???


Another aside:

What would you call an object that produces brilliant flashes in
the daytime sky? It has the following appearance:

- Appearance: 2 to 10 flashes per second

- Brilliance: similar to sun reflected off a car windshield

- Colors: range from white to pure spectral colors, change
  from one color to another

- Angular size: distant plane
- Shape: short fat sausage with domes above and below

- Tactics: hovering, erratic movements or jittering, occasional
  tilting, and vertical flight

- Sound: none

From: bruce maccabee <brumac@compuserve.com>
Subject: Re: Re: Arrey Sighting / Re: Voyager Newsletter - Issue No. 7

UFO Research List - http://web.ukonline.co.uk/voyager/

Larry wrote:
>
The mirages of headlights over a hot road at night are reflection
mirages, not refraction ones. They are due to the total internal
reflection case of refraction physics, where refraction through
the junction would require a speed of light faster than that in a
vacuum. The image is inverted.

<
The typical mirage over a road is caused by the road heating the
air just above it, decreasing the density of the air. Light bends INTO the
more dense (higher refractive) air the is higher up than the heated air
near the road. If you want to call this a form a reflection, then so
be it. The light travels faster in the air next to the road and more
slowly in the
air several feet above the road. Hence a light path that started downward
toward the road (at a VERY slight angle) would ultimately be bent upward
after reaching a minium heght above the road.
This is NOT the reflection of the headlight in the road itself, which can
occur
because of a semi-specular phenomenon called "foward gloss."

just filling in the 12-mile distance given by ground radar. No, it isn't a
question of UFO's using war surplus but of PARTIALLY mimicking our ground
radars. There were several signal characteristics out of 11 that were
discrepant with the known ground radar. I agree an ECM/Stealth-type exercise

of Electronic Warfare Lab, George Rappaport, if an ECM or electronic warfare
game or test could account for the case but he said NO. As for the airliner
hundreds of miles away in West Texas, Klass was trying to explain the ground
radar trackings in the Dallas area with it, NOT the ELINT detections of
ground radar signals which can be received at longer ranges than the
fourth-power reductions of a ground radar trying to pick up back reflections.

really, don't listen to those nasty people who keep attacking us",etc). As

situation is to listen only to themselves, and ignore everyone else!

And that's only some of their most recent objectionable acts!

Their obession with secrecy and underhand dealings is notorious. BUFORA
must be the ONLY group who feel the only way to win people's trust is to
create a culture of total secrecy, keep information from them, and give
group workers (those NOT within their "Inner Council" clique) no real say
in running the group. The group they want YOU to work yourself into the
ground for! And I know; I was editor of the Bulletin for 8 months of hell,
where my life was not my own. Where my life was effectively dominated by

with getting the Bulletin ready; only to find that all the work I did was
"bumped" by another issue of the BULLETIN which Steven Gamble did behind my
back. He oh-so-kindly said I could incorporate my work with the next
issue; but that was only said so the "inner" council could censor what I
had to say about the Max Burn's fiasco!

- A fiasco that NO member of council has had the guts to explain to the
members of the association within the BULLETIN.
For that you have MY total undying shame and contempt.

Rather than pay court to such mealy-mouthed attitudes I ripped up my work
and threw it away; better for it to die in honor than live
in dishonor!

The only future the BUFORA "Inner council" clique offers British Ufology
is one where THEY dominate. One where THEY remain in power, but where WE

BUFORA is a group controlled by a self-interested clique who's only

We have forgotten NONE of this, BUFORA council!

What a total waste!

Date: Mon, 20 Sep 1999 18:09:33 -0400
From: joel carpenter <ufx@mindspring.com>
Subject: Arrey, New Mexico sightingMessage-id:
<000701bf03b4$d20988a0$0100a8c0@mindspring.com>

UFO Research List - http://web.ukonline.co.uk/voyager/

A few days ago I mentioned the Navy Viking rocket launch that took place at
White Sands a few days after Moore's sighting on 24 April 49 - it reached 51
miles altitude and about 2500 mph, basically straight up and down. I did
neglect to mention another important flight at White Sands two months before
the Arrey sighting -- "Bumper" shot 5.
This was a V-2 with a WAC-Corporal second stage, designed to study the
problems of multi-stage rockets. It was launched at 3:15 PM MST on 24 Feb
49. At 20 miles altitude, the WAC-Corporal was ignited, reaching top speed
of 1.39 miles per second. The WAC made it to 250 miles just 6.5 minutes
after launch. It was going so fast that it exceeded the abilities of the
tracking facilities at White Sands and its wreckage wasn't discovered until
early the next year, 85 miles uprange.

The next phase of the Bumper project moved to the Florida Firing Range, and
this time the object was not altitude but range -- the Bumper 7 V-2 climbed
to 10 miles and pitched over, then the WAC fired, peaking at 22 miles and
traveling in a shallow ballistic arc 190 miles downrange at very high speed,
Mach 9 peak, the fastest man-made object in history (so they say). This
flight was on 29 July 50.

It's probable that Moore's team knew of the Feb 1949 Bumper launch and its
potential. Although the second flight never could have happened at White
Sands due to the limited size of the test range, it's conceivable that some
might have suspected a secret launch from the USS Norton Sound, the
rocket-launching ship which was then off the California coast on sounding
rocket launching mission. This may explain the concept that the Arrey object
was something secretly launched off Baja California.

I'm not asserting that that's what the Arrey object was -- just noting
possible explanation for the _idea_ that it might be a secret man-made test
object.

Joel Carpenter

COMMENT: The ELINT direction-finders only give angles not speeds or

exactly the same ANGULAR speed as the direct image of the ground radar, not
double in speed. The only way to get an absolute LINEAR speed that is twice
that of the RB-47 is to ASSUME a distance equal to the distance to the ground
radar (in that case by law of similar triangles the ground track of the image
would twice that of the RB-47 in the same interval of time). But we have no
such data.

Dear All,

Over the least 18 months you will have been aware of the controversy
surrounding Maxwell Burns, a self-styled British Ufologist.

He claimed, amongst other things, to be an 'abductee', a journalist, a
former DJ, a respectable researcher and much more besides.

Today, at Sheffield Crown Court he was found guilty of very serious drugs
dealing charges and is now in prison awaiting sentencing.

A small group of us in the UK warned that he was a dangerous,
criminally-minded drug dealer. Our warnings were not taken seriously - even
after it became public knowledge that Burns had been arrested and charged
with the serious offense of "possessing 875 amphetamine tablets with intent
to supply".

Not surprisingly Burns claimed he'd never taken drugs, that he'd been
'set-up by the intelligence services' DESPITE the fact that he was caught
in possession AND that his two co-conspirators pleaded guilty to the same
charges!

In recent months Burns had engaged in a lunatic smear campaign against
myself, in conjunction with another dubious character called Larry O'Hara,
and several other researchers who were trying to warn the UFO community
about his criminal activities. Burns posted a variety of illiterate,
libelous and defamatory material that indicated exactly what kind of person
he was.

The jury at Sheffield Crown Court soon realised that Burns was guilty on
both counts - it's just a pity that his supporters within British and
American Ufology - and we all know who they are - were blinded by his
fifth-rate research, his lies and deception and the wild conspiracy
fantasies that he forced upon us all. They will have to answer the
inevitable charges of having supported a criminally-minded drug dealer who
tried to flood Sheffield's streets with illegal substances.

In addition, you may remember that the British UFO Research Association
invited Burns to speak at one if its flagship London Lectures despite our
warnings. Whilst there are some excellent workers within BUFORA some
serious questions must now be asked of those who invited Burns to speak and
who claimed that they were 'upholding free speech'...
Furthermore, serious questions will be asked of the Cornwall UFO Group,
who, in their utter stupidity and in full knowledge of the facts, invited
Burns to address their forthcoming Conference. If they need a decent
speaker who does lectures of expenses only without recourse to criminality,
threats and drug-dealing then I volunteer to replace Burns....

(It should be noted that Burns made threats, via a supposedly secret
hotmail account, against both myself and my wife Lynda - now pregnant with
out first child. He admitted that he'd sent the emails later on.)

It's a pretty sad state of affairs when piece of drug-dealing trash like
Burns can be taken seriously by researchers who frequently appear on TV
documentaries and debates. Can we trust their judgement any longer? Can we
take the fence-sitters, who gave Burns the benefit of the doubt even though
his con-conspirators had pleaded guilty, seriously??

What does this say about Ufology and the lunatics who claim that Burns was
'set up'?

After all, in court Burns carried a folder with alien stickers all over
it..........

For two years both myself, David Clarke, Andy Roberts and a handful of
others tried to tell people about Maxwell Burns - but to no avail. Perhaps
next time we'll be taken rather more seriously.

Tim Matthews.

BY DAY, harmless UFO buff Max Burns wrote about his own ''alien abduction."
But by night the Sheffield city centre DJ was involved in the seedier world
of drug dealing.

Now he faces being abducted for real - courtesy of Her Majesty's Prisons.
Burns, aged 37, became well-known to UFO enthusiasts on the internet where
he
described how he was "abducted" by aliens when he was youngster.
Cheshire-born Burns said he wanted to act as a counsellor for other people
who claimed they had been kidnapped by aliens.

He claimed they left an "implant" in his leg and believed aliens were
responsible for spreading ME - so-called yuppie flu - to people they
abducted.

Burns became convinced the police and security services had launched a
massive cover up.

In an article in a UFO fanzine, Burns wrote that he believed a flying
saucer
had shot down an RAF Tornado jet after a chase over the city in 1997.
And he believed he was being followed by security services who were bugging
his phone because of what he had discovered about the case.
Burns claimed he was involved in probing what he calls "the Sheffield UFO
incident" when he was arrested on suspicion of drug dealing.
Sheffield Crown Court heard this week that Burns WAS being followed by the
police - but they were looking for illegal drugs, not UFOs.
Drugs Squad detectives had been following the DJ as part of a covert
operation against dealers.

And officers saw Burns speaking to a man in another car and retrieving a
bag
from a grass verge after a late night rendezvous at a motorway junction.
When police swooped on the car driven by a woman friend of Burns as it left
the M1 near Tinsley they found almost 1,000 amphetamine tablets hidden
inside a carrier bag.

Burns denied any knowledge of the drugs, but back seat passenger Suzanne
Bradley told the jury she had bought 50 of the tablets - designed to look
like the dance drug Ecstacy - from him on the journey back to Sheffield.
Bradley told the court she met Burns when he was a disc jockey and
described
him a "strange" because of his obsession with aliens and UFOs.
(David Clarke and Roy Emery, Sheffield Star newspaper.)
