Hi,

I have no axe to grind about Nick Pope. I like the guy. Frankly, if he's
made a mint out of UFOs and a monkey out of the MoD after his undoubtedly
genuine interest in the subject, good luck to him. But there are a few
points worth noting.

Firstly, I was BUFORA Director of Investigations during most of his posting
at Air Staff 2A. Several times during that period our paths crossed. From
these contacts it seemed that Nick was interested by and at least partly
convinced of UFO reality during his posting, not merely afterwards.

We do not know what impact the Florida CE 4 saga had - the one that happened
to witnesses Peter and Jenny but apparently impressed Nick. This case
occurred, of course, before his posting so its a point we need to ponder.
Since it seems reasonable such an incident - if it drove Peter to be
regressed (by Budd Hopkins) - has to have at least piqued the interest of
anyone in contact with it.

I find the extent of Nick's prior interest intriguing, only in the sense
that the evidence coming into the MoD appears to be no big deal. Most of the
interesting cases in 'Open Skies, Closed Minds' and 'The Uninvited' are
not - as many outsiders might assume -
MoD originals. They are, in fact, cases already in the UFO community - ie
the public domain. If the previously unknown reports in these books (ie
those that came to the MoD and not at all to UFOlogy) are reflective of the
essence of data the MoD received during Nick's tenure then it is hard to see
how anyone would be convinced of alien reality from them. But if they were
not represenative and there were other, better cases, that were more
persuasive why have we never heard about them? Or was Nick mostly convinced
about alien contact by cases that did not go directly to the MoD? In which
case why are the MoD missing all the good cases? Or, indeed, is it simply
Air Staff 2A not getting to see such stuff and is another, more covert,
department getting the higher calibre stuff? Such questions are of far more
importance than anyone squabbling over Nick. What really matters is what
Nick's data can tell us about the real goings on behind the scenes at the
MoD.

I did hear from BUFORA colleagues that during his MoD tenancy Nick had
private tete a tete's with some UFOlogists. I think these were never openly
promoted by him or these people (and understandably so ) because they might
upset the delicate balance of things during his posting. That was proper
then but is surely irrelevant now. It would be interesting to know what
opinions of Nick and the then current MoD stance on UFOs these UFOlogists
received during such soirees.

During the time he was at 2A and I was BUFORA D of I there were cases which
I considered solved (eg the March l993 west country sightings that I was
convinced were a space junk burn up). In my exchanges at the time with Nick
he accepted this was a likely source for some sightings that night but
sought to persuade that other reports that night were unexplained. This
was a curiosity - a UFO group arguing for a solution and the MoD trying to
suggest otherwise. Nick, of course, may well have been right. I am not
proposing anything sinister in his denials. But it was certainly a point I
noted and wrote
of in the UFO literature (eg an article in IUR that Nick evidently read as
he mentions it in 'Open Skies').

I interviewed Nick for my BBC TV documentary the year before his first book
appeared. I had read his MS then (and he certainly knew of this because I
tried to suggest changes where I had noted errors). For
instance, he had comments on the Peter Day film (a solved case) but these
were wrong. When I pointed out why these were wrong Nick did not even
recognise the case
as being in his book. As such, much later claims that Nick was surprised to
learn I had read his book before it was sold to a publisher do seem
puzzling.
Yet his agent reacted in horror long afterwards by
writing to editors I was associated with complaining in a way
that could have led to trouble with the publishers from
whom I make my daily living. It was a bit of a mean act by this man, I
thought. He is agent for Tim Good, Nick Redfern and Georgina Bruni
too and it seems odd if he was unaware that publishers do sometimes have
specialist
MS read by people who know the subject and can determine if the text
makes a contribition to knowledge. That letter from his agent to my
publishers was in the Spring of l999. Yet Nick knew the situation from my
meeting with him in December l995 and never indicated that this was an
upsetting
event despite our meeting face to face at least four times in the
intervening three
years. So why was there such a delayed reaction by his agent?

At the 1995 interview Nick told me he had not seen any gun camera film
by RAF crews when taking the 2A posting. Also that the MoD had never
sent people to interview witnesses - and so those claiming this event (eg
the
several witnesses in the book I was then researching - 'Behind the MIB' -
were
perhaps deluded by 'Walter Mitty' UFOlogists who were playacting.) I asked
these questions for good reasons. Firstly, Ralph Noyes (whose MoD posting
connected with
UFOs was superior to Nick's) was no supporter of the ETH. He thought most -
if not all - UFOs were IFOs and UAP. But he described to me
in detail his access to RAF gun camera footage taken during mid
air encounters. This was part of his briefing when taking the job. Access
was said to be restricted . Nick declined to discuss his
clearance level (which was fair enough) but it left me suspecting that it
could not match that of Ralph Noyes.

As for the denial that any MoD people had
visited witnesses, documents at the PRO prove this was untrue.
For instance, Wilmslow police officer Colin Perks was interviewed by staff
from an MoD Defence Intelligence gathering unit working in conjunction with
Nick's
then equivalent officer. This was in l966. It seems a safe bet to me that
other
witnesses claiming similar things for my book were probably being truthful -
despite Nick's suggestions.

Nick later told me when I raised the point again at a panel discussion
during an X Files conference that he now realised that RAF officers might
occasionally in the past have visited witnesses. But this sort of thing had
apparently not occurred during his time.

I interviewed one of Nick's predecessors in this posting, Pam Titchmarsh,
inside the MoD in August l983 when Brenda Butler, Dot Street and I turned up
unannounced with
the just released Halt memo and asked for affirmation as to its status. A
shocked officer told us that her time spent on UFO matters was just a
fraction of the week (an hour or two at most) - the rest of her working week
was spent on mundane duties far removed from any X files.

Thus either a massive increase in time alloted by the MoD to UFOs occurred
in the period l983 to l991 (in which case the MoD owe the public an
explanation as to
why), Nick did not spend as many hours a week on this role as some are
assuming
or else Nick invested extra time (perhaps out of work hours?) on a task
that he was personally interested by. If there are any other options here,
maybe someone can suggest one that I have missed. Understanding which is
true is important to unravel what is going on at the MoD, not to 'get at'
Nick - which is a pointless, shabby act, for I dont doubt his sincerity.

These are just a few points to be mulled over. And they are offered as
constructive
comments to try to get to the bottom of the MoD position on UFO study - not
in any sense as anyi Nick Pope propoganda, which I regard as the last refuge
of the jealoius mind. What surely matters is comprehending what the MoD are
up to and Nick's arrival on the public scene gives us an opportunity to do
that.

The apparent MoD interest indicated by the status of Nick's job frankly
makes little
sense on the usually stated premises of Whitehall. If UFOs are not
spaceships and no cases are ever shown to be unsolved then what could
possibly justify boosting the role of their UFO office from 2% of the
working week in l983 to what Nick implies was a lot more hefty proportion of
his time in l991?

That really is to me the issue we need to sort out here - for such an upturn
is either a gross waste of extra taxpayers money on a topic that the MoD
themselves publicly seem to regard as trivial or an increase in funding
because they know something we do not.

Which is it?

Best wishes,

Jenny Randles

I will shortly reply in detail to some recent comments re this
topic. In the meantime, I would be interested to know if there's
any further information about the following newspaper report:

'Salt Tribune', 24 July 1949

Pilot Reports Winged 'Vs' Over Idaho.

BOISE, July 24

Seven V-shaped objects which appeared about the size of fighter
planes were reported flying within 1500 or 2000 feet of a
civilian aircraft over the Mountain Home desert Sunday.

The pilot told the Idaho Statesman, Boise, that so far as he
could determine the objects were not United States planes.

He notified the Civil Aeronautic administration radio station of
his experience and the 190th fighter squadron of the Idaho
national guard reported it to McChord Field, Washington.

The Statesman quoted the pilot as saying he was "frightened and
shaken" by the experience. He said the objects, in tight
formation, but not the type of formation used by military
aircraft, were flying "at tremendous speed".

The pilot, the Statesman said, had wide experience in aviation.
He trained pilots during the war and operates an airport in the
Boise valley. He made his information available only on the
condition that his name would not be used, the paper said.

The pilot described the objects as being in the shape of a V,
with a solid, circular body under the nose of the V.

There was no evidence of any means of propulsion, he said - no
propeller and no smoke trails indicating jet or rocket power.

There were no markings of any kind. The colour, he said, was a
shade "he couldn't describe and hadn't seen before".

He said he had the objects under observation for two minutes.

The pilot said he was about ten miles west of Mountain Home,
flying towards Boise at about 10,000 feet on the right side of
the highway. He said the objects were flying at about 9000 or
9500 feet.

He described the formation as in two lines of three each with the
seventh object either in the center, between the two lines, or
above them.
[End]


This 'Salt Tribune' report is intriguing as it goes against the
grain in the prevailing 'flying saucer/disk' climate, makes no
reference to them and reports a sighting of objects which are
notably comparable to what Kenneth Arnold actually described.

Does anyone have a copy of the referenced source 'Idaho
Statesman' article?


James.

Indianapolis IN Mar 77 (Report by children)

Huffman TX Dec 80 (Helicopters were flying with the UFO)

The following newspaper clipping might be of interest - I'm not
sure how well known it is:

'Florida Journal', 4 July 1964

'Won't Tell Soul Next Time'
UFO Witness Sighs At Reports of What He Supposedly Said

By CHARLES RICHARDS

SOCORRO (UPI) - A Policeman who gained sudden national attention
Friday after he saw an egg-shaped flying object near Socorro said
Sunday his experience had taught him something.

Socorro Policeman Lonnie Zamora said he would turn around and
run, just like he did Friday evening, but next time he'd never
mention it to a soul.

"There have been so many phone calls," he sighed. And most of
Sunday he spent shaking his head over some of the reports of what
he supposedly said about the incident.

"Maybe you'd better ask some of these other guys," Zamora told
reporters. "I'm the only one who saw it, but they seem to know
more about it than I do."


_Denies Seeing Creatures_

Zamora denied he had seen any little creatures around the object
and said the unusual machine rose off the ground and flew slowly
away in a southwesterly direction until it faded out of sight. It
never got more than 20 feet off the ground while he was watching
it, Zamora said, contrary to reports the object had zoomed up and
away from him at a high rate of speed.

Two investigating officers from Kirtland Air Force Base in
Albuquerque said reports a man from the Pentagon would come to
Socorro were also false.


_Termed 'Fantastic'_
Capt. Richard T. Holder, a White Sands Missile Range commander,
termed the incident 'fantastic' but referred to Zamora as a
reliable witness.
[End]

I have come across the following article which could be the first
ever 'flying triangle' newspaper report. It mentions the central
red light which is a distinctive feature of so many later
accounts.

Not much else to go on I'm afraid and apparently no structured
object was actually seen. Pity.

Worth noting though:

'Newcastle Evening Chronicle'

MYSTERY FLYING TRIANGLE IS SPOTTED OVER NORTH

REPORTS of a mysterious flying object sighted over Tyneside last
night have been sent to the Air Ministry in London for
investigation.

The object, described as "a triangular formation of lights with a
red light in the centre," were seen by people in Consett, South
Shields, Fawdon and Fenham, Newcastle.

A spokesman at R.A.F. Station Acklington said today that he had
received reports on the phenomenon from at least two sources and
these had been passed on to the Air Ministry.

"I have no further information about this," he said "and even if
I had we are not allowed to release information".

Mr J. Leslie Otley, secretary of the Tyneside Unidentified Flying
Objects Society, said his wife and two neighbours saw the lights
between 9.15 and 9.40 last night circling over Deanham Gardens,
Fenham.

_BALL OF LIGHTS_

"A friend of mine, Mr A. Miller, telephoned to say he saw them
too, over Consett at 8.30 p.m.," said Mr Otley.

I reported the sighting to Acklington, who told me they had
received a similar report from a man in South Shields. In the
early hours of today I received a phone call from the Fighter
Command Headquarters at R.A.F. Stanmore, asking me for further
information."

Mrs Otley said she first saw a single light in the sky, but later
this was followed by "a triangular formation of lights with a red
light in the centre."

After 20 minutes, the formation moved off northwards, she said.
[End]


Assuming the lights were in fact attached to an object, its
characteristics were presumably sufficiently unusual for it to
have generated more than one 'UFO' report and from different
locations.

I wonder why 'Fighter Command' were apparently so interested. By
default, it was likely to have been an aircraft and surely they
wouldn't normally follow up on a 'UFO' report anyway?

Do our knowledgeable UK subscribers have any thoughts on this and
info on what exactly ''Fighter Command/RAF Stanmore' was then
concerned with?

This article was published on September 9th, 1960, which dates
said incident as the night of September 8th, 1960 and now the
earliest 'flying triangle with a central red light' case I'm
aware of.

>Do our knowledgeable UK subscribers have any thoughts on this and
>info on what exactly ''Fighter Command/RAF Stanmore' was then
>concerned with?

RAF Stanmore Park (to give its correct name) was the home to the
Headquarters of No 11 Group of Strike Command and was responsible for Air
Defence. It closed at the end 1998 and its operations were transfered to
RAF Bentley Priory. There are plans to re-develop RAF Stanmore Park for
civilian housing / schools etc.

Hope that helps

Cheers

John

Chaps,
Fighter Command was tasked with the interception of aircraft intruding into UK
airspace. Until 1968 the RAF was split into various "Commands" ie Bomber, Fighter,
Support, Coastal, etc

In 1968 Bomber Command and Fighter Command were merged into Strike Command.

Fighter Command was what scuppered Goering's plans for destroying the RAF in
1940 and its HQ was at RAF Stanmore Park (in Middlesex, I think). In the period up
to 1968 Fighter Command was tasked with guarding the UK's airspace from the
Soviet threat, so they would be interested in a possible intrusion into UK airspace.
Then they would decide whether it had, ahemmm...any defence significance.

Fighter Command also controlled the Bloodhound II SAMs on the east coast of the
UK and may have been a bit jumpy that something had appeared in that area
undetected. This was also the era of the Tripwire, so that jumpiness can be understood.
Don't you know there was a Cold War on?

Chris

At 02:16 AM 10/6/99 +0100, James posted:
>UFO Research List - http://web.ukonline.co.uk/voyager/
>
>The following newspaper clipping might be of interest - I'm not
>sure how well known it is:
>
>'Florida Journal', 4 July 1964
>
>'Won't Tell Soul Next Time'
>UFO Witness Sighs At Reports of What He Supposedly Said
>
>By CHARLES RICHARDS
>
>SOCORRO (UPI) - A Policeman who gained sudden national attention
>Friday after he saw an egg-shaped flying object near Socorro said
>Sunday his experience had taught him something.
>
>Socorro Policeman Lonnie Zamora said he would turn around and
>run, just like he did Friday evening, but next time he'd never
>mention it to a soul.

I find it interesting that a United Press International (UPI) story has a
byline (author). This would lead one to believe that Charles Richards was
a UPI reporter, rather than a "stringer" or a reporter for the 'Florida
Journal'. On the other hand, it is unusual (at least today) for a UPI
reporter to get a byline in a local paper, unless they are a known
columnist. If he did work for UPI, where was he when he got this
information, and from whom? I suspect we'll never know.

It has been well known that Zamora was not treated well by the press, and
the fact that his native language was spanish was one of the factors in
that. One radio station apparently made fun of his phrasing in english,
which allegedly caused him great embarassment. This treatment did nothing
to foster good will toward the news media, and to this day he remains
elusive to investigators and the media.

Let's keep in mind that all newspaper and wire stories were written by
reporters who often infuse their own beliefs and suspicions into the text
of their work. How many people on this "list" have been quoted by a
reporter at one time or another and found the text of their comments have
somehow become mis-construed? This is often the result of a reporter
trying to tell a story and asking a lot of questions until they finally get
the quotes that he (or she) needs. It is important that we analyze all
such reports for information that might become lost, but we must also
understand the limitations of that information and take it for what it is.

Steve

Date: Wed, 06 Oct 1999 12:09:39 -0400
From: bruce maccabee <brumac@compuserve.com>
Subject: Re: Socorro

UFO Research List - http://web.ukonline.co.uk/voyager/

REGARDING THE FOLLOWING
>
>The following newspaper clipping might be of interest - I'm not
>sure how well known it is:

>'Florida Journal', 4 July 1964

>'Won't Tell Soul Next Time'
>UFO Witness Sighs At Reports of What He Supposedly Said

>By CHARLES RICHARDS

>SOCORRO (UPI) - A Policeman who gained sudden national attention
>Friday after he saw an egg-shaped flying object near Socorro said
>Sunday his experience had taught him something.

SNIP

>"Maybe you'd better ask some of these other guys," Zamora told
>reporters. "I'm the only one who saw it, but they seem to know
>more about it than I do."


>_Denies Seeing Creatures_

>Zamora denied he had seen any little creatures around the object
>and said the unusual machine rose off the ground and flew slowly
>away in a southwesterly direction until it faded out of sight. It
>never got more than 20 feet off the ground while he was watching
>it, Zamora said, contrary to reports the object had zoomed up and
>away from him at a high rate of speed.


The problem with this is the same as the problem with all newspaper
publications of interviews: I don't care how "honest" or a reporter is
or how accurate he claims to be.... what he publishes can be wrong.

Now, I'm not saying that the above is wrong, only that we can't be sure.
Look at all the consternation over the newspaper accounts of the
McMinnville
case, for example. What did Evelyn Trent really say to the press?
What did Paul really say? Why was there disagreement between their
stories. WAS THERE disagreement, or was the apparent disagreement
merely an artifact of the way the newspaper stories were written?
  The fact is that a person being asked a question
tends to formulate an answer that answers the question and may leave
out other information that would change the context. This problem is
compuounded by the tendency of the questioner to already have an answer
in mind, and so he/she/ listens for the response he wants and shuts out
everything else.
   Suppose in the above the reporter wanted to find out if the story was
true that "small beings" were seen next to the saucer and suppose that
he asked the question this way, desiring to emphasize the wierdness
or "extraterrestrialness" of the sighting:
 " Lonnie, did you see any weird creatures, like any little spacemen, near
the flying saucer?"
  If Lonnie assumes the two
"children" were humans, he would have to answer,
 "No, I didn't see
any weird creatures or little spacemen near the flying saucer, but I did
see two children."
The reporter takes this answer, ignores the response about two children
because he was only looking for "weird creatures" and he writes,
truthfully in his mind, that Lonnie did not see any "creatures" near the
object.

Regarding the speed of departure, this could also be a matter of
"Relativity."
If the reporter askes,
"Did the UFO rise up and then zoom away?"
and if Lonnie wants to get across the idea that it rose up and moved away
slowly
at first and then accelerated he might say,
"No, it rose upward and hovered for a second or two and then moved away
slowly, and then seemed to speed up as it moved ."

As compared to (relative to) other stories about a fast departure, this
answer might seem
to the reporter to mean that Lonnie really meant it moved away slowly, and
so that's
what the reporter writes.

The bottom line is, in depth personal interviews are likely to provide more
accurate
information than newspaper interviews.

If, during the in depth interviews with the FBI, Air Force, Hynek, etc.,
Zamorra
described seeing two "children".... then he saw two "children" ...whatever
they were.

A while ago James posted some stuff about UFO files held
at the PRO.

My colleague dave Clarke and I have just returned from a four
day stint there looking mainly at the recently released 1967 files.
This has turned up some interesting material, including much]new
stuff about UK government UFO policy, and this will be released
in a month or two as a UFOIN research document on the pivotal
1967 UFO 'wave'.

Whilst we were there I checked out the 'Bang On' reference
James gave. This consisted of a five page newsletter
published by 115 Squadron. It was issue no. 1, dated Dec 31
1943. I couldn't find any references to other issues.

In a section headed 'Phenomena' the following was written:

>PHENOMENA

>Under this heading there occur from time to time reports of
>weird and wonderful apparitions seen during our (and the
>American) attacks on Germany. We have asked our local
>Inner Circle bloke to comment on the latest species of wizardry. Here
>is his story....believe it or not.

>On the 11th December the Yanks paid one of their daylight visits
>to Emlen. Visibility was good and the weather clear."An unidentified
>object was seen in the target area. It was about the size of a
>Thunderbolt and passed 50/75 yards beneath the formation. It
>flew STRAIGHT and LEVEL. (No chaps it was not a Lanc gone mad..)
>at a terrific speed, leaving a streak like a vapour trail which was all
>white and which remained visible for a long time. The object passed
>so quickly that the observer could not determine it more accurately..."

>Suggestions will be welcome...serious ones...as to what this Loch Ness
>Monster of Emlen might have been.

A couple of paragraphs later, after some general stuff about the raid
it says:

>In another attack...this time on Bremen...there were many reports of
"silver
>and red discs above the formations". These have been seen before
>but up to now no-one has been able to decide their purpose.
>Suggestions please.

So, there y'go.

On a related note, I checked several of the files for the Schweinfurt
raid to search for the reference, originally given by Martin Caiden,
to small discs flying in and amongst the formation. I couldn't
find anything which was relevant.

Happy Trails

Andy

Emden was a favourite target for the 8th AF and the RAF as it was on the NW coast
with little or no overflying of flak batteries. The RAF performed numerous
"Gardening" missions to plant vegetables (that's minelaying missions to you and me).

A small aircraft traveliing really fast trailing a single vapour trail would be a Me 163
Komet.

According to The Warplanes of the Third Reich,

Tactical testing by Erprobungskommando 16 on the Me 163B commenced at
Peenemunde in early 43, but after Bomber Command flattened it in July 43, moved to
Bad Zwiscenahn near Oldenburg. Oldenburg according to my Atlas is just down the
road from Emden as the Komet flies.

so, calm down, calm down.

ever seen on the case.

The one point I thought notable was that Zamora reportedly denied
seeing any 'little creatures'. Interesting, if only confirmation
that we know he was reticent to acknowledge any sighting of
'figures'.


>The bottom line is, in depth personal interviews are likely to
>provide more accurate information than newspaper interviews.

For sure. I suppose we have to take any case material on merit,
there's always the possibility it contains some key and little
known/long forgotten evidence.

Which, in retrospect, is exactly what lies behind recent
'resurrection' of the Socorro story. Was there a magazine article
in which a hot-air balloonist recalled how his balloon spooked a
local cop and does that refer to Zamora.

Still unanswered questions, with, as discussed, Tracy Barnes
being the most likely candidate. It's being pursued and hopefully
can be clarified shortly.

If that is the explanation - although puzzling why it was never
picked up on at the time of any such article - this doesn't in
any way detract from Zamora as a witness.

We can surely now understand how he was only able to obtain brief
glimpses of the object, with rarely a clear view, or without
having lost his glasses.

Zamora could only describe what he observed. Unresolved, the fact
it became a celebrated UFO encounter was inevitable and arguably
justified.


What comes out of this article is Zamora's regret he ever
mentioned the incident.

As Mac Brazel would doubtless concur.
I wonder how many people have been influenced by such publicised
regrets, or the general 'stigma' sometimes associated with 'UFO'
reports and have never 'told a soul' about their own experience.

Would that particularly apply to pilots, police officers,
politicians, 'professionals' in the medical, legal, business etc.
fields, ministers/priests etc., 'minority groups', 'respected'
academics and scientists?

Add the vast number of military personnel and government
employees, plus doubtless other 'categories' which can be thought
of, it encompasses a sizeable percentage of the population who
are possibly unlikely to ever report a 'UFO' or related incident,
although of course some therein will.

In addition to those who have a 'position' or 'reputation' to
consider, there is the opposite end of the spectrum - those who
would want nothing to do with 'authority', or simply never
consider they should contact the media and least of all a 'UFO
organisation'.

That's excluding the recognised 'third world', numerous other
countries where the culture or communications preclude the very
idea, and/or where merely surviving is enough to contend with.


It's a digression, however, not unrelated to the question - would
you report a 'UFO'?

[And if so, to whom?]

At a (very) rough guess, maybe some eighty per cent of the
world's population wouldn't - perhaps ninety per cent?

In an ideal research world, which might be attainable if UFO
research had any perceived scientific merit or other funding
obtained, investigators could be sent to arbitrary 'third world
etc. locations and conduct an analysis of local
sightings/experiences.

I'm sure it would be insightful, whatever the results.

I will personally volunteer for two weeks, all expenses paid, in
the Bahamas.

Yes, I know it's a tough assignment, but somebody has to do it.


James.

Luis,

Thank you for the interesting observations.

This 'Brooklyn Bridge' story is one I have in the past referred
to as a landmark example of how incredulous claims are eagerly
accepted to be plausible 'evidence'.

How can anyone complain that isn't representative of 'ufology'.
It is, as proven by how frequently Budd Hopkins or Linda
Napolitano (apparently Cortile's real name) are invited to
recount the tale at UFO related conferences.

What I can add to your posting is that the following comments
were published on a CompuServe forum by someone who seems to have
an insightful knowledge of the affair. Although some subscribers
will probably know who the writer is, I won't disclose their name
as they probably wouldn't wish to be identified:

Date: 14 August 1997

Hi. I've been involved with the case since around 1992 and helped
Budd with some of the investigation. There are numerous problems
that have surfaced with the case that we are still in the process
of checking, however since this is still ongoing I am not at
liberty to discuss all of them. What I can say is that this case
either happened pretty much the way Budd reported it, OR, it was
a well orchestrated, well engineered hoax. I lean toward the
latter, however the keywords to remember here are "well
orchestrated". This isn't a simple hoax. If it was in fact a
hoax, someone did their homework, at least more than marginally.
But there are some things that are as plain as the noon day sun
that should be questioned (and never were) and we are in the
process of questioning them.

If the story is true these things will hold up to scrutiny. If
not we should be able to ferret out some *more* damning evidence
before long. We have quite a bit right now that taken as a whole
puts the entire case in question. But others before have tried
and more or less failed to dissuade the main proponents of the
case from believing it hook, line and sinker. In plain English -
The BS detector went off bigtime but not everyone sees this as
yet.

**EDITED** I decided to edit the rest of my original response for
the time being. Never know who's lurking. Stay tuned. <G>
[End]


Date: 15 August 1997

I just spent the better part of this morning responding to this
post and then filed it away rather than send it. It's was too
explosive and I need to confer with some associates before
blowing any whistles and also need to take care of a personal
matter before I take on certain people. But I will. I'm
contemplating publish my findings right here in this section and
basically punt the ball into the hoaxers field. I'm sick of the
nonsense and lies. I spent 2 1/2 hours on the phone last night
with one of the "witnesses". This person confirmed my suspicions.
I need to look into legal and criminal remedies before going any
further. That could take a little while. But I promise you
haven't heard the last of me. <g>
[End]
The full revelations never came out.

I recently wrote to this person asking if they would like to now
comment further and was informed the situation hadn't changed.

That's understandable if they are, or were, so close to those
directly involved and anxious not to be responsible for hurting
anyone.

However, _considerably more_ was publicly revealed by this writer
in 1997 (I still have all the correspondence on file), especially
concerning the inadequacies of Hopkins' research.

I also note that Joe Stefula publicly claimed on CompuServe of
Linda Napolitano, "I have copies of her telephone calls to Rich
Butler in which she states she gets 50 per cent of all money made
by Hopkins on her story".

If this 'Brooklyn Bridge' of ufology is significant, it might be
the questions it asks of proponents and publicists who supported
any premise that the story was ever conceivably credible.

of the deepest concern.

I doubt ET had anything to do with it......

Feds curious about high-tech conclave on extraterrestrials

By Matt Beer
EXAMINER TECHNOLOGY WRITER                  Friday, October 8, 1999

NASA agent probes Silicon Valley meeting with UFO theorist

An upcoming private meeting between Silicon Valley high-tech executives,
NASA scientists and a high-profile UFO enthusiast has sparked an
investigation by a government agency.

Special Agent Keith Tate, an investigator with the Long Beach branch of
NASA's Office of Inspector General, has been calling Silicon Valley sources,
including The Examiner, seeking information about a planned Tuesday meeting
between research scientists and Silicon Valley high-tech executives.

At that meeting, first reported by The Examiner, attendees, including
scientists from the NASA Ames Research Center in Mountain View, will discuss
propulsion technologies.

"We're trying to determine if any proprietary information will be talked
about at that meeting," said Tate. "We're very concerned about this."

Staging the meeting will be the International Space Sciences Organization.
Its founder is Joe Firmage, a 28-year-old, high-tech executive who made
headlines late last year when he published a Web site and book in which he
recounted his beliefs in space aliens. On the ISSO site, he claims to have
been visited in his bedroom one night by such an alien.

Firmage also has stated that some of the high technology of today was
obtained from the legendary alien space craft crash at Roswell, N.M., in
1947. Firmage stepped down from his post as CEO of the giant Santa
Clara-based USWeb Internet consulting firm following his revelations, due to
shareholder concerns about his extraterrestrial pursuits.

ISSO spokesman Tony Young had no comment on the NASA probe.

Over the last several years, NASA has been researching an array of exotic
propulsion technologies through a small program dubbed Breakthrough
Propulsion Physics.

Some of these techniques thumb their noses at Albert Einstein's theory of
relativity, which postulates that nothing can travel faster than the speed
of light * 186,00 miles per second. These include using technologies
familiar to science fiction fans: worm holes and warp drives.

Firmage, according to his Web site, believes "there is stunningly good
evidence that UFOs are real starships." He writes that "whatever did or did
not happen at Roswell in 1947 will ultimately prove to be a rounding error
when the implications of this phenomenon become widely known."


©1999 San Francisco Examiner

Yes. I have copies of the photos. They are in Craig's book. The
object in the photos is bright red. The background contains
nothing but sky.

The object is the lid off a large plastic cannister. The
cannister was clear, made in the shape of Santa Claus, and was
sold full of cookies. The lid was a stylized Santa hat made of
red opaque plastic. It is shaped like a disk, with a peak in the
center and a beveled rim, and is bright red. It is maybe 7 inches
in diameter and 3 inches tall at the peak.

I used to have the same cannister, bought in 1965 or 1966 for
$3.95. I recognized the object as soon as I saw the photos. They
also sold a fat elf cannister, with an identical lid (made of
green plastic), full of the same cookies. Another similar
cannister had a similar top, but was in the shape of a fire
hydrant and was full of dog biscuits.

Also, there were two other photos taken in between the two UFO
photos, according to the numbers on the film.

To recap on Paul Hanmer's case report:

"As a Chartered Accountant, I often have to oversee audit
assignments with a strict timetable. This leads to the need to
work long hours. In March 1978, I was working on such an
assignment in my home county of Lincolnshire, UK. One Thursday
night, I finished work at about 10.30pm and drove a colleague
home to the village of Alford. In general, the coastal areas of
Lincolnshire are very flat. However, Alford lies on the edge of
gently rolling countryside - the Lincolnshire Wolds.

My route home took me up a hill on the A1104 towards Ulceby
Cross. Part way up the hill, at around 11:00 p.m., I was dazzled
by what I took to be the undipped headlights of an oncoming car.
I flashed my own headlights and slowed. To my astonishment, the
oncoming lights slowly "took off" from the road and gracefully
flew to my right. Excitedly, I stopped my car, wound down the
driver's side window and peered out. The sight that greeted me
will stay in my memory forever.

I saw that the lights were coming from a massive, beautiful
aircraft which had now turned, was flying at a height of about 50
feet and was now heading towards the coast directly over my car!
The craft was shaped like a delta, very similar to the Vulcan
bombers based in Lincolnshire at the time.

However, it was about four times the size of a Vulcan, flew
extremely slowly and was absolutely silent! All leading edges of
the delta were beautifully rounded - there were no sharp
protuberances such as a tailplane. The underside of the craft was
coloured sky blue. It just glided over me and headed towards the
coast - no noise, no smoke, no vibrations, no smell - just an
aircraft of sheer gargantuan beauty".

reflection from the white. At one point the all RAF aircraft lost
their underwing serials and the roundals became very small. The
current fashion is light grey with toned-down markings which are
very hard to see.<<

applied if a go around was required. A Vulcan landing was a

slow the aircraft on landing e.g the pilot kept the nose high
until the speed dropped and nose wheel touched the runway when

From: Chris Gibson <cgibson@skomer.u-net.com>
Subject: Odd phenomena over Germany in WW2Message-id: <E11c7mI-0002zD-
00@serv1.is1.u-net.net>


UFO Research List - http://web.ukonline.co.uk/voyager/

Air crew on day and night raids over the Reich saw all sorts of odd stuff, much of
which turned out to have a logical, if unpleasant explanation. These led to all sorts of
beliefs and myths amongst the crews.

Bomber Command, being mainly night operation oriented, had many such stories. eg
Keeping the H2S radar and Monica tail warning radar turned on as it was believed
these protected the bomber from nightfighter attack. The Luftwaffe in fact used these
to home in on the bombers and it was only after a long period of time, (after a
Luftwaffe Ju-88 nightfighter defected to the UK), that the order went out that these
were to be turned off, or in the H2S case, unless they were actually being used.

One of the more enduring myths was the Scarecrow. Bomber Command crews
believed (or perhaps had been told) that the German flak defences had a shell that
could emulate an exploding Lancaster. These "Scarecrow" rounds were meant to
show the crews that many of their number were dying as bombers were destroyed by
flak. In actual fact, again discovered later on, the Nachtjaegers were using upward
firing cannon called "Schrage Musik" to hit bombers from below without the use of
tracer. Any on-looking crew would see a large explosion with no plausible reason, no
gunfire, no flak. The airmen called them "ScareCREWs". Bomber Command operated
as widely spread streams, so it was rare to see other aircraft on a raid, until they went
on fire or exploded.

The Luftwaffe also employed various lights and flares to guide the nightfighters.
Bomber Command raids were characterised by their profligate use of flares and
target markers. I'd be cautious about any interpretation of these war stories from a
UFO viewpoint. I think before reading too much into combat reports from the war,
you must appreciate that these guys went through a traumatic experience and some of
this might come out in the reports. Some idea of the tactics and equipment of the
period helps as well. John's revelation of the gliding Vulcans shows how innovative
tactics were evolved to meet the needs, so perhaps some of the tactics from the era
remain buried in the archives.

If you want to read more about these guys who went out night after night, in
vulnerable aircraft with dodgy Oxygen supplies AND some-one trying to kill them,
Martin Middlebrook has published a series on particular raids of the war. (including
an excellent one on Schweinfurt)

Could the red and white disks actually be parachutes? Aerial mines were a favourite
wonder weapon on all sides whch invariably proved to be largely innefective.

I still think the high speed aircraft trailing vapour is a Me 163. It's in the right place
(Emden) at the right time (late 43) and acting in a similar fashion.
Chris

In addition, I have a source* that says that the French
Underground was using tissue-paper fire-balloons to give the
Germans something to waste ammunition against. Even the name
fits: Feu fighters. Feu means fire, and is pronounced "foo." So,
as Smokey Stover always said, "Where there's foo, there's fire".

This was over occupied France, not Germany. The balloons were
easy to hide from German troops, because they could be used
upside-down as party lanterns (thus, finding a stock of them in
a home would not seem suspicious).

They were almost impossible to shoot down. If the Germans did hit
one, they couldn't find the wreckage of the "enemy plane," just
some spent party decorations.

I also saw a movie once showing the Underground launching some of
these, but I can't remember which movie it was (I hadn't heard
of foo-fighters at the time, so the need to record the title of
the war movie was not present).

Additionally, I know the Japanese were using fire balloons, both
at home (to confound enemy fighters), and over California, flying
in bombs that set many fires (mostly in what were then sparsely
populated areas). The 1942 "air raid" over LA was probably one of
these.

Hi Bruce -

Again, I need to know the weapon being used. However, as an example the
American Browning M-2, fifty caliber machine gun has a muzzle velocity of
about 2900fps (884mps).
Once the round leaves the barrel (muzzle velocity) it begins to deteriorate,
as I'm sure you know. The effective range is about 11,000 feet (though the
round can climb higher). Looking at the muzzle velocities of a number of
machine guns put the range at about 2800 to about 3000fps. If I had the
precise weapon, I might be able to find the exact numbers, but if we're
talking about German weapons during WWII, that information might be more
difficult to locate. The tracer rounds would burn out within five or six
hundred yards, then all you have is a light weight bullet.

If you remember those scenes of the being of the Gulf War, with the green
glowing images of the rounds being fired, what we saw were the tracers and as
they winked out, it meant that the combustible material had burned out, but
the round continued climbing until its energy was expended and the round
began to fall back to earth. The reason you don't want people firing into the
sky at holiday time is because those bits of lead return to earth, falling
like little bits of lead rain. Drop an 185 grain bullet from 5000 feet and it
can do a great deal of damage.

Hope this helps.

KRandle

therefore 800(81.6) - ,5 x 9.8 x (81.6)^2 = 32,653 m.

This is pretty high up. I expect a lot higher than the aircraft, meaning
that tracer rounds would be still going up as they passed the planes. At
6,000 m altitude (planes?) the time would be (solve quadratic eqn) about
7.9 sec and the velocity about 800 - 9.8x7.9 = 722 m/sec upward.

Of course, if fired at an angle, not vertical, the vertical component would
be lower than calculated (and so would the ultimate height). If fired at
45 degrees only th vertical component is affected by gravity: 800 cos 45 =
565 m/sec.
Now the time to 6,000 altitude is about 11 sec and the vertical component
of velocity is 565 - 9.8 x 11 = 457 m/sec. The horizontal component would
be 800 sin 45 = 565 m/sec, so the composite velocity would be (565^2 +
457^2)^.5
= 727 m/sec at an angle of arctan(457/565) = 39 degrees.

OK, take the lowest of these velocities at 6000 m: in 1/30 of a second the
round would move, say, 727/30 = 24 m. That means the tracer round would
cross the fuselage of a plane (no more than 10 m high) in 1 video frame
(or, if film at 24 frames/sec, would travel 727/24 = 30 me in one frame).

Of course, this calculation is related to tracer fire going up. By
conservation of energy..ignoring friction, if the tracer lasted long enough
to arc over and come down and still be glowing, it would be traveling at
essentially the same rate, but downward.

Bottom line: the objects filmed lasted too long to be tracer fire under
conditions such as considered here.

@Primary reasons why Arnold's nine Cascade mountain objects might
@not have been birds was their highly reflective nature and
@apparent airspeed. He would therefore have to be deceived by
@both, particularly about the velocity.

This is the primary cause of misidentifications of conventional
objects as UFOs:

1. When the identity of the object is known, then the observer
has a rough idea of its true size, and then can make a reasonable
estimate of its distance, speed, and altitude.

2. But when the identity is unknown (a UFO), then the estimate of
the size is based on nothing but guessing either the identity or
the distance. Then the estimates of distance, speed, and altitude
are based on the guessed size. Often an assumption that the
object is a piloted craft causes the size estimate to be far off
the mark.

3. Halation (scattering) inside the retina of the eye makes
bright objects seem larger than they are.

The recent Berwyn 'UFO Crash' piece in the Daily Mirror cannot
be allowed to pass without comment.
So.......


>HOW ALIEN'S MY VALLEY?
>Farmer claims he saw UFO
>A TOP-SECRET Government research base was used to store alien
>bodies after their UFO crashed in a remote Welsh valley, it was
>claimed yesterday.
>The mysterious craft came down in the Berwyn Mountains, Clwyd,
>according to a new book by top UFO investigator Nick Redfern.
>In a chilling echo of the infamous Roswell Incident in New
>Mexico, scores of troops were dispatched on a secret mission to
>recover the wreckage.
>One soldier, quoted in the book under the pseudonym James
>Prescott, was ordered to Llandderfel with four others and loaded
>two oblong boxes into their armoured truck.

The source of this 'information' has always been anonymous.
Tony Dodd _claims_ to know who was involved but, as usual,
won't share his secrets. No-one actually saw a _craft_ of any
kind!

>They then ferried the bodies back to the Chemical and Biological
>Defence Establishment at Porton Down near Salisbury, Wilts,
>under strict orders not to stop for anything.

Again this is information derived from an anonymous and
almost certainly non-existant source.

>Retired Mr Prescott, who is too afraid of reprisals to be named,
>said: "Once inside, the boxes were opened by staff at the
>faculty in our presence. We were shocked to see two creatures
>.which had been placed inside decontamination suits.

Consider: Would the 'delivery boys' be allowed to stay around
to see the Greatest Secret In The Universe being unveiled?
And with no protective garb being worn? Why were the 'bodies'
transported by truck and not helicopter?

>"It was obvious the creatures were not of this world and, when
>examined, were found to be dead.
>"The bodies were about five to six feet tall, humanoid in shape,
>but so thin they looked almost skeletal with a covering skin.
>"Although I did not see a craft at the scene of the recovery, I
>was informed that a large craft had crashed and was recovered by
>other military units."
Research in the villages of Llandrillo, Llanderfel, Bala and Corwen
indicates that there were very few military personel around
for this 'incident'. Police (who had initially thought a plane had
crashed) and a three man team from RAF Valley were involved.
There is no evidence, other than the anecdotal, to the contrary.

>Farmer Huw Lloyd, 39, was a boy of 14 watching TV at home in
>nearby Llandrillo on the night of the crash in January 1974. He
>said there was a huge bang followed by a tremor and a blinding
>blue light.
>Huw recalled: "I was amazed at how quickly the police responded
>and how many people came here."

In an interview I conducted with Lloyd in 1998 he stated that there were
no more than two car loads of police, which is not an unreasonable
amount if they suspected a plane crash. They arrived at his father's
farm about 30-40 minutes after the earth tremor. Not a particularly
fast response time.

>The incident has remained classified and the Ministry of Defence
>refuses to comment.

Utter nonsense! The MOD are quite happy to answer letters about the
'event' but will say they have no knowledge other than the fact
that RAF Valley was called out. The squadron log for RAF Valley for the
relevant date is entirely freely available and was not classified.

>Details were uncovered by expert Mr Redfern after years of
>research and are published in his book Cosmic Crashes.

Even Nick now says that the Berwyn Case isn't as clear cut as he once
thought, although we agree to differ in our conclusions.

I hope to be able to post a full analysis of the 'James Prescott'
scenario in a week or so. Kevin McClure has done some
excellent work on this aspect and I have asked him if he will
write a summary.

It seems that there are certain UK ufologists who are desparate
to turn a mundane incident into our very own Roswell.
Fun ahead!

Happy Trails

Andy

It's in the "Encyclopedia of UFOs," along with another fake
produced by the same photographer.

A lady's coat button was placed on a print of the aerial shot.
Then another photo was taken at an angle.

The fact that the "shadows" are so large and dark indicates a
fake all by itself. It is very hard to find the shadow of your
plane on the ground unless you are flying very low. If the plane
is high enough, there is only a penumbral shadow. This happens
any time the angular size of the plane (as seen from the shadow
point on the ground) is smaller than the angular size of the sun.
This, or course, it the UFO angular size reported as "distant
plane."

BTW, if the "plane shadow" is of the "camera plane," and the
round shadow is cast by the UFO, then there would have to be two
suns in the sky.

Yes, the ever reliably useless Daily Mail. The one that serialised all of
Nick Popes greatest works. I used to write regularly for James Black's
'Answers to Correspondants' for them at his request. I resigned after their
series of terrible reports on UFOs that were so bad and so frequent and
often provably wrong but about which they declined to do a thing when I
complained to the editor.

Then they displayed a remarkable attitude to 'Something in the Air' - buying
rights weeks in advance, gaining a PR embargo to give them an exclusive,
then declining to publish without telling the publisher of this decision.
After weeks of struggling to find out why the rights officer at Robert Hale
gave up but I was told by an embarrassed features reporter that the editor
insisted he would not publish 'that sort of stuff' in his paper.

As you know SITA is anti ETH and I dont think sensational. As such this
attitude given the things they do regularly publish is to say the least
strange. I dont know if my refusal to write for James Black again or my
complaints over their prior UFO coverage is connected. It did predate the
decision over the book. But it also predated their purchase of rights in the
first place (for which they still paid Robert Hale despite never printing a
word, incidentally).

So the Mail approach to UFOlogy is to say the least curious.

BTW I carried the Heathrow story on UFO Call six weeks ago. Nothing like (as
they regularly claim to be) Britains most successful paper being up to date

Hi,

The Manchester case was (I am 99% certain) a fireball meteor, as I have
reported at length in several sources. Ian Ridpath supports that view. The
main difference with the Heathrow case is that this was a daylight episode.
The Manchester case (actually it occurred 3 miles from me over Whaley
Bridge) was in the dark above thick cloud.

There are - however - similarities and daylight bolides do occur but tend to
generate more witnesses. So at this stage I am not that sure these two cases
are connected - although its a possibility.

I've always wondered on what basis they made such range estimates. Pilots are
notoriously unreliable that way, as even Dr. Hynek pointed out, and
justifiably so: they interpret any sudden visual cue in its most hazardous
avatar, and by so doing, usually live to draw a pension. They don't idly
speculate about that beautiful light or that fascinating shadow -- they
defend themselves and their passengers.

Cases abound of estimates of "a few hundred feet" really being a hundred
kilometers. So in these cases, what is the basis of the range? If it's merely
a guess based on angular size and assumption of 'classic' airplane size, then
it's not necessarily so.

Jenny,

I agree that the meteor explanation is a reasonable, probably
default, deduction.

I'm still not convinced about this though!

Why?

Because there are clear indications that the flight crew did in
fact witness a structured craft.

Here we have the essence of an anecdotal 'UFO'. Damnably
frustrating, we simply can't replicate what was witnessed, how it
was perceived, remembered and subsequently maybe embellished into
legend.

The Manchester incident is a significant 'UFO' case as there were
two witnesses, the pilot and co-pilot, who come under the
archetypal 'reliable, experienced and trained observers',
especially of aerial artefacts.

I thought this was arguably one of the most intriguing reports in
recent years, given that they both witnesses did rule out a
meteorological explanation and identified aspects consistent with
another 'craft', i.e.:
Date: Monday 5th August, 1996.
[End]


This is quite specific and nothing seems to suggests a bolide -

A "silvery grey wedge-shaped object".

"a solid object which I believed had black or grey stripes down
the side".


That was 'First Officer' and co-pilot Mark Stuart's summary.

The pilot, Captain Roger Wills was publicly more 'reserved'. In
all of my archived newspaper clippings, there's only one reported
comment from him and its reliability may be questionable. From
'Bild' (a German 'tabloid' newspaper) and dated 30 January 1995:

Captain Roger Wills stated: "We were already above Great Britain.
Suddenly a mysterious, fiercely illuminated triangle was heading
towards our machine in a straight way. We thought of the worst.
We drew in our heads because we thought we are going to collide.
But in the last second the object passed our airplane on the
right side".
[END]

It maybe loses a little in the translation.

However, referencing the CAT report, we have dependable evidence
that Wills, "remained convinced that the object was itself lit"
and "described it has having a number of small white lights,
rather like a Christmas tree".


How can we reconcile both witness accounts with a fireball
meteor?

Hi,

James. Absolutely. I used similar arguments with the Civil Aviation
Authority (one of the Air Miss investigators in the l995 British Airways
case attended a lecture I gave at a Stockport bookstore where I presented
the Bolide solution and its close similarity to the Eastern Airlines case
from l948).

The CAA had rather foolishly suggested the air crew could have seen a
spaceship after eliminating normal planes such as military aircraft as the
cause. It never was really suspected that there was no craft there at all -
because the pilot and co pilot read such a structure into their two second
sighting. The CAA had accepted the description of the crew at too much face
value assuming their report of an aircraft sized object at close proximity
was what they had really encountered. In fact, it was probably a far larger
object much higher in the atmosphere (and outside radar detection range).

As you rightly say the air crews first thought was for the safety of the
plane (which was not buffeted by any turbulence - a key indication that the
'UFO' was not as close as they thought).But the problem was the lack of
familiarity with how people perceive UFOs that the CAA possessed. Serious
UFOlogists have such knowledge. But most hook onto the expectation that such
an encounter truly was an alien craft and, frankly, dont use their
experience or expertise from past cases nearly enough. If we dont can we
blame the CAA for not doing?

Too often pilots, who undoubtedly are skilled investigators, are considered
gods by the public - understandably as we psychologically need to regard
them as super human and incapable of making errors. This because we trust
our lives to them so often. Airlines feel the same way. When writing
'Something in the Air' I came upon several major airlines and disgruntled
pilots who deliberately censored UFO data for fear of its effects on
passenger confidence.

 But air crew are subject to exactly the same sort of misperception as
ordinary mortals. Unfortunately, the CAA (and FAA in the US) should learn
from the investigations of UFOlogists who have dealt with many cases in the
past - cases that immediately allowed us to suspect the cause for the
January l995 British Airways encounter. However, this same event was
something the air miss investigators appear to have been blinkered into
seeing in very limited terms (a military craft or a craft from somewhere
else). They were constrained by experience to treat something too literally
because they lacked the relevant background in UFO study.

Here is an example of how UFOlogists can work with the authorities in a
postive way - but, sadly, all too often the image we project is one geared
up to find spaceships and little else. It ought to be more often directed
towards solving cases as this is something we can do well when we bother to
try. Why UFOlogy regards solved cases as garbage to be swept under the mat
in an often forlorn quest for aliens constantly baffles me. We should make
more out of our strengths and seek to show the world how sometimes
UFOlogists can do other things than seek out cover ups and conspiracies.

Best wishes,

Jenny Randles

I've read accounts of 'routine' aviation accident investigations in which the
investigators conclude that the very WORST type of witness to an aviation
accident is a pilot. The reason: they do not report raw perceptions, but
force these cues into interpretations, and subsequently re-arrange or even
conjure up memories to fortify the way they are SURE things happen. This is
because they ARE so familiar with the technology, and the need to make
actionable conclusions FAST.

I've always been much more impressed with witness descriptions of phenomena
they did NOT understand but which clearly gave hints they were seeing real
events -- one Russian emigré from the Urals, discussing the nuclear disaster
in 1957, wrote to me (I quoted him in "Uncovering Soviet Disasters", 1988)
about how along a radioactive creek the pine trees died but the leafy trees
didn't (or the other way around -- I forget right now), which is a classic
characteristic of low-level radiation exposure. He didn't KNOW it was
classic, he reported RAW observations, and this established his authenticity
in my mind.

And there's the classic literature example from Herodotus, as he describes
the story of a Phoenician circumnavigation of Africa, and the reason HE
dismisses the claim as an empty boast: "After all ,those Phoenicians (giggle,
chuckle) claimed that as they passed westward around the southern point of
the continent, they saw the sun on their LEFT hands (haha!) instead of on the
right hand which is normal." Normal only for people in the northern
hemisphere, of course!!

On Tue, 26 Oct 1999, David Clarke wrote:

@UFO Research List - http://web.ukonline.co.uk/voyager/
@
@The following appeared in the London Daily Mail, 26 October, 1999:
@
@"Riddle of UFO at Heathrow
@
@"A PASSENGER jet's close encounter with a mysterious,
@fast-moving craft seconds after taking off from Heathrow
@had experts baffled yesterday.
@"The crew of an MD-81 reported an object 'like a bright
@light' passing within 20ft of them at 3,500 ft.
@"Air accident investigators were unable to shed any light
@on the mystery as radar records show there were no other
@planes in the area at the time.
@"A dossier on last month's incident is thought to have
@been passed to the MOD to see if the UFO could have
@been a radar-invisible spy plane or a stray British
@test craft."
@
@Am I correct in thinking this claimed sighting has been
@mentioned somewhere on Updates before?
@Does anyone recognize this case - or is it something
@completely new?

* Do we have the time of day on this?

* Since the sighting date is Oct 25, 1999, I doubt that this
exact case has appeared before. Maybe one very similar has.

* Anything passing only 20 feet away (the length of a large car)
would be within the range of binocular vision. If the object
really came that close, and the crew was unable to identify it,
the velocity of their own airplane was probably responsible. One
would wonder why the pilot did not attempt evasive action.

* Anything as large as an airplane would loom large and be easily
identified long before it came within 20 feet. Therefore, the
object was either very small, or the 20 foot distance estimate
was in error.
* This is an example of the "Gorman Effect," where a small,
nearly stationary object is perceived as a larger object, farther
away, and moving at high speed.

* One possibility is the prank fire balloon. The following
elements of the story fit:

1. The object was perceived as nothing but a light source.

2. The object did not appear on RADAR.

3. The object could not be identified at close range.

4. Nobody else saw it. But it's possible that when the plane
passed close to it, the wake may have destroyed it.

Of course, this theory only fits if it was night, or if the
balloon was a lighted weather balloon, or a helium balloon with a
road flare hung from it.

* Another possibility is a misperceived meteor.

* A third possibility is a high-powered model rocket.

* A terrorist's missile (shudder) is a possibility, although a
remote one.

There was a similar close encounter in Jeffersonville Indiana
(USA) several years ago. A police helicopter chased it, and the
crew reported that the object darted around at fantastic speeds
to evade the helicopter. The object was unidentified until the
person who launched the balloon came forward. In an experiment to
measure wind direction aloft, he had launched and tracked a fire
balloon. The "fantastic speeds" were the result of the
helicopter's own motions, combined with misperception of the size
and distance.

a thing (cf the reactions of ground witnesses in the l997 Peak District
incident). A bolide on the other hand is a fast moving burn up miles high in
the atmosphere and visible for maybe 2-3 seconds. It would also be silent.
The likelihood of many - or any - witnesses seeing this silent and brief
flare from the ground below thick cloud with only scattered breaks is much
lower than if the UFO was a military plane. Note also that a miltary
plane would take some minutes to pass the Boeing. Even after it was out of
sight from the restricted cockpit view it would fly down the right side of
the BA plane and be in view to all witnesses on that side. As a plane is on
final approach to Ringway (I know as I have flown this exact route many
times) a lot of people are looking out of the windows. I find it hard to
believe that not one passenger would see this secret plane streak past their
aircraft as they would have had a longer chance to see it than the pilots
did. On the other hand a very transient streak of light from a bolide would
depend on someone through the more narrow field of view looking in the right
place during a very short period of time and makes much more sense of the
lack of passenger witnesses.


>If the testimony of trained pilots, ATC staff and police can't be relied
>upon - and I take your point that anyone can be mistaken. Who makes a
>credible UFO witness ?


I am not suggesting pilots are not credible witnesses. What I am saying is
that human perception operates in what are known to be strange ways when UFO
sightings occur. Training is an irrelevance because these things are odd and
they happen quickly. Your training allows you to cope without putting the
aircraft at risk. It does not make you any less likely to suffer perceptual
deception. just like Einstein can look at an optical illusion and still be
fooled. You wrongly assume that problems with human perception infer lack
of skill or competence. Indeed I have been attacked by UFOlogists for
suggesting this case is solved because it will put off pilots reporting
sightings given that I am disparaging their story. But I am doing no such
thing. I am merely relating what 25 years as a field investigator tells you
about how people see UFOs. Any people.


>Who was closer to the object ? As you comment, the incident took place very
>quickly, so whoever was closer - and I imagine it would be the co-pilot,
>would be in a better position to observe the UFO. Sitting in the left seat,
>the pilot would have to be looking across the cabin, taking his eyes away
>from a potentially disasterous situation.

The co pilot actually semi ducked instictively. But I dont think proximity
matters. It would if we were talking about something 20 feet from the
cockpit. If it was 20 miles away (as I believe) two or three feet either way
is no issue. The object sped past them to the right. Neither really
registered it before it was almost gone. If you have ever seen a bolide (I
have) you'll understand.

Re: Manchester Airmiss

Hi Jenny,

Your meteor theory is interesting, but it sounds rather unlikely to me,
given the crew's description of the object and the duration of the
sighting.
 The technical description of a bolide meteor, is one which appears to
explode, ie, a detonating fireball, or ablating meteorite. (A fireball
has to be brighter than magnitude -5, which is more than Venus)
 Fireballs are spectacular but rare events and in many years of night
sky watching, I've only seen half a dozen true fireballs and two
bolides. (Current estimates suggest that no more than about 5000 bolides
occur within the Earth's atmosphere every year)
 If you are suggesting that the object which passed the airliner was a
large meteorite in the terminal phase of its flight, would you care to
put a size to it?

I'm not saying that something along these lines can be totally ruled
out, but the stray classified vehicle theory strikes me as the most
plausible.
 In my part of the world, (East Anglia) there have been quite a few
cases of conventional military aircraft straying into prohibited areas,
usually met by total denial when issues have been raised with the
authorities.
 One event which comes to mind from a few years back, involved an A-10,
which came close enough to a Royal helicopter flight (carrying Princess
Anne, I think) to cause real concern. This was filmed by a BBC (or
possibly Anglia TV) news team, but the MoD and USAF insisted it had
never happened and suggested the video footage had been shot elsewhere
or at a different time.

One particular section of Airmiss Report 2/95 says, "Unfortunately, the
nature and identity of this object remains unknown. To speculate about
extraterrestrial activity, fascinating though it may be, is not within
the Group's remit and must be left to those whose interest lies in that
field."
 This statement, could be seen as an attempt to shift interest away from
the possibility that Flight 5061 narrowly escaped collision with an
"off-course" classified (possibly stealthy) manned/unmanned vehicle.

An incident with some similarities occurred on August 5 1992 at 1.45PM
when a United Airlines Boeing 747 narrowly missed what may have been an
experimental aircraft as it approached George AFB in California.
 The airliner had just left Los Angeles International Airport on a
flight to London and the aircraft's TCAS (Traffic Alert and Collision
Avoidance System) warned the crew that a unknown contact was approaching
almost head-on at very high speed.
 There was insufficient time to take evasive action and the UFO passed
beneath them, narrowly missing the 747 by an estimated 500 feet.
 The crew described the UFO as having the forward fuselage of an SR-71
and an overall lifting body shape, with some kind of a tail.
 Of course, the USAF denied any involvement with the incident and
insisted that no secret aircraft had been responsible!


Bill Rose

Re: Bolides/Air Incidents

Hi Jenny,

While I agree with what you are saying about air traffic density,
I would suggest that serious incidents involving stray military aircraft
can occur, regardless of the location.
 I don't want to sound like a conspiracy buff, but just because someone
in authority says that certain things can never happen, it doesn't mean
this is the truth.

Going back to witness descriptions, Mark Stuart is quoted as telling
the CAA that his attention was diverted to something in his peripheral
vision. He looked up in time to see a dark (some reports say gray)
object pass down the right side of of the aircraft at high speed. He
said, it was wedge shaped, with what could have been a black stripe down
the side. He estimated the object's size was somewhere between a light
aircraft and a Jetstream.
 Looking at several newspaper cuttings I have, it seems the crew thought
it most likely they had encountered a USAF stealth aircraft, although
the writers clearly preferred the alien spaceship angle.

I'm not saying your fireball theory is unacceptable and I'm not
suggesting that the crew's report was flawless, but I certainly don't
think anyone has a really solid answer to this story.

The 1948 DC-3 incident above Alabama was certainly interesting and I'm
quite open minded about it. However, correct me if I'm wrong, but wasn't
the object involved reported as climbing up through the clouds after
passing the aircraft?

Bill

On Wed, 27 Oct 1999, Jenny Randles wrote:

@>If the testimony of trained pilots, ATC staff and police can't
@>be relied upon - and I take your point that anyone can be
@>mistaken. Who makes a >credible UFO witness ?

@I am not suggesting pilots are not credible witnesses. What I am
@saying is that human perception operates in what are known to be
@strange ways when UFO sightings occur. Training is an
@irrelevance because these things are odd and they happen
@quickly. Your training allows you to cope without putting the
@aircraft at risk. It does not make you any less likely to suffer
@perceptual deception. just like Einstein can look at an optical
@illusion and still be fooled. You wrongly assume that problems
@with human perception infer lack of skill or competence. Indeed
@I have been attacked by UFOlogists for suggesting this case is
@solved because it will put off pilots reporting sightings given
@that I am disparaging their story. But I am doing no such thing.
@I am merely relating what 25 years as a field investigator tells
@you about how people see UFOs. Any people.

It doesn't matter if the witness is a trained pilot or not.

My work in the Kinesiology Department has taught me one important
fact that is quite germane to this case: If an object is more
than 30 feet away, then NOBODY can accurately estimate the size,
distance, speed, or altitude, unless the witness has more
information in one of the following forms:

1. The witness knows the identity of the object.

2. The object was or passed in front of and behind known objects
at known distances.

3. The witness uses pecial instruments to increase depth
perception (and the training to use them).

Convincing amateur UFOlogists that the human body is limited in
this way is an ongoing task. They think that because trained
observers can estimate the distance, speed, and altitude of a
flying airplane, they should be able to do the same thing with a
UFO. But the airplane observer has one important advantage: the
size of the airplane is known.

And that makes all the difference.

Witnesses to unknown objects tend to guess either the distance or
the size, and then base all of their other estimates on that
guess. Often the mistake made is to assume that the unknown
object is a vehicle. All subsequent impressions are then based on
this error. There are cases in my files where the size
and distance estimates were off by a factor of over a billion
(a milliard for those not in the US).

So there is absolutely no way those pilots could have estimated
the distance of the object, unless:

1. It flew between the cockpit and the wing of the airliner.

2. It was recognized as a known aircraft.

3. It flew between the plane and clouds (which establishes an
upper bound on distance).

4. It flew between the plane and the ground (again establishing
an upper bound on distance).

5. It went behind the wing of the airliner (establishing a lower
bound on distance).

We need to get this little fact about the limits of human
perception publicized, so people don't blame pilots for these
incidents. There is nothing they can do to improve their
perceptions of these events.

Stuart suggested this might be a reflection from their own

You are of course correct that they didn't agree on the exact
substance, however, they did concur about the similarity of a
'triangular' shape. As the CAT report confirmed, "Following the
incident, the captain and first officer independently drew what
they had seen, both agreed about the shape but differing in their
opinions about the lighting aspects".

Stuart further reportedly explained, "The objects we drew were
the same shape, but they differed in texture - mine was a solid
object which I believed had black or grey stripes down the side."

"The Captain drew a similar shape, but his was made up of lots of
different little lights."

"I felt his drawing could be explained by a reflection from our
landing lights as the object went down our right-hand side."

It was that stated shape which led to the CAT investigation
spending so much time debating whether a hang-glider was maybe
responsible and then discarding it as unrealistic, given the
overall conditions.


>>The Manchester incident is a significant 'UFO' case as there
were two witnesses, the pilot and co-pilot, who come under the

>Sorry, but I disagree. I have seen many times witnesses -
