I don't actually disagree with your good self or anyone about
this at all.

The phrase "archetypal 'reliable, experienced and trained
observers'" was intentional. That's what they are generally
considered or claimed to be.

Jim Oberg's comments are highly pertinent. I personally don't
conceive any purportedly 'trained observer' to necessarily be
more dependable. I'm not aware that anyone is trained in the
observation of 'UFOs'.

Incidentally, given my research into Kenneth Arnold's 'flying
saucers', I'm probably the last person who would argue that
pilots are beyond reproach as witnesses!

We have to assess each case on its own merits.


>>I thought this was arguably one of the most intriguing reports
in recent years, given that they both witnesses did rule out a
meteorological explanation and identified aspects consistent with
another 'craft', i.e.:<<

>Well, again, I am sorry, we disagree.

There can be no disagreement that both witnesses dismissed
meteorological phenomena, it's confirmed in the CAT report.

If we look at this in reverse; a pilot and co-pilot witness an
unidentified object, apparently in close proximity, such that the
co-pilot "instinctively ducked" (CAT report) fearing an imminent
impact. They both sketch what was perceived and seemingly depict
a similar, triangular-shaped object. The pilot believes it
displayed a number of small white lights, whilst the co-pilot
recalled the object was a silver-grey colour, wedge-shaped and
had a 'stripe' down one visible side.

Despite both perceiving the object to be triangular-shaped,
ruling out a "Met phenomenon", individually ascribing that said
object either displayed a number of small white lights or was
resplendent with a 'go faster' stripe and that the co-pilot
'ducked' as he expected an immediate impact... they were both
consummately mistaken in all of this and it was in fact a 'fiery
meteor' some twenty miles away.

That's what has to be reconciled in this case and whilst
meteors/space debris often result in reported observations of an
airplane crash or 'UFO(s)', we rarely have such an ostensible
'close encounter' and comparisons with ground based experiences
may neither be appropriate or reliable.
Supposing the witnesses did in fact observe a triangular/wedge-
shaped object, maybe 'stealthy', or, for whatever reason, not
detected on radar.

Wouldn't you perhaps still conclude it was a bolide?


>I think if you read my data in 'UFO Reality' you will have a
>hard time not accepting your touching faith in the certainty of
>witness testimony just does not work in the real world of UFO
>sightings.

You mean like my faith in Arnold, Zamora, Burroughs, Penniston...

Again, I have to call it as I see it and we can't dismiss every
case, as could be construed by your comments. I'm sure that's not
what you mean and recall it wasn't so long ago you said of my
critique re Burroughs, Penniston and the entire 'Rendlesham'
case:

"Easton fails to address another issue: the nonmilitary
witnesses. Half of 'UFO Crash Landing?' deals with these matters.
There simply are too many reliable people who saw strange things
that weekend for us to dismiss their stories".

Somehow, we seem to have since swapped our respective viewpoints
on witness evidence!

That will happen... depends on our perspective of any case and
always likely to be influenced by our view of the 'bigger
picture'.

For example, one important realisation which has come out of
discussions on this list is that witnesses do sometimes provide
important, accurate accounts of their experiences. It's that
reliability which provides evidence to maybe explain the
occurrence.

If we look back on the topic of high altitude triangles of lights
moving across the sky, it was the precise detail in those reports
which led to Chris Gibson recognising they may be 'triplets' of
spy/surveillance satellites. And so it, almost certainly, proved.

Zamora's account leaves us with invaluable, first-hand
documentation, still untainted and reliable even if the hot-air
balloon theory is substantiated [hopefully news on this shortly].

As discussed, Paul Hanmer's extraordinary 'triangular UFO'
testimony, although now looking from discussions to be explicable
as a 'silent' Vulcan, gliding in to land, would still be quite
accurate, other than his estimate of the size.

There are surely countless examples of dependable witness
accounts.


I'm especially not troubled that the Manchester incident involves
an enigmatic 'wedge-shaped' object. There are comparative
sightings of 'UFOs' described as 'wedge-shaped' and it isn't too
far removed from an aircraft planform.

That said, many of these 'wedge-shaped' accounts are not easily
explicable. See, for example, a case which I documented in great
detail and taken at face value, remains quite baffling to me:

http://web.ukonline.co.uk/voyager/j.htm


As noted at the outset, I do believe that a suggested bolide
explanation for the Manchester air-miss is a reasonable deduction
and the default solution.

That doesn't of course mean it is the actual explanation and I
see enough in the witness testimonies and refutation of that
possibility to indicate this case should remain, as the CAT
report concluded, "unassessable".

I would like to comment on the bolide hypothesis for this sighting:
James wrote:>
>As noted at the outset, I do believe that a suggested bolide
>explanation for the Manchester air-miss is a reasonable deduction
>and the default solution.>

>That doesn't of course mean it is the actual explanation and I
>see enough in the witness testimonies and refutation of that
>possibility to indicate this case should remain, as the CAT
>report concluded, "unassessable".
<

AS I understand it the plane was under 4000 ft altitude at the time.
It would be important to know the "Exact" angle of elevation above the
plane's
altitude when it was first seen, and the angle when last seen. If we knew
these
numbers we could make a more accurate estimate based on "bolide physics."

But, anyway, here goes,

Typical bolide/meteor burns brightly at 50 down to 30 miles altitude. If
it gets too
low it can slow and "go out" (temperature drops).
Therefore the bolide hypothesis contradicts the witness' claim that the
object was close.

Imagine for the purposes of argument that the initial sighting elevation
angle was
45 degrees. Now, this seems higher than I would expect for a man
(copilot)_ to duck...
I would expect the angle to be a few degrees for him to think the object
was going to hit the plane.

But, anyway, assume it's initial angular elevation was 45 degrees. Assume
the final elevation
(when it went out of sight) was 90 degrees. Now, I know, you're all
saying, "Hey, they can't look straight up." Fine. Then tell me how "up"
they can look.

The choice of 45 degrees is "fortunate" for calculation because the
horizontal distance traveled
by the bolide (not quite parallel to the curvature of the earth, which is
nearly a straight line for this
distance) will be the same as its altitude above the plane. That is, if
its altitude above the plane when directly overhead was 30 miles, then it
was 30 miles from directly overhead when first seen.
(45 degree right triangle: sides equal; hypotenuse is 1.414 times a side)


Now a typical meteor speed exceed 17,000 mph which is low altitude orbital
speed. But lets assume a really slow bolide at 17,000 mph. To travel 30
miles horizontal distance requires about 6 seconds
[(30/17000) x 3600 sec/hr = 6.4 sec]. This is about 6 times larger than
they estimated.
If the highest angle they could see was only 80 degrees, then the last 5.3
miles of travel was blocked from view and they watched it traveled 30-5.3 =
24.7 miles corresponding to 5.2 seconds,

If one REALLY stretches the bolide hypothesis and suggests it was at an
altitude of 10 miles (I don't know if it would even glow at that altitude,
furthermore it would probably be noticeably falling downward) then the
times calculated above should be divided by 3. Still longer than they
estimated.

On the other hand, if the initial elevation angle was low, say 10 degrees,
so that they MIGHT
think it was going to hit, then the straight line path from overhead would
be

30(tan[90-10]) = 170 miles. Now the time duration is 36 seconds. Hardly
a "fantastic speed" from their point of view.

You can see that as the initial elevation angle drops the distance to of
the bolide when first seen
increases rapidly (at 5 degrees the distance is 30 tan(90-5)=343 miles,
etc.0.

Therefore one cannot simply bandy about the bolide hypothesis without
exploring the consequences of same.

The failue to test prosaic hypotheses is the "failure of UFO skepticism."
(See Prosaic Explanations, the Failure of UFO Skepticism, at www.isso.org
and look in the "library")

Don't forget another possibility -- launch phase of space vehicles. I'm
attaching a note about some spectacular views over Alaska a few years earlier.

Kosmos-2335 was launched December 11, 1996, from Baykonur into a 65 degree
inclined orbit, BUT any connection would require:
1. Timing correspondences
2. Proper LIGHTING in the sky over the area of the sighting
3. Correspondence of viewing direction and MOTION, relatively rapidly ( ~one
degree/sec) right to left, which seems to NOT match witness accounts.
4. Ground track match -- this looks at first hand like a killer, since even
at 71 degrees, the launch described below barely made it within view of
western Alaska.

I'll look into this, but I doubt the connection -- most satellite launch
inspired reports have classic perceptual characteristics which allow them to
be 'suspected' before they are confirmed.

Somebody has got to set up a ufology research service that knows how to
1. Obtain reentry reports rapidly
2. Obtain and process satellite navigation data -- the 2-line 'element sets'
-- to correlate with sightings
3. Document visual characteristics of entries and launch phenomena, for all
researchers to access.

I can't be a 'single point' access to this data, and I am dismayed that these
easily-obtainable records and software are not more widely used within the
ufo research community, even after decades of close connections between
space/rocket events and SOME (but often most SPECTACULAR) UFO reports.

Note of Interest: "UFO" sightings in western Alaska night of March 17-18,
1987, were caused by Soviet satellite launch.
From: J. Oberg, Rt 2 Box 350, Dickinson, TX 77539,April 29, 1987


The launching of the Kosmos-1833 satellite from TT at 1987 March 18 / 1830
UT led to a large number of UFO reports from western Alaska. The spacecraft's
upper stage was venting leftover rocket propellant when it passed off the
Seward Penninsula at about 1857 UT (11:57 PM March 17, Yukon Standard Time).
Two reports came from observers on St. Lawrence Island in the Bering Sea:
Savoonga (63.40N, 170.31W), "It was round and it seemed bigger than a
jetliner". Gambell (63.46N, 171.45W): "There seemed to be a big bright cloud
of smoke thrusting downward with one red and one white light.... The object
seemed to be bigger than a 747 jet at that altitude. No body was visible,
justthe bright cloud of smoke and the lights."

Other reports came from mainland observers out late to watch the mushers in
the Iditarod dogsled race. Tanunak (60.34N, 165.15W): It "looked like a
satellite-bright, white light within a glowing area...", like "aircraft
landing lights as seen through the fog." Elim (64.35N, 162.20W), saw a
"bright aqua-blue-green colored, oval-shaped object approximately the size of
two football fields with three lights on the side and an egg-shaped cloud
around and leaving a smoke trail behind." Newsmen talked to more than forty
witnesses in these areas.

The mayor of Pilot Station (61.58N, 162.59W) in the Yukon River delta is a
subscriber to The Skeptical Inquirer, and he received the Winter 1987 issue
(with my article on the Great East Coast UFO of August 1986) a few days after
his sighting. The startling simularities prompted him to write a letter to
me. The apparition "brightened and began jetting out a plume of milky
nebulous material. This plume was slowly rotating and formed a cloud around
the star-like object with a diameter of between 4 and 5 times that of the
full moon. This wondrous show continued for around 3 minutes, then rapidly
faded and disappeared." David E. Cartier, 3/30/87 postmark. He originally
reported it as moving from northeast to southwest, but on plotting it against
star charts reconsidered and concluded that it had been moving largely west
to east. "The story of this sighting got around and local eskimo parents are
now using it in stern admonitions to their children as a prime example of why
'You shouldn't stay out late at night!!!'", Cartier, letter of 4/16/87.

Army National Guard observers reported to Anchorage that they watched lights
moving southeast at about 30,000 feet altitude.

The event was caused by the launching from Tyuratam of an SL-16 vehicle (the
USSR's new intermediate Saturn-I-class military booster), carrying a
"1603-class" satellite (possibly military ELINT) into an unusually high
inclination (71 degrees, highest ever from TT), high altitude (850 km) orbit.
Computer plots generated by Nicholas Johnson (Teledyne-Brown Corporation,
Colorado Springs, CO) showed the object's groundtrack crossing the Aleutians
about 900 km from the Yukon River delta, at an altitude of about 310-320 km.
Such launchings, while rare, will occur again, and under the proper twilight
and weather conditions will probably again be widely visible throughout
western Alaska.

This was one of the first cases reported in my home locality, and
it caused a big ruckus in the papers at the time. All of the
witnesses said the object was flying low and close, some saying
it was at treetop level. The object was definitely identified as
the re-entry of the Soviet Zond 4 satellite, many miles up. The
local papers did not bother to print the story of the object's
identification -- it wasn't news like the strange story was.

(snip)

@I agree which is half the problem. Nobody is disputing these two
@men are good witnesses or not reporting effectively pretty much
@what they saw that night. By arguing from prior similar UFO
@cases I am merely suggesting why I think we can see what that
@was. This in no way demeans the witnesses. Those UFOlogists who
@argue that it does clearly have not much background in how UFO
@witnesses perceive what they do.

People are expecting witnesses to perform beyond their capability
if they expect an estimate of the size, distance, speed, or
altitude of an unknown object. Human beings do not come with the
necessary equipment to do this.

@>If we look at this in reverse; a pilot and co-pilot witness an
@>unidentified object, apparently in close proximity, such that the
@>co-pilot "instinctively ducked" (CAT report) fearing an imminent
@>impact. They both sketch what was perceived and seemingly depict
@>a similar, triangular-shaped object. The pilot believes it
@>displayed a number of small white lights, whilst the co-pilot
@>recalled the object was a silver-grey colour, wedge-shaped and
@>had a 'stripe' down one visible side.

(snip)

@Like I said you are treating witness testimony too literally in
@my opinion.

Right! Unless the object is identified, or other visual clues are
supplied, humans cannot distinguish between:

1. A small close object and a large distant object

2. A slow close object and a fast distant object

3. An approaching object and an expanding object

4. A receding object and a contracting object

5. An approaching light and a brightening light

6. A receding light and a dimming light
What humans do perceive well includes angular size, changes in
angular size, angular motion, and changes in brightness.

Additional clues that can shed light on the true nature of the
observations include:

1. The object goes in front of something known.

2. The object goes behind something known.

3. The object casts a shadow.

4. Atmospheric scattering is detectable between a distant object
  and the observer. It's absence indicates a close object.

5. Strobe and navigation lights.

6. Tactics: Birds fly in a particular manner, bugs have different
  tactics, airplanes behave in still different ways, and
  helicopters have flight characteristics of their own. These
  are recognizable and can provide clues to the identity of an
  unknown. Each type of flight depends on the aerodynamics and
  guidance systems available.

7. Other witness accounts from different locations.

In an experiment performed by the Psychology Department here, a
lighted balloon was displayed in an otherwise darkened and masked
environment (to eliminate other visual clues) The illumination
and size of the balloon, and its distance from the subject could
be varied by the experimenters.

If the balloon was within 20 feet (6 m) of the subject, an
accurate description of what happened was given, due to the
binocular vision of the subject. Beyond 30 feet (10 m), subjects
were unable to tell whether the balloon was moved radially, or
its size and illumination were changed. When the balloon was
small, changing illumination alone was enough to cause subjects
to report radial motion. With one eye covered, the confusion
happened at any distance.

@>For example, one important realization which has come out of

The trick is sorting out which parts are accurate descriptions,
and which parts are impressions based on a guess of the size,
distance, speed, altitude, or identity of the object(s).

(snip)

@Are you familiar with the experiments that have been conducted
@into UFO witness perceptions? Some of the things we can concur
@from these are that the briefer the sighting the less accurate
@is its perception. The fewer the surrounding features to afford
@perspective, the least accurate the judgement of height,
@distance etc. Long duration (ie several minute) sightings of
@things that can be judged against ground objects clearly are
@more likely to be well perceived than very transient things
@against a vast expanse of blackness. It is this principle that
@makes the scary roller coaster (Space Mountain in Florida) work
@because here you are submerged in darkness and don't see a small
@set of lights shaped like a rocket on the wall but a huge rocket
@mass flying suddenly and looming terrifyingly large right at
@you. Anyone who has been on Space Mountain will have something
@of an inkling of what that BA crew went through and if they
@think about it - why they went through it.

There is a very good book on this subject: "Observing UFOs." I
don't have it with me, but I will try to give the details of
author, publisher, etc on Monday. It delves deep into the
problems of perception. Another good source is Allen Hendry's
"UFO Handbook," which covers misperceptions quite well.

(moby snip)

We have to remain objective here. Assuming facts not in evidence,
or assuming that testimony is more accurate than is humanly
possible, leads us to conclusions that are not warranted. We have
to carefully evaluate the meager evidence we have, and allow for
imperfections in the observations that are made.

Here are my thoughts and impressions:

* I noticed how quickly the witnesses all thought of UFOs.

* Many of them expected ET effects.

* Their eyes had to adjust to the darkness to see the objects
after a car passed. That means the lights weren't very bright.

* All but two of the witnesses reported the object to be to the
north, northwest, or northeast. One reported that it ended
up in the southeast after being in the northwest, north, and
east. The other reported that it was overhead at one point.

* The lights went out at different times. This suggests that the
lights were on different objects, not on one large object.

* The lights were already there when noticed in each case.

* The "area where stars were blocked out" might be just the area
in the north where there are no bright stars, combined with the
relative brightness of the object lights.


Here are some suggestions to add to your list:

4. Multiple light sources on airplanes in a military exercise
miles north of the observers.

5. A barium-cloud experiment with multiple releases.

6. A prank involving flares tied to balloons.

7. Lighted balloons released for some reason.

8. Multiple releases of fire balloons, similar to the secondary
sightings in the March 1997 Phoenix case.

9. A combination of any of the 8 possibilities.

From: Chris Gibson <cgibson@skomer.u-net.com>

,
Thankyou Larry for possibly the most sensible post I have come across in a long time.
People always interpret what they see in terms of their own experience.

I was lucky when I saw my triangle, I had three other known aircraft to compare it
with.

Another example (which I think I've talked to Dave Windle about is as follows.

I see a silver cigar shape flying over my house. it has two smaller objects flying in
formation alongside, halfway along the cigar on either side. None of this trio are
contrailing. What is this?

1) i lived under the main route north over the English Midlands
2) the sky is clear and blue
3) I spend quite a bit of time looking up (annoying habit, but ive done it for years)

So, being familiar with my manor I know that this is unusual.

Watching this formation for a bit longer I see that it's actually a Boeing 737 whose
wings and tailplanes have a luminence matching the sky, so all that can be seen is the
fuselage and the engines. Until it shape shifts into a 737, it is impossible to guage its
size or altitude.

How would some-one else have perceived this? How would I have perceived this had
I seen it pass across a gap in the cloud? Would it have been a cigar shaped Mothership
with two scouts?

There is an old addage that people never look up


As for the short duration of the Manchester airmiss sighting. In the ROC we were
required to identified an aircraft image with an exposure time of 0.5 seconds. Ok, so
we had a list of 200 possibles and we were expecting the image, but we also
discovered that we could identify an aircraft type at exposure times of 1/100th of a
second under the right conditions. (darkened room, eyes adjusted to the light, good
silouhette). This relied on a residual image on the retina. So in a darkened cockpit,a
bright object appears suddenly, you duck, shut your eyes, you can still see it. (Try it)

Another interesting aspect we found was that the longer the period you saw an image
for, the greater the chance of a misidentification. We put this down to having more
information to raise doubts with. Perhaps with a longer sighting the brain fills in for
absent info?
As for the object being about the size of a Jetstream (small 18 seat airliner). I
wondered about that at the time. Perhaps I'm alone in this but I always think aircraft
when seen close up on the ground seem to be smaller than they should be (I now
expect a plethora of Father Ted jokes ie "Those cows are small because they are far
away, Dougal") So I have to agree with Larry in his posting. How often have we
heard of UFOs the size of battleships How many people have seen a battleship? Not
many about nowadays.

I've always been wary of witnesses interviewed by aviation specialists and UFO
specialists alike. (eschewing the word UFOlogist, professional or otherwise) Perhaps
it is time for a standard format questionaire for this type of sighting. Is this available
already?

I have long maintained that how can something be termed as being unusual (ie a UFO)
if the witness and those interpreting their testimony do not know what is usual?
Trained observers, pilots, bobbies or any-one else, are trained in looking at a situation
and in relating what they saw at a later date. That is the good side of trained observers.
The downside is that if they see something tht doesn't fit, they may fill in some detail.

Chris,

A couple of years back, another witness and myself observed high
above nearby hills a dazzling, silver, saucer-shaped object,
reflecting the early morning sun.

Even though it was stationary, I knew this wasn't a star.
We watched it for around a minute, with no further clue what it
might be. I suggested it could be an airplane, however, using the
hills as a reference, it didn't appear to be moving.

We agreed this was an unusual sight and did look like an upturned
'saucer', although realising it wasn't a 'flying saucer'.

It was only after about a minute's observation that the object
slowly began to alter shape. Within the next 30 seconds it
evidently was in fact moving and a further 30-60 seconds revealed
the mysterious object to be no more than a jet aircraft.

The brilliance of the silver reflection was caused by the
relative angle of the sun, that was clear. Why it seemed to be
stationary and remain the same size and shape for so long was
presumable also due to relative factors.

It was an interesting lesson.


Although I always knew this was likely to have a mundane
explanation, it was easy to understand how someone who had an
unresolved sighting under similar circumstances could believe
they had definitely seen a 'UFO'.

It was by definition a striking, stationary, saucer-shaped 'UFO'
for more than a minute.

James & List,

Your sighting would never pass my initial screening criteria for visual
sightings as UFO Best Evidence, which requires a minimum angular size of the
full moon (0.5 deg) for a minimum of 1 minute observation with full details
reported by at least 2 witnesses on each of these criteria. Your aircraft
was evidently close to the apparent size of a star and we are given no
corroborating data from your other witness on angular size and duration.

The purpose of my screening criteria is to avoid wasted time on marginal
cases. Cases still have to pass through further filters. My screening test
does not automatically generate "best evidence" UFO cases. It only sets up a
list for further review. I DON'T want to hear from anyone mindlessly
generating lists of cases that pass my screening criteria and then saying
"see!! aha! these were weather balloons, Venus, ad planes, thus were
obviously not UFO Best Evidence so your criteria don't work." My screening
does work. Cases going through my screening need further investigation or
analysis, but they are at least of a much higher caliber of observation,
having sufficient duration and size as to enable many conventional causes to
be eliminated right from the outset.

By analogy to video data systems, human visual perception can be quantified.
An object at the limit of visual resolution, just under 1 arcminute or just
over 0.01 deg, is an image that is effectively made up of 1 pixel (picture
element). Suppose for purposes of illustration that for every second of the
UFO sighting some 10 bits of data on brightness, color and position are able
to be extracted by skillful investigators. Then your one-minute sighting
would yield a potential of only 600 data bits assuming a star-like angular
size (1 pixel x 10 bits/sec x 60 secs = 600 bits).

But a one-minute sighting of an object with full moon angular size, an image
of roughly 1,000 pixels, would yield a potential data return of roughly
600,000 bits -- a vastly greater collection of information than a mere 600
bits.

Brad Sparks

As Bruce said, the object's trajectory is a key issue in this sighting. My
rough 'back of the envelope' calculation of closing speed, assuming a
relatively flat, reciprocal course:

We know the B737 was travelling at around 200 mph - suppose the object was
travelling at the same speed and just broke through the cloud base, close
the Boeing. This gives us a closing speed of around 400 mph or approx. 600
fps. So in less than 0.2 seconds, it could have flown the entire length of
the B737 or clearly any part of it in even less time.

Let's not forget the report says visibility was 10+km. If the very brightly
lit object was on a flat-ish trajectory in relation to the B737, then the
crew could hardly have missed seeing it even further out than 10km. In that
case, it covered that distance in around 2 secs, giving it a velocity of
around 11,000 mph...!

I'm not saying the object was an a/c of any type...I'm just kicking the
various possibilities around.

Brad's high standards are obviously not maintained by a lot of people in this business.
There is a grey area where all the mathematical analysis in the world won't answer the
question "What was that I saw?". Many people prefer the more exotic explanation to
the mundane. Some-one will provide that explanation. I must side with the mundane
explanations.

I'm not comfortable with the "lights in the sky" sightings and I've had a few (lights on
the sky sightings, that is) but there are many who are happy with lights and take it to
the media, who lap it up from both the "Wow, aliens" and the "Here's another nutter"
viewpoints.

But as I have said in the past you can't just ignore these sightings as they are a part of
the phenomenon. Ignoring data is the road to ruin, ignoring results is the next step.
Classify (ie categorise) them by all means, then analyse particular classes, but
ignoring what doesn't fit your particular model is dodgy pratice. I'd rather put more
emphasis on the structured craft, but what percentage of sightings are structured craft?

I'll get my coat.

Chris

Date: Sun, 31 Oct 1999 17:05:03 -0500 (EST)
From: RB47Expert@aol.com

UFO Research List - http://web.ukonline.co.uk/voyager/

Hi Chris,

Thanks for your comments. I guess I don't really consider my standards so
very high, but actually bare minimum acceptability for further consideration
as "Best Evidence." A good case could be made that these standards are too
lenient because of witness error (e.g., an alleged "5-minute" duration might
actually only be 1 minute, etc.) Hynek introduced us to the multiple-witness
requirement for visual sightings (see The UFO Experience) so that's nothing
new. I'm not saying the Nocturnal Lights (or any other category) must be
totally discarded, in fact I'm a strong advocate of ongoing studies of IFO's
in order to provide "control studies" to validate Unexplained UFO cases. I'm
only saying that if cases fail a minimum angular size of the full moon (0.5
deg), minimum duration of 1 minute, and minimum of two witneses fully
reporting these data and others for cross-comparison and corroboration, then
the cases should not even be considered for the "Best Evidence" category,
though certainly a lesser category is acceptable. It's a matter of
PRIORITIZATION of effort. (I'm only considering non-instrument visual cases
here, as I haven't worked out screening criteria for instrument /
photographic / radar cases.)

I think UFOlogy has a fixation on the idea that some alien scheme can be
discerned by analyzing "patterns" in masses of poor UFO data using the magic
of "statistics" and "computers." There is little or no appreciation for the
devastating confusion and nonsense factor caused by a tiny "signal" (if any)
getting swamped or lost in a mass of "noise." It's like Rohrshach ink blots
-- you can read any message you want into the alleged "UFO data."

Therefore I challenge UFO researchers to avoid wasting precious research time
by setting aside marginal categories of UFO cases unless and until such time
as demonstrated otherwise. For example, low-strangeness, brief duration
pinpoint-sized sightings should be set aside unless someone can discover some
pattern that reveals a certain subset of such sightings to be real UFO's.

Brad Sparks

I hate to be redundant and repeat myself, but:
Since I got scarcely any response from my meteor/bolide comments the first
time I posted them (and got a message saying that the message had not been
delivered because the "mailbox was full")
So, lest anyone assume that th default solution is a "good one" simply
because
all others fall by the wayside for one reason or another,
let me point out that the bolide hypothesis can also be questioned on
reasonable grounds.

If it were the case that the trajectory was nearly horizontal and the
initial elevation angle was nearly zero, then the bolide hypothesis is
strained to the breaking point....I don;t think any bolide would be glowing
if at an altitude of 4000 ft; furthermore, the trajectory should be
downward, so it should have appeared to be dropping, even in the short time
observed.

WHAT I POSTED SEVERAL DAYS AGO:
>AS I understand it the plane was under 4000 ft altitude at the time.
It would be important to know the "Exact" angle of elevation above the
plane's
altitude when it was first seen, and the angle when last seen. If we knew
these
numbers we could make a more accurate estimate based on "bolide physics."

But, anyway, here goes,
Typical bolide/meteor burns brightly at 50 down to 30 miles altitude. If
it gets too
low it can slow and "go out" (temperature drops).
Therefore the bolide hypothesis contradicts the witness' claim that the
object was close.

Imagine for the purposes of argument that the initial sighting elevation
angle was
45 degrees. Now, this seems higher than I would expect for a man
(copilot)_ to duck...
I would expect the angle to be a few degrees for him to think the object
was going to hit the plane.

But, anyway, assume it's initial angular elevation was 45 degrees. Assume
the final elevation
(when it went out of sight) was 90 degrees. Now, I know, you're all
saying, "Hey, they can't look straight up." Fine. Then tell me how "up"
they can look.

The choice of 45 degrees is "fortunate" for calculation because the
horizontal distance traveled
by the bolide (not quite parallel to the curvature of the earth, which is
nearly a straight line for this
distance) will be the same as its altitude above the plane. That is, if
its altitude above the plane when directly overhead was 30 miles, then it
was 30 miles from directly overhead when first seen.
(45 degree right triangle: sides equal; hypotenuse is 1.414 times a side)


Now a typical meteor speed exceed 17,000 mph which is low altitude orbital
speed. But lets assume a really slow bolide at 17,000 mph. To travel 30
miles horizontal distance requires about 6 seconds
[(30/17000) x 3600 sec/hr = 6.4 sec]. This is about 6 times larger than
they estimated.
If the highest angle they could see was only 80 degrees, then the last 5.3
miles of travel was blocked from view and they watched it traveled 30-5.3 =
24.7 miles corresponding to 5.2 seconds,

If one REALLY stretches the bolide hypothesis and suggests it was at an
altitude of 10 miles (I don't know if it would even glow at that altitude,
furthermore it would probably be noticeably falling downward) then the
times calculated above should be divided by 3. Still longer than they
estimated.

On the other hand, if the initial elevation angle was low, say 10 degrees,
so that they MIGHT
think it was going to hit, then the straight line path from overhead would
be

30(tan[90-10]) = 170 miles. Now the time duration is 36 seconds. Hardly
a "fantastic speed" from their point of view.

You can see that as the initial elevation angle drops the distance to of
the bolide when first seen
increases rapidly (at 5 degrees the distance is 30 tan(90-5)=343 miles,
etc.0.

Therefore one cannot simply bandy about the bolide hypothesis without
exploring the consequences of same.

The failue to test prosaic hypotheses is the "failure of UFO skepticism."
 (See Prosaic Explanations, the Failure of UFO Skepticism, at www.isso.org
 and look in the "library")
/........................


Further comments: I presume that the witnesses got the impression that th
obejct was approaching because its angular size increased and perhaps the
brightness increased. If it were a bolide 30 miles up its angular size
and brightness would not change much because th distance between it and the
plane would nmot change much. On the other hand, if it were seen at a
very low elevation angle initially, then its distance to the plane would be
shrink as rapidly as the closing velocity between it and the plane. If H
is the altitude ABOVE the plane and D is the horizontal distance from the
plane to the object, then the range, R, from the plane to the object is R
= (H^2 + D^2)^1/2 (thanks to Pythagoras and
predecessors, from whom Pythagoras "stole" this rule). Now, from some
initial starting distance when first seen, Do, the distance is D = Do-
(Vp+Vo)t where Vp= velocity of plane and Vo = velocity of object and t is
the time). For very large H (e.g., 30 miles) small changes in D don't
create large changes in R. But as H is reduced, the variation of R with
t becomes closer and closer to being
R (approximately) = Do - (Vo+Vp)t, which shrinks in proportion to the
velocity sum.

OK, no assume the object had some intrinsic size (several feet, several
meters, whatever) as seen head on. Then the ANGULAR or APPARENT size, AS,
equals the actual size, S, divided by the distance, R or AS = S/R (for R
> S). Therefore if H were large, R wouldn't change much and AS wouldn't
change much so the witness, one presumes would NOT get the impression of an
object coming right at them at a high rate of speed. But if H is small,
then the rate of angular size
is inversely proportional to the velocity sum, AS proportional to S/(Vt)
where V is the sum of velocities.
If the velocity sum is large the angular size can grow at a truly "awesome"
rate....
If the copilot ducked, I would deduce that the angular size grew at a
tremendous rate.
The same analysis holds for apparent brightness which is the intrinsic
brightness (intensity) divided by the range.
The point is that if the object truly approached the plane at a HUGE speed,
then it was likely close to the altitude of the plane and NOT likely a
bolide.

On Mon, 1 Nov 1999, bruce maccabee wrote:

@
@If it were the case that the trajectory was nearly horizontal and the
@initial elevation angle was nearly zero, then the bolide hypothesis is
@strained to the breaking point....I don;t think any bolide would be glowing
@if at an altitude of 4000 ft; furthermore, the trajectory should be
@downward, so it should have appeared to be dropping, even in the short time
@observed.

Not so. A meteor can appear to be going up from the observer's
viewpoint due to perspective. If a meteor starts to glow over
Springfield Ohio, has a trajectory directly toward Lincoln
Nebraska, and burns out over Muncie Indiana, I would see it
rising in the northeast sky from my viewpoint in Bloomington
Indiana. This is because Springfield is much farther away than
Muncie. The meteor would appear lower in the sky at first because
its altitude subtends a smaller elevation angle at a greater
distance.

A similar thought: Why is it that all of the planes that are 20
miles away are seen near the horizon? And why does the airplane
about to land at the airport behind me appear to rise in the sky
as it approaches to fly over me to get there? It is constantly
descending, yet from my viewpoint, it rises clear to the zenith
as it overflies me.

So you can't say that all meteors have need a constantly lowering
elevation angle as seen by a witness. I saw one with a
definitely rising elevation angle two weeks ago.


One also has to take halation into effect. This is the expanding
of the apparent size of a bright object due to scattering of
light within the retina.


That doesn't mean that I think the B737 object was a meteor. I
favor something quite small, like an escaped toy balloon.
Remember that nobody can estimate the size, distance, or speed of
an unidentified object. The reported speed could be a bad
estimate of size combined with the 737's own velocity. See the
Ruppelt discussion of the Gorman case.

You're right Larry. Squaking 5734 simply means the transponder is
transmiting that number which has been assigned by ATC. Normally a/c (here
in the UK at least) transmit 7000, but in controlled airspace you will be
given a unique number in order to identify your plane.

Mode C or Mode Charlie also transmits altitude data

Hi Larry,

Actually, the Soviet Zond 4 satellite is still in orbit (around the sun)never having
decayed on 3/3/68 or any other date. It was supposedly the Zond 4 Rocket Body that
re-entered in March 1968, presumably the third stage of the Proton booster rocket.
But I'm not convinced that the rocket re-entry was responsible for the sightings in the
Eastern U.S. on 3/3/68. It may have been a spectacular meteor fireball. Phil Klass
mistakenly claimed that NORAD had "records" of the Zond 4 decay but when I
contacted NORAD and ADCOM in 1976 they said they didn't. And they wouldn't
either because there was no network of infrared early warning satellites available to
observe and track a re-entry in March 1968.

At that time all NORAD could do was make very uncertain Tracking & Impact
Predictions (TIP's) based on projections of flight path and estimates of highly variable
aerodynamic factors. But NORAD didn't even have a TIP on the Zond 4 rocket body
when I asked for such. At best Phil found a Navy radar fence detection of a relatively
low object at around the time of the sightings, over the fence at 32 N latitude in the
Southern US, but the flight direction was wrong (as I recall it was headed South rather
than North etc.).

Intensive study of the massive Blue Book file on the case might settle the question
one way or another.

I'm rather unclear on whose remarks are whose in the posting I'm addressing here.
The sighting in Indiana?? on Oct 16, 1999 (UTC) has no linkup with any satellite
decays on Alan Pickup's website. He has one at Oct 15.33 or about 0755 UTC or 2:55
AM EST but that is almost a day too early. I did a catalog query on the NASA
Orbital Information Group website (http://oig1.gsfc.nasa.gov/) but found nothing else.

The Web link you gave for satellite re-entry data didn't work. The "vshop" portion of
the URL has a transposition error and should be "vsohp" for Visual Satellite
Observers' Home Page.

Brad Sparks

Dear Jim & List,

I'd feel more comfortable about assigning the 3/3/68 (EST) sightings to Zond 4's
upper stage if there were accurate durations in the minutes versus seconds (typical of
meteor fireballs) -- and there may be -- and if the NAVSPASUR radar fence had
picked it up going in the right direction at the right time. A meteor could conceivably
have missed the radar fence at 32 N latitude by coming in on a more easterly course
but the Zond 4 rocket body could not possibly have done so. I have not been able to
study the scores and scores of sighting reports in the Blue Book file (I don't have a
copy). But duration would be an important factor as well as accurate headings (most
accurate when passing directly overhead of the witness). There is no disagreement
over the fact that this was NOT a UFO and it was either a satellite re-entry or a meteor
fireball.

The important lesson to take from the March 1968 sightings is what Hartmann in the
Condon Report called the "airship effect." Here were hundreds of eyewitnesses who
believed they saw "windows" in a dark outer body when in fact their brains were
imposing a perceptual design on the fiery fragments -- imagining they were bright
"windows." Cf. Chiles-Whitted.

Brad Sparks

Bruce,

Thanks for the detailed analysis. It might further help to see
the full reported interview from that 'Daily Mail' article dated
5 August, 1996:

"We were coming back from Milan and were on the last stages of
approach, at about 4,000ft," recalls Stuart. "We were on a
northerly course direction heading towards the airfield, just in
the tops of the clouds."

"The captain was flying the aircraft. I was monitoring what was
going on; my job was to keep an eye on the settings."

"My peripheral vision was drawn to something out of the front
window. I actually saw the object coming towards me. It was a
silvery grey wedge-shaped object"

"My reactions was to reach for the control column, to try to get
away from what I felt was an object in very close proximity. My
hands never really went further forward than maybe an inch or
two. The object passed very, very close down the right-hand
side."

"I asked the Captain if he had seen it, to which he replied
'yes', he had. We decide to ask air traffic control if they had
seen anything on the radar. They replied that they hadn't and
asked us if we'd like to file an air miss, which would lead to an
investigation."
"The object didn't alter its course. There was no deviation on
the part of either aircraft. It just came down the side, making
no attempt to avoid us, and we didn't have a chance to take any
evasive action. It was over very quickly, so there wasn't much
that could be done."

On landing, both pilots discussed what they had seen. "I
suggested to the Captain that it would be a good idea to draw
what we had seen. We both did so."

"The objects we drew were the same shape, but they differed in
texture - mine was a solid object which I believed had black or
grey stripes down the side."

"I didn't see any windows or anything like that. The Captain drew
a similar shape, but his was made up of lots of different little
lights."

"I felt his drawing could be explained by a reflection from our
landing lights as the object went down our right-hand side."

"We then phoned air traffic control and decided that we would
file an air miss, which meant that all the traces from radar
would have to be examined in further detail."
[End]


Also, from the CAT airmiss report:

"An extract from the RT recording on 119.4, which shows that the
B737 was given decent clearance to 4000 ft at 1845:30, follows:

From:
B737 (1848) - 'c/s we just had something go down the RHS just
above us very fast.'

Manchester - 'Well, there's nothing seen on radar. Was it er an
ac?'

B737 - 'Well, it had lights, it went down the starboard side very
quick.'

Manchester - 'And above you?'

B737 - 'er, just slightly above us, yer.'

Manchester - 'Keep an eye out for something, er, I can't see
anything at all at the moment so, er, must have, er, been very
fast or gone down very quickly after it passed you I think.'
B737 - 'OK. Well, there you go!'

James posted a copy of the report. My comments are added:
>
>"My peripheral vision was drawn to something out of the front

>silvery grey wedge-shaped object"

This does not provide an estimate of the angular elevation,
although one get's the impression that it probably APPEARED
to be at about the elevation of the aircraft. Had there been a
very noticeable angle up, it seems to me it would have appeared
less threatening.

>"My reactions was to reach for the control column, to try to get
>away from what I felt was an object in very close proximity. My
>hands never really went further forward than maybe an inch or
t>wo. The object passed very, very close down the right-hand
>side.">

This suggests that he barely had time to react before it passed
the aircraft . He says right hand side. Implication is that it wasn't
far above the aircraft.
This stretches the fireball explanation to the limit.
Also, it has been suggested that it might have been a mylar
balloon. Well, let's just say some reflective object. It was
nighttime, so it had to be seen either by self-luminosity or
by reflection. Although reflection from city lights MIGHT be
a possibility,it has been suggested that the object was illuminated
by aircraft heaedlights.

(SNIP)
>"I didn't see any windows or anything like that. The Captain drew
>a similar shape, but his was made up of lots of different little
>lights."

>"I felt his drawing could be explained by a reflection from our
l>anding lights as the object went down our right-hand side."

The landing light suggestion is "ingenious" if not amusing.
Consider that the langing lights form expanding beams in
front of the aircraft. How far could one see an object
illuminated by these beams? If it were directly ahead and
and hence in the beam, perhaps a mile or so. Aircraft headlights
are intended as beacons for oncoming aircraft and they are very
bright. But detection of an object requires not only a bright
beam but also a bright reflection and then the light after
reflection diverges quickly, i.e., does not form a beam (unless the
object happens to be a flat mirror). I don't know what size a mylar
balloon might be, but let's pick 1 meter as a large size. At
1 kilometer the angular size is 1 milliradian....detectable in daylight
viewing. Optimum reflection alignment in the aircraft beam, could make
such a thing
appear as a bright point way off in the distance. Naturally this point
would appear
to grow brighter and larger IF (a) the balloon remained within the beam,
and
(b) the orientation of the balloon relative to the beam remained constant

Hi,

The two primary cases that you are confusing are one that occurred in June
l998 involving a plane on take off from Heathrow. This was reported by the
CAA last month but recently posted on the net as if it were a very recent
incident. The balloon option is possible here as this was a mid day
sighting. No radar tracking occurred.

The other case is an event in January l995 that was reported by the CAA Air
Miss group in l996 as a possible alien craft (an amazing comment) . That
involved a British Airways Boeing 737 from Milan on final approach to
Manchester. This was at night above thick cloud and again only the aircraft
appeared on radar. This is the case where I have long argued it to be a
meteor and that has close similarity with the Chiles Whitted Eastern
Airlines sighting from l948 - which I also believe to be a fireball meteor.

I mentioned when you raised the balloon idea a third case, involving a
Britannia Airways Aircraft near Gatwick Airport in l991 if I recall the date
correctly, where there was a radar tracking of the visually observed
daylight object. A second inbound plane was vectored away by ATC. Although
it has many similarities with the l998 case above in the Gatwick case a
balloon is unlikely due to the radar tracked speed and direction change of
the object.

The latter two cases (the l998 case is too recent) as well as many others
are discussed in my book 'Something in the Air' (Robert Hale, London, l998).
The US publishers are Sterling, New York. They released their edition this
summer but changed the title to 'UFO Danger in the Air' (a sad indictment of
the difference between UK understatement and a US publishers need for in
your face PR to try to sell a book that is purposefully not discussing
aliens ).

Good luck in finding it. The UK edition has sold 747 copies and no paperback
rights so is on target for the least successful UFO book in history -
although there is a nice Fortean irony in the number of copies sold I guess.
So much for efforts at understatement! I suspect Sterling will fare better
with it in the USA given their overt UFO .

In a message dated 11/2/99 1:13:56 AM, ufx@mindspring.com wrote:
<< It doesn't seem to make sense that anything stayed in Earth orbit to

decay a day later. >>

Don't extend your "sense" too far in the unearthly realm of space flight!
<grin>

The Proton third stage carries the fourth stage and payload into a low,
unstable parking orbit. The fourth stage fires before the end of the first
pass, leaving behind the third stage and some ejected covers and other
hardware, and they burn up within a few hours or days at most (as with the
Tampa Bay UFO fireball last September 7). The fourth stage ("Block D" in
Russian terminology) leaves with the interplanetary payload, or in the case
of a geosynchronous payload, goes into the 'transfer orbit' (say 200 by
40,000 km); the payload later circularizes its orbit, and the fourth stage
slowly decays and enters within a year or two (as with the Proton fourth
stage which entered over the Cal/Oregon line last September 1).

<< it seems as though the reentry would have been short and

steep, rather than long and flat...>>

Almost without exception, satellite entries are shallow and long, because air
drag slowly lowers the path around the earth. But when ufologists assume that
the entry must be steep and fast, they unfairly rule out the correct
explanation of many spectacular events (such as the Sept 1 and Sept 7 entries
in the US, both 'classic' Proton entries). Read Allan Hendry -- 20 years ago,
he got it right, and people who forget -- or never took -- his advice will
continue to embarass themselves.

In a message dated 11/2/99 9:32:36 AM, ufx@mindspring.com wrote:

<<But isn't it true that everything that the Proton put on its simulated lunar

trajectory (ie, except for the third stage in its unstable LEO parking

orbit) DID come back down in steep fast reentries along with the Zond

spacecraft?>>

Without active steering, it's unlikely any of it ever hit Earth again,
considering the trajectory dispersions caused by the lunar fly-by. Some would
be thrown entirely clear of Earth, others would hit the moon or enter orbits
with higher perigees -- like, tens of thousands of km, and never (in terms of
geologic time!) re-enter. Compare these vehicles with the Saturn S-4B stages
and discarded post-insertion debris, mainly the SLA panels. None of them ever
hit Earth. Certainly it is physically possible, but in practical terms I'd
rate it extremely unlikely.

Larry,

Actually the NORAD radar "fence," operated by the Navy and called the Naval
Space Surveillance system, usually catches satellites in orbits above 32 degs
inclination a few times per day, rather than once per orbit. The fence only
covers the Southern US over roughly 40 degs of longitude and the earth
rotates under a satellite's orbit about 22 degs of longitude or more per
orbit. So in about three orbits a satellite would completely miss the radar
fence.

Brad

Joel,

I stand corrected on the Zond 4 story. Your reference to the internal Soviet
history reveals that Zond 4 did not go into heliocentric orbit after all but
went into a simulated circumlunar trajectory and underwent controlled
re-entry after 5.22 days, but was destroyed by ground control at about 2346
UTC on March 7, 1968, about 12 km above the Gulf of Guinea in the Atlantic.
Presumably the fourth stage was left in the high apogee orbit and it is
unclear to me whether it would have impacted the earth or not after 5 days or
so or without a braking burn (I'm sure Jim Oberg can clarify).

I've read the subsequent postings between you and Jim Oberg and I see it's
just a misunderstanding. What you were talking about Joel was the obviously
fairly steep 20 g re-entry of the Zond 4 itself on March 7, 1968. But this
was an extremely unusual situation, not normal for 99.99%+ of orbiting space
objects. What Jim is talking about is the Proton third stage which put the
Zond 4 payload into low-earth parking orbit. When this third stage
re-entered, presumably on March 4-5, it would have had a long shallow
re-entry like most re-entering space debris or satellites.

What this Soviet history introduces is the prospect that the Russians might
have an exact record of the Proton third stage's re-entry, if there was some
way of contacting the appropriate sources in Russia.

Brad

away from the moon. On reentry, the guidance system failed, and the planned

James posted a copy of the report. My comments are added:
>
>"My peripheral vision was drawn to something out of the front
>window. I actually saw the object coming towards me. It was a
>silvery grey wedge-shaped object"

This does not provide an estimate of the angular elevation,
although one get's the impression that it probably APPEARED
to be at about the elevation of the aircraft. Had there been a
very noticeable angle up, it seems to me it would have appeared
less threatening.

>"My reactions was to reach for the control column, to try to get
>away from what I felt was an object in very close proximity. My
>hands never really went further forward than maybe an inch or
t>wo. The object passed very, very close down the right-hand
>side.">

This suggests that he barely had time to react before it passed
the aircraft . He says right hand side. Implication is that it wasn't
far above the aircraft.
This stretches the fireball explanation to the limit.
Also, it has been suggested that it might have been a mylar
balloon. Well, let's just say some reflective object. It was
nighttime, so it had to be seen either by self-luminosity or
by reflection. Although reflection from city lights MIGHT be
a possibility,it has been suggested that the object was illuminated
by aircraft heaedlights.

(SNIP)
>"I didn't see any windows or anything like that. The Captain drew
>a similar shape, but his was made up of lots of different little
>lights."

>"I felt his drawing could be explained by a reflection from our
l>anding lights as the object went down our right-hand side."
The landing light suggestion is "ingenious" if not amusing.
Consider that the langing lights form expanding beams in
front of the aircraft. How far could one see an object
illuminated by these beams? If it were directly ahead and
and hence in the beam, perhaps a mile or so. Aircraft headlights
are intended as beacons for oncoming aircraft and they are very
bright. But detection of an object requires not only a bright
beam but also a bright reflection and then the light after
reflection diverges quickly, i.e., does not form a beam (unless the
object happens to be a flat mirror). I don't know what size a mylar
balloon might be, but let's pick 1 meter as a large size. At
1 kilometer the angular size is 1 milliradian....detectable in daylight
viewing. Optimum reflection alignment in the aircraft beam, could make
such a thing
appear as a bright point way off in the distance. Naturally this point
would appear
to grow brighter and larger IF (a) the balloon remained within the beam,
and
(b) the orientation of the balloon relative to the beam remained constant

Hello Jean-Pierre

Here are my responses below:

J. Pharabod wrote:

>
> 1) Hoax (JPP)
>
*A hoax by the witnesses*
Very unlikely. First I'll give some background on how the case
developed. The following day after the sighting, FOX2 and FOX3
approached a local radio station and some details of the Fox Lake
sighting was broadcast. However, that broadcast was as far as it went.
Another radio station got calls regarding other sightings around the
Yukon. I didn't happen to hear any of the broadcasts, and to my
knowledge the news didn't spread to other media local or otherwise. Some

time in 1998 CRM1 anonymously called a UFO research associate of mine
saying that his sighting took place about 1.5 hours before the sightings

over Fox Lake. This was our first clue of the incident suggesting a
large UFO with multiple witnesses. However, we weren't given a date, not

even a year. Then in February of 1999 (more than 2 years after the
event) we got our break, FOX2 telephoned us long distance as a result of

a UFO article in a Yukon wide newspaper (the article described some
unrelated cases). FOX2 gave his name but asked to keep it confidential
he felt uncomfortable giving the names of other witnesses. However, he
did mention that several of the witnesses independently stopped in at
Braeburn Lodge and described their sightings to Steve Watson, the Lodge
owner. I went to talk to Steve the following week and he gave me the
names of several of the witnesses who he said stopped in the same
evening although not all together. He also mentioned that they were very

excited about what they saw. I contacted these people. Many where
reluctant to talk but eventually opened up. They gave me more names and
this "snow balled" into a total of 22 witnesses. Finding these people
took considerable effort, many didn't have phones so I just had to drive

the 2 or 3 hours to their community hoping that at least one would be
home. This process took about 7 months.

If it were an orchestrated hoax by these people they would not had sat
around for someone to show up at their door for 2.5 years. I don't think

they would have arranged to stop consecutively at Braeburn Lodge and
tell
a made up UFO story to the lodge owner.

With some of these witnesses I have met several times, often invited
into their homes. I have got to know them fairly well and consider many
of them as friends. Among the ones I have met frequently are FOX1,
FOX2, FOX3, FOX4, FOX5, PEL1 and PEL2. I can guarantee to you on a
personal level that these people are telling the truth as they recall
it. Even the ones I
only met on one occasion, their demeanor was consistent with that of on
honest person confronted with something that they seen that they could
not explain in terms of conventional means.

*a hoax by me*
This is equally improbable as I would be risking loosing my credibility
as a professional engineer and risking my future employment and
livelihood for myself and my family.

> 2) Aurora Borealis (JPP)

There was too much structure (equally spaced rectangular lights in a
row) for it to be Aurora Borealis.

See drawing by FOX2: http://www.ufobc.org/yukon/2206fox2draw1neg.htm
See drawing by FOX3: http://www.ufobc.org/yukon/2203fox3draw1neg.htm
See drawing by FOX4: http://www.ufobc.org/yukon/2210fox4draw1neg.htm
See drawing by FOX5: http://www.ufobc.org/yukon/2211fox5draw1neg.htm

Most if not all of the witnesses have been brought up in these remote
villages and lead at least partly a subsistanance life style and
therefore have spent a lot of time
outdoors. They know what Northern Lights look like.

been different UFOs but there could be other reasons for the differences
in the drawings:

1. It was 2.5 to 3 years ago from the time the sighting occurred to when

the witnesses were asked to make the drawings. Memories do change.

2. Perhaps witnesses at different locations saw different sides of the
UFO
that may have had a different number/configuration of lights. The
distance
to the UFO also varied so certain details would not be seen by those
further away.

3. Different witnesses spent different amount of time on their drawings.

Some paid a lot of attention to detail while others just provided a
quick
sketch. Some drawings were constructed in just seconds while others, and

one in particular probably over 5 minutes . Artistic talent varied.

4. The UFO may have had certain lights turned off and certain lights
turned on during that evening. It may have varied the "on lights and
"off
lights" between the times when various witnesses observed it.

Note: Drawings by FOX2, FOX3, FOX4 and FOX5 were very similar with the
minor differences that could easily be attributable to points 1 ,2 and 3

above. The differences in drawings of PEL2 and PEL3 I believe could be
mostly attributable to points 1 and 3. The differences between the
drawing
of PEL1 and the other Pelly witnesses I think may be attributable to
points 2 and 4.

5. Points 2, 3 and 4 do not explain the differences in drawings by
witnesses who were together during the sighting. To provide some
explanation for this, one may consider the following. All the the
witness
observed the UFO for several minutes. During their observation the UFO
traversed a considerable distance across the sky thereby changing their
perspective view of it. It likely looked much different from the
different
angles which it was observed. Each witness was asked to draw the UFO. I
would suppose that each witness would pluck one image from their mind
that
corresponded to one of those perspectives. They would likely choose the
one image that had the largest impression on them. This may explain the
differences between the drawings of CRM1 and CRM2, and also between PEL6

and PEL7.

Will do for now. Interested in your further thoughts.

In a message dated 11/5/99 11:27:34 AM, pharabod@in2p3.fr wrote:
<<Aside from the inconsistency already stated, the angular expanse of the
sky by the UFO reported by the witnesses is much too large for any
manmade launched vehicle entering orbit. Also, the UFO possessed too
much structure that would only be noticeable at close range. Again,
refer to drawings by FOX2, FOX3, FOX4 and FOX5.>>

This is a sound response -- however, do not fall into the trap of trying to
imagine how a phenomenon SHOULD look, and eliminating it based on these
theoretical and baseless grounds. Space vehicles entering orbit are often
surrounded by large spherical clouds, or even spiral clouds (if the rocket is
tumbling as it spews), that can be several degrees -- up to ten or more
degrees -- in angular size. As for structure, don't forget the common
perceptual error of seeing lights in formation and deducing the existence of
a joining structure -- it happens with satellite entries ALL of the time.

I've attached a report I did on a 1986 'gas cloud' UFO. The same type of UFOs
made watches stop in China and "chased" several airliner pilots.

=======


The Great East Coast UFO of August 1986
James E. Oberg
Rt 2 Box 350, Dickinson, TX 77539
appeared in skeptical inquirer and MUFON UJ

At about 10 PM EDT on Tuesday, August 12, 1986 (0200 UT Aug 13), nearly the
entire eastern half of the United States was treated to a spectacular
celestial apparition. Millions of people were outside looking for Perseid
meteors, and many of them had their astronomical instruments and cameras at
the ready. So when a bright cloud-like UFO (for it was a genuine Unidentified
Flying Object, at least for a day) appeared in the eastern sky, moving from
right to left, it had probably the largest audience of any UFO ever witnessed
in North America. Sightings occurred from Georgia (Florida was socked in with
clouds) to Louisiana to Houston, Texas, to Tulsa and Oklahoma City, to
Illinois, Kentucky, Michigan, Ontario and Quebec, and all points in between:
South Carolina, Virginia, Massachusetts -- the whole eastern seaboard.

Descriptions of the object and its motion varied, but a general picture soon
emerged. It was called a pinpoint, a moving spiral, a glowing cloud, and a
big ball of fire. In Houston, Don Stockbauer described an orangish nebulosity
surrounded by an irregularly shaped white cloud elongated vertically, with a
dim starlike nucleus. Brenda Newton of Rochester, New York, recalled: "It
started to get bigger and it had a tail. By the time we got out of the truck,
it had begun to spiral. It lasted for a few minutes, then became like a dim
star and floated toward the west." The vice president of the Syracusan
Astronomical Society (New York) said it resembled a "reflection of the moon
off a cloud, but it was very iridescent, very vivid." Wayne Madea, an amateur
astronomer in northern Maine, saw a bright star-like object emit a luminous,
rapidly expanding donut-shaped cloud; through a telescope Madea saw "a
pinpoint of light, like a satellite, traveling with the cloud".

As it turned out, amateur radio listeners -- "hams" -- were also receiving
radio signals from space at that very moment. And that was the key which led
many independent observers to solve the apparition quickly and accurately.
Others (such as myself) did it the hard way, with application of basic
principles of spaceflight and orbital motion.

My involvement began at noon Aug 13 when, at a luncheon "brown bag" meeting
of astronomy enthusiasts, a report of a bright light in the eastern sky, seen
from Houston, was discussed. Returning from lunch, I received a phone call
from David L. Chandler, a writer for the 'Boston Globe' with whom I had
discussed other spaceflight stories months before. He filled me in on the
sightings, and I suggested he check about space launchings, particularly the
Japanese launch (which I had also learned of that morning). At first there
was difficulty in ascertaining the exact launch time (International Date
Line, and confusion at the Japanese representative's office over EST vs EDT),
but an hour later, armed with a good liftoff time and with known orbital
inclination and period, I was able to produce a hand-calculated map which
showed the object heading up the east coast at about 10 PM EDT. Its altitude
was about 1500 km (almost a thousand miles), well high enough for it still to
have been sunlit even though the ground below had been dark for more than an
hour.

Part of my advantage was a long familiarity with similar apparitions caused
by space launches elsewhere in the world, most notably over South America
(Soviet launchings from Plesetsk) and Australia (American launchings from
Cape Canaveral). So my initial hypothesis about a propellant venting sprang
quickly to mind. Such a phenomenon was unheard of over North America, but the
new Japanese rocket test was also the first of its kind.

The names of the vehicles involved were a little confusing. The booster was
called the "H-1" and it was the first launch. It's second stage was powered
by the new "LE5" engine, using super-cold liquid hydrogen as fuel. Two
payloads were deployed: an amateur radio satellite variously called JAS-1
(Japanese Amateur Satellite #1), JO-12 (Japan OSCAR 12), or "Fuji" (by the
builders); the geodetic mirror satellite, EGP ("Experimental Geodetic
Payload"), or "Ajisai" ("Hydrangia Flower"). The booster was launched from
Tanegashima Island off Kyushu at 5:45 AM JST August 13 (2045UT Aug 12), after
a 14 minute hold. Precise tracking data from NORAD allowed a perfect match of
sightings to space vehicle.
I then reported my results to the Smithsonian Scientific Event Network in
Washington, DC, to NORAD Public Affairs in Colorado Springs, to the Committee
for the Scientific Investigation of Claims of the Paranormal (which got me on
a Buffalo, New York radio show which had aired LIVE accounts of the UFO on
Tuesday evening), to NASA Public Information at the Kennedy Space Center in
Florida, and to the MUFON research group in Texas. This in turn resulted in
my receiving about twenty additional telephone calls from news media
throughout the east.

Chandler's story appeared in the 'Boston Globe' (page 6) on Thursday, August
14. It moved over some national news wire, too, since it also appeared in the
same day's 'Houston Chronicle', some Tacoma, Washington, paper, and
presumably elsewhere. On Friday, I did an interview with an Associated Press
reporter from Louisville, Ky, and that story moved nationally over the
weekend.

Within a week, the "UFO" was stuffed, boxed, and buried (it should also have
been seen from Central America, the Caribbean, and the north coast of South
America -- those reports may dribble in over the next few months). But it was
a marvelous experience for the witnesses and for the analysts, and several
interesting points can be raised about "UFO reports" based on this fortuitous
experiment.

Several interesting events involved coincidences. Caught up in the
excitement, Air Traffic Controller Tim Jones in Syracuse reported three
different-colored lights randomly moving and hovering for 45 minutes (but it t
urned out he was watching B-52s land at nearby Rome AFB, several hours after
the real UFO); his account was carried in the nationwide news media, but the
solution rarely was. In Clark County, Kentucky, residents were panicked by an
explosion while the light show was going on -- but the sheriff later got an
anonymous phone call confessing to setting off illegal fireworks. Recalled
County Deputy Larry Lawson: "The people said their homes shook and windows
vibrated as if there had been an explosion or earthquake... They said the
whole sky lit up. All these people weren't imagining or seeing things. Some
of them were very terrified over it right after it happened." These
illustrate the power of coincidence, in which two concurrent independent
events can easily (and erroniously) be integrated into a single unsolvable
mystery. Also, the emotional state of witnesses (such as fear) is no measure
of the authenticity of their original perception.

One other amusing aspect was the wide variety of half-baked explanations
offered for the "UFO". Some speculation associated it with the meteor shower,
a barium cloud, or a satellite burn-up, while other guesses associated it
with an explosion of the Japanese satellite. Professor Richard Stoner of
Bowling Green State University in Ohio was quoted as saying: "It is caused by
little bits and pieces of dust from the comet. They're very small, if there
were a larger piece, an icy piece of material, something about the size of a
snowflake, it might well cause something like this. It would vaporize and
leave a glowing cloud behind it." Astronomy professor Martha Haynes of
Cornell didn't trust the observers: "When people who watch the stars once,
maybe twice a year go out and look hard for a while, they're bound to see
things they think are strange.... When you're in that mind set anything like
the light of a plane on the horizon looks strange." John Bosworth of NASA's
Goddard Space Center scored a near-miss when he attributed the reports to
glints off the EGP satellite's mirrors, reflecting moonlight: "I suspect
that's what they saw", he told a reporter. The National Weather Service and
the Seattle-based National UFO Reporting Center agreed "it was some sort of
natural phenomenon."

A number of people, however, got it right, and right from the start. Tom
Bolton of the David Dunlap Observatory north of Toronto told newsmen it was
caused by release of something from a satellite: "The satellite was actually
seen in the telescope here and we had a report from an amateur astronomer
(who) saw it and saw the release of material from it -- but we're not sure
which satellite it was and we're not sure what the material was that was
released." A number of amateur radio people also told their local papers
exactly the true story: for example, Richard C. Eaton of Fayetteville, NY, a
retired GE engineer, was quoted in the 'Syracuse Herald Journal' as
suspecting the cloud was part of the Japanese launch.

The spiral form also was intriguing. In Syracuse, amateur astronomer Denise
Sabatini reported: "It started out as a pinpoint of light. It was as if it
were releasing some type of reflective gas into the air, and as the gas was
released into air, it was as if it was spiraling around the pinpoint of
light." The spiral was "like pouring milk into coffee." Astronomer Karl
Kamper at the David Dunlap Observatory in Richmond Hill, Ontario, described
the object as starlike surrounded by a small spiral cloud (he told newsmen
the spiral could have been fuel spilling from a damaged satellite, and said
it must have been extremely high in the sky). Chuck Barnes, head naturalist
at the Troy Farm and Nature Center near Detroit, had been giving an outdoor
lecture on meteors when the UFO appeared: "It was glowing like a spiral
pinwheel standing on end and moving on a line from southeast to northwest",
he told newsmen (the motion was actually from SE to northEAST); "It appeared
to be five or six times larger than a full moon." In Massachusetts, an
amateur astronomer watched the plume from the rocket perform two full turns
in four minutes, painting the spinning spiral as he watched.

The relevance of these perceptions to other UFO reports is connected with a
series of night-time sky spirals seen over China in the late 1970s. While UFO
enthusiasts have accepted them uncritically, experienced analysts have voiced
the suspicion that they actually involved space launchings (much like the H-1
over America on August 12). These intuitive suspicions were encouraged by a
recent official Chinese disclosure of the cancellation of the "Windstorm"
space booster, which through the 1970s was being developed in competition to
the "Long March 3" booster; there were several flight tests, including one
unsuccessful satellite launching, although precise dates were not provided.
Further disclosures may allow a precise connection between "Windstorm" space
shots and the "spiral UFOs" over China.
Another interesting phenmomenon was the way in which UFO groups seemed to get
a different type of descriptions than did the national news media. Robert Grib
ble of the National UFO Reporting Center in Seattle got more than a hundred
telephone calls, consistently describing an object shooting straight up into
the sky until it mushroomed at a certain altitude ("It seemed to hold in a
certain airspace", he recalled, adding "I got NO reports of it moving across
the sky"). Sherman Larson, with the Center for UFO Studies in Illinois, said
his group received numerous calls: "In each case, witnesses said an object
appeared to have exploded in the sky and then moved into a cloud." In these
accounts, sub-conscious interpretations by the collectors had evidently
colored the straightforward pure perceptions, and without other accounts the
stories collected by the UFO groups could well have coagulated into a "true
UFO" if the solution had not been published so quickly. This is a
long-recognized (but evidently still serious) problem with anecdotal data
collection.

All in all, the great cloud UFO of August 12, 1986 was an exciting,
illuminating experience, in more ways than one!


******JEO******

In a message dated 11/5/99 11:27:34 AM, pharabod@in2p3.fr wrote:
<<The angular expanse of the sky by the UFO reported by the witnesses is
much too large for it to be the re-entry of rocket or satellite, or
strange meteor. There was also too much detailed structure (rectangular
lights, search beam, many smaller lights that formed a pattern)>>

Without arguing FOR this explanation, I must REPEAT my caution that this
passage is based on a very faulty understanding of what satellite entries
actually DO look like. The December 1991 entry over the English channel, for
example, or the Sept 7, 1999 entry across the Gulf of Mexico, BOTH included
graphic descriptions of "searchlights" from the 'UFO'. Lights forming a
pattern -- that's practically a CLASSIC phrase used by witnesses to entries
(or shallow meteors).

HOWEVER, an entry crosses the sky at an angular rate of about a degree per
second, and if this motion is utterly inconsistent with the witness reports
in this case, this strongly argues AGAINST such an explanation.
