PATROL CAR ILLUMINATED BY UFO
Damon, Texas, September 3, 1965

About 11:00 p.m. on a Friday night, Deputy Sheriff Bob Goode, 50,
was driving his patrol car south out of Damon toward West
Columbia on Highway 36. Since he had suffered a bite on his left
index finger earlier that day from a baby alligator, he had asked
Chief Deputy Billy McCoy, 38, to ride with him in the event the
pain flared up and interfered with his driving. It was a
sparkling clear moonlit Texas night, and Goode rested his arm in
the open window of the door as they drove through the prairie.
Suddenly McCoy spotted a bright purple light on the horizon to
the southwest which appeared to be about five to six miles
distant. At first they thought it might be something in the
nearby oil fields, perhaps an oil-drilling rig. But then a blue
light, smaller in diameter than the purple light, emerged from it
and moved to the right before stopping. Both lights remained in
this orientation for a while before beginning to drift upward.
This upward floating motion continued until the objects reached
an elevation of 5-10 degrees above the horizon.

Goode then studied the lights through a pair of binoculars, but
could not make out any additional features. As their curiosity
mounted, the officers began to look for back roads that might
take them closer to the lights. They stopped again, and this time
the lights suddenly swooped toward them, covering the intervening
distance in 1-2 seconds, abruptly stopping practically overhead.
Their patrol car and the surrounding terrain were brightly
illuminated in purple light. They could now see that the purple
and blue lights were attached to opposite ends of an enormous
object, hovering about 150 feet from them at about a 100-foot
altitude.

In his later statement to the Air Force, McCoy described what he
saw:

"The bulk of the object was plainly visible at this time and
appeared to be triangular shaped with a bright purple light on
the left end and the smaller, less bright, blue light on the
right end. The bulk of the object appeared to be dark gray in
color with no other distinguishing features. It appeared to be
about 200 feet wide and 40-50 feet thick in the middle, tapering
off toward both ends. There was no noise or any trail. The bright
purple light illuminated the ground directly underneath it and
the area in front of it, including the highway and the interior
of our patrol car. The tall grass under the object did not appear
to be disturbed. There was a bright moon out and it cast a shadow
of the object on the ground immediately below it in the grass."

To both men, the object seemed to be "as big as a football
field." Goode could feel strong heat emanating from the object
onto his left arm, through his shirt-sleeve.

After a few seconds, with the strange object hovering almost
directly overhead, they fled the scene and headed toward Damon
"as fast as we could go," making speeds of up to 110 miles per
hour. McCoy kept watching the object out the rear window of the
car. For 10 to 15 seconds, the UFO continued to hover above the
pasture. Then it abruptly shot back in the direction from which
it had come. "After arriving at approximately its original
position," McCoy reported, "it went straight up in the air and
disappeared at 25-30 degrees above the horizon."

Back at Damon, the shaken officers calmed themselves, and then
decided to go back and investigate again. This time they drove
down the Damon-West Columbia road, but saw nothing. Finally they
returned to the area where they had first seen the lights, and
once again spied the purple light on the horizon, and again saw
the smaller blue light emerge with a strange two-step motion and
float upward. Fearing another close encounter, they again fled
the area.

Goode and McCoy continued on their shift until three or four in
the morning, then stopped for breakfast at a cafe. Goode noted
that his alligator bite was no longer sore, and when he unwrapped
the bandage he discovered that the swelling had gone down and
that the wound was nearly healed. Next day, the wound showed
virtually no scarring.

The deputies reported the sighting to Ellington Air Force Base,
and Major Laurence Leach, Jr., arrived on September 8, 1965, to
interview McCoy and Goode and take a statement. Leach's report to
Project Blue Book headquarters at Wright-Patterson Air Force Base
reflected his puzzlement. "There is no doubt in my mind," he
said, "that they definitely saw some unusual object or
phenomenon....Both officers appeared to be intelligent, mature,
level-headed persons capable of sound judgement and reasoning."
(Air Force unidentified case, Project Blue Book files, National
Archives. For more detailed information, see Donald E. Keyhoe and
Gordon I.R. Lore, Jr., UFOs: A New Look, NICAP, Washington, D.C.,
1969, pp. 7-8; McCoy statement, Brazoria County Sheriff's
Department, Sept. 8, 1965; "Ellington [AFB] Probes UFO Seen by
Local Deputies," Brazosport Facts, Sept. 6, 1965; Rhonda Moran,
"The Night of the UFO," Brazosport Facts, Sept. 13, 1995.)
[End]


Was there ever any question of a hoax, or evidence which could
conceivably explain this 1965 incident?

Jean-Pierre,

One possible explanation for this interesting case was that, if a
structured object at all, the witnesses might have observed an
airship.

The object's apparent huge size and relatively slow airspeed
would seem to rule out most other probabilities.

However, the difficulty is being uncertain of whether the
testimonies are accurate, especially those which were not
documented until much later.

Presumably investigations so far have found no evidence for an
airship being in that area at the time.

Although we have no known connection to this story, there is at
least one Canadian company, based in Ontario, who manufacture and
fly large, unusual airship designs - 21st Century Airships Inc.
See examples at:

http://www.21stcenturyairships.com/H1994.htm
http://www.21stcenturyairships.com/H1995.htm
http://www.21stcenturyairships.com/H1996-97.htm

similar in the Yukon area on 11 December, 1996, or can suggest
someone who might have.

can be accessed from the 'Airship Manufacturer Database' at:

http://hotairship.com/database/index.html

Also at:

is the only on-line photograph I could find of a 'kytoon', used
in Meteorological research.

Stadium'. There are of course comparisons between this case and

of instantaneous, rapid acceleration (or so it seemed).

I have highlighted some of those accounts on the list and it
seems we have yet to find an explanation for them - again
assuming the data is reliable in the first place.

from David L. Chandler, a writer for the 'Boston Globe' with whom I had
discussed other spaceflight stories months before. He filled me in on the
sightings, and I suggested he check about space launchings, particularly the
Japanese launch (which I had also learned of that morning). At first there
was difficulty in ascertaining the exact launch time (International Date
Line, and confusion at the Japanese representative's office over EST vs EDT),
but an hour later, armed with a good liftoff time and with known orbital
inclination and period, I was able to produce a hand-calculated map which
showed the object heading up the east coast at about 10 PM EDT. Its altitude
was about 1500 km (almost a thousand miles), well high enough for it still to
have been sunlit even though the ground below had been dark for more than an
hour.
Part of my advantage was a long familiarity with similar apparitions caused
by space launches elsewhere in the world, most notably over South America
(Soviet launchings from Plesetsk) and Australia (American launchings from
Cape Canaveral). So my initial hypothesis about a propellant venting sprang
quickly to mind. Such a phenomenon was unheard of over North America, but the
new Japanese rocket test was also the first of its kind.

The names of the vehicles involved were a little confusing. The booster was
called the "H-1" and it was the first launch. It's second stage was powered
by the new "LE5" engine, using super-cold liquid hydrogen as fuel. Two
payloads were deployed: an amateur radio satellite variously called JAS-1
(Japanese Amateur Satellite #1), JO-12 (Japan OSCAR 12), or "Fuji" (by the
builders); the geodetic mirror satellite, EGP ("Experimental Geodetic
Payload"), or "Ajisai" ("Hydrangia Flower"). The booster was launched from
Tanegashima Island off Kyushu at 5:45 AM JST August 13 (2045UT Aug 12), after
a 14 minute hold. Precise tracking data from NORAD allowed a perfect match of
sightings to space vehicle.

I then reported my results to the Smithsonian Scientific Event Network in
Washington, DC, to NORAD Public Affairs in Colorado Springs, to the Committee
for the Scientific Investigation of Claims of the Paranormal (which got me on
a Buffalo, New York radio show which had aired LIVE accounts of the UFO on
Tuesday evening), to NASA Public Information at the Kennedy Space Center in
Florida, and to the MUFON research group in Texas. This in turn resulted in
my receiving about twenty additional telephone calls from news media
throughout the east.

Chandler's story appeared in the 'Boston Globe' (page 6) on Thursday, August
14. It moved over some national news wire, too, since it also appeared in the
same day's 'Houston Chronicle', some Tacoma, Washington, paper, and
presumably elsewhere. On Friday, I did an interview with an Associated Press
reporter from Louisville, Ky, and that story moved nationally over the
weekend.

Within a week, the "UFO" was stuffed, boxed, and buried (it should also have
been seen from Central America, the Caribbean, and the north coast of South
America -- those reports may dribble in over the next few months). But it was
a marvelous experience for the witnesses and for the analysts, and several
interesting points can be raised about "UFO reports" based on this fortuitous
experiment.

Several interesting events involved coincidences. Caught up in the
excitement, Air Traffic Controller Tim Jones in Syracuse reported three
different-colored lights randomly moving and hovering for 45 minutes (but it t
urned out he was watching B-52s land at nearby Rome AFB, several hours after
the real UFO); his account was carried in the nationwide news media, but the
solution rarely was. In Clark County, Kentucky, residents were panicked by an
explosion while the light show was going on -- but the sheriff later got an
anonymous phone call confessing to setting off illegal fireworks. Recalled
County Deputy Larry Lawson: "The people said their homes shook and windows
vibrated as if there had been an explosion or earthquake... They said the
whole sky lit up. All these people weren't imagining or seeing things. Some
of them were very terrified over it right after it happened." These
illustrate the power of coincidence, in which two concurrent independent
events can easily (and erroniously) be integrated into a single unsolvable
mystery. Also, the emotional state of witnesses (such as fear) is no measure
of the authenticity of their original perception.

One other amusing aspect was the wide variety of half-baked explanations
offered for the "UFO". Some speculation associated it with the meteor shower,
a barium cloud, or a satellite burn-up, while other guesses associated it
with an explosion of the Japanese satellite. Professor Richard Stoner of
Bowling Green State University in Ohio was quoted as saying: "It is caused by
little bits and pieces of dust from the comet. They're very small, if there
were a larger piece, an icy piece of material, something about the size of a
snowflake, it might well cause something like this. It would vaporize and
leave a glowing cloud behind it." Astronomy professor Martha Haynes of
Cornell didn't trust the observers: "When people who watch the stars once,
maybe twice a year go out and look hard for a while, they're bound to see
things they think are strange.... When you're in that mind set anything like
the light of a plane on the horizon looks strange." John Bosworth of NASA's
Goddard Space Center scored a near-miss when he attributed the reports to
glints off the EGP satellite's mirrors, reflecting moonlight: "I suspect
that's what they saw", he told a reporter. The National Weather Service and
the Seattle-based National UFO Reporting Center agreed "it was some sort of
natural phenomenon."

A number of people, however, got it right, and right from the start. Tom
Bolton of the David Dunlap Observatory north of Toronto told newsmen it was
caused by release of something from a satellite: "The satellite was actually
seen in the telescope here and we had a report from an amateur astronomer
(who) saw it and saw the release of material from it -- but we're not sure
which satellite it was and we're not sure what the material was that was
released." A number of amateur radio people also told their local papers
exactly the true story: for example, Richard C. Eaton of Fayetteville, NY, a
retired GE engineer, was quoted in the 'Syracuse Herald Journal' as
suspecting the cloud was part of the Japanese launch.

The spiral form also was intriguing. In Syracuse, amateur astronomer Denise
Sabatini reported: "It started out as a pinpoint of light. It was as if it
were releasing some type of reflective gas into the air, and as the gas was
released into air, it was as if it was spiraling around the pinpoint of
light." The spiral was "like pouring milk into coffee." Astronomer Karl
Kamper at the David Dunlap Observatory in Richmond Hill, Ontario, described
the object as starlike surrounded by a small spiral cloud (he told newsmen
the spiral could have been fuel spilling from a damaged satellite, and said
it must have been extremely high in the sky). Chuck Barnes, head naturalist
at the Troy Farm and Nature Center near Detroit, had been giving an outdoor
lecture on meteors when the UFO appeared: "It was glowing like a spiral
pinwheel standing on end and moving on a line from southeast to northwest",
he told newsmen (the motion was actually from SE to northEAST); "It appeared
to be five or six times larger than a full moon." In Massachusetts, an
amateur astronomer watched the plume from the rocket perform two full turns
in four minutes, painting the spinning spiral as he watched.

The relevance of these perceptions to other UFO reports is connected with a
series of night-time sky spirals seen over China in the late 1970s. While UFO
enthusiasts have accepted them uncritically, experienced analysts have voiced
the suspicion that they actually involved space launchings (much like the H-1
over America on August 12). These intuitive suspicions were encouraged by a
recent official Chinese disclosure of the cancellation of the "Windstorm"
space booster, which through the 1970s was being developed in competition to
the "Long March 3" booster; there were several flight tests, including one
unsuccessful satellite launching, although precise dates were not provided.
Further disclosures may allow a precise connection between "Windstorm" space
shots and the "spiral UFOs" over China.

Another interesting phenmomenon was the way in which UFO groups seemed to get
a different type of descriptions than did the national news media. Robert Grib
ble of the National UFO Reporting Center in Seattle got more than a hundred
telephone calls, consistently describing an object shooting straight up into
the sky until it mushroomed at a certain altitude ("It seemed to hold in a
certain airspace", he recalled, adding "I got NO reports of it moving across
the sky"). Sherman Larson, with the Center for UFO Studies in Illinois, said
his group received numerous calls: "In each case, witnesses said an object
appeared to have exploded in the sky and then moved into a cloud." In these
accounts, sub-conscious interpretations by the collectors had evidently
colored the straightforward pure perceptions, and without other accounts the
stories collected by the UFO groups could well have coagulated into a "true
UFO" if the solution had not been published so quickly. This is a
long-recognized (but evidently still serious) problem with anecdotal data
collection.

All in all, the great cloud UFO of August 12, 1986 was an exciting,
illuminating experience, in more ways than one!


******JEO******

Summarised in, I believe, a public document on FUFOR's web site:


PATROL CAR ILLUMINATED BY UFO

Damon, Texas, September 3, 1965


About 11:00 p.m. on a Friday night, Deputy Sheriff Bob Goode, 50,

was driving his patrol car south out of Damon toward West

Columbia on Highway 36. Since he had suffered a bite on his left

index finger earlier that day from a baby alligator, he had asked

Chief Deputy Billy McCoy, 38, to ride with him in the event the

pain flared up and interfered with his driving. It was a

sparkling clear moonlit Texas night, and Goode rested his arm in

the open window of the door as they drove through the prairie.
Suddenly McCoy spotted a bright purple light on the horizon to

the southwest which appeared to be about five to six miles

distant. At first they thought it might be something in the

nearby oil fields, perhaps an oil-drilling rig. But then a blue

light, smaller in diameter than the purple light, emerged from it

and moved to the right before stopping. Both lights remained in

this orientation for a while before beginning to drift upward.

This upward floating motion continued until the objects reached

an elevation of 5-10 degrees above the horizon.


Goode then studied the lights through a pair of binoculars, but

could not make out any additional features. As their curiosity

mounted, the officers began to look for back roads that might

take them closer to the lights. They stopped again, and this time

the lights suddenly swooped toward them, covering the intervening

distance in 1-2 seconds, abruptly stopping practically overhead.

Their patrol car and the surrounding terrain were brightly

illuminated in purple light. They could now see that the purple

and blue lights were attached to opposite ends of an enormous

object, hovering about 150 feet from them at about a 100-foot

altitude.


In his later statement to the Air Force, McCoy described what he

saw:


"The bulk of the object was plainly visible at this time and
appeared to be triangular shaped with a bright purple light on

the left end and the smaller, less bright, blue light on the

right end. The bulk of the object appeared to be dark gray in

color with no other distinguishing features. It appeared to be

about 200 feet wide and 40-50 feet thick in the middle, tapering

off toward both ends. There was no noise or any trail. The bright

purple light illuminated the ground directly underneath it and

the area in front of it, including the highway and the interior

of our patrol car. The tall grass under the object did not appear

to be disturbed. There was a bright moon out and it cast a shadow

of the object on the ground immediately below it in the grass."


To both men, the object seemed to be "as big as a football

field." Goode could feel strong heat emanating from the object

onto his left arm, through his shirt-sleeve.


After a few seconds, with the strange object hovering almost

directly overhead, they fled the scene and headed toward Damon

"as fast as we could go," making speeds of up to 110 miles per

hour. McCoy kept watching the object out the rear window of the

car. For 10 to 15 seconds, the UFO continued to hover above the

pasture. Then it abruptly shot back in the direction from which

it had come. "After arriving at approximately its original

position," McCoy reported, "it went straight up in the air and

disappeared at 25-30 degrees above the horizon."


Back at Damon, the shaken officers calmed themselves, and then
decided to go back and investigate again. This time they drove

down the Damon-West Columbia road, but saw nothing. Finally they

returned to the area where they had first seen the lights, and

once again spied the purple light on the horizon, and again saw

the smaller blue light emerge with a strange two-step motion and

float upward. Fearing another close encounter, they again fled

the area.


Goode and McCoy continued on their shift until three or four in

the morning, then stopped for breakfast at a cafe. Goode noted

that his alligator bite was no longer sore, and when he unwrapped

the bandage he discovered that the swelling had gone down and

that the wound was nearly healed. Next day, the wound showed

virtually no scarring.


The deputies reported the sighting to Ellington Air Force Base,

and Major Laurence Leach, Jr., arrived on September 8, 1965, to

interview McCoy and Goode and take a statement. Leach's report to

Project Blue Book headquarters at Wright-Patterson Air Force Base

reflected his puzzlement. "There is no doubt in my mind," he

said, "that they definitely saw some unusual object or

phenomenon....Both officers appeared to be intelligent, mature,

level-headed persons capable of sound judgement and reasoning."


(Air Force unidentified case, Project Blue Book files, National

Archives. For more detailed information, see Donald E. Keyhoe and
Gordon I.R. Lore, Jr., UFOs: A New Look, NICAP, Washington, D.C.,

1969, pp. 7-8; McCoy statement, Brazoria County Sheriff's

Department, Sept. 8, 1965; "Ellington [AFB] Probes UFO Seen by

Local Deputies," Brazosport Facts, Sept. 6, 1965; Rhonda Moran,

"The Night of the UFO," Brazosport Facts, Sept. 13, 1995.)

[End]



Was there ever any question of a hoax, or evidence which could

conceivably explain this 1965 incident?

UFO fly over his place south to north, than north to south, then south to
north, changing color each time. If I hadn't been watching myself at the
time while walking somewhere, I wouldn't have seen the three airliners
that flew over the town in succession, each disappearing behind one of two
clouds just before the next appeared from behind the same cloud. Since
they had their landing lights on, they were not immediately obvious as
airplanes. The three planes were coincidentally in the right places at
the right time to make the effect.

This direction ambiguity could be a difference between the actual
direction the object was heading versus the directions the witness
observed the object in. The object's actual flight path cannot go from
southeast to northeast unless the object turns. Likewise, I can watch an
airliner which is heading toward the northwest that disappears in my
northeast. The question is whose compass the motion reported is relative
to - the object's, or the observer's? The same ambiguity of type of
direction reporting appears in the Lakenheath/Bentwaters case. Perspective
between the actual flight path and the witness location can have an effect
on the report too.

@suspicions were encouraged by a recent official Chinese disclosure of the
@cancellation of the "Windstorm" space booster, which through the 1970s
@was being developed in competition to the "Long March 3" booster; there
@were several flight tests, including one unsuccessful satellite
@launching, although precise dates were not provided. Further disclosures
@may allow a precise connection between "Windstorm" space shots and the
@"spiral UFOs" over China.

@Another interesting phenomenon was the way in which UFO groups seemed to
@get a different type of descriptions than did the national news media.
@Robert Gribble of the National UFO Reporting Center in Seattle got
@more than a hundred telephone calls, consistently describing an object
@shooting straight up into the sky until it mushroomed at a certain
@altitude ("It seemed to hold in a certain airspace", he recalled, adding
@"I got NO reports of it moving across the sky"). Sherman Larson, with the
@Center for UFO Studies in Illinois, said his group received numerous
@calls: "In each case, witnesses said an object appeared to have exploded
@in the sky and then moved into a cloud." In these accounts, sub-conscious
@interpretations by the collectors had evidently colored the
@straightforward pure perceptions, and without other accounts the stories
@collected by the UFO groups could well have coagulated into a "true UFO"
@if the solution had not been published so quickly. This is a
@long-recognized (but evidently still serious) problem with anecdotal data
@collection.


These could also be observational overlaps with unconnected (coincidental)
airplanes and clouds visible only from the viewpoint of certain witnesses.
The fact that different UFO groups got different descriptions may have to
do with where each group had handy field investigators, and which group
each local law enforcement agency suggested that witnesses should call.
It has been my experience that they usually have a handy phone number (of
one local investigator or one national group) to get rid of UFO calls to.

@illuminating experience, in more ways than one!

@Summarized in, I believe, a public document on FUFOR's web site:

@PATROL CAR ILLUMINATED BY UFO
@Damon, Texas, September 3, 1965
@
@About 11:00 p.m. on a Friday night, Deputy Sheriff Bob Goode, 50,
@was driving his patrol car south out of Damon toward West
@Columbia on Highway 36. Since he had suffered a bite on his left
@index finger earlier that day from a baby alligator, he had asked
@Chief Deputy Billy McCoy, 38, to ride with him in the event the
@pain flared up and interfered with his driving. It was a
@sparkling clear moonlit Texas night, and Goode rested his arm in
@the open window of the door as they drove through the prairie.
@Suddenly McCoy spotted a bright purple light on the horizon to
@the southwest which appeared to be about five to six miles
@distant. At first they thought it might be something in the
@nearby oil fields, perhaps an oil-drilling rig. But then a blue
@light, smaller in diameter than the purple light, emerged from it
@and moved to the right before stopping. Both lights remained in
@this orientation for a while before beginning to drift upward.
@This upward floating motion continued until the objects reached
@an elevation of 5-10 degrees above the horizon.
@
@Goode then studied the lights through a pair of binoculars, but
@could not make out any additional features. As their curiosity
@mounted, the officers began to look for back roads that might
@take them closer to the lights. They stopped again, and this time
@the lights suddenly swooped toward them, covering the intervening
@distance in 1-2 seconds, abruptly stopping practically overhead.
@Their patrol car and the surrounding terrain were brightly
@illuminated in purple light. They could now see that the purple
@and blue lights were attached to opposite ends of an enormous
@object, hovering about 150 feet from them at about a 100-foot
@altitude.
@
@In his later statement to the Air Force, McCoy described what he
@saw:
@
@"The bulk of the object was plainly visible at this time and
@appeared to be triangular shaped with a bright purple light on
@the left end and the smaller, less bright, blue light on the
@right end. The bulk of the object appeared to be dark gray in
@color with no other distinguishing features. It appeared to be
@about 200 feet wide and 40-50 feet thick in the middle, tapering
@off toward both ends. There was no noise or any trail. The bright
@purple light illuminated the ground directly underneath it and
@the area in front of it, including the highway and the interior
@of our patrol car. The tall grass under the object did not appear
@to be disturbed. There was a bright moon out and it cast a shadow
@of the object on the ground immediately below it in the grass."
@
@To both men, the object seemed to be "as big as a football
@field." Goode could feel strong heat emanating from the object
@onto his left arm, through his shirt-sleeve.
@
@After a few seconds, with the strange object hovering almost
@directly overhead, they fled the scene and headed toward Damon
@"as fast as we could go," making speeds of up to 110 miles per
@hour. McCoy kept watching the object out the rear window of the
@car. For 10 to 15 seconds, the UFO continued to hover above the
@pasture. Then it abruptly shot back in the direction from which
@it had come. "After arriving at approximately its original
@position," McCoy reported, "it went straight up in the air and
@disappeared at 25-30 degrees above the horizon."
@
@Back at Damon, the shaken officers calmed themselves, and then
@decided to go back and investigate again. This time they drove
@down the Damon-West Columbia road, but saw nothing. Finally they
@returned to the area where they had first seen the lights, and
@once again spied the purple light on the horizon, and again saw
@the smaller blue light emerge with a strange two-step motion and
@float upward. Fearing another close encounter, they again fled
@the area.
@
@Goode and McCoy continued on their shift until three or four in
@the morning, then stopped for breakfast at a cafe. Goode noted
@that his alligator bite was no longer sore, and when he unwrapped
@the bandage he discovered that the swelling had gone down and
@that the wound was nearly healed. Next day, the wound showed
@virtually no scarring.
@
@The deputies reported the sighting to Ellington Air Force Base,
@and Major Laurence Leach, Jr., arrived on September 8, 1965, to
@interview McCoy and Goode and take a statement. Leach's report to
@Project Blue Book headquarters at Wright-Patterson Air Force Base
@reflected his puzzlement. "There is no doubt in my mind," he
@said, "that they definitely saw some unusual object or
@phenomenon....Both officers appeared to be intelligent, mature,
@level-headed persons capable of sound judgement and reasoning."
@
@(Air Force unidentified case, Project Blue Book files, National
@Archives. For more detailed information, see Donald E. Keyhoe and

@1969, pp. 7-8; McCoy statement, Brazoria County Sheriff's
@Department, Sept. 8, 1965; "Ellington [AFB] Probes UFO Seen by
@Local Deputies," Brazosport Facts, Sept. 6, 1965; Rhonda Moran,
@"The Night of the UFO," Brazosport Facts, Sept. 13, 1995.)
@[End]
@
@
@Was there ever any question of a hoax, or evidence which could
@conceivably explain this 1965 incident?


There is certainly an inconsistency:

The object was said to have cast a shadow on the ground from moonlight. It
was also said to have illuminated the ground under it, and to have given
off enough light to read by. No change in illumination was reported. How
can the same object do both?

Also, we have to remember that UFOs had just hit the news a month earlier
in the same area, when thousands of people (many being police) in the
plains states reported UFO activity. People were primed to turn mundane
objects into UFOs, and the cranks were turning out fake photos and
sighting reports. One would wonder what the officers would have discovered
if they had remained at the scene (assuming it wasn't a hoax).

for bringing this important story to our attention:

ANOMALY FOUNDATION, Apartado 5041, 39080 Santander, Spain
Web site address: www.anomalia.org
Press Officer (Mr. Ricardo Campo) e-mail: rcampo@datalogic.es

PRESS RELEASE

20 YEARS OF MYSTERY ARE OVER
THE ANOMALY FOUNDATION SOLVES THE 'MANISES' UFO CASE

On the 20th anniversary of the most infamous Spanish UFO
sighting, the Spanish "Anomaly Foundation" (www.anomalia.org) has
presented to the press a detailed report written by engineer Mr.
Juan A. Fernandez Peris from Valencia, which definitely closes
this emblematic aerial UFO incident, which occurred on 11/11/79
over the Mediterranean Sea. After a scientific and painstaking
investigation of almost two decades, the 'Manises UFO' case has
been solved.

On November 11th, 1979, a flight of the now defunct TAE air
company with 109 people on board made an emergency landing in the
Manises airport (Valencia) forced by the risk of a collision with
two weird red lights that were seen from the cockpit. According
to the statements by pilots, the lights were first observed at
23:05, but then the lights appeared to come near the aircraft the
crew became very nervous. Barcelona's air transit control centre
denied that there was any other aircraft in the area, so pilot
Francisco-Javier Lerdo de Tejada decided to abort the flight and
make an emergency landing in Manises, where he arrived at 23:45.
Consulted the military radar, it did not confirm any anomalous
traffic nearby.

Ground observers based on the airport reported a number of
strange-looking lights. Witnesses included the flight controllers
and airport staff personnel. Because of that, one hour later, at
00:40 of November 12th, a Spanish Air Force Mirage aircraft was
scrambled from Los Llanos Air Force Base to find out what was
going on. The combat jet pilot observed various unknown lights
that he pursued with his aircraft over an extended period of
time. Although he was unable to reach the lights, some
electromagnetic disturbing effects on radio communications and
weapon systems manifested during the flight.

The Spanish Anomaly Foundation granted its "Ricardo Caruncho"
research prize to Mr. Fernandez Peris for his 200-page analysis
report on the circumstances surrounding this incident.
Investigation resolved that the original lights observed from the
civil airplane were prompted by flare-ups raised from two
combustion towers located in the major oil refinery of
Escombreras, near Cartagena, Spain. The direction of lights as
well as their apparent angular size matched exactly with the
luminous flashes emitted from the chemical industry complex.
Their brightness and special features produced an optical
mistake, but the main culprit was a strong temperature inversion
developed that night, one with an exceptional visibility. All
factors together contributed decisively to the sighting
distortion.

As far a the pilot was concerned, he had some important family
problems underway which unleashed an anxiety attack facing the
remote lights which he considered to be anomalous in nature. As
Barcelona's air transit control centre did not offer any
solution, the pilot took an obviously disproportionate decision,
deviating the flight off-route (it was scheduled Mallorca-Canary
islands) and landing in the Manises airport.

It is a noteworthy fact that during those days the Spanish media
was overflowed with UFO reports and the atmosphere was quite
favourable to believing that extraterrestrial crafts were flying
our skies. This sociological ambient took a weight on the pilot's
reaction as well, no doubt.

The tight situation lived at the airport during the air UFO
encounter, with much radio exchange with the pilot, moved the
staff personnel to start looking for any strange light in the
sky. Afterwards those were identified as stars and planets, but
not at that precise time.

On the other hand, the Mirage aircraft manned by captain F.
Camera returned to its base at 02:07, after and unsuccessful
pursuit of several non-defined luminous stimuli, which had not
any relationship with the lights seen from the TAE airliner. The
most amazing part of the incident, the EM interference suffered
by the military jet when flying over Valencia city, these were
caused by the electronic countermeasures adopted by US Navy
helicopter's carrier "Iwo-Jima", a US Sixth Fleet's ship sailing
near the Columbretes islands. The US Navy ship was at the highest
alert due to Iran's hostages' crisis developed at the time.

In summary, an extraordinary and unusual mixture of chance
circumstances lead to an exaggeration and distortion of events,
otherwise trivial.

The Anomaly Foundation (Apartado 5041, Santander, Spain) has
established a fund to publish the ultimate book on this UFO
classic case. Both donations and queries are welcome.
[End]

Date: Wed, 10 Nov 1999 03:35:38 +0000
From: James Easton <voyager@ukonline.co.uk>
Subject: Reports of Closely Observed UFOsMessage-id:
<008a01bf2b2c$a8eb1fc0$a4c628c3@cis.compuserve.com>

UFO Research List - http://web.ukonline.co.uk/voyager/

*LIST ONLY PLEASE *

Anecdotal 'UFO' stories are inherently frustrating to
researchers. There's usually no corroborative witness accounts
and only exceptionally, corresponding photographic/video
evidence.

That acknowledged, there's one particular testimony which I was
able to document in detail and having 'left aside' for some four
years now, I've taken another look at and realise, in hindsight,
has some features which may be intriguing. if not unique.

Although I doubt they can be explained, it's a case I consider
worthy of contemplation as I had lengthy correspondence with the
claimed witness and have no reason to suspect any elaborations in
her account. Indeed, the reverse maybe applies as Julia had
grounds to believe the incident probably involved an experimental
military aircraft.

I no longer believe that's a comfortable explanation - the USAF
surely doesn't have an aircraft capable of what she describes
[they wish!].


Anyway, Julie's affidavit follows and for the first time publicly
I will add some further comments from her correspondence. As it
was understood I intended to publish this story, plus I'm not
identifying Julie and of course never would, these will hopefully
help set the case in the context I understand.

This was Julie's recollections, as summarised from her
correspondence, which she confirmed to be an accurate synopsis:

[START]
I swear this craft just appeared over my head. This was at about
10:00 a.m. on a bright, sunny day. There was one of those
skyquakes, then in a minute or two after that, (I was outside)
the atmosphere seemed to get "heavy" like it was pushing down on
me, and it got warm. I have dogs and they were growling and when
I looked up, suddenly this craft was over my head, fairly close
too. I felt it there before I actually saw it. I did not see it,
or hear it approach except for noticing the change in the
atmosphere, suddenly it was just there, as if becoming visible
for the first time.

It appeared to be gunmetal gray, almost black, but not quite. I'd
say the shape was - triangular, a regular triangle. It was
exactly like the craft - well, no, but very close to the craft in
the second episode of the X-Files.

I'm not sure how to describe how big this craft was. It was big,
but not giant. It was wider than a helicopter but not as wide as
the stealth fighter wing span, or maybe it was close to that. And
it was very close to me, so close that I had a hard time keeping
my eyes open because of the pressure it caused in the air. The
eerie part was the silence for a craft hovering so close. It
wasn't far above the roof of our kennel and looked close enough
to almost touch. I'm not a very good judge of measurements so I
can't say for sure how high above me it actually was, but it
seemed rather close, I'd guess about 25 feet.

I was almost directly below it, so I only saw the bottom. It had
lights around the edges of the triangle, but I couldn't say how
many and they didn't appear to be on. I can say for certain that
I saw lights at each one of the three corners of the craft and at
least one on each of the sides. I did see what appeared to be
either a large light or a window directly in the centre of the
triangle.

I can't say if the edges were round or flat as I couldn't really
focus on it for a long time because I couldn't keep my eyes open.
It was sort of like standing under helicopter blades - you have
to shield your eyes. I didn't hear any engines or whirring or
humming, and there was no real air movement to speak of, just
this pressurized feeling and the warmth.

It was there about a minute, give or take a few seconds, then it
disappeared from view - I did not see the craft move at all, it
just wasn't visible anymore. It disappeared just as suddenly as
it appeared and was gone again without any visible movement. It
was pretty creepy. I'm not unused to seeing things in the sky. I
don't live that far from Edwards Air Force Base, as the crow
flies and I'm used to seeing the stealth planes, even when they
denied the existence of them. Those looked like giant bats in the
distant sky. This triangular craft was the same color as the
stealth planes, which leads me to believe they are experimental
military planes.

J.N.
[END]


Initially, Julia said she couldn't be certain about the date,
only that it was sometime during 1993 or 1994. She later noted
that it was definitely before the January,1994 Los Angeles
earthquake and at a time when the 'skyquakes' were being
reported, with speculation these related to the 'Aurora'
aircraft.

It's an unusual tale as Julia insisted this 'craft' exerted that
'downwards pressure', similar to a helicopter.

The 'X-Files' reference is somewhat 'chicken and egg', as the TV
program drew heavily on previously reported 'UFO sightings'.

A triangular-shaped 'black' aircraft which can 'decloak', hover
and 'disappear'...

Maybe 10 years from now?


Although controversial and open to interpretation, Julia added:

"I don't know if I mentioned this to you previously, but someone
close to me was Navy air a few years back and had more than a few
UFO sightings that were without a doubt NOT military. It was his
job to fly around the world testing on-board tracking systems
under various weather conditions. He spent much time in the
Aluetian Islands in Alaska and other remote places where there
was a lot of activity. They always reported what they saw, even
recorded some of it on video tape, but the tapes were always
confiscated and they were debriefed and told not to talk about it
ever".

Naturally, I endeavoured to understand this and Julia
subsequently elaborated:

"The person I mentioned who was Navy Air is my brother. He
didn't discuss details with me, I had a hard time getting him to
admit he saw strange things, because he takes his "oath"
seriously and when the Navy says don't talk, he doesn't. I trust
his word though, he isn't given to making up stories and he
doesn't really believe in extraterrestrials, although he
does know he saw things he can't explain".


Which, overall, is ostensibly encouraging. No apparent ET
hysteria here and instead some rational appraisals of what
constitutes the 'UFO' phenomena.

Julia seemed to have an appreciation of aircraft technology and
concluded her experience was within that perspective.
Perhaps the most significant aspect of this case and many others
where a silent, 'tree-top' level, hovering, triangular object is
reported and especially where we find such detail of said
'object' provided, is that they limit conceivable explanations.

It appears to basically come down to a conclusion that the
witnesses are fabricating their stories, or that these reports
may have some substance.

No 'strange lights in the sky' in these cases.

Is it agreed there isn't a rational explanation and we must
therefore be faced with 'unreliable' accounts or..... what?


James.

On Tue, 9 Nov 1999, James Easton wrote:

> UFO Research List - http://web.ukonline.co.uk/voyager/

> A few weeks ago, I mentioned there was a published claim that the

> Government Files', Peter writing:
>
> "Belgian skeptic Wim van Utrecht and members of the Belgian Royal
> Military School have shredded technical aspects of the image and

I don't know what are the present conclusions, but in May 1997
(May 5, I think) I spent several hours in this Belgian Royal
Military School where a meeting was entirely devoted to this
photograph. There was Marc Acheroy, Professor and head of a lab
at the Royal Military School, who has studied the photo for
several years (professionally speaking, the analysis of
photographic documents is one of his expertises). He said that
the photograph did not at all look like an hoax and added that,
in his opinion and though he had not definitive proof, it was
the photograph of something which was in the sky. Marc Acheroy
had absolutely not any interest in UFOs before the photograph
was brought to him.

In 1990 or 1991, Wim van Utrecht tried to make a photograph
looking like the 'Petit-Rechain' one. This photograph also was
studied by Marc Acheroy, who concluded that van Utrecht did not
reproduce some characteristics of the original photograph, in
particular the differences in size of the lights in "false
colors" red, green and blue.

There has been some suspicions regarding the 'Petit-Rechain'
photograph because the photographer said that he made it, showed
it to several people in his factory, and put it away somewhere
at home; then (a couple of months after) somebody talked of it to
a professional photographer who bought the photograph. An inquiry
has been made by the SOBEPS who found back all the witnesses
(the people in the factory who initially saw the photo, the
man - also a worker of the factory if I remember correctly -
who contacted the professional photographer). All confirmed
exactly what said the original photographer. Also, when the
photograph was (allegedly) taken, the photographer was with
his girl friend, who confirmed what he said.

I will add that, when the photograph was taken, everybody and
all the media were speaking of "triangles". On the photograph,
it's not exactly a triangle, but a shape with "kink" in the
leading edge, which corresponds to the more precise sightings
of November 29, 1989, when the object was seen at close distance
when it was not yet complete night. Few people knew of this
when the photograph was taken.

[To John Burtenshaw: there was "kink" in the leading edge,
but no "nose", which excludes the Vulcan bomber, at least for
these November 1989 sightings... also the Vulcan bomber does
not hover silently, and was no longer flying in 1989. On the
photograph, there is no "nose", and if there are kinks, maybe
they correspond to the Vulcan's ones, but they correspond also
to the visual sightings of November 29, 1989.]

I am not surprised by the fact that Wim van Utrecht thinks that
the photograph is a hoax. It is possible that some members of
the Royal Military School (which is a rather big institution)
think the same, but they have not the same competence as Marc
Acheroy. I would like to know the date of van Utrecht's
statement: was it before or after May 1997 ? All that I can
say is that, at the beginning of May 1997, practically nobody
in this meeting at the Royal Military School questioned the
authenticity of this photograph (I say practically nobody
because at least I myself questioned it - but I use to question
everything...).

> If they did have doubts, what was behind them, both in relation
> to the photograph, allegedly taken on 31 March 1990 by a Belgian
> factory worker, and witness testimonies?

Just a minor point: the photography was taken at the beginning of
April 1990 (after the 1st !).

Jean-Pierre Pharabod

Does this calculation assume that Daylight Savings Time was in effect
then? Since this happened before the Uniform Time Act (1968), Texas
may not have been observing daylight time. Most western states chose
to avoid the hassle of changing clocks twice a year before 1968. Now,
only Indiana, western Kentucky, Arizona, Alaska and Hawaii do not
observe daylight time.

The moon was 6 days old (almost first quarter) on September 3. I have
that in my file on Exeter NH, which happened about 22 hours earlier on
that same day. That means that just under half of the face of the moon
was lighted. The moon had gone down by the time of the Exeter
sighting.

@In any case, I see no inconsistency in purple not covering up
@"silvery" moonlight (unless the purple were so bright as to "wipe
@out" the eyesight...which it evidently was not).

In that case, the shadow would appear greenish. Of course, if the
object was "nearly overhead," then (due to the low moon elevation) the
shadow should have been to the left of the patrol car, not "under the
object" as reported.

They said the light was bright enough to read by. If it really shed
that much light on the patrol car, I would think that the brilliance
at the object would have wiped out the shadow.

Of course, that statement may have been an observational error. In the
October 1967 Milledgeville GA case (Condon 37), police officers stated
that the planet Venus was "bright enough to read by." Maybe it depends
on what you are trying to read (at low light levels, a billboard is a
lot easier to read than legal notices in a newspaper).

The fact that the lights shifted in exactly the same way each time the
officers approached could indicate that the effect was somehow created
optically. Not knowing the details of the surroundings, I can't
speculate how.

It seems to be about the same year that I saw a 3D billboard here with
a real car body (no engine or drive train) supported in a hole in the
sign panel. If the moonlight hit that just right.... But it wouldn't
explain the motions made while the police car was stopped.

One has to remember that they were within 50 miles of what is now the
Johnson Space center. "Houston, we have a problem!" In this case, they
might have rented a farm for some early LEM experiments.



There seems to be a discrepancy between the different accounts of the
sighting I have:

One account says the deputies were driving to West Columbia after
attending a high school football game at Sweeny. Damon is NOT between
Sweeny and West Columbia.

Another account says they had visited someone in Damon before the
sighting.

A third account says they were on duty and were patroling Highway 36
before the sighting.

Can anybody clear this up?

row over Phoenix was actually the result of a training exercise in
parachute-flare dropping. It was not immediately identified because

tied together. The lights over Tucson and the lights observed later in
the night on the 13th were groups of free fire balloons.

Upon rereading this post, I fond that I have some better answers for
you (I got kinda rushed the other day, because I had a meeting to
attend).

I could not include the text I am responding to directly, because my
email editor can't do much with attachments.

When I said "diffused," I was really thinking "extended," but in my
haste to get done, I just couldn't think of the word I wanted.

There were several sketches with extended patches of light. One of
them seemed kind of diffuse, which is where I nabbed that word.


The barium cloud I observed started out the size of a star, and
expanded to slightly larger than the full moon. I checked the angular
sizes at the time of the sighting.


This is one of the most puzzling cases I have encountered in years. Of
course, we still haven't ruled out several effects:


A. The "stimulated report" effect: This is where publicity seekers or
hecklers give fictitious reports after a real sighting. Some of the
sightings might be stimulated reports. Of course, any sighting
reported before the witnesses could have found out about the other
sightings could not be stimulated.
B. Optical mirages. Who knows what this could have been an image of?
But without very unusual light bending effects, the differences in
observed direction tend to rule this out.

But it does happen. See the "Handbook of Unusual Natural Phenomena" by
William R Corliss (Anchor/Doubleday 1983). While driving, I once saw
the image of a truck approach me in my lane, then rise into the air,
flatten out, and disappear. A few minutes later, the real truck passed
me (in the correct lane, of course).


C. Exagerated angular size: Many witnesses do not understand the
concept of angular size, and try to report their perception of real
size instead.

One of my favorite size errors is a description of an object that was
later identified as a fire balloon: "A boxcar at arm's length." The
witness thought the question was "How big would the object be if it
had approached within an arm's length?"

On the other side, I got a description: "The size of a baseball." A
baseball at arm's length is huge in the sky (Try it). The object was
Mars scintillating on the horizon. The witness described how a
baseball hit in the air and seen from the stands looks.


Most people are poor judges at angular size. As an exercise in
observation in an astronomy class, the professor asked students to
pretend that they held objects at arm's length, and to write down what
objects best fit the zenith moon, and the horizon moon.

He collected their guesses. Most chose a larger object for horizon
moon than for zenith moon. Horizon moon guesses ranged from "quarter"
to "basketball" ("car" was thrown out as misunderstanding the
question). Zenith moon guesses ranged from "dime" to "softball." Every
guess was at least twice the correct size ("pea," for both horizon and
zenith moons).

Of course, there was one drawback to the experiment: It took place in
a classroom without windows. This means that it would be very helpful
to:

1. Actually take the witness to the scene of the sighting.

2. Give them an ordinary pencil with eraser tip to use as a tool.

3. Have them practice angular sizes on common objects (house, car,
road sign, bird, etc) first.
4. Finally, ask them to estimate the angular size of the unknown
object.


D. There is another effect at work here: One has to remember that some
people's visual systems tend to exaggerate the size of an object being
concentrated on (at least mine does). This is not an effect in the
eye, but in the way the brain processes the image to root out detail
(again, try it). If you aren't aware of this effect, you might
overestimate the angular size.


E. Beware of witness statements claiming the object was "directly
over" a distant landmark. Since the witness has no indication of
actual size or distance, the object could have been a lot smaller and
closer, yet appear to be far enough to be over the landmark.
Conversely, it might be farther away.


F. I am reading the same reported effects in this case as those
reported in the 1997 Phoenix AZ case (the flights that were confirmed
to be parachute-flare drops):

1. A solid body that blocked out stars was reported, with the
lights attached to it

2. The lights were perceived as being on a larger object

3. A searchlight effect

4. Different colored lights (from identical flares)

5. Square lights

6. Distortion of the shape of the lights


G. Nobody suggested parachute flares.

@I wondered if you knew the answers to these questions:

@1. What type of film was allegedly used - am I correct in

@2. I believe a zoom/telephoto lens was reportedly used - do we

Knowing the exact kind of lens used would give a range of
magnification factors. Also find out if an extension was used -- that
changes the magnification range.

@3. Were the actual negatives examined and is it known what images
@were on the roll of film before and after this photograph?

@4. Was only one photograph of the 'object' taken?

This is what bugs me about UFO photo cases. The photographer takes
only one photo. If I saw something strange, and I had a camera in my
hand, I would keep shooting until I ran out of film, or the object
left. (Actually, the only time I saw something strange when a loaded
camera was available, I didn't chance losing sight of the object to go
inside to get it. If I had, I wouldn't have gotten a picture, and I
wouldn't have identified the object.)

@5. What was the claimed altitude of this object when
@photographed?

This is impossible for the witness to determine without special aids.
Any such number is totally worthless, unless the object is
photographed going behind something (which gives a lower bound on
distance).

@6. I presume the image we're all familiar with is an enlargement
@(either that or the object was very close overhead, or it was an
@incredibly powerful lens!).
@
@Can you clarify this?

If it is cropped, I want to know if anything else shows in the
uncropped photo.
@
@Just an observation - the object's 'top' edge is distinctly
@longer than the bottom.
@
@Would this be consistent with a low altitude object, photographed
@at such an angle from below?
@
@
@If we have all of the above data and assuming there remains no
@significant evidence to believe the photograph was hoaxed
@(although it does seem 'too good to be true') - maybe we can
@calculate a theoretical size?

Not without knowing the distance! And you can't find the distance
unless you know the size. Angular size is the best anyone can do.
This is the common trap in UFOlogy. Too bad there aren't any landmarks
in the shot. They would give a frame of reference, and allow testing
the focus and depth of field.

From: Larry Robinson S/AP/EIS <lrobins@indiana.edu>
Subject: meteors

UFO Research List - http://web.ukonline.co.uk/voyager/



Several posts a few weeks ago questioned the possibility of either
curved meteor paths or mirages changing the apparent path of a meteor.
I now have a reference with examples of both:

Handbook of Unusual Natural Phenomena

William R Corliss

Anchor/Doubleday
Garden City NY
1983

It cites a few interesting cases:

10/20/1893 1049 GMT (location not given). Zig-zag meteor made two
bends in its path.

11/4/1960 2046 GMT aboard the SS Hector, Adelaide to Aden. Meteor
followed undulating path

8/10/1972 Meteor bounced off the earth's atmosphere, tracked by
satellites. It burned blue-white, went 15 Km/s, and left a "smoke"
trail.

4/17/1934 Over Oregon and Nevada (300 mi path) in sight for 25...35
seconds!

4/28/1938 Rhodesia. Went south to north, visible for 1/2 hour.


There are also some unusual mirages cited that defy current theory.

"The path of meteorites is usually described as perfectly straight or only
slightly curved, but exceptions occur. The stone meteorite of
Prambachkirchen, in Austria (fell November 5, 1932) broke in two at an
altitude of 14 kilometers. The smaller of these two parts, with a final
weight of 2 kilograms, moved in a circular arc of 10-kilometer radius,
thereby changing its direction by more than 180 degrees."

- Fritz Heide, "Meteorites", 1964

Was it spinning like a curve ball, or was there some kind of jet effect? The
other thing is that it must have been falling as it turned, so maybe the
real path was more like a descending spiral?

Date: Sat, 13 Nov 1999 00:39:44 +0000
From: Bill Rose <bill.rose@virgin.net>
Subject: `Petit-Rechain' PhotographsMessage-id: <382CB350.47C1@virgin.net>

UFO Research List - http://web.ukonline.co.uk/voyager/

Hi Jeanne-Pierre,

Re: `Petit-Rechain' Photographs

You make a fair point about computer graphics packages and I wasn't
suggesting this picture had been made in such a way. I probably should
have made that a little clearer.

As far as the picture is concerned, I'm sorry, but I can't accept there
is any realistic evidence to suggest this is genuine, although I'm not
arguing about the other events of that period.

In an average week, I shoot several hundred pictures on a variety of
different film formats and this is how I earn my living. I've also been
involved in astrophotography for the around last 25 years and have
written several manuals on the subject for telescope companies and have
produced a fair number of articles for technical publications. So I
think I have a pretty realistic idea of what is possible under poor
shooting conditions.

To me, this FT picture looks like a simple piece of not especially good
magazine artwork and it would present no technical challenges to create
using simple photographic techniques.

However, looking at the technical info you provided, the only way such a
picture could have been taken, (assuming it's genuine) would be with the
camera mounted on a tripod. Handholding is not an option and the
apparent image movement is not camera shake.

Because of this, you must accept that the photographer had a tripod on
hand, found sufficient time to set it up and position his camera and
wasn't flustered by the rapidly developing situation.
 Let me add, that I've seen more than one press photographer drop a
camera body or lens during a really busy picture shoot.

As Larry pointed out, anyone trying to capture something as important as
this would keep shooting pictures until they ran out of film.
 Furthermore, throwing away the next frame does nothing to prove this
photographer's case and it suggests another motive.

I doubt if an ISO 200 film used in conjunction with a lens opening of
f/4 would provide any detail of the craft's outline behind the lights
with a 1-2 second exposure under fully dark conditions.
(Do you have a reasonably accurate time of day?)
I also wonder why an alien FT or top secret "black" project vehicle
would be attracting so much attention with its disco lighting!

It's unlikely that the E-6 reversal process carried out by the lab had
any bearing on the final images and I'd just add that any sequence of
holiday images can be followed by a copy of another picture.
 Hs anyone examined the original transparency?

If anyone is interested, in exact angles of view for various 35mm camera
focal lengths, here are some details:

50mm lens 27.0 X 39.6 degrees
100mm lens 13.7 X 20.4 degrees
150mm lens 9.15 X 13.7 degrees
200mm lens 6.87 X 10.3 degrees

Unfortunately, there's no way of estimating the size of this object that
I am aware of.

To briefly return to James's points about the ouija pointer, I would
suggest that a model maker would be likely to significantly alter one of
these things before making any pictures.

Sorry guys, but I see no evidence whatsoever that this picture is in any
way authentic.

Bill

background or foreground. And conveniently the one and only other photo
allegedly taken was "thrown away." For some strange reason the photographer
didn't exhaust his roll of film on the alleged UFO.

How about discussion instead on the mysterious F-16 radar trackings of the
highly maneuverable UFO on March 31, 1990? Are there any recent
developments? When I last checked there were corrections of the video
recording rate for the radar display data and the time. I calculated nearly
400 g's linear and centripetal acceleration at one point but have not
bothered to recalculate until the basic input data are settled.

Brad Sparks

Hi Jeanne-Pierre,

Re: `Petit-Rechain' Photographs

You make a fair point about computer graphics packages and I
wasn't
suggesting this picture had been made in such a way. I probably
should
have made that a little clearer.

As far as the picture is concerned, I'm sorry, but I can't accept
there
is any realistic evidence to suggest this is genuine, although
I'm not
arguing about the other events of that period.

In an average week, I shoot several hundred pictures on a variety
of
different film formats and this is how I earn my living. I've
also been
involved in astrophotography for the around last 25 years and
have
written several manuals on the subject for telescope companies
and have
produced a fair number of articles for technical publications. So
I
think I have a pretty realistic idea of what is possible under
poor
shooting conditions.


To me, this FT picture looks like a simple piece of not
especially good
magazine artwork and it would present no technical challenges to
create
using simple photographic techniques.

However, looking at the technical info you provided, the only way
such a
picture could have been taken, (assuming it's genuine) would be
with the
camera mounted on a tripod. Handholding is not an option and the
apparent image movement is not camera shake.

Speaking only as an amateur with several years experience... it
certainly doesn't seem to be consistent with camera shake as the
central light and object itself appear to unaffected, something
which had always been 'unusual'.

If this was taken with a zoom lens - especially on 200mm max - as
you well appreciate, the conditions would be horrendous.
Presumably hand-held, with the magnification greatly intensifying
camera-shake, not particulary fast film, almost no light and an
object which was assumed to be moving at the time.

That the object would also have to be conveniently overhead, plus
the absence of a sequence of shots, perhaps further argues
against the authenticity of this picture.

However, we need to look at the evidence on the site Jean-Pierre
highlights.

It's claimed therein that , "a doorpost replaced the stand".

Although using a stable, nearby source as a temporary 'tripod' is
standard practice, how could anyone do so when photographing an
object directly above - how could you see through the viewfinder?

Would that really provide much, if any, more stability?
Absolutely not, in my experience.

It's further claimed the object, "hung motionless for a few
seconds, at a distance of about 150 meters, before it started to
move and disappear behind the rooftops of neighbor houses".

In those 'few seconds', our photographer therefore had to find a
soild base for the camera and would have been extremely fortunate
that something suitable was close at hand. Then of course you
have to locate the image in the viewfinder, adjust your zoom lens
to maximise the shot, focus...

No way that can all be done in a few seconds, I'm sure you will
agree.

Why, incidentally, was our photographer carrying his camera with
a zoom lens at night?

As you note, we don't seem to know the time when this photograph
was allegedly taken - maybe it wasn't so dark as we surmise?

From: Bill Rose <bill.rose@virgin.net>
Subject: `Petit-Rechain' PhotographsMessage-id: <382E0224.75CB@virgin.net>

Re: The way this FT picture was alledgedly made.

James,

I think it's really stretching a point to suggest this photograph might
have been taken using a doorpost, presumably on the side of a building?
 Was the camera supposed to have been held against the edge of the wood?

Assuming the photographer had already set the shutter speed to B, opened
the lens to its widest aperture, (fiddly in the dark) he would then have
to adjust the focal length, focus and hold the camera very still while
depressing the shutter and holding it down.
 I'd add that many "one touch" zooms tend to slip or self adjust when
held vertically, although the exact type of lens was not mentioned.
 I do not think the coolest pro would expect to secure anything
meaningful in those conditions, especially with the equipment available.
 As you rightly point out, it would be almost impossible to take a
photograph vertically and focus/frame the subject without a tripod.

Although I didn't mention this in my previous post, the jpeg image
certainly did not show any reasonable resemblance to an full frame or
largish image made on ISO 200 reversal film. My assumption was that it
had been duplicated, perhaps enlarged or manipulated with computer
software. (Which now appears to be the case)

Was the original material ever submitted to Kodak for an opinion?

I hope you find my comments helpful!

Bill

Auto-focus cameras are excellent and can focus faster than a person if there
is enough brightness and contrast in the subject. The shutter speed would be
determined by the brightness of the subject itself not by the fact that it
was night time. Therefore it is still possible to get the photo in question
without a tripod.

autopsy' footage! Still, it applies across the board, or perhaps
in Tim Matthews' case, the bored.

The problem with any 'UFO' picture which _could_ be authentic is
that there may be enough 'suspicious' elements to label it a
hoax, even though that's not true.

The 'Trent' photographs come to mind as a prime possibility (we
might discuss this case in depth sometime).


The bottom line, whether a reported 'UFO' sighting, photographic
or even video material, is that we keep coming up against the
same frustrating termination - insufficient data. We analyse and
surmise and still end up where we started.

Fortunately that's not always so, yet how many 'UFO' cases are
actually ever resolved.

Usually, we can't prove any explanation and conclusions are open
to interpretation, often impelled by preconceived beliefs.
Hopefully we distance ourselves from faith and rely on whatever
scraps of tangible evidence are thrown our way!


Isn't it a popular misconception that ninety-five percent of
'UFO' cases 'can be explained'?

Where did that come from - is it an evolution from one of the
early USAF proclamations?

In practice, certainly in my experience, it's accurate to say
that some ninety-five percent of 'UFO' cases are never solved.
Blatantly, it doesn't follow that any unidentified artefact is
non-terrestrial, even though that occasionally seems an unimpeded
possibility.


>And conveniently the one and only other photo allegedly taken
>was "thrown away." For some strange reason the photographer
>didn't exhaust his roll of film on the alleged UFO.

Didn't Ed Walters only take one photograph of every 'UFO' he
claimed to have noticed?
Paul Trent only took two photographs (so far as we know). Why
didn't he take more - wasn't there ample opportunity?

And we have to remember Billy Meier did take an 'impressive'
sequence of 'UFO' photographs. True, when investigated the tree
shown in these photos didn't exist and Billy apparently claimed
it had subsequently been 'vaporised' by the Pleiadean spacecraft.
Which wasn't very nice.

It is, as always, a question of perspective.

Any 'UFO' case, whatever it constitutes, has to be considered on
its own merits - there are no 'rules'. What you see is what you
get, or maybe what you get is only what you can see.

That's the really frustrating part - we rarely get to see the
proverbial panorama.


What ostensibly credible sequences of 'UFO' images do exist?

Off-hand... the 'Lubbock lights'...arguably the 'Trent'
photos..erm...maybe not that many during the past 50 years?

It would be interesting to hear of other known examples - there
must surely be quite a few.

Conversely, how many 'single shot' photos of a 'UFO' exist by
comparison?

At a guess... would some ninety five percent of 'UFO' photos be
'one-offs'?

So, how can we criticise our Belgian photographer in that
respect. Either we don't, or agree that this 'single-shot'
property is tantamount to an indication of dubiety, consequently,
most 'UFO' photographs are by default dubious.


I assuredly don't know and merely highlight some questions which
seem to be prevailing.


James.

Re: Auto focus Cameras

Hi Martin,

Sorry to disagree, but not all AF SLR cameras are excellent and the main
area they tend to fall down in is focus speed and the ability to lock-on
in difficult conditions.
 We have not established the true image size of the FT on the frame, but
even it it had been substantial, the subject would have confused the
best AF systems of that time.
 10 years ago, AF was not nearly as good as it is today.
 For example, when the state-of-the-art AF Nikon F4 was introduced in
1988, most pros continued to use them as a manual focus bodies and even
now, many still use the far superior F5 in manual mode, considering
their brains better computers than camera chips.

On a fully automatic camera, the shutter speed would, as you say be set
by the camera's metering, but this is not an issue because we know that
a time exposure was made.

However, I am unaware of any suggestion that an AF camera is claimed to
have been used for the FT pic and it would have probably hindered
picture taking rather than than improving it.

Sorry, but it would just not be possible to produce this picture (if it
were genuine) without rigid support for the camera.

Bill

Jean-Pierre,

Thank you for this latest on the Belgian radar cases of 1990. I have seen
detailed F-16 radar data but never have seen detailed data from the ground
radar sites, especially anythning to correlate with the F-16 trackings. Can
you make that available?

How was it determined that the F-16's chased "ground clutter"? Normally,
ground clutter is eliminated by MTI (moving target indicator) filters.
Strange effects from inversion layers are usually found near the horizon as
ducting and superrefraction only occur at horizontal grazing angles.
Aircraft onboard radars usually do not have the range to pick up distant
horizon effects.

Brad Sparks

Look in John Spencer's "World Atals of UFOs, where one of the Lubbock

@It would be interesting to hear of other known examples - there

How about these:
Great Falls MT, 1950 cine.

Tremonton UT, 1952 cine.


Some that were later identified:

Keflavic Iceland 1954: Multiple photographers came away with multiple
sequences of "invisible UFOs" on film while trying to photograph a
solar eclipse. I have copies of at least 12 different photos. Lens
flares abounded that day!

Ft Belvoir VA, 1957: This WAS a UFO to the witness. It was a simulated
atomic bomb explosion that detached a black smoke ring.

Condon Case 54: Four photos of a sub-sun (a meteorological phenomenon
that reflects the sun). A UFO to the witnesses, but not to the
investigators.


Some borderline cases:

The 1958 Trinidade Island photos -- although the photographer had
previously faked other UFO photos, and a halftone effect is observed
in a square surrounding the object when the photos are copied on as
digital copier.


On the other hand, quite a few un-credible sequences exist:

George Stock's 7 photos in Passaic NJ in 1952 provide much detail --
so much that you can see the two spots where the handle broke off the
cup that was glued to the upside-down saucer. The object is also too
dark to have been a distant flying object.

The 1952 Barra Da Tijuca photos: Much work has been put into analyzing
photo number 4, and which way the light struck the palm tree. A quick
look at number 5 throws the whole sequence into the hoax category. The
object is sunlit from underneath!

Natal South Africa, 1956: Two shots, taken through a cloud filter, of
a toy spin-and-balance-on-a-stick circus plate thrown into the air. I
still have the one I got back then.

3/18/59 Denville NJ: For some reason, two people attempted to take
time exposures of the moon on the same night, and came away with
different time exposure effects. One captured the flashing lights of
an airplane and trails of bugs circling a streetlight, while another
caught a bug flying across a telescope's view, illuminated by a
fluorescent (or mercury) lamp flashing at the normal 120 Hz rate.
Piata Beach, Itapoan Brazil, 1959: An identical object transfers power
from the motor to the record-changing cycle cam in my Collaro Conquest
record changer (manufactured 1953-1967). This is a part that needs to
be periodically replaced.

Ligao Philippines 1966: The photographer took a time exposure of a
night scene, then gyrated the camera before (or while) closing the
shutter). Electric lights in the scene produced dashed trails due to
the flashing caused by alternating current.

Gulf Breeze FL 1994: A staged "dogfight" between part of a light
fixture and a model of an Air Force fighter. The two objects are
always in the same attitudes and relative positions, but the camera
has moved entirely around them within a clearing.



@Conversely, how many 'single shot' photos of a 'UFO' exist by
@comparison?
@
@At a guess... would some ninety five percent of 'UFO' photos be
@'one-offs'?

Seems about right.

@So, how can we criticize our Belgian photographer in that
@respect. Either we don't, or agree that this 'single-shot'
@property is tantamount to an indication of dubiety, consequently,
@most 'UFO' photographs are by default dubious.

Most UFO events are usually brief in nature. This leads to four
important facts:

1. A witness with a simple camera has a better chance of getting a
good picture, if not several, just because he doesn't need to fiddle
with it before shooting.

2. The only valid reason a witness would take UFO shots with a tripod,
a cloud filter, or some other accessory, is if he ALREADY had it set
up for another purpose before the UFO appeared.

3. The wrong kind of film is likely to be in the camera, since a UFO
was not anticipated.

4. A time exposure is unlikely unless the UFO stayed stationary
for a while before the photo was attempted.


In addition, we always need to remember these cases when looking at
UFO photos:

1. Shots where the flash failed to go off are a common source of
bright objects on a black background.

2. The wrong frame can be picked when the photos come back from being
developed. The 8/2/65 Tulsa OK and the 10/21/65 St. George MN photos
are examples of people seeing things in the sky, trying to photograph
them, and then selecting frames resulting from flash failures when
they get their pictures back.

(I once photographed the navigation lights of a plane flying overhead
at night. I had to hunt really hard with a magnifying glass to find
the lights in the resulting print, and on the negative.)

3. Birds and insects are "frozen" in flight by the camera.

4. A focal-plane shutter can distort quickly moving objects (a photo
of a race car with oval wheels and a slanted body).

5. Objects that are easily identified in color are sometimes
mysterious in black and white. It's almost as mysterious as figuring
out where an amateur photographer got black and white film after 1980.
It hasn't been on store shelves around here since then.

6. Halation can expand a very bright object on film, in a video
camera, and in the eye. It can also change the color.

7. Teen age photographers are greatly over-represented in my
collection of UFO photos (compared to population size).

8. If there are ANY anomalies of focus in the shot, the photos are
suspect. Most UFO photos should be taken with the camera focus set at
infinity.

9. Sometimes the "sky" in a photo is not sky. In the 3/14/54 photo
taken at Puddingstone Dam CA, the "UFO" is a man rowing a boat on the
body of water beyond the dam. A speedboat in the foreground is the
subject of the photo, and the real horizon is above the top of the
frame.

10: Motion can cause blurring and transparency. The UFO in the 1958
Redlands CA photo is a rapidly fluttering wind sock.

11. Never forget objects reflected in a window the photo was taken
through.

12. Under low-light conditions, the colors rendered by color film and
video cameras can be very wrong.

photographic operations themselves. But the object itself
hovered or nearly hovered during about 5 minutes (maybe more;
the photographer - if he tells the truth - saw it during 5
minutes, but maybe it was already hovering before). Towards
the end of these 5 minutes, the photographs were taken; then
the object went away.

This is Alfarano's video. It has been analysed by
Patrick Ferryn, the professional photographer who
inquired about the history of the Petit-Rechain
photograph (Reference: Vague d'OVNI sur la Belgique -
Un dossier exceptionnel, SOBEPS, 1991, pages 405-408).
His conclusion is that it looks very much like an
ordinary air liner flying over Bruxelles... and
Occam's razor tells us that, with extremely high
probability, it's only that.

This is a problem with non professional video
cameras (and maybe also professional ones): the
definition is far worse than with a good old
photographic apparatus. At night, you get only
the lights (with a poor definition) and not
the shape (if the lights are on a solid object).

Jean-Pierre Pharabod
