Further to the "Deep Throat" episode of the X-files.

There is a scene, shot inside the bar, where Mulder buys a photograph taken by the
landlady. When I saw the photo I did a double take and almost spilled my 12 year old
over my kilt (wasn't wearing my tartan anorak, James) said "Hoots Mon" and played a
pibroch.

The photo was of a delta similar to what I had seen in 1989.

Also, skyquakes were discussed fairly regularly in the aviation press around the world
and in the mass media around LA (an area with a helthy interest in seismics) from
1989 until 93, so I wouldn't take them as being a sign that some-one has been reading
the UFO mags. It was the skyquakes that first tweeked my interest in Aurora, as being
a geology graduate, an aircraft that tripped seismometers in such a way had a double
interest. It was only after seeing the Sweetman drawings in 1992 that I put two and
two together (and got something between 3.5 and 4.5, but I better check it with a
calculator, as the old joke goes).

I've been out of the loop on all this business as I've been away. I note that Tim has
spat the dummy and the teddy is out of the pram.

I find his departure worrying as I believe a forum such as this needs the input from the
likes of Tim. While I don't agree with Tim's methods and specific opinions, (as long
term subscribers will know) I tend to lean to his viewpoint on the military, or rather
terrestial, origin while trying to maintain an objective stance.

So, I have to say "Come back Tim, you can't have any influence on the content from
the outside". I suspect it is the repeated raking over of old cases that concerned Tim,
but as usual I have to say (in a inversion of the concept of uniformitarianism), the past
is the key to the present. Anyone for a "Save the Tim" campaign? (Stop that
sniggering at the back, Easton).

Chris

1746. Bet that's confused a few folk.

Jean-Pierre,


The fact that a photographer called G.Mossay holds the copyright of this
FT picture strikes me as rather suspect, unless he just happens to run a
photo library specialising in paranomal pictures?

When illustrative (or other) material is reproduced in books/magazines,
on TV etc, the owner normally receives a fee which is agreed in advance.
 This is covered by International copyright law.
If for example you wanted to use one of my pictures for your latest
book, we would first agree a single payment, possibly based on the
anticipated sales figure.

So a widely published photograph like this FT image, should have earned
quite a lot of money for the copyright owner. Do you see the point I'm
making?

Out of interest, do you know if any duplicate transparencies of the
original were made or a high resolution scan was put onto a CD?

Date: Wed, 17 Nov 1999 02:31:04 +0000
From: Bill Rose <bill.rose@virgin.net>
Subject: `Petit-Rechain' PhotographMessage-id: <38321368.5C73@virgin.net>

UFO Research List - http://web.ukonline.co.uk/voyager/

Larry said:

Most UFO events are usually brief in nature. This leads to four
important facts:

1. A witness with a simple camera has a better chance of getting a good
picture, if not several, just because he doesn't need to fiddle with it
before shooting.
2. The only valid reason a witness would take UFO shots with a tripod,
a cloud filter, or some other accessory, is if he ALREADY had it set
up for another purpose before the UFO appeared.
3. The wrong kind of film is likely to be in the camera, since a UFO
was not anticipated.
4. A time exposure is unlikely unless the UFO stayed stationary
for a while before the photo was attempted.
---------
Comment:

1. Reasonable point, assuming they are inexperienced, although simple
should not mean unsophisticated, especially with so many high-spec AF
35mm and APS compacts around.
 Disposable cameras will only produce worthwhile pictures in fairly good
daylight conditions and their lenses are not stunningly sharp.
2. Partly true. For cloud filter, I believe you actually mean a U/V or
skylight? Most experienced amateurs and pros fit these to expensive
lenses and leave them on all the time to protect the front element.
(The just take a little of the blue out, that's all) Some other
accessories may be permanently attached, but I agree with what you say
about a tripod.
3. Not really true these days. Many photographers stick to something
like an ISO 400 color negative film for all conditions. This film is
fast, fine grained and has plenty of latitude.
4. You may have no control over the exposure if an automatic camera is
used. If the EV level is low and a slow film is loaded the exposure time
can be as long as the camera decides.
 I think you are indicating that a reasonably sharp picture in dark
conditions can only have been produced if the subject was stationary and
the camera supported, which will have allowed an appropriate, perhaps
lengthy exposure time?
------------

Larry said:

In addition, we always need to remember these cases when looking at
UFO photos:

1. Shots where the flash failed to go off are a common source of
bright objects on a black background.
2. The wrong frame can be picked when the photos come back from being
developed. The 8/2/65 Tulsa OK and the 10/21/65 St. George MN photos
are examples of people seeing things in the sky, trying to photograph
them, and then selecting frames resulting from flash failures when
they get their pictures back.
(I once photographed the navigation lights of a plane flying overhead
at night. I had to hunt really hard with a magnifying glass to find
the lights in the resulting print, and on the negative.)
3. Birds and insects are "frozen" in flight by the camera.
4. A focal-plane shutter can distort quickly moving objects (a photo
of a race car with oval wheels and a slanted body).
5. Objects that are easily identified in color are sometimes
mysterious in black and white. It's almost as mysterious as figuring
out where an amateur photographer got black and white film after 1980.
It hasn't been on store shelves around here since then.
6. Halation can expand a very bright object on film, in a video
camera, and in the eye. It can also change the color.
7. Teen age photographers are greatly over-represented in my
collection of UFO photos (compared to population size).
8. If there are ANY anomalies of focus in the shot, the photos are
suspect. Most UFO photos should be taken with the camera focus set at
infinity.
9. Sometimes the "sky" in a photo is not sky. In the 3/14/54 photo
taken at Puddingstone Dam CA, the "UFO" is a man rowing a boat on the
body of water beyond the dam. A speedboat in the foreground is the
subject of the photo, and the real horizon is above the top of the
frame.
10: Motion can cause blurring and transparency. The UFO in the 1958
Redlands CA photo is a rapidly fluttering wind sock.
11. Never forget objects reflected in a window the photo was taken
through.
12. Under low-light conditions, the colors rendered by color film and
video cameras can be very wrong.
--------
Comment:

1. Failed flash pictures can produce this effect, but small built in
flashguns only provide enough light for subjects up to about 10ft (3m)
2. The wrong picture will only be selected if nobody bothers to check
the frame number on the negative or transparency. Many minilabs now
print the frame number on the back of the picture as routine.
4. This depends on the design of the focal plane shutter/slit width and
is not generally noticeable with a modern "Copal" vertical run type.
5. Color film is most peoples automatic choice, although most proper
camera stores in the US/Canada and Europe carry black and white film
which is still popular with serious amateurs.
6. The usual problem with "lights in the sky" type pictures of UFOs shot
with AF camcorders is their inability to automatically focus on the
subject. This always produces dancing globes of light or sometimes shows
up features within the camera's optical system. However, TV producers
always seem to like these effects.
8. Agreed, but inexperienced photographers seldom check.
12. Manufacturers predetermine the exposure ranges of color films.
Outside these parameters, they all undergo shifts. Color temperature
varies with the time of day. In terms of white balance, camcorders are
better than they used to be and most people leave this function on
automatic.

Bill

In summary, a brief reply to Jean-Pierre's recent postings -

Jean-Pierre,

Thank you for clarifying so much about this photographic case.

I'm sure we have all learned a great deal and I didn't realise
you had actually had a meeting with the [claimed, of course]
photographer.

So, the object reportedly hovered for maybe up to five minutes.

That would be an extraordinary 'UFO' sighting by any definition
and especially if there were multiple witnesses.

What we seem to be missing are clear testimonies from the
photographer, his girlfriend and any other observers. We have
unanswered questions and if the answers do exist in publications,
they may need to be translated for the majority.


Presumably the reported observation took place in a populated
area such as a small town?

If this object did hover for even, say, two minutes, we would
expect several people had corroborated some of the details. Do
you know how many actual witness accounts exist - even if only of
'strange' lights in the sky at that time?

Obstacles to this photograph being authentic remain that the use
of a zoom lens without a tripod and especially if a night-time
exposure of more than one second was used, is that 'camera shake'
should be evident and consistent throughout the picture.

Another is that this object must surely have been massive, or was
at _extremely_ low altitude to explain how large it appears.

Could of course be that either were true, or possibly both.

These and other reservations acknowledged, no urgency to dismiss
this as a hoax until facts are established and hopefully they can
continue to be.
Aside from 'Petit-Rechain', we should keep in mind what a
remarkable phenomenon the 'Belgian flap' was.

A couple of years ago, a colleague kindly provided copies of
lengthy articles about these events from old issues of 'Flying
Saucer Review', including translations from French of :

'Belgium Haunted by Huge Triangular Craft', by Joel Mesnard and
Editorial Committee of 'Lumieres dans la Nuit'.

'The UFO 'Wave' of November/December 1989 Over Eastern Belgium',
also by Joel Mesnard and Editorial Committee of 'Lumieres dans la
Nuit'.

Although I'm not certain when these were featured in the
magazine, it looks like they date from 1990.

I was wondering if the articles would be of general interest and
whether you had any comments about reliability of the original
sources - I believe 'Lumieres dans la Nuit' is/was [maybe no
longer published?] well regarded. Essentially, the articles (four
and seven pages respectively) seem to be a summary of various
reported sightings.

It's claimed there were over two thousand separate reports during
the 'flap' - is that a gross exaggeration?

[Incidentally, can someone please confirm if 'Flying Saucer
Review' is also still published?].

As there is no mention I can find therein about the 'Petit-
Rechain' incident, when was the sighting first reported and when
did the existence of this photograph become known?


James.

Date: Wed, 17 Nov 1999 03:25:08 -0500
From: joel carpenter <ufx@mindspring.com>
Subject: Rationale for the FT shapeMessage-id:
<001f01bf30d5$430631f0$0100a8c0@mindspring.com>

UFO Research List - http://web.ukonline.co.uk/voyager/



Here's an anorak-like thought: is it utterly pointless to speculate about
the function of UFO shapes? There was a discussion on UpDates that contained
this little statement:


>This is just my opinion. I believe triangular UFOs are all human
>prototypes, and their shape might serve multiple purposes:

>1. To make it look more or less like a plane.

>2. To allow for standard flight mechanisms to be activated in
>case something goes wrong with the main (gravitational, etc.)
>propulsion and maneuvering systems.


I don't buy number 1 (why would "They" care?), but could there be something
to the second item?

Is it true that FTs generally fly point-forward, like a delta-wing plane? I
seem to recall cases where they were flying edge-first.

This wouldn't really matter, I suppose, since an edge-first triangle could
be thought of as a variant of a flying wing like the old Arup or Flying
Flapjack, which were more or less "D-shaped."

It would be of interest to document cases where the "leading point"
_changed_ over the course of the observation, since that would immediately
tend to rule out (as far as anything can be ruled out, I suppose) the idea
that the object was flying aerodynamically. You just can't send Concorde
shooting off sideways.

Are FTs generally equilateral triangles (Is the data good enough to
generalize from)? If they have a short edge, do they fly with that as the
trailing edge?

Additionally -- this may be belaboring the obvious -- do FTs always fly
parallel to the ground, or do they bank to turn, like conventional aircraft?
If they bank to turn, it implies that whatever lift force they use acts
normal to the plane of the triangle, and can be redirected by reorienting
the vehicle. Alternatively, this behavior could imply that the object is in
fact a misidentified conventional aircraft. (Well, helicopters don't need to
bank to change direction at low speed, but the _rotor_ tilts, at least)

If the objects really are ET and use antigravity technology, why would they
maintain a horizontal orientation at all times? If they can defy gravity and
aerodynamic considerations, it seems that they would be essentially free of
the need to maintain a fixed orientation. Weightless, drifting like the
Space Shuttle, in their antigravity field or whatever it is.

If they're really secret, advanced lighter-than-air vehicles, the
similarities to normal aircraft behavior would make more sense. Airships
have "tops" and "bottoms." They also have altitude limits, due to the
expansion of the gas as the vehicle climbs. Do FTs tend to stick to low
altitudes? Offhand, I get the sense that they do, with the exception of the
cases that were obviously sightings of the tetrahedral high-altitude
balloons. An aerostat couldn't go higher than, say, 15,000 feet, if that.
(Well, I guess some of the bomber Zeppelins did go that high in WWI, but
that was different).


It is an interesting fact that while almost every permutation of flying
machine that could be conceived has been built by someone somewhere, there
seems to have been no such thing as a jet-powered hybrid aerostat -- meaning
a high-performance, aerodynamically-shaped airship with jet engines.
Obviously such a thing _could_ be built, but it would be tricky to maintain
the needed structural strength with low weight. Even a 1,000 kg payload
would require an enormous volume of gas and considerable structure. I wonder
if something the size of a Vulcan could even lift that much. It would have
to be very thick.

Again, maybe all this is pointless, but I have a hard time with the idea
that UFOs aren't amenable to analysis because they may operate on principles
we can't grasp.

Joel Carpenter

"Il devait etre entre 21 h 30 et 23 h lorsque S., qui avait lache

Je suis ressorti aussitot et j'ai pris deux photos dont une seule
a donne un resultat. L'objet semblait relativement loin, assez
haut dans le ciel. Je n'ai pas eu l'impression qu'il se tenait
en position vraiment horizontale, car il presentait sa base
inferieure a moi. Il devait donc etre en position inclinee. Il
paraissait plus grand qu'un avion de tourisme; je dirais 5 cm
a bout de bras. Quant a l'altitude, il m'est impossible de
l'estimer exactement: peut-etre 150 metres?... Aussitot la
deuxieme photo prise, le phenomene jusqu'alors quasi immobile,
s'est mis a se deplacer assez lentement, pointe en avant, en
direction du zoning de Petit-Rechain (nord). Il a disparu apres
quelques instants, cache par le toit des maisons. Pendant
l'observation, j'ai percu un leger sifflement. Ce soir-la
le ciel devait etre couvert; il ne faisait pas bon mais il
ne pleuvait pas. Ce qui m'a le plus impressionne, c'etait
l'immobilite apparente du phenomene."

2) his girlfriend (this testimony is less clear, especially
regarding the immobility and the disappearance of the phenomenon,
but is coherent with the first one):

"J'ai vu trois points lumineux blanc-jaune, disposes en triangle,
et par la suite, j'ai distingue une autre lumiere au centre.
Pour moi, cette lumiere etait fixe et semblait de meme couleur
que les autres. Je n'ai pas vraiment remarque la forme d'un
triangle; je l'ai plutot devinee en raison de la position des
feux. Je ne peux pas dire si ce phenomene etait immobile ou
s'il se deplacait. J'ai alors appele P. Apres que ce dernier
ait pris les photos, le phenomene est parti d'un coup, pffuit...!
La vitesse etait assez rapide et j'ai percu un leger sifflement.
Le chien n'a pas reagi anormalement. Quand l'objet s'est deplace,
il est alle vers la droite (nord). J'avais l'impression qu'il
etait incline, car il presentait son cote inferieur a moi. Je
suis incapable de dire de quelle maniere le phenomene a disparu
puisque, en fait, je ne l'ai pas vu se deplacer. A vrai dire,
lorsque P. prenait des photos, je ne faisais plus attention.
Quand j'ai regarde a nouveau, l'objet avait disparu."

(Questioned again in April 1991, she confirmed that she was in
fact looking mainly at his boyfriend taking photographs, and
practically paid no attention to the object during these last
seconds. Ref: Vague d'OVNI sur la Belgique - 2 - Une enigme non
resolue, SOBEPS, 1994, page 225).

> Presumably the reported observation took place in a populated
> area such as a small town?
>
> If this object did hover for even, say, two minutes, we would
> expect several people had corroborated some of the details.

Not necessarily. There is another example of a sighting in a
small town (Basecles, December 21, 1989) above which the
object hovered from 7 h 15 to 7 h 50. There were only five
witnesses. Fortunately, during 5 minutes some of these
witnesses observed it from two different locations, which
enabled to make the only triangulation in the whole "wave".
The size of the basis of the triangle, if the triangulation
is correct, was about 50 meters; the two other sides of this
isocele quasi-triangle were slightly greater (height of the
triangle: about 55 meters).

>                                          Do
> you know how many actual witness accounts exist - even if only of
> 'strange' lights in the sky at that time?

See above. It seems that people don't often look at the sky. And
at Petit-Rechain, it was during the TV hours...

> Obstacles to this photograph being authentic remain that the use
> of a zoom lens without a tripod and especially if a night-time
> exposure of more than one second was used, is that 'camera shake'
> should be evident and consistent throughout the picture.

This is not what Patrick Ferryn, a professional photographer,
thinks. The zoom was secured on the edge of a wall, and, because
of his profession (turner-miller), the photographer should
normally have a firm hand.

> Another is that this object must surely have been massive, or was
> at _extremely_ low altitude to explain how large it appears.

See above the results of the triangulation.

> Could of course be that either were true, or possibly both.
>
> These and other reservations acknowledged, no urgency to dismiss
> this as a hoax until facts are established and hopefully they can
> continue to be.

> Additionally -- this may be belaboring the obvious -- do FTs always fly

The Belgian FT could at least hover in any position (horizontally,
vertically with leading edge up or down, at about 45 degrees like at
Petit-Rechain - which points to a lighter-than-air). Note that the "Big
Wing" reported in Popular Mechanics, December 1991, which allegedly
flew over Antelope Valley (California), could hover horizontally and
vertically. According to the Popular Mechanics article ("America's
New Secret Aircraft"), it was probably a huge lighter-than-air.

The US ZMC 2 metalclad experimental airship of 1929 had a useful lift of
3127 lbs to be precise. It was 149 ' x 43' with a volume of 202,000 cu '.
*Source: Giants in the Sky by Dr Douglas Robinson

What makes this so interesting is that it was classed as a pressure rigid in
that its envelope was made of very thin aluminium sheeting. It was one of
the most robust LTA craft ever built and showed no signs of corrosion or
structural problems after 12 years of test flights.

What's even more interesting is that it weighed less per foot than
Goodyear's America or
Columbia II conventional blimps of recent years.

With modern composites and lightweight propulsion systems, a small rigid
airship would probably look more like a lifting body a/c rather than an
advertising blimp - an Aereon in fact. A monocoque
hull would be very strong and light, so fragility isn't an issue.

If people really are seeing these things - and a journalist I interviewed
here in the UK claimed to have done exactly that - my hunch is that they use
helium for aerostatic lift combined with an efficient overall shape for
aerodynamic lift.

You're right - as usual :) about the early Zepps. The modified so called,
Height Climbers flew at around 20,000 ft altitude and thus rendered the
entire UK defence system obsolete for a time.


Best

DaveW

These were 4 daytime shots taken on May 12, 1994, by a motorist (who
wished to remain anonymous) who said he saw the UFO, and ran into a
clearing to get a better look at what was happening. The photos are
obviously fake:

1. The bottom of the UFO and the bottom of the jet are much darker
than the darkest parts of the background.

2. The focus on the objects is sharper than the focus of the
background. This indicates only one thing: small objects close to the
camera.

3. In one shot, part of a background tree is behind the jet.

4. The photographer moved a large distance from shot to shot.

5. Only two of the photos overlap in the background features they
show, other than a tree branch that is "over" the objects (but
facing a different way) in each photo. It is quite obvious that the
object and jet are models hung from the tree branch.

@like an ISO 400 color negative film for all conditions. This film is
@fast, fine grained and has plenty of latitude.

Right. But the one time a camera was handy when something unusual
happened at night, the ASA 50 special portrait film my father had in
his camera was totally useless.

@4. You may have no control over the exposure if an automatic camera is
@used. If the EV level is low and a slow film is loaded the exposure time
@can be as long as the camera decides.

@ I think you are indicating that a reasonably sharp picture in dark
@conditions can only have been produced if the subject was stationary and
@the camera supported, which will have allowed an appropriate, perhaps
@lengthy exposure time?

Actually, I was just indicating various aspects of a sudden,
unexpected event, versus those of a planned hoax.


@------------
@
@Larry said:
@
@In addition, we always need to remember these cases when looking at
@UFO photos:
@
@1. Shots where the flash failed to go off are a common source of
@bright objects on a black background.
@2. The wrong frame can be picked when the photos come back from being
@developed. The 8/2/65 Tulsa OK and the 10/21/65 St. George MN photos
@are examples of people seeing things in the sky, trying to photograph
@them, and then selecting frames resulting from flash failures when
@they get their pictures back.
@(I once photographed the navigation lights of a plane flying overhead
@at night. I had to hunt really hard with a magnifying glass to find
@the lights in the resulting print, and on the negative.)
@3. Birds and insects are "frozen" in flight by the camera.
@4. A focal-plane shutter can distort quickly moving objects (a photo
@of a race car with oval wheels and a slanted body).
@5. Objects that are easily identified in color are sometimes
@mysterious in black and white. It's almost as mysterious as figuring
@out where an amateur photographer got black and white film after 1980.
@It hasn't been on store shelves around here since then.
@6. Halation can expand a very bright object on film, in a video
@camera, and in the eye. It can also change the color.
@7. Teen age photographers are greatly over-represented in my
@collection of UFO photos (compared to population size).
@8. If there are ANY anomalies of focus in the shot, the photos are
@suspect. Most UFO photos should be taken with the camera focus set at
@infinity.
@9. Sometimes the "sky" in a photo is not sky. In the 3/14/54 photo
@taken at Puddingstone Dam CA, the "UFO" is a man rowing a boat on the
@body of water beyond the dam. A speedboat in the foreground is the
@subject of the photo, and the real horizon is above the top of the
@frame.
@10: Motion can cause blurring and transparency. The UFO in the 1958
@Redlands CA photo is a rapidly fluttering wind sock.
@11. Never forget objects reflected in a window the photo was taken
@through.
@12. Under low-light conditions, the colors rendered by color film and
@video cameras can be very wrong.
@--------
@Comment:
@
@1. Failed flash pictures can produce this effect, but small built in
@flashguns only provide enough light for subjects up to about 10ft (3m)

RIGHT! I think the Lubbock Lights photos are residue of exactly that.

@2. The wrong picture will only be selected if nobody bothers to check
@the frame number on the negative or transparency. Many minilabs now
@print the frame number on the back of the picture as routine.

@4. This depends on the design of the focal plane shutter/slit width and
@is not generally noticeable with a modern "Copal" vertical run type.

On the ones I have used, the slit changes "width" with the shutter
speed. The opening blade is released, then after the exposure is
timed, the closing blade is released. Newer cameras move the blades
faster than older cameras.

@5. Color film is most peoples automatic choice, although most proper
@camera stores in the US/Canada and Europe carry black and white film
@which is still popular with serious amateurs.

You have to go out of your way to get it. Of the many stores that sell
film, only two in Bloomington sell B&W.

@6. The usual problem with "lights in the sky" type pictures of UFOs shot
@with AF camcorders is their inability to automatically focus on the
@subject. This always produces dancing globes of light or sometimes shows
@up features within the camera's optical system. However, TV producers
@always seem to like these effects.

That's because most auto-focus systems work on sonar. Any object
closer than the actual subject of the photo fools the sensor. But what
I am talking about is where the light is so bright that it scatters
inside the CCD chip and activates adjacent pixels. I have recordings
(off network TV) of several dazzling lights in the daytime sky which
were probably airliners reflecting the sun.

@8. Agreed, but inexperienced photographers seldom check.

Any time the focus of the UFO is DIFFERENT than that of the
background, the UFO is close to the camera. That is the focus anomaly
I referred to.

@12. Manufacturers predetermine the exposure ranges of color films.
@Outside these parameters, they all undergo shifts. Color temperature
@varies with the time of day. In terms of white balance, camcorders are
@better than they used to be and most people leave this function on
@automatic.

Distant nighttime UFOs are usually outside the range. Also, a video
taken with a new camera at the special night church service we had
last week came out totally black and green.

Hi Larry,

Re: photo technicalities

There are all sorts of relatively simple cameras on the market and even
some of the new budget Kodak models are quite sophisticated with AF and
program exposure. I think its just a little difficult to tie down a
definition for a "simple" camera these days.

Okay, I take your point about an orange filter, But I wouldn't
personally read too much into that, because an experienced photographers
who only used B&W film might decide to leave one on for all outside
shots. Let me add that you don't always need a filter to bring out
clouds on B&W film.

ISO 50 (50 ASA) film would undoubtedly be too slow for any difficult
available light picture, even with a fairly fast lens. However, ISO 200
or 400 is the main type sold these days in many different countries. I'd
add that Kodak's "Fun Gold" 35mm Throwaway cameras made in France and
sold throughout Europe are loaded with very fast ISO 800 color neg film
as standard.
 I know this, having just dismantled one and retrieved the cassette for
processing.

Regarding shutters, older horizontal travel cloth shutters, especially
those used for larger format cameras could provide image distortion and
the famous Edwardian picture of a racing car taken Jacques-Henri
Lartigue comes to mind which shows elongated wheels.

In some parts of the States I've visited you can only buy 24 exposure
rolls of 35mm 200/400 speed color print film in supermarkets, gas
station etc. But most of the proper camera shops in bigger US towns do
still carry B&W film.
 In Britain, you can buy B&W film in almost all larger towns and most
supermarkets/hardware stores carry 36 exposure rolls of color 35mm film
and 40 exposure casettes of APS. Different markets, but no hard and fast
rules.
 That said, I think we'd probably agree that the average man/woman is
likely to choose color print film these days and B&W is now the province
of enthusiasts. A few years back, the Fuji rep told me that their color
negative films out sold all other types by a ratio of three to one. I
would suspect it's even higher now.

Sorry Larry, but you're wrong about AF camcorders working on sonar.
 Most work by passive contrast detection. It's just possible that some
earlier designs used infrared, but this system is really the province of
small compact still cameras. Polaroid have a unique sonar system for
their awful instant picture cameras.
 With CCDs, there can be some spillover in a high contrast situation and
the use of a lens in low light at its widest aperture doesn't help
matters. The older video tubes were far worse in low light than chips.
 Many recorded nightime UFO "globe" lights are simply defocused images
where the AF system has failed to find the subject.
 Perfect color balance is rarely possible under artificial lighting and
domestic lamps usually lean strongly towards red and fluorescent tubes
have a green color temperature, although the brain adjusts for this.
 If you have a camcorder that's producing really strange colors, it may
be that the auto white balance is turned off.

Hope you find my comments useful and this discussion isn't getting too
far away from UFOs!

I'm now going out to (hopefully) photograph some Leonids.

Bill

PHOTOGRAPHER'S STATEMENT:

It must have been between 21.30 and 23 H when S., who had released
the dog in the court, called me to come to observe an odd object
in the sky. When I left, I saw the practically motionless object
towards south-west, at approximately 45 degrees of elevation.
The thing was this: three white lights, round, laid out on a hardly
perceptible triangular surface. In the center, there was a
flickering point of same color, or perhaps a little redder than the
other lights. As the phenomenon practically did not move, I went to
take my camera. I went out again at once and I took two photographs,
only one of which has given a result. The object seemed relatively
far, rather high in the sky. I did not have the impression that it
stood in really horizontal position, because it presented its lower
base to me. It must thus have been in an inclined position. It
appeared larger than a private plane; I would say 5 cm at end of arm.
As for altitude, it is impossible for me to estimate it exactly:
perhaps 150 meters?... Immediatly after the second photo was taken,
the hitherto quasi motionless phenomenon, began to move rather slowly,
point ahead, in direction of the zoning of Petit-Rechain (north).
It disappeared after a few moments, hidden by the roofs of the houses.
During the observation, I have perceived a slight whistle. That evening
the sky must have been covered; it was not fine weather but it did not
rain. What has the most impressed me, was the apparent immobility of
the phenomenon.


GIRLFRIEND'S STATEMENT:

I saw three luminous white-yellow points, laid out in triangle, and
thereafter, I have distinguished another light in the center. For me,
this light was steady and seemed of same color as the others. I really
do not have noticed the shape of a triangle; I have rather guessed it
because of the position of lights. I cannot say if this phenomenon was
motionless or if it was moving. I have then called P. After the latter
took the photographs, the phenomenon started from a blow, pffuit...!
Speed was rather fast and I have perceived a slight whistle. The dog
has not reacted abnormally. When the object has moved, it has gone
towards the right (north). I had the impression that it was inclined,
because it presented its inferior side to me. I am unable to say how
the phenomenon disappeared since, in fact, I did not see it move. To
tell the truth, when P. took photographs, I did not pay any more
attention. When I have looked at again, the object had disappeared.

Maybe there. Here, the Occupational Safety and Health Administration
(OSHA) frowns on such techniques as unsafe. If a machinist used such a
technique while the inspector was present, or if an injury resulted
from a tool being thrown, the company could face a stiff fine.

Also, to make precision parts, the use of the dials in imperative.
When a strang shape is required, either a template-tracking follower
controls the tool (with the machinist just controlling the maximum
cut depth on each pass), or a computer controls the entire operation.
I use tables of feed and cut settings I calculate earlier on a
computer when I need strange shapes.

With softer materials like wood, there is very little chance the tool
would be thrown, so wood lathes are still operated by hand.

MOVIE film by David Crockett while on board a freighter aircraft flying off

I know a LOT about this multiple witness, radar, visual and radar visual
event that
was documented in real time by a recording made by a reporter on the plane
and by the Wellington Air Traffic. The object seen by the air crew of two,

two reporters on board and the cameraman.

The section of the movie film that contains the ampersand image contains
also dozens of useable focused images that were not smeared by motion
because
the camera vibration happened to reverse direction at the time a frame was
taken
(10 frames per second, 44% efficiency factor, if I recall correctly).
The ampersand
image probably occurred as the camera bumped into something (was supported
on\the cameraman's shoulder as he crouched down to film through the cockpit
windows).
Considering that the film magazine was sticking abve his head and
considering that he was
c routching or almost kneeling behind the copilot's seat, the camera could
have bumped into
the copilot's seat...or even into the copilot (LOL)... it may have bumped
on the control panel
above the camerman's head (controls on the ceiling above the copilot).
Anyway, the ampersand image became useful for analyti purposes because the
image itself
was not badly overexposed, whereas more compact image were greatly
overexposed. I determined the exposure level for the ampersand image and
converted this into absolute energy
deposited (or the equivalent in lumens) and, using the known focal length
of the camera and the
estimated distance of the object, estimated the radiance under the
assumption of 4 pi radiation.
The ampersand image was "featured" in a letter to the Editor of Applied
Optics, a technical magazine, in August 1979 (vol 18, #15 page 2527)_
A response to my article was published in the same journal in December,
1979 (vol 18 #23, page 3889). My rebuttal to the response was published
in the same journal in June, 1980 (Vol 19 #11, pg 1745) . So far as I
know this is the ONLY UFO sighting ever "argued out" in a professional
technical journal. How I happened to get my article on this sighting
published is in this referreed journal is explained in "STILL IN DEFAULT"
which is available at www.stardrive.org (scan the "front page").


The ampersand mages and hundreds of others were taken with a 100 mm focal
length lens.
Then the cameraman switched to a 240 mm lens. I determined during the
investigation (carried out in New Zealand and Australia), unfortunately, in
the dark and on the vibrating flight deck, the cameaman had not mounted the
lens correctly. It turned out to have been either too far .. I think ...
from the focal.
He said he set the lens at its infinity focus mark and then zoomed in on
the light. My analysis of the film, frame by frame, indicated that as he
zoomed he actually went through the focus and "out the other side" thereby
creating a huge (2 mm on the film) defocused image. In th "heat of the
moment" h didn't realize that something was wrong. He though he was
looking at a magnified view of what he had been filming wit the 100 mm
lens.

I determined, with the help of a skeptic in Australia, that the horizontal
lines across the large image, which one guy called the "rings of Jupiter"
(!!), were actually caused by slight varations in thickness and composition
of the airplane windows. (This effect could be duplicated by filming a
distant bright light at a slight angle through window glass when the lens
is wwaaayyy out of focus. )

Fortunately for the few frames when the film was in focus or nearly so it
was possible to get an estimate of the shape of the light source.... sort
of a bell shape.

Recently I have had a paper published in the Journal of Scientific
Exploration entitled "ATMOSPHERE OR UFO". This paper is a direct rebuttal
to comments by the skeptical review panel of the so-called
"Sturrock/Rockefeller Panel" of two years ago, (So far, this is the only
direct rebuttal.)
That paper discusses a radar event in Switzerland but most of the paper is
a discussion of radar and radar visual sightings that occurred an hour
earlier than th sighting which resulted in th ampersand image. I
demonstrated that some object was actually flying along with the aircraft
for about a minute, although there was no known aircraft other than the one
carrying the witnesses. For more information see www.sse.org and the link
to the Journal of Scientific Exploration.

> them seemed kind of diffuse, which is where I nabbed that word.
>
> The barium cloud I observed started out the size of a star, and
> expanded to slightly larger than the full moon. I checked the angular
> sizes at the time of the sighting.
>
> This is one of the most puzzling cases I have encountered in years. Of
> course, we still haven't ruled out several effects:
>
> A. The "stimulated report" effect: This is where publicity seekers or
> hecklers give fictitious reports after a real sighting. Some of the
> sightings might be stimulated reports. Of course, any sighting
> reported before the witnesses could have found out about the other
> sightings could not be stimulated.

21 of the witnesses can be ruled out as publicity seekers since they wish to remain
anonymous. Furthermore, with the exception of the first witness that contacted me
(FOX2) they didn't "seek" me out or "seek" out the media. I had to track them down.
The remaining one, Don Trudeau(PEL1) is regarded by his community as a person of
high integrity and trust. He is the assistant director of Lands for that area of
the Yukon.

Interview data that was gathered was not released until as many witnesses as
possible were located and interviewed.
None of the of the witnesses presented a demeanor consistent with that of a heckler
during their interviews.

> B. Optical mirages. Who knows what this could have been an image of?
> But without very unusual light bending effects, the differences in
> observed direction tend to rule this out.
>
> But it does happen. See the "Handbook of Unusual Natural Phenomena" by
> William R Corliss (Anchor/Doubleday 1983). While driving, I once saw
> the image of a truck approach me in my lane, then rise into the air,
> flatten out, and disappear. A few minutes later, the real truck passed
> me (in the correct lane, of course).

Interesting, but like you say the different directions tends to rule this out.

>
>
> C. Exagerated angular size: Many witnesses do not understand the
> concept of angular size, and try to report their perception of real
> size instead.

I largely agree with this statement. I have come across this challenge many times.
However, I use several methods to help mitigate the inaccuracies. See below:

>
>
> One of my favorite size errors is a description of an object that was
> later identified as a fire balloon: "A boxcar at arm's length." The
> witness thought the question was "How big would the object be if it
> had approached within an arm's length?"
>
> On the other side, I got a description: "The size of a baseball." A
> baseball at arm's length is huge in the sky (Try it). The object was
> Mars scintillating on the horizon. The witness described how a
> baseball hit in the air and seen from the stands looks.
>
> Most people are poor judges at angular size. As an exercise in
> observation in an astronomy class, the professor asked students to
> pretend that they held objects at arm's length, and to write down what
> objects best fit the zenith moon, and the horizon moon.
>
> He collected their guesses. Most chose a larger object for horizon
> moon than for zenith moon. Horizon moon guesses ranged from "quarter"
> to "basketball" ("car" was thrown out as misunderstanding the
> question). Zenith moon guesses ranged from "dime" to "softball." Every
> guess was at least twice the correct size ("pea," for both horizon and
> zenith moons).

When I first started doing UFO investigations, I was not satisfied with many of the
"at an arms length" angular size estimates by witnesses either. I decided to
calculate the arms length size of the moon for myself, and like above it is about
the size of a "pea". This somewhat surprised me. If asked the blind question at the
time I probably would have said the size of a "dime".

Hi Larry-

My wry sense of humor will get me in trouble one of these days... HAARP is a
favorite hobby-horse of the paranoid crowd ... I wasn't serious (or was I?).

Some people think HAARP is the New World Order's death ray, mind-control
machine, or worse...

The official story is :

http://w3.nrl.navy.mil/projects/haarp/haarpFactSheet.html

What Is HAARP?
HAARP (High frequency Active Auroral Research Program) is to be a major
Arctic facility for upper atmospheric and solar-terrestrial research. HAARP
is being built on a DoD-owned site near Gakona, Alaska. Principal
instruments include a high power, high-frequency (HF) phased array radio
transmitter (known as the Ionospheric Research Instrument, or IRI), used to
stimulate small, well-defined volumes of ionosphere, and an ultra-high
frequency (UHF) incoherent scatter radar (ISR), used to measure electron
densities, electron and ion temperatures, and Doppler velocities in the
stimulated region and in the natural ionosphere. To further the scientific
capabilities and usefulness of the IRI and ISR, HAARP is supporting the
design and installation of the latest in modern geophysical research
instruments, including an HF ionosonde, ELF and VLF receivers,
magnetometers, riometers, a LIDAR (LIght Detection And Ranging) and optical
and infrared spectrometers and cameras which will be used to observe the
complex natural variations of Alaska's ionosphere as well as to detect
artificial effects produced by the IRI.

"A BAC 111 aircraft, which had been reconfigured to carry a

refueled about 1800 to 1900 nautical miles into the Atlantic by a
KCl35".

or Raven, was transferred to a facility at Langley Center. Most
of the training at that time occurred at Air Force bases
throughout the U.S., at the Center and in the Vienna, VA area. He
was transferred to advanced flight schools at Shepard Air Force
Base, TX.

According to the BUFORA report Farlow was taking a load of cookers from the
midlands. This might help locate his bosses. Both the vet and Farlow were
interviewed until 4.30 am at the Christchurch Police Station (a definitely
checkable source). The woman passenger in the vets car, suffering from
severe shock, was taken to a local hospital and kept in overnight for
observation. Again there should be records. She refused to speak about the
sighting afterwards. The vet and Farlow were supposedly put up in a nearby
guest house arranged by the police and the next morning collected and taken
to Bournemouth Police Station (checkable source three). It was here that the
MoD officer interviewed them.

After the interview Farlow was driven by police to Ringwood to collect some
personal effects. Does this imply he lived there? It was on this trip that
he passed the site of the incident. This confuses the issue greatly because
to get from Bournemouth to Ringwood you would more likely use the A road
that does not go through Avon and Sopley. Unless of course police
deliberartely drove him this way. However, there is no reasonable manner
that you would travel between these two towns and go via Ibsley, which is
north of Ringwood - thus making the alternative story of the sighting
location seemingly incompatible with this sequel event. Thats one reason why
I have always assumed the Ibsley location was in error and the 'road between
Avon and Sopley' location reported by Tony Pace correct.

The truck was held at the police compound at Christchurch (another checkable
source) until late on 7 November, according to Farlow. To leave he required
a tow from an army lorry to get the thing started due to the massive
electrical faults. It was a long slow journey to return the truck to the
headquarters of the haulage firm that owned the truck. This was located in
Shropshire.

Theres quite a bit to work from here - Andy. And if this is a concoction it
can surely be exposed with so much checkable data.

It's possible that they were ejecting smoke or something similar into
the air, but I helped set up the stage equipment, and I didn't see any
equipment for such a use. They had a fog machine, but since it used
dry ice, the fog went down, not up. Also, they didn't use it until
after the tornado effect was used.
Also, given enough moisture or dust in the air, the image produced by
a laser light show can be seen in the sky without clouds, but only if
the viewer is within a few degrees of the projector beam. At wider
angles, the witness would see a vague color patch, a searchlight beam
effect, or nothing at all. It's like the time I went to a drive-in
movie, and fog rolled in during the show. We went over and sat right
below the projector window, and we were able to see the image
projected on the fog. At the car, we could only see the projector beam
itself making a streaked cone on the fog.

Subject: McMinnville "object" is outdoor light cover
Date: Mon, 24 May 99 18:02:48 PDT
From: "Max C. Standridge" <mstandridge@aristotle.net>

Hello, all:

I've been doing some intensive research on a subject that has
fascinated me for several years now: the famous McMinnville/Trent
photograph. It was snapped shortly after I was born in 1950. I've
searched the web for more information about it, and I've perused
several books by both "skeptics" and "believers" in an effort to
get a clearer idea as to what the "object" was and how the
photograph came to be.

It's an outdoor light cover. It probably goes back quite a way:
to about the 1920s or 1930s. I recently saw it in a photograph of
a group at Lausanne Girls School in Memphis from 1933. That's
what it is: the light cover for an outdoor light from the 1920s.

In the Lausanne photo, no attempt is made to claim the light
cover is anything but a light cover. A group of girls are posing,
in the evening twilight, beneath a row of them. They are strung
along wires, over the girls' heads.

It's sad but true: the greatest "proof" of ufos is probably not
that at all.

I'd love to believe otherwise, after all these years of work. If
someone would come forward, THIS VERY DAY and say they had
absolute proof that this thing WASN'T an old outdoor light cover,
I'd jump to believe it. The fastest way, would be to produce
clear evidence that the photographer of the Rouen, France 1954
"object" was, in fact, an actual French military pilot AND the
photograph WAS taken from inside the cockpit of a French military
aircraft--as originally claimed (to Frank Edwards) by someone.

Otherwise, the closest thing I've found, is an outdoor light
cover on the cover of the _Lausanne Locket_ for 1933. The truth
sometimes hurts. But I'm trying to be an SPJ style "professional"
journalist, here--whether it pays anything or not.

I've scoured several sources for more information about that
Rouen, France "object" of 1954. There simply isn't much. Even
Jerome Clark, UFO expert, has been unable to find much info. It
was simply supplied to a UFO investigator by a Frenchman--some
say a military pilot. It was published in the RAF _Flying Review_
in the hopes that it's owner--the photographer, presumably--would
come forward. It was alleged to have been taken from the air--
from the cockpit of a French military aircraft. But the French
military has NEVER confirmed this, and the original photographer
has NEVER come forward to claim it.

Instead, what we have is a light cover, from "near" a small
French town--and a light cover, from a small Oregon town. And
now, a lightcover from the _Lausanne Locket_ of 1933. No wonder
they all look alike.

Wow, how depressing!

Phillip Klass has illustrated many interesting possible ways the
object could have been a deliberate hoax, using a "small model"
or a "hubcab," including smudging the camera lens with oil or
something, simulating the way the Trents inadvertantly smudged up
their camera lens when they closed the camera--and thereby
produced a background sky that "blended in." This, in turn, made
the "object" appear further away than it actually was via
blurring the light lines.

However, nothing so complicated as that occurred. That is, no
model was involved. This thing was already hanging there. It was
the light between the farmhouse and the other houses, including,
evidently, that of Mr. Trent's mother, who only lived 400 feet
away (and never saw a UFO). (Years later, the Trents claimed Mr.
Trent's father had seen the object briefly, as well. However,
they didn't say this in the early reports. It was strictly a "two
witness" phenomenon.)

It's 1999. The Rouen photo was taken in 1954. If the photographer
was going to come forward, they'd have done so by now. There have
been several attempts to locate them, all having failed. Isn't it
interesting, too, that there is this uncanny resemblance to the
outdoor light cover? And in such a logical place for a light
cover to be!

Mr. Trent probably had no intentions of pressing this on the
public as a "UFO" until his "friends"--the Wortmanns or others--
manipulated the situation, suddenly seeing green. He didn't make
money--but he was trying.

He'd been told by _Life_ and the International News Service that
he'd be paid for it--as well as by the local paper. He didn't
press the issue, because he knew it was really just a picture of
his backyard on one misty morning. He probably had suspended the
light cover beneath the outside electric wire with catgut fishing
line, with never a thought of deception. Only after he showed it
to friends did "ideas" start to form up.

Depressed, but sincerely yours,
Max Standridge
mstandridge@aristotle.net
[End]


A photograph of the 'light cover' would have been useful
supporting evidence - has anyone seen it?


James.

Joel and list,

I have given considerable thought to your comments. In doing so,
I revisited most of the `triangular' UFO reports on file and
realised more than ever that there is no rationale to so many of
them.

I wonder if we really have a basis for theorising the
possibilities of a `jet-powered hybrid aerostat' or any other
manufactured planform, when it seems evident that a `hard core'
of data is inconceivably explicable in this context.

Perhaps the first step is backwards, to look at the overall
perspective and agree what exactly constitutes that core of data.

We must exclude all reports of triangular/delta/boomerang shaped
aerial objects which are relatively consistent with aircraft.
These could simply be civilian flights, military exercises,
observations of unfamiliar `stealth' airplanes, or possibly even
unrecognisable `black projects'. At least all feasible
explanations.

We can also dismiss the high-altitude `triangle of lights'
reports identified on this list as being almost certainly
triplets of reconnaissance satellites.

Essentially, leave aside anything which comes under the category
of explainable in a `standard' context and what remains resilient
to rationalisation are the _reported_ observations of an object
which:

- is observed at extreme low altitude, frequently described as
`tree-top' level

- is with rare exceptions completely silent at all times, a
distinctive attribute

- can hover, sometimes reportedly for several minutes.


Additionally, typical properties include:

- it can come to a standstill in mid-air; absolutely just stop
- it can rotate on a central axis

- it's lights are, in several accounts, noted as intensely
brilliant, yet still diffused

- it is frequently reported as having a light at each apex

- it is also often reported as having a central red light

- it can seem to suddenly just disappear

- it is, alternatively, sometimes reported as able to `take off'
from a standstill and at an `incredible speed'

- it is almost exclusively encountered at night, usually the
claimed witness(es) being in a car

- `it', is not always the case, there are claims of more than one
such object and when that occurs, generally `two or three', in
proximity.


How can we equate this with aircraft or helicopters; a primary
obstacle is that most accounts remark about the bewildering
silence of an airborne craft encountered at close range.

Therefore, we surmise which aerial vehicles a witness might
perceive to make no noise, or whether these reports are evidence
of clandestine, maybe `exotic', technology. Surely though,
there's nothing even in those realms which can be reasoned to
make sense of the overall testimonies.

In order to do so, it seems we must accept there is `something'
being flown - on numerous occasions over many years - and which
explains commonly reported attributes. Yet, that `something',
would be an anathema to and irreconcilable with `secret' aviation
development, whether commercial or military.

In the majority of cases, any premise of a deliberate hoax is
also incongruous with what is described.

My conclusion has to be that we will find no answer to this
intriguing facet of the `UFO phenomenon' by contemplation of yet
to be unveiled aviation technology.

The explanation must lie elsewhere.


The puzzle is; these aren't `strange lights in the sky'
sightings, they are detailed testimonies of an object observed at
close quarters and often for several minutes. We can't dismiss
them outright and must remember that the clue to those triplets
of satellites were uniform and insightful `UFO' reports.

If, as appears to be the only judicious possibility, it comes
down to consummate witness misperception, fantasising and/or
fabrication, that in itself would be an important understanding.

As an invaluable `snapshot', I have mentioned before that, with
the permission of the `National UFO Reporting Centre', I
extracted some two hundred plus accounts of
`triangular/boomerang/delta' UFO reports from their records and
these are available as a text file on my web site at:

http://web.ukonline.co.uk/voyager/nuforc.txt

It's easy to identify the above distinguished cases within.


Joel wrote:

>It would be of interest to document cases where the "leading
>point" _changed_ over the course of the observation, since that
>would immediately tend to rule out (as far as anything can be
>ruled out, I suppose) the idea that the object was flying
>aerodynamically. You just can't send Concorde shooting off
>sideways.

For information, taking that NUFORC data and searching on the
word `rotate[d]', the following (I haven't corrected spelling,
etc.) were found:

Occurred : 4/5/1998 23:35 (Entered as : 04/05/98 23:35)
Reported : 4/5/1998 03:35
Posted : 1/28/1999
Location : Channahon (near Joliet), IL

It was April 5, 1998, approx 23:35. It was sunday night. I am a
student and we had no school the next day. I left my friends
house to take another friend home. After I dropped him off I
headed towards my house, when I noticed three lights in the sky
to the east by northeast of my direction of travel (east) I was
observing this over a farm field. As the road curved right, I
lost sight of the object over a small wood. when I cleared the
trees the object was much, much closer. over the initial
hydrenaline rush I was able to tell the three lights were a
perfect equalateral triangle. The lights continued to expand
outward, as the object appeared to come closer. I slowed to see
the object as it stopped and hovered beyond a neighborhood,
nearby an old rock quary. The lights rotated clockwise, then the
lead light turned towards me as the object banked, as an aircraft
would turn, I thouht it to resemble the B- 2 stealth bomber.

The shape of the triangle was incorrect though. The object was
equal on all sides, as the stealth has a longer base at the tail
than the shorther two wings (an isosolece triangle). As the
object moved towards me, sped down the winding road, only looking
back as I could, to horrifyingly see that this object was moving
parallel to my direction of travel. the road curved, and i lost
sight of the object over more trees. A few seconds later I
stopped to turn left on US route 6 and saw that these lights were

Some of the 1980s `Hudson Valley' material is an intrinsic
component of this data and we find references to a `rotating'
triangular object therein, for example, in a relatively well
known article, `The Westchester Wing - A Closer Look', by R.
Perry Collins:
"It can be stated that many thousands of individuals in the New
York/Connecticut area were witness to an unusual aerial object in
1983 and 1984. The object was consistently described as extremely
large, structured, `V' shaped, silent and flying slowly at low
altitudes. It also was seen to accelerate `very, very quickly,'
to rotate on its axis in flight, make abrupt right-angle turns,
hover motionlessly and display variable lighting as well as
`searchlight-like' beams extending to the ground.

The reactions of local police were touched on in the previous
article. Many police officers who were witnesses to the low
overflights of the UFO were adamant in their statements. They
agreed that what they saw was not a plane or groups of planes.
One officer reported a very large, structured craft which glided
silently over his cruiser, stopped, rotated on its axis, and
moved slowly over his position again.

[...]

In July of 1984 I interviewed a family of four living in the
suburbs of Danbury, Connecticut. The husband had been leaving
work later than usual and was moving out of the parking lot when
he noticed some odd looking lights in the nearby sky. At first he
paid little attention to them, thinking only that a plane was
flying around at low altitude. As he drove home (a trip of
several minutes) he began noticing that the lights seemed to be
pacing him. Still he took little notice until he pulled into his
driveway and got out of his car. He then could clearly see a huge
array of colored lights drifting slowly towards his house.
Calling his wife and children, they all gathered on the back
porch just as the object came directly over them. It was clearly
triangular in shape and as it moved overhead it executed an
abrupt ninety degree turn without slowing or showing a turn
radius. The husband described the turn, `The tip of the triangle
was moving in the direction of flight when the thing seemed to
slowly rotate on its central axis, so that the tip was finally
pointing ninety degrees from where it started. Then, without any
change in speed, just as the tip completed its rotation, the
thing just moved off in a completely separate direction, back
over the front of my house.' The couple had spoken to only a few
close friends about the incident and seemed relieved to hear that
many other people were having similar experiences in the area.

[...]

On the evening of October 17th, 1985, an estimated two thousand
witnesses saw the object as it appeared over Bridgeport,
Fairfield and Danbury, Connecticut. As it moved over these towns
it was seen, by separate witnesses, to `change shape' from a `V'
to a straight line and back to a `V.' The witnesses, some of them
police officers, again referred to rows of large lights that
defined the shape of the object. It moved very slowly, rotated on
its axis and accelerated very rapidly. It was described as
`larger than an airliner at low altitude' by witnesses I
interviewed. Visiting the Fairfield and Bridgeport, CT police
departments, I found that there had been a very large number of
calls that night from people concerned about the object

[...]

Thursday, October 17th - `V' shaped white, red, green and blue
lights were first seen over Main Street, Bridgeport, CT at
approximately 8:35 p.m. The `lights' moved slowly north to the
area of St. Vincent's hospital, stopped, hovered for three to
five minutes, then rapidly accelerated away to the north. It
apparently turned to the east and was next seen hovering over
Fairfield University, Fairfield from 8:45 to 8:55 p.m. Again
stopped, hovered, `V' unfolded to straight line. Altitude
verified at less than one thousand feet by `trigging out' witness
positions and angles of observation. All witnesses agree the size
of the display was larger than a jet airliner. After hovering
over Fairfield, while viewed by police officers, object rotated
on its own axis and moved away. Reports came in from Trumbull,
Monroe and then Danbury. Shortly after 9:00 p.m., over Danbury,
police chief John P. Basile saw it with over thirty other
witnesses. Also seen over Bethel and New Fairfield areas and then
Candlewood Lake. Articles on page four of the Bridgeport Telegram
of Friday, October 18th and page 13 of the Danbury News-Times of
the same date. Approximately thirty calls to the Bridgeport
Police Department, approximately three hundred calls to the
Fairfield Police Department, calls also to the Danbury police,
local radio stations and newspapers. Estimated number of
witnesses, two thousand."

There is a recognised question mark that the `Hudson Valley'
sightings included a formation of `ultralight' aircraft, their
pilots intent on creating the illusion of a `UFO'.

Personally, I'm cautious about these statements where the lights
change from a `V' shape to a straight line or vice-versa.

Adding Jean-Pierre's references to comparative `rotating
triangles' reports from Belgium, there is clearly a body of
testimony for such sightings.

Realising there are likely to be other claimed incidents where
this seeming aerodynamic mastery of `stopping' and `rotating'
isn't specifically mentioned, or described otherwise, it_could_
indicate that similar alleged observations - when hovering, low-
altitude, silent, triangular objects were _not_ noted as rotating
- also have some substance.

Whatever that might be, the countenance of these stories is
perplexing and again, I can only now resolve this by suggesting
it must all come back to, basically, confusion,
misidentifications and/or totally unreliable tales.

If so and in either event, where did this body of unique
characteristics come from?
We appreciate how the underlying `flying saucer' conception came
to prominence and where later boundless associations originated,
- `alien abductions', `crop circles', `cattle mutes', etc. - ,
however, what was the genesis of `low altitude, hovering, slow
moving, silent' triangular UFOs'?

Perhaps more than anything, that's what I've been searching for
and can't determine a source. However, I have previously
emphasised what seems to be a significant landmark - the 1975,
North Carolina `flap', reported in the press at that time:
highlights key points:

`Triangular-Shaped Saucer Shakes Up Five North Carolina Counties'

@I don't agree that the picture Spencer used is a fake, although it has

The picture I have in his book has the following differences:

- The UFO is much closer to the garage than in the real photo.

- Foliage has grown (at least two years worth) since the
originals were taken. This would be difficult to fake.

- The fuel tank is taller.

- The garage door is in a different position on its track.

- The camera is in a different location. This is shown by
parallax between the power pole and the garage door track.

- The UFO has a bubble dome instead of the pole.

The shape of the UFO is different. There is only one convex
"bump" on each side, and a sharper rim. It bears only superficial
resemblance to the original photo.

- The contrast is completely different, This image would
definitely fail the tests the Colorado Project used.

- The photo is in color. The Brookesmith copy has different
colors than the Spencer copy, but they are the same image.

- Striking clouds are there that are not visible in the original.

- None of the buildings used for photometric comparison in the
originals are visible.


Now, where did it come from?

- It may have been an attempt to sidestep royalty payments by
creating a new image.

- If Trent faked the first ones, he may have done it again.

- Somebody else wanted to get in on the action, and created a
fake at the site.

- An investigator may have later tried to duplicate the photo at
the site, and his attempt survived.

- Somebody obtained an authentic photo taken between 1952 and
1966, and added in the UFO.

- The image could be one of the photos created when investigators
were throwing objects into the air and photographing them. The
Trents said this happened shortly after the sighting (according
to Bruce Maccabee). The foliage growth tends to disprove this
possible origin of the photo in question.

- If the object is the Chrysler hubcap I remember, then the
photos would have had to have been taken several years later (as
the foliage shows), after the hubcap was produced. The hubcap was
one of the first that covered most of the wheel (not just the
center hub and lug nuts), and those did not appear until later in
the '50s.

- The image had to have been taken before the Colorado Committee
investigated the sighting, because the power pole had been
replaced with a larger one by the time their photos of the site
were taken.

In each case, the photo was altered to make titles or charts
fit into a magazine page.

In each of those cases, the basic photo was cut and pasted to
make a closely related image (using 1960s technology). But there
are too many differences in the "new" version of the Trent photo
to allow it to be an altered version of the original.

@Bill

@
@TRIANGULAR UFO HOVERS NEAR FRENCH AIR BASE
@
@On December 1, 1998, a motorist driving through Evreux, a city in
@the department Eure approximately 150 kilometers (90 miles) east
@of Paris, spotted a triangular UFO hovering nearby at 5:50 p.m.



The following is garbage data, since the witness had no idea how
far away the object was:

@The witness described the UFO as "having a length estimated at 40
@meters (132 feet). The object's speed was about the same as a
@conventional French military aircraft." He first saw it hovering
@"at an altitude of perhaps 20 to 30 meters,"

He would have to know what the object was, or have clues from the
object going in front of or behind something to be able to judge
size, distance, speed, or altitude. The vehicular assumption
theory comes into play here. The witness assumes that the object
is probably a vehicle capable of carrying a man, and this
assumption colors all further observations.



@and the object "had a series of eight white luminous windows
@along its edge and also a rotating reddish light underneath."
@Stopping his car, the witness watched as the UFO passed silently
@overhead. The object was moving toward BA-105 of the
@Evreux-Fauville air base operated by the Armee de l'Air (French
@Air Force--J.T.)



@As the UFO passed over, the car's electrical system suddenly
@went dead. The car engine, the radio and the headlights all shut
@off. When the witness tried to turn the ignition key, all he
@heard was the dead thump of the solenoid. The "blackout" lasted
@only 30 seconds. When he tried again half a minute later, the
@engine roared back to life.

The very same thing happened to me without a UFO. There was a nut
loose where the battery ground cable, the engine block ground,
and the ground strap to the car frame all came together at the
starter solenoid. Repeated tries jiggled the lugs around until
they made good enough contact. The question is whether the car
later required repair for the same thing. My car tended to pull
the stunt rarely and randomly at slow idle before it got it
fixed, but not very often.

Another thing that can cause such an effect is a combination of
an intermittent ignition module and a bad battery cable (which
can damage the ignition module). Over the past two months, my van
shut down the engine suddenly once every four or five days. I
thought there was water in the gas tank, so I added some Heet. A
week after that, the engine refused to start. Replacing the
ignition module cured it, and it hasn't shut down since.

One would wonder if it is possible that a strong RADAR beam can
affect an ignition module, making it shut down temporarily. Of
course, this would only affect cars with electronic ignition.



@"Right afterward I went to a phone and called the base at

@James & Listmembers

@I didn't see any mention of the jerky movements often associated
@with FT sightings in these extracts.

Fire balloons jerk, and produce all of the other reported
effects. The size, however, is usually misreported by the
witness, because they cannot conceive of a device so small.


@When witnesses describe fantastic acceleration from a standing
@start, do you know if they actually see the FT pulling away, or
@do they simply see it in another location which makes them think
@it's accelerated away at unearthly velocity.

Both have been reported. One very mundane possibility (which I
have seen myself) is that the object is a lot smaller and closer
than the witness believes. Since nobody can visually find out the
size, distance, speed, or altitude of an object more than 30 feet
(10 m) away without additional aids, the true speed of an unknown
object is unknown. Reducing the size and range of the object also
brings the speed down.


@An issue on which I'd like to hear Bruce's ..or of course any
@else's comments, is that if a witness sees bright lights close
@by, which suddenly move away at great speed, would the
@persistence of the eye draw a line between the two points ?

It should show a brief bright streak, provided it emits light
continuously over the entire motion. On the other hand, if I move
my filed of view rapidly past a radio tower with a strobe light
on top, I see a series of dots showing each flash of the strobe.
Human persistence lasts about .05 to .1 second, although a bright
source on a dark background can last longer.


@I'm thinking of the way lasers 'draw' patterns which are never
@really there, it's just that eye recognizes them because of the
@speed at which the laser tracks.

Those usually repeat 24 times a second or faster. Motion pictures
use a speed of 24 frames per second.


@A witness I interviewed wrt. a close up and personal FT sighting
@was adamant the thing seemed to 'snap' from A to C without
@passing through B. This made me wonder if more than one FT was
@creating this illusion. She remained in her car- terrified
@during her two minute or so sighting, and was therefore unable
@to say whether the FT was still above her, but with its lights
@turned off.

If the FTs were fire balloons, the witness might not have noticed
a second one until the first one burned out. It's also possible
that an object simply turned out its lights while moving.

One other possibility is an unmanned reconnaissance craft.

@David

I just caught up to the existence of this thread, with this
post. So someone may have mentioned the following curious
fact already.

A couple of years ago or more someone asked me about the
version of the Trent photo in my so-called "Complete
Sightings Catalogue". I checked with Hilary Evans (Mr Mary
Evans Photo Library, from where we hired the picture). He
was unable to find out anything about it, and had (as one
might, working purely from memory) simply taken it to be a
hand colored version of one of the original B&W shots. He no
longer knew where they'd acquired the shot, either. As I
recall we also used it in "The Unexplained", circa 1981, so
it has been around for quite some time.

Well there's helpful, boyo. If anyone can track down any
reliable info about how the shot was taken/created/&c and by
whom and why, I'd be more than interested to know, and so
would Hilary. It's interesting that no one has complained
about breach of copyright in 18 years or so...

Larry, John, Clas,

Re: Trent Photo/The Mary Evans Picture Library Copy.

I agree with all the main points of Larry's analysis.

The UFO is in a slightly different position to some other images and
there are certainly other minor differences.
 However the only reason I can see for removing the scratches/damage
and adding color tints would be to improve the appearance and this
could have easily been done by any competent (pre-PC) artist. The motive
for doing this would be to improve saleability.

There are actually several different Trent pictures around and I have
just located an image printed by Quest Int,(UK UFO Mag) which shows the
craft with a spike on top.
  The UFO we are discussing in the tinted picture does have a more
rounded appearance, perhaps as a result of a cut and paste job, maybe
as a consequence of being copied several times or perhaps the artist
simply liked it like that.
 I believe it was simply moved to aid composition and make the picture
more attractive. The added foliage may have been added for the same
purpose.

Conceivably, someone might have done this in an attempt to evade
copyright, but the image is undoubtedly close enough to the original
(does anyone have what might considered a good unaltered original?) to
be accepted as a fair representation of the genuine picture.
 My guess is that in a dispute, most courts would decided this picture
was a fair representation of the original.

I would briefly mention my own dispute with Paragon Publishing in
1996. Without my permission, they used one of my pictures which was
copied from a science magazine, extensively modified with Adobe
Photoshop and placed on the front cover of one of their own titles.
 This eventually resulted in an "out of court" settlement.

Okay, you might argue that this particular "Trent" image is not an
original and shows a re-enactment. Establishing this would be very
difficult indeed. My point is, does this really matter? The picture is
after all, just a paperback graphic to illustrate content.

Where does reasonable modification give way to an outright fake? Well,
the pictures in almost every high quality fashion magazine sold in the
Western World are modified to improve their appearance. Just because
you move strands of hair, erase lines and take out zits doesn't make
the girls/guys imposters, but does improve sales figures!

Bill

Nice work Joel - the Dinosaure is an interesting one because it was a
multi-hulled ship - (a design Dr Solomon Andrews used in the 1860s in his
Aereon 1 & II ships) but it was also to feature
suction pads under its hulls to keep it on the ground !
Another not-too-well-known hybrid was Nasa's (Ames) Megalifter concept of
1974. It had a non-rigid hull, 650 feet long that contained 7Million cu.ft.
of He, surrounding a central cargo bay with a
180 tonne capacity. Propulsion was to be via four turbofans. Cruise range
would have been around 10,000 miles@ 200mph.

It was an odd one - for those familiar with the Thunderbirds TV programme,
it looked like #2
but with a/c-like, straight wings around its midsection. Engines were fixed
to the wings like an
airliner. Never made it to become rubber on the ramp - but an interesting
concept.

The Aereon Deltoid with discussed before.
In France, the Centre National Recherche Scientifique (CNRS) proposed a
number of very large flying saucer airships, such as the 'Pegase' high
altitude research craft ( around 1,000 ft or 300m)
dia. and the smaller 'Titan' flying crane to move around 900 tonnes.
In the UK, the Thermo-Skyship saucer was another attempt to combine a more
efficient shape to enhance aerodynamic lift with the aerostatic or buoyant
lift of He. - which itself was going to be enhanced by heating it.
In Mexico a saucer-shaped airship, the MLA-32-B was built and flown by
Spacial headed by the late Mario Sanchez Roldan. It was around 100 feet or
33 metre diameter saucer standing four storeys high.
In the US again, Mike Walden who was involved in the Spacial saucer is still
designing solar powered disc-shaped airships (among other types) - including
a hypersonic- LTA craft called
Hyper. He's currently building a small UAV called Cambot. His company's
called LTAS.
Would you agree that political factors are often more likely to affect a
programme being funded to completion rather than engineering hurdles ? Look
at Concorde - the political imperative was there
to build the world's first supersonic passenger jet - and despite problems,
it was done.
If there was a need to build an LTA craft to act as a platform for radar,
ECM or Intel missions, it could be done without any problems. The question
arises: would an LTA craft be useful in these roles ?
The answer is a resounding 'Yes.' More antennae area, especially in depth,
means dramatically improved resolution of stealthy or fast moving, surface
hugging targets. Endurance of weeks rather than hours, and payload
capabilities off the scale compared with HTA machines.

Dave
