OK, I read this web page.

I am not really competent about other cases, but I think that
fire balloons can't explain the Belgian wave (maybe some cases,
but not all):

1. I don't think that they can illuminate parts of the ground
(or, in some cases, witnesses themselves) like car headlights:
Eupen, 1989/11/29, 17h30, 1 witness: "a very neat area of
the road was illuminated"
Jallay, 1989/11/29, 18h30-18h45, 1 witness
Herve, 1989/11/29, 2 witnesses
La Calamine, 1989/11/29, 2 witnesses + 3 witnesses (not same)
Natoye, 1989/12/12, 21h30, 4 witnesses
(and other cases...)

2. I don't think that they can make 180 degrees turns and
describe loops. For example:
Ernage, 1989/12/11, 18h45, 2 witnesses (Lt.Col. Amond and
his wife). By the way, I met them in Bruxelles in February
1991, and discussed with Lt.Col. Amond, who seems perfectly
normal.
3. I don't think that, in a group of 4 lights obtained
with such balloons (3 whitish at the corners of the "triangle",
and 1 reddish at the center), the central one can detach itself,
describe an autonomous trajectory, and even come back and
re-attach itself:
Eupen, 1989/11/29, 19h30, 2 witnesses (gendarmes) (in this
case the central light did not come back, but went away in
another direction)
Jemeppe-sur-Sambre, 1989/12/11, 18h50, 2 witnesses (the
central light re-attached itself after having come at
close distance from the witnesses - a few meters, just
above the ground).

4. I don't think that such a balloon, when it comes at
such a close distance, looks like a cluster of 10 to 20
small red lights, the whole thing having approximately
the size of a car (Jemeppe-sur-Sambre case, quoted above -
of course this assumes that the witnesses did not lie/
hallucinate, were not victims of an optical illusion)

5. There is an interesting daytime sighting:
Pont-de-Loup, 1990/04/22, 8h25, 2 witnesses. Here the
quasi-triangular object was hovering or slowly moving
vertically, one angle down, two angles up, illuminated
by the rising sun; however the lights were still visible.
Of course, this assumes that the witnesses did not lie/
hallucinate, were not victims of an optical illusion.

6. During the night April 22-23, 1990, two witnesses in
the court of their factory at Basecles saw the "object"
flying at very low altitude over them, and very low speed.
They noticed (or thought so) rectangular plates between
the front and rear lights, the object looking like an
"aircraft carrier upside down". They estimated the length
of the object, which covered more than the court of the
factory, at 100 meters or more. No noise at all; the
object flew slowly over them for more than one minute.
Of course, this assumes that they did not lie/hallucinate,
were not victims of an optical illusion.

Jean-Pierre Pharabod

@streetlamps and you "streak" your eyes sideways, you can see a
@series of dots. This is because the light goes on and off 60 or
@50 times per second with the AC power. (Or 30 times if it acts
@like a rectifier... not sure)

It depends on where you are.

In the US and Canada, the lights flash 120 times a second (twice
the power line frequency of 60 Hz, because the line alternates
first positive, then negative, and the light flashes on for
each). A half-wave rectifier would make it flash 60 times a
second.

In the UK and most of Europe, the power line frequency is 50 Hz,
so the light will flash at 100 times a second. A half-wave
rectifier would cause the light to flash 50 times a second.

Some places have a 25 Hz power line frequency, and the light will
flash 50 times a second.

Most gas discharge lamps work just fine on AC, so rectification
is not often used.

The flashing of a gas-discharge lamp at a reliable frequency is
used to calibrate the speed of record turntables, disk drives,
and other rotating devices through the use of a stroboscopic
disk. When the device is rotating at the correct speed, the marks
on the disk appear to be stationary when illuminated by the
gas-discharge lamp.

David,

Although this is a reported attribute I'm aware of, it doesn't
often feature. However, a couple of accounts where it's mentioned
are particularly notable testimonies.

The first comes from Jay Ward and was posted in 1994 to, if I
recall, alt.paranet.ufo:

"In the summer of 1975, I saw a pair of triangular objects while
stargazing with binoculars. At the time, I assumed that they must
have been aircraft. But it's been a long time since then, and I
haven't ever seen any airplanes, or whatever, that even remotely
resemble the objects I saw.

I was laying on the ground, looking through a pair of 20 power
binoculars. My feet were pointed east, and the binoculars were
pointed slightly to the right of straight up, at about the one
o'clock position. Something went through my field of vision,
moving right to left. I caught up to it quickly, and saw two
objects flying in close formation, one in front, and the other
behind, and to the right. They were both the same size, shaped
like equilateral triangles with straight edges, flying point
forward. Their color appeared to be flat slate gray, against a
deep black sky. There were no features, and I saw no lights, or
glow of any kind. They appeared to be illuminated by the city
lights. It looked something like this:

There was something very peculiar about the way they looked as
they flew. The craft in front appeared more steady than the
trailing one, and the distance between them fluctuated randomly,
varying from nearly touching, to a maximum of a triangle length.
When the rear one began to lag, it would suddenly snap back to a
comfortable distance from the front one. My impression was, that
it looked as though they were being manually controlled by
pilots, and as if they had very high power to weight ratio, and
like they were somewhat hard to control.

I watched them for about 8 to 12 seconds. During that time, they
maintained a due north heading, and covered about 80 to 90
degrees of azimuth. After I lost sight of them, I waited for
several minutes for any sound. I heard nothing.

The binoculars were 20x50, with a field of view of 157 feet at
1000 yards. If you assume that the objects were about 100 feet
long, and took up about 1/3 of the field of view, then their
altitude would be 2000 yards, or 6000 feet, and their speed would
be 568 mph. That seems pretty conventional, but I think I would
have heard jets at that altitude. Furthermore, what jets have a
perfect equilateral silhouette? The closest thing I can think of,
is the B58 Hustler. But my view was clear enough, that I could
have seen the little bit of fuselage in the front and back of the
delta wing.

I probably blew the simple geometry I used for the altitude and
speed calculations, but I've given enough facts that one could
calculate height and speed for any craft of a known size.

If anyone has any information about similar sightings, I'd love
to hear about it.

border. In the foothills of the Hauchuca mountains".

"The one I saw didn't have the light in the middle. Just the one
on each corner. It went out of sight behind the mountains. But
for almost a minute, I watched it hover, 'jump', hover, 'jump'
etc. I say 'jump' because it wasn't a smooth motion. It was
almost like it was hopping. Not any motion that I had seen
before, nor have I seen it since. It caught my attention because
I thought it should fall out of the sky doing that".

recalled seeing and I've attached a 'thumbnail' copy of this.

Just to get the ball rolling, here are my thoughts -assuming that we aren't
dealing with technology from anywhere other than Earth - in which case all
bets are off and anything's possible:

An object travelling in a straight line - let's call it A - C must pass
through B. Whether it will be seen to pass through B is another thing
altogether. The only explanations that make sense to me - and I don't claim
any particular insight - is that:

1) More than one object is involved - the bright illumination may be a clue
here. Your eyes are drawn to the lights and by the time they're gone - i.e.
turned off, and your eyes re-adjust, you see a similar object some distance
away which is now lit up - you'll imagine it's the same object which has
snapped from A to C without travelling through B. An aerial shell game.

What would confuse matters even more would be if the lights on the second
craft were in a similar relative pattern further inboard, you would assume
the object is further away than it actually is.

2) The object is using an electro-chromatic coating which allows it to
change colour and brightness.
Moving stealth technology into the visual spectrum is a stated goal of
defence chiefs. It's already been tested in a crude but effective form
decades ago ( project Yehudi). Bright lights were fitted to the leading
edge of a/c wings which helped them to blend in with the sky.

The key issue is why illuminate it in a way which has often been described
as "..a Christmas Tree' in the first place ?

Thinking from an "extraterrestrial" point of view, there are some
other reasons these lights might be on vehicles:

1. They are part of a necessary "exhaust" of whatever drive the
vehicle has.

2. The emitted light is not in the visible spectrum seen by the
extraterrestrials, and they tend to ignore it. Infrared is not in
our visible spectrum, but other animals can detect it. Imagine
how our cars and planes look to them.

3. Intergalactic law requires navigation lights on all
interplanetary vehicles.


Thinking from an earthly viewpoint:

1. Those unmanned recon vehicles have lights, to provide enough
light for the cameras.

2. Fire balloons use candles for both propultion and visibility.
Usually these are pranks intended to make people see UFOs, but
some have been used for amateur weather research (at least one
science magazine detailed their construction for such purposes).

3. War veterans may have been reenacting the 50th anniversary of
the French Underground's use of fire balloons by launching some.
They were used to confound the Germans and make them waste ammo.
(the Japanese also used them on our west coast, triggering an
"air raid" scare in LA in February 1942 -- sometimes touted as
the first time we shot at UFOs.)

4. We has sort of a scare like this here in the '60s. A flashing
triangle of 3 lights appeared momentarily every few seconds,
moving in a straight line. One of the points of the triangle was
to the rear, and a flat was to the front. It's apparent motion
was shown by where it flashed next. What was it? It was a high
altitude plane with high power strobe lights attached to the
wings and tail. It belonged to a company that was taking
aerial photos to make a new map of the area.

@> Of course, a fire balloon is very small compared with the
@> reported descriptions of most of these FTs, but it is also
@> impossible for observers to determine size, distance, speed, or
@> altitude when the object is farther than 10 m away. The most
@> common type is made out of a dry-cleaner's garment bag.
@>
@> Fire balloons are silent, but many of the "humming" sounds
@> associated with them actually came from nearby buildings or pole
@> transformers.
@
@OK, I read this web page.
@
@I am not really competent about other cases, but I think that
@fire balloons can't explain the Belgian wave (maybe some cases,
@but not all):

@1. I don't think that they can illuminate parts of the ground
@(or, in some cases, witnesses themselves) like car headlights:
@Eupen, 1989/11/29, 17h30, 1 witness: "a very neat area of
@the road was illuminated"
@Jallay, 1989/11/29, 18h30-18h45, 1 witness
@Herve, 1989/11/29, 2 witnesses
@La Calamine, 1989/11/29, 2 witnesses + 3 witnesses (not same)
@Natoye, 1989/12/12, 21h30, 4 witnesses
@(and other cases...)

This is a very common feature of fire balloon cases. In most
cases, it results from the dark adaptation of the witness
increasing their sensitivity to light so they see it as bright as
a non-adapted person would see a pool of light from car
headlights. Of course, candles couldn't outshine a real car's
headlights if they were present, but some fire balloons have been
made from flares instead.



@2. I don't think that they can make 180 degrees turns and
@describe loops. For example:
@Ernage, 1989/12/11, 18h45, 2 witnesses (Lt.Col. Amond and
@his wife). By the way, I met them in Bruxelles in February
@1991, and discussed with Lt.Col. Amond, who seems perfectly
@normal.

What the witnesses are describing in some cases is the swinging
and oscillating of the bag (all of it but the bottom is
invisible). In other cases, winds really do make such turns,
especially near a stand of trees. One time, I watched an escaped
child's balloon go round and round in a clearing before it
finally escaped out the top. Similarly, I have seen vertical
loops of wind carrying debris. No, a fire balloon can't actually
loop the loop like a plane does, but it can follow such a path
remaining nearly upright.



@3. I don't think that, in a group of 4 lights obtained
@with such balloons (3 whitish at the corners of the "triangle",
@and 1 reddish at the center), the central one can detach itself,
@describe an autonomous trajectory, and even come back and
@re-attach itself:
@Eupen, 1989/11/29, 19h30, 2 witnesses (gendarmes) (in this
@case the central light did not come back, but went away in
@another direction)
@Jemeppe-sur-Sambre, 1989/12/11, 18h50, 2 witnesses (the
@central light re-attached itself after having come at
@close distance from the witnesses - a few meters, just
@above the ground).

Some questions:

Did the central light leave the vicinity of the triangle? If not,
it might have been a reflection of one of the other lights off
parts of the balloon, or from "hangies" (strips of foil hung
from the balloon to make it sparkle and appear on RADAR).

When the central light approached witnesses, did it move
laterally to their line of vision, or only radially? At night, it
is impossible to determine whether a distant light has
brightened, expanded in size, or moved toward the witness. Fire
balloons are notorious for making sudden rushes directly toward
the witness (brightening) or rushing away at high speed (dimming
until they go out).

Was the central light seen to actually return to the object, or
was it "there again" after the moving central light disappeared?
Putting fireworks in a fire balloon, to be ignited by a candle as
it burns down, is a common trick. Another common description is
that the object dropped bombs or fired missiles at the ground. In
each case, a falling candle or flare produced this effect. If the
last candle falls, the object shoots "toward the horizon" at
fantastic speed.

A related effect is that birds tend to circle fire balloons and
be reported as "satellite objects." Actually, they are eating the
bugs attracted to the fire balloon.

Another thought will be presented below.



@4. I don't think that such a balloon, when it comes at
@such a close distance, looks like a cluster of 10 to 20
@small red lights, the whole thing having approximately
@the size of a car (Jemeppe-sur-Sambre case, quoted above -
@of course this assumes that the witnesses did not lie/
@hallucinate, were not victims of an optical illusion)

Must I repeat it again and again? Any unidentified object in the
night sky that is farther away than thirty feet LOSES ALL SIZE
AND DISTANCE INFORMATION to an observer on the ground, unless
special instrumentation (and training) is used!

The "size of a car" is the witnesses' guess without data. Most
UFO witnesses tend to guess the size of a man carrying vehicle
under such circumstances. It is not a question of the witness
lying, but a question of how much information the witness
actually had, and how much his subconscious supplied to fill in
gaps.

The candles of a fire balloon tend to reflect off of the bottom
of the bag, creating effects like lots of tiny lights, or long
rectangular windows. Again, this is a ubiquitous effect of the
fire balloon.



@5. There is an interesting daytime sighting:
@Pont-de-Loup, 1990/04/22, 8h25, 2 witnesses. Here the
@quasi-triangular object was hovering or slowly moving
@vertically, one angle down, two angles up, illuminated
@by the rising sun; however the lights were still visible.
@Of course, this assumes that the witnesses did not lie/
@hallucinate, were not victims of an optical illusion.

My other thought: A triangular kite with lights attached to the
ends of the sticks. I have done this myself in an experiment.
There is also a neat device that allows a kite to drop an object
to slide down the kite string at the bidding of the "pilot," and
another device that can send an object up the string.



@6. During the night April 22-23, 1990, two witnesses in
@the court of their factory at Basecles saw the "object"
@flying at very low altitude over them, and very low speed.
@They noticed (or thought so) rectangular plates between
@the front and rear lights, the object looking like an
@"aircraft carrier upside down". They estimated the length
@of the object, which covered more than the court of the
@factory, at 100 meters or more. No noise at all; the
@object flew slowly over them for more than one minute.
@Of course, this assumes that they did not lie/hallucinate,
@were not victims of an optical illusion.

This is again based on an estimate of size and distance without
data. Their estimate of size was based on their guess of how far
away it was and vice versa. We do not know (and have no way of
knowing) if the object was actually smaller and closer, or larger
and farther. Oh, how I wish that multiple witnesses would
separate and try to triangulate when confronted by an unknown
object.

On a fire balloon, the "plates" might have been the bag
or understructure reflecting the candlelight.


****


One of my favorite accounts was of a witness who was fishing from
a boat near New Albany IN on October 17, 1973. He saw a lighted
object that seemed "larger than a semi" (65 ft) hovering almost
overhead. Then it moved close to a nearby tree, which it
illuminated the FRONT of. His depth perception recalibrated to
the tree, and he realized how small and close it really was. He
cast his fishline, caught the fire balloon, and took his catch to
the Floyd County Sheriff as evidence of what was causing the
October 1973 UFO wave here in Indiana.

Three days earlier, a policeman in Linton described another fire
balloon as "a flying two-story house with golden transparent
rooms." Later a juvenile admitted launching it.

In Jefferson County KY, on February 26, 1993, after receiving
many reports of a large UFO from citizens, police dispatched a
helicopter to investigate. The helicopter chased a lighted
object, which was reported to have made "ramming attacks" on it.
The object was described as being extremely maneuverable. A man
called the next day and said he had sent the fire balloon up as
an experiment to measure air currents. He said he didn't dream
that his amateur balloon would cause so much trouble. Again,
observers misjudged the distance and size, even though they saw
it against the city lights below at times. The downwash of the
rotors also caused the object to dodge, and eventually put out
the candles.

On October 18, 1973, thousands at a high school football game saw
a UFO over the stadium. A police helicopter was dispatched, and
witnesses saw it trying in vain to get close to the object, which
repeatedly dodged the helicopter. It was another fire balloon,
proven when police watched it fall and recovered it. Again,
misjudgement of size and rotor downwash contributed to an effect
of extreme maneuverability.


See what I mean about witness size descriptions?

Point 2. The object seen by Lt.Col Amond and his
wife did "loop the loop" (according to their testimony)

Point 3. Eupen, 1989/11/29
In that case the light slightly dropped vertically,
then went away horizontally (I think it was at
"moderate" speed but I have to check that).
      Jemeppe-sur-Sambre, 1989/12/11
The central light was seen to actually return to
the object.
Note that this sighting at Jemeppe-sur-Sambre occurred
just after the Amond's sighting near Ernage, about 10
km north of Jemeppe-sur-Sambre. The Amond saw the object
flying away to the south "at high speed" at the end of
their sighting.

Point 4. Jemeppe-sur-Sambre, 1989/12/11
The witnesses said that the cluster of lights was only
a few meters away. If we assume that this was 10 meters
or less, then their "size of a car" estimate is not bad.
If in fact the cluster was further away, it's size had
to be bigger (for example, if it were 100 meters away,
the linear size of this cluster would have been 10
times the linear size of a car, and its volume 1000 times
the volume of a car - very rough reasoning, I agree)

Point 6. The front of the object had already disappeared
beyond the end of the court of the factory, and the rear
part was still behind the beginning of this court
(defining "end" and "beginning" with respect to the
motion of the object). I shall read again the size of
this court, my memory is 50 meters but I am not sure.
I am rather skeptical about this testimony, because it
looks too much like the Star Wars space cruiser...
The only triangulation made, from the testimonies of
witnesses who observed the object from two different
locations at Basecles, in December 1989, gives:
basis of the isocele quasi-triangle: about 50 meters
length of each of the 2 other sides: about 60 meters

Not quite a Latin scholar, but I got my own share of Latin in my five years
of Classical High School (well, more than 20 years ago...).

I also asked for help from some fellow who know more than me about
symbolism and the like.

Here's what I can offer.

The Latin sentence is not written in a style-perfect Latin, but its rough
meaning mght be something like:

1) "Don't ask from the multitude of blind people in the night"

or also

2) "Don't ask about the many blind nights"

- "multa" is not a penalty, as suggested but the feminine form of multus,
that is "much", "many"
- "nocte" is the ablative of "noctis", i.e. night
- "noli" is the imperative of nolo (means "I don't want" or better "I want
not to"), so a stronger "don't you"
- "rogare" means to ask
- "caece" is the ablative of "caecus", meaning blind

The phrase (expecially its first version) does sound like a Masonic one,
and the whole patch does contain heavily Masonic simbols: the triangle, the
hooded men (not ghosts). It wouldn't be the first time that some Latin
sentences pass into the American slang through Masonry (can you remember
the APRO logo?).

Hope this is of some help.

Best regards

David, Edoardo and list,

I may now be able to add some clarification to your helpful
translations.

The phrases are:

CLASSIS CAECE
DE MULTA NOCTE
NOLI ROGARE


A key word may be CLASSIS, which, I understand is a Latin word
used to described a group of ships that moved together.

CAECE as noted means 'blind' and can also mean 'sightless', i.e.,
unsighted - not permanently blind.

Which could give us 'unseen ships'.


MULTA NOCTE apparently specifically means 'late at night' - could
maybe also be 'many nights'?'

DE translates as 'down from, from, concerning, about'.


NOLI ROGARE can be found in the well known text:

'Noli rogare quid faciat tibi patria tua'

which means, 'Ask not what your country can do for you'.

I've located some information which states, 'The imperatives noli
and nolite (from the verb nolo, nolle, nolui) followed by the
infinitive are used to tell somebody NOT to.


All together, the patch's message perhaps translates as something
close to:

Ask not about the unseen ships late at night .
and is intended as a cryptic allusion to

'invisible aircraft which fly at night'.


Any advances on this?


James.

Hello Jim!

At 19.18 05/12/99 +0000, James Easton wrote:

>A key word may be CLASSIS, which, I understand is a Latin word
>used to described a group of ships that moved together.

Maybe so, but also "class" or "group".

>Which could give us 'unseen ships'.

Not so: classis is either nominative or genitive, while caece is ablative:
an attribute must be consistent with the name both as of number, gender and
case.

>MULTA NOCTE apparently specifically means 'late at night' - could
>maybe also be 'many nights'?'

Many nights should be plural (multis noctibus). I can't remember ever
having met "multa nocte" meaning "late at night", but I will check.

>DE translates as 'down from, from, concerning, about'.

Right so: de + ablative means "about"

>I've located some information which states, 'The imperatives noli
>and nolite (from the verb nolo, nolle, nolui) followed by the
>infinitive are used to tell somebody NOT to.

As I told you, indeed.

>All together, the patch's message perhaps translates as something
>close to:
>
>'Ask not about the unseen ships late at night'

Er... no: if it's Latin we cannot combine words as we like, without having
them to match by case/number/gender, as I said.

A more literal translation would rather be: "Ask not about the late (?)
blind night of class" [whatever THAT may mean].

>and is intended as a cryptic allusion to
>
>'invisible aircraft which fly at night'.

This sounds too much a logical jump to me.

Re: Trent Photo/The Mary Evans Picture Library Copy.

Larry,

I believe that I've now established (by making a direct photographic
comparison between the various Trent pictures) that the image used in
John Spencer's book does contain essentially the same UFO as the
original Trent picture, although this version undoubtedly lost some
detail during a cut and paste job or copying.

It has exactly the same orientation/overall shape as the original and I
can see no reason to suspect it is Chrysler hub cap or a model.

Of course, you are right, this colored picture is not exactly authentic,
but I'm sure you would agree that an image in a paperback is not suited
to serious detailed analysis.

Even a photograph that looks pretty good in a book or magazine, will
probably have all sorts of inbuilt technical faults such as distortion
and will suffer from reduced resolution in comparison to a print made on
photographic paper.

Of course, it would be useful to have a picture like this captioned as
a representation rather than a reasonably accurate reproduction.
 But that said, I doubt if there are many publishers who would really
care much one way or the other, providing the illustration looked good!


Bill

CLASSIS CAECE is intended to mean the blind/unseen fleet', (or
brought up to date, the 'unseen squadron').


MULTA NOCTE apparently specifically means 'late at night' - could
maybe also be 'many nights'?'

ever having met "multa nocte" meaning "late at night", but I will
check.

I picked this up from a couple of references at:

http://ccat.sas.upenn.edu/~jod/AG/allgre.293.html

http://members.aol.com/medusaexam/cqb/cqb105.txt


DE translates as 'down from, from, concerning, about'.

Right so: de + ablative means "about"

Understood... could DE MULTA NOCTE therefore be intended to mean
'we go _about late at night_', i.e., we operate during the night?


All together, the patch's message perhaps translates as something
close to:

'Ask not about the unseen ships late at night'

Er... no: if it's Latin we cannot combine words as we like,
without having them to match by case/number/gender, as I said.

I'm making allowances there may be no strictly correct literal
translation - that these few Latin words are possibly a humorous
allusion to 'formal' Latin.

Or considered in reverse, the objective was to include a
meaningful declaration in the squadron patch and translate it to
Latin as is 'traditional'. However, wouldn't it be difficult to
find an accurate 'backwards' translation?

What's the Latin for Stealth!


I now suggest the message reads:

'Ask not about the unseen fleet which is about late at night'

and the contemporary translation is something like -

'Ask no questions about the undetected aircraft which operate at
night'.


If our depicted 'ghosts' are meant to be 'spirits', could it be a
patch connected with the 'B-2 spirit'?

One thing I believe can be concluded for certain - we may first
have read the 'map' on this patch in reverse!

It's that 'black' area, not the white, which is our landmass and
seems to represent the north and south American continents.

The apparent small 'triangle' shown looks to possibly be in the
general area of Whiteman AFB, Missouri - home of the B-2.

Could that be the explanation?

What might the 'star' shown on the US mainland therefore
represent?

Date: Mon, 06 Dec 1999 18:44:40 +0100

Hello Jim!

At 02.27 06/12/99 +0000, James Easton wrote:
>
>As CLASSIS ROMANA was the Latin term for the Roman navy and
>PORTUS CLASSIS means 'Port of the Fleet', I still suspect that
>CLASSIS CAECE is intended to mean the blind/unseen fleet', (or
>brought up to date, the 'unseen squadron').

The problem is that CLASSIS and CAECE do not match: the first is either a
nominative or a genitive; the latter is an ablative. You cannot put'em
together.

As of:

>>Many nights should be plural (multis noctibus). I can't remember
>>ever having met "multa nocte" meaning "late at night", but I
>>will check.

a list member privately sent me the following references:

>http://ccat.sas.upenn.edu/~jod/AG/allgre.293.html
>
>"...in sera (multa) nocte, late at night..."

That's interesting, though "late" is SERA (and the meaning of that MULTA
within parentheses is unclear).


>www.csl-web.de/gebonn/internet/pbuecher/rez0507/annelt.htm
>
>[Latin:]
>"Multa nocte dum alii dormiunt dominus van Daan furtive in
>culinam procedit et alimentum edit."
>
>[Seven languages total at this site, offering translations
>of Anne Frank's diary.]

The second reference is useless:

a) its Latin is really rudimentary and what we call "Macheronic Latin" (and
I'm still ROFL at its Italian version);

b) the translation of that same sentence gives "one night" in English (and
the same in all the other languages which I can read therein: French,
Spanish, German or Italian); now if you use "multa" to say "one" (i.e. its
true opposite), it sounds like "multa" means nothing at all...

>>>DE translates as 'down from, from, concerning, about'.
>
>>Right so: de + ablative means "about"
>
>Understood... could DE MULTA NOCTE therefore be intended to mean
>'we go _about late at night_', i.e., we operate during the night?

Not at all: the specific time is given by a simple ablative: eg. "multa
nocte".

DE + ablative means either an argument (talking "about" something) or a
movement "from" a place.

Anyway, that's enough for me, unless new elements surface. It's risking to
become a boring issue for the list, more so as it is purely an exercise in
Latin for a UFO-unrelated issue.

If any of my consultants can offer some other perspective, I'll let you know.

Best regards

I would just like to add to / confirm Bill's comment that although I
obviously prefer a picture to be as authentic as possible when illustrating
a book I don't feel concerned unless the picture is actually creating a lie,
or perpetuating a myth (in which case I wouldn't knowingly use it). No
book-illustration picture is really suitable for true research, an original
print and preferably the neg are the only really useful sources I would
think. Stretching, colouring, contrast-adjusting etc are all 'normal'
publisher techniques none of which harm a general impression but all of
which may harm any scientific analysis.
John Spencer

Date: Wed, 08 Dec 1999 16:19:50 +0100 (MET)
From: "J. Pharabod" <pharabod@in2p3.fr>
Subject: SETI signals?Cc: nwm@acm.org, pharabod@in2p3.fr
X-Authentication-warning: polhp2.in2p3.fr: pharabod owned process doing -bs

UFO Research List - http://web.ukonline.co.uk/voyager/

LIST(S) ONLY - LIST(S) ONLY - LIST(S) ONLY

(Preliminary remark: what follows has nothing to
do with the recent HD119850 hoax)

I found on a French SETI discussion group a
very interesting message, written by Norman
Molhant, a scientist who lives in Canada and
has a very broad scientific knowledge, especially
in astronomy and physics. According to him,
the SETI people have very probably already
intercepted several dozens ET "messages", in fact
very likely ET radar signals. He agreed that
I forward this message (which he wrote on
December 4, 1999, in answer to questions from
a subscriber). I already heard and read that
the SETI people had received apparently
artificial messages, but did not what to do
with them because they were not repetitive
(see the probable explanation below). It is
my understanding (according to some rumors)
that a fraction (small or big, I don't know)
of the SETI people think that these messages
are of ET origin, but are happy that the
SETI "protocole" asks that this kind of
message had to be seen twice in the same
area of space - this request prevents the
turmoil which would happen if they say that
they already have got the signals...

So, here it is:

----------------------------------------------------

> Is SETI a worthwhile search?
> What I mean is that our chances of ever receiving a message are
> so low that we can take for granted the eventual failure of SETI.
> Consider for instance:
> - the number of intelligent life forms that develop a civilization
> able to send messages we could receive, i.e.: civilizations more
> or less compatible with ours,

The "planetary radar"-like signals we already detect (the famous "Wow!"
was the first, Gugliemo Lemarchand's team in Argentina has detected 19
other similar signals, Horowitz's team in Harvard also has one or two
dozen such detections) enable us to estimate that technological
civilizations compatible with ours are aplenty in the Galaxy. There
are probably hundreds of them within 1000 light-years, if not even more.

> - la volonté de ces civilisations d'envoyer des signaux dans l'espace,
> their willingness to broadcast signals in space,

We haven't detected any beacon or "call-for-contact" (QSO) signals yet.
Maybe there are none. Signals detected up to now all seem similar to
what planetary radars (used for scientific research) would send without
any intention to attract attention. Furthermore, that's *precisely* our
current attitude: the behavioural similitude is striking.

> - do they send at random or do they now and target us,

Same remark: inasmuch as the signals already detected form a typical sample
of what coherent radio signals there are to be detected in the Galaxy, one
can expect that *nobody* is targeting us or transmitting a beacon signal.

> - our ability to intercept the message, to recognize it as such and
> to understand it ...

To intercept or detect the message: our capabilities in that direction
are slowly getting better.
To recognize the message: the biggest problem is the absence of any
repeat detection. That's understandable if the signals we detect are
not messages but transmissions from planetary radars, as seems to be the
case.
To understand the message: unless it is an actual QSO expertly designed
to be easily understood by any technological society (i.e.: a radio
"Rosetta stone"), we have but extremely poor odds to ever understand it.

> There are so many unknowns therein that SETI starts to look more
> like a wild gamble than a scientific project.

Depends on what one expects... ;^)
For a *positive* confirmation of the existence of extra-terrestrial
intelligences, one must have repeat detections of either a beacon
or a QSO signal, and that ... Maybe there are none. :^(
For a *statistical* confirmation that we are not alone in the Galaxy,
one can dispute forever the validity of the signals already detected.
My personal opinion is that we have enough evidence already. ;^)
We are not alone.

> Furthermore, receiving a message isn't enough: on must know what to
> do about it, with all the human risks this entails...

It seems to me that the odds of detecting an understandable message are
extremely low, because the probability that someone somewhere sends a
QSO seems practically nil while any other message will most likely stay
undecipherable.
So, I don't expect we'll be able to do anything with whatever signal
we will finally accept as positive proof of the existence of ETI.
Hence the human risks look to me quite similar to those coming from
the dissemination of any other scientific information.

> And the worst problem is of course the speed of light.
> It may be cool to receive a 50 000 years old message, but
> establishing reciprocal contact is then out of the question.

Not necessarily. In 50 000 years, these people will certainly have
made some technical progress. The odds that they still are at the
same distance from us look pretty low to me. We will thus probably
contact them much nearer to us, or else they aren't anywhere anymore.
This is implicit in Fermi's paradox: the Galaxy must have already
been "conquered" or "invaded" many times, the "conquerors" or "invaders"
are in all likelyhood much less warlike than one might fear and have
patrolled our galactic neighbourhood since time immemorial. ;^)

> Even a message sent from only 30 or 40 light-years away would be

signal is a QSO, of course! ^)

You should understand some basic information about these
scans. First, they are 8 bit grey level (255 levels) which means
that there are "abrupt edges" where there should be gradations.
Second, the original negatives have lots of flaws, including finger
prints and scratches. I suspect that the lies you have seen are
scratches. Third, they have been looked at intensely with excellent
equipment at JPL and Los Alamos as well as by myself, and
most recently (summer of 1998) by Rand Molnar, president of the
Brooks Institute of Photography. No one has previously suggested
that features such as you mention here could be images of supports.

Because of the "flaws" (dirt, scratches, etc.) and the problems inherent
with digitization these .jpg versions should NOT be used for
sensitive photographic investigations. They are OK for seeing generl
shapes, general variations in brightness, general sizes, etc.
and they are authentic...... what you see is what they photographed....
plus some photographic garbage, of course. Please keep in mind that
the first reporter to talk to the Trents, Bill Powell, found th negatives
under the sofa/divan in their house. The kids had been playing with
them. What is absolutely remarkable is that, considering the lack of
care and the cheap camera, etc.., the photos are nevertheless
clear enough so that one can see te images of the power
wires hundreds of feet from the camera The edges are sharper than
appear in this X-Y (horizontal-vertical) digitized version.

James,

The "white line" you notice in the Trent photos is obviously a crease, scratch or film
defect as even you point out it crosses in front of the UFO in Photo 1 so the object
could not possibly be suspended from it. Moreover, it is NOT "extremely thin" but
quite THICK relatively speaking and indeed in Photo 2 it is DOUBLED in parallel.
Where did the other line go in Photo 1 if it was actually a line stretched taught over
the Trent yard?

I would not be surprised if these defects don't appear on early copies of the photos
made from the original negatives, e.g., McMinnville Telegraph-Register prints in
1950 or Condon Committee prints in 1967. It is unclear to me what generation from
the negatives these copies represent.

Bruce could clarify for us whether the negatives show these lines or not. I have
noticed over the years damage or artifacts on the negatives not present back in 1950
or 1967 -- for example Sheaffer's "tangle of threads" above the wire in one photo
doesn't show up in the Condon Committee copies (and of course it never shows up in
the other photo even today on the negative). It is apparently an artifact or defect
picked up over the years.

Max Standridge's unsubstantiated and wild allegations about the Trents' "fire
insurance fraud" and such have been exhaustively refuted.

I have to ask James why you seem to be deliberately stirring up trouble on this case
by bringing in caustic and abusive people such as Standridge to this List? He accused
me and Bruce Maccabee of "character assassination" and all sorts of emotionally
derisive charges of "unethical" conduct and such -- all because we stuck to sober
unemotional discussions of scientific facts refuting his claims (weather observations,
particulate densities, object proportions and dimensions, etc., refuting his claims). We
studiously avoided emotional-laden rebuttals but it didn't do any good, he still lashed
out with wild emotional attacks instead of sticking to sober facts. I don't need to have
to deal with this. It's not fair and not right.

If you bring him aboard I will no longer remain dispassionate about this and may
leave this List. I will not put up with this crap and will seriously consider legal action.
I do not need this gratuitous aggravation of my health from maliciously inflicted
stress.

Brad Sparks

Date: Thu, 09 Dec 1999 10:08:00 -0500 (EST)
From: Larry Robinson S/AP/EIS Kinesiology <lrobins@indiana.edu>
Subject: Trent photos

UFO Research List - http://web.ukonline.co.uk/voyager/



Does anyone else see what I am seeing in the scanned versions of
the Trent photos?

These appear in both sets of scanned photos, found on:

www.konsulting.com/Trent/Trent1.jpg
www.konsulting.com/Trent/Trent2.jpg

and

web.ukonline.co.uk/voyager/trent1.jpg
web.ukonline.co.uk/voyager/trent2.jpg


In the lower right of the photo "Trent1," just above the ground
and to the left of the tall power pole, I see a faint image of a
pickup truck in the sky. It faces to the right and slightly away
from the camera. I didn't notice it until I returned from
answering the door, and I was several feet from the computer. I
would think it was just an artifact of the mind trying to make
sense of random pixels (which I have studied) but the license
plate being in the right place is too much of a coincidence.

In the lower right of "Trent2" there seems to be a white blotch,
but on closer examination, it resolves itself into the Adamski
"chicken brooder" saucer, tilted sideways, complete with the
three balls.

"Trent2" also is covered with fingerprints.


The question is, how did these faint images get into the
scans of the photos?

The fingerprints are obvious: the negatives were mishandled at
some point.

One possibility is that traces of a previous image scanned can
sometimes be carried over to the next scan, especially if a
drum-type combo scanner/copier/laser printer was used (in which
case, the "previous image" could have been copied or printed).
Another is that the negatives were sandwiched with negatives
of other images, and selectively faded.

A third is that the photographic paper used was faintly exposed
to other images in some way.

The pickup truck could be a reflection in a piece of glass.

Possibly a frame was reused when a flashbulb failed.

Or it might be that my brain is simply processing random noise
and trying to make sense of it. I have studied this effect
before. That's why I want to know if anyone else sees these
things in the images.

It is interesting that the images are both in the lower right
sides of the photos.


I will have to check the other copies of the Trent photos I have
to see if the images appear in them too.

Provo a tradurre.

Credo che si debba costruire "Caece classis noli rogare de multa nocte".


Il verbo che regge la frase e' senz'altro "noli", imperativo di nolo, che
presuppone una seconda persona. Questa seconda persona è individuabile a
mio avviso in "caece", vocativo maschile singolare di "caecus -a -um",
aggettivom in questa frase sostantivato. "Noli" assieme ad un infinito
presente esprime l'imperativo negativo del verbo all'infinito. Quindi
"Cieco non chiedere", o forse, traducendo meglio in questo contesto,
"ignorante non domandare" o "stolto non fare domande" (il senso di "caecus"
in latino in questo può essere vario come quello di "cieco" in italiano).
"De multa nocte" significa "a notte inoltrata": non e' frequente che de +
ablativo esprima il complemento di tempo, ma qui e' cosi' e frasi come "de
multa nocte" o "de medio die" ("in pieno giorno") esprimono il complemento
di tempo.
"Classis" e' un femminile parisillabo della terza declinazione: puo' essere
nominativo, vocativo o genitivo singolare e significa o "flotta, esercito"
o "gruppo, classe". Secondo me e' un genitivo. Non puo' essere un
nominativo perche' il soggetto e' al vocativo e "classis" non puo' essere
un vocativo perche' e' femminile e quindi non concorderebbe con "caece" al
vocativo (in tal caso avremmo "classis caeca"). Penso dunque sia un
genitivo e che dipenda da "caece", perche' solo cosi' mi sembra che si
riesca a trovare qualche senso.

Concludendo, per me si potrebbe provare questa traduzione: "ignorante del
gruppo, non fare domande nel cuore della notte", frase che potrebbe
significare, traducendo meno alla lettera e cercando di capire il senso del
motto, "tu che nel gruppo sei un ignorante, non fare domande quando non hai
la capacità di dissipare le tenebre dell'ignoranza", dove il "gruppo"
potrebbe essere la loggia massonica o anche il genere umano.

Questa e' la mia proposta di traduzione. Aspetto osservazioni e
controproposte.


MASSIMILIANO GRANDI

On Wed, 8 Dec 1999, Larry Robinson S/AP/EIS Kinesiology wrote:

> See the December 1999 Scientific American. That "WOW" signal and
> other similar ones at that station were eventially correlated
> with break times at the station, not something in the sky. They
> tracked it down to a microwave oven in the break room.

Still no December issue in our library (in fact, they have
only the October issue - shame on them!). But I got an answer
from Norman Molhant. According to him, the microwave oven
hypothesis is very unlikely. One of his friends has studied
the WOW signal, and he found that:

- it was not at the microwave oven frequency (which was about
2.4 Ghz), it was not an harmonic (it was at about 1.4 Ghz),
it was not a beat with a local oscillator of the Big Ear
receptor;

- the WOW is a modulated signal (2 sidebands + wave carrier),
a microwave oven sends a rather pure signal (practically
without sidebands);

- the WOW wave carrier drifts in frequency with a speed which
corresponds rather well to the galactic drift in our
neighborhood, once substracted the effects of the rotation
of the Earth, of its orbital motion and of the orbital motion
of the solar system around the center of the Galaxy.

Since I don't know when our library will receive this December
1999 issue, could you (or any other happy reader of this issue)
summarize how it was demonstrated that the microwave oven
hypothesis was eventually the good one?

Jean-Pierre Pharabod

I made a boo-boo.

I gave the wrong information on the article about that microwave
oven causing SETI signals. It seems I had read two different
articles on SETI the night before, and had forgotten that I
switched magazines between them. A phone call interrupted me
while I was reading. She's cute and cuddly -- Need I say more? I
wrote down the magazine info after the phone call, not checking
to see if the article was the correct one.

The article was actually in the May issue of UFO Universe, not
the December Scientific American.

The microwave oven receptions occurred at the Australian Parkes
Observatory last year. They had nothing to do with the Wow!
signal, which was in another part of the article.

A SETI researcher was getting excited because he was receiving
signals from the same parts of the sky at the same times every
day. He was about to call in others to verify when he noticed
that the times corresponded to the station break times. A brand
new microwave busily warming tidbits in the break room on the
floor below was responsible.

***

One possibility that must be considered in SETI is spy satellite
transmissions, which governments keep secret for obvious reasons.
Some of them use short (under 2 minutes) transmission bursts at
randomized intervals, durations, and frequencies to keep
evesdroppers from getting a whole message.

This in one area where governments prefer to let UFOs and SETI
receptions remain unidentified as man-made activities. They want
the public to believe that aliens are doing these things, rather
than divulge their clandestine activities.

There are still sources of QRM that both systems could pick up:

1. Deep space probes (such as Pioneer 10). But at least we know
where they are.

2. Very strong sources (such as the noise generated when a large
power grid fails), strong enough to get through the back
lobe of an antenna.

3. Pranks. Once the system becomes publicized, pranksters could
arrange two microwave transmitters to operate simultaneously
close to the telescopes.

(How do we know that the few unidentified receptions they have
weren't the result of pranks or unlicensed transmitters?)



Now, does anyone have enough money to rent time on TWO telescopes
at the same time?

telescopes aren't designed to detect motion. Instead, they would
observe a strengthening and weakening of the signal as the
satellite moves into and out of the telescope's filed of "view."
The antenna can't detect motion as such, because it doesn't scan
like a RADAR antenna. Instead, it stays focused on one part of
the sky at a time.

the locations or details of the other side's spy satellites, to
avoid diplomatic repercussions.

Not only would spy satellites give away their identity as earth satellites by
their positions but also by the Doppler shifts of their radio signals due to
orbital motion. Most geosynchronous satellites are not in perfectly
geostationary orbits. Many trace out figure-8 patterns in order to cover
more area north and south of the equator. And most send out encrypted
digital signals which would be quite obvious to radio astronomers.

Brad Sparks

sufficient to dismiss it as a probable hoax.

Interestingly, in the new negative scans Bruce has made
available, the line in T1 is visible, yet nothing is evident in
T2.

I can vouch for having some negatives which exhibit a similar
'scratch', occurring due to a speck of dirt in the shutter
movement, or resulting during commercial processing. Fortunately,
it rarely happens, though it seems to be always when its
otherwise one of my better pictures.

I dare say Mr Trent could have said the same.


>Max Standridge's unsubstantiated and wild allegations about the
>Trents' "fire insurance fraud" and such have been exhaustively
>refuted.

I'm not familiar with the extent of these claims or their
refutation.

When I wrote, asking if Max could provide a copy of the 'Lausanne
Collegiate School' magazine which he had cited as showing light
covers similar to the Trent's 'saucer', I had invited him to
contribute on the topic.

I certainly wasn't aware of any previous debates involving Max,
Bruce and yourself, indeed, when I recently highlighted his
claims, it was with the express question - what became of them,
was the magazine photograph ever produced, etc.

As mentioned, any participation from Max, which I deduced as
unlikely anyway, would have been in the longer term and please
don't be concerned about any 'caustic' confrontations here. I'm
now aware of the situation.

I think there's more than enough to consider about the
photographs themselves. I saw the 'Adamski' saucer, but (sorry
folks) just can't see a pickup truck in the sky. ;)

However... isn't the 'blob of light', which does resemble a
sideways 'saucer' in T2 (the latest scans show a more anomalous
shape), in the same location as the 'ball of light' in T1?

At first, I presumed they were both 'lens flare'; is that
possible if the photographs were taken from different
positions/angles?

I'm about to upload the latest scans and will post details.


James.

From: Larry Robinson S/AP/EIS Kinesiology <lrobins@indiana.edu>
Subject: Trent Photos

UFO Research List - http://web.ukonline.co.uk/voyager/



I did a survey of most of the copies of the Trent photos I have.
Here are the results:



The following publications cropped the areas containing the
anomalies out, since they were nowhere near the UFO:

* Look 1967 special "FLYING SAUCERS"

* The Condon report

* Peter Brookesmith "UFOs - The Government Files

* Jenny Randles "UFOs and How to See Them" (Trent2 only)

* Jenny Randles "Alien Contact: The first fifty years"

* J A Hynek "The Hynek UFO Report"

* Hynek and Vallee "The Edge of Reality"

* Paris Flammonde "UFO Exist

* Time-Life "The UFO Phenomenon" (Trent2 - see below)



The following publications printed the photo too lightly for the
anomalies to appear if they existed in those copies. Other than
the phone wires and pole, the background is white:

* The true report on Flying Saucers (1967 - only Trent2)

* Philip Klass "UFOs Explained" (only Trent1)

* Ronald Story "Encyclopedia of UFOs" (Trent1 - see below)



The following publications printed copies with the pickup truck
actually visible:
* Bob Larson: UFOs and the Alien Agenda

* Time-Life "The UFO Phenomenon" - Not only is the pickup truck
visible, but other cars are parked to the left of it.

* Sagan and Page "UFOs - a Scientific Debate" The pickup truck is
cropped out, but the other cars visible in the Time-Life print
are there.



The following publications printed copies with the "Adamski
object" visible.

* Ronald Story "Encyclopedia of UFOs"




After further investigation, I think the "Adamski object"
happened when developer was dripped on the negative, then wiped
off. The "three ball effect" was an artifact of pixelation and
was visible in only one magnification.

The pickup trick looks similar to what happens when a photo is
taken through a sheet of glass reflecting another scene faintly.

As for the effect being created in the mind, I have experimented
with this, and I find that, if the effect is psychological, I can
make it change into something else. I can't make the pickup truck
change.

I have attempted to bring out the truck images even more:

contrast enhancement.

Seymour Hess was NOT a professional astronomer but a meteorologist who made
his observation from Lowell Observatory.

Do check Hynek's 1952 report on astronomers for Project Blue Book for more
leads. Also the famous LIFE magazine article of April 7, 1952, lists a very
detailed observation by an astronomer and his family in 1947. And definitely
contact Peter Sturrock at Stanford.

Brad Sparks

Dear All & Whomsoever

Some years ago, a European colleague wrote to me with
various corrections and comments on my wonderfully mistitled
book "UFO: The Complete Sightings Catalogue" (1995). He
mentioned that the Moreno family's CE-2 at Trancas,
Argentina on 10/21/63 had been debunked, or perhaps more
accurately revealed, as a set of misperceptions of military
manoeuvres.

I am lurking out of sight of the coming Apocalypse with the
betrothed & various equines on the other side of the
mountains from my files, and can't recall who gave me this
snippet. If my rudely forgotten informant is on either of
these lists, could you raise your right hand, and give me
(or all of us - prima facie it's a remarkable case) the
details of how, when, by whom &c, the case was debunked?

best wishes
and season's greetings, one & all
Peter B

Hi Martin and Larry,

FOX3's angular size estimate of holding his arms 4 feet apart on site is not
too accurate a method. I would have thought he could pinpoint specific
landmarks for the righthand and lefthand edges of the object, though subject
to the moving target problem. That would be more accurate than the arms'
length method (which works better with small objects held at arm's length).

I noticed some other odd discrepancies in the witness accounts:

1. In your account of FOX2 there is no mention of him and FOX3 walking
towards each other then driving to the campground to discuss the incident
together after the UFO left. This is not mentioned in FOX3's Jan 1997
written account either (http://www.ufobc.org/yukon/22fox3.htm), it's in your
interview report with FOX3. In his Jan 1997 story FOX3 specifically states
"As I continued to go on my way I was stunned into "Silence". We just got
into our vehicles and drove towards Carmacks in tranquility."

2. There is no mention of FOX3 getting out of the car to frantically look
for the camera in FOX3's Jan 1997 written account, it's in your interview
report. In FOX3's written account he states he "stayed in the car" then
drove away in silence.

3. FOX3's Jan 1997 report states that when FOX2 came over he (FOX3) was
waiting for his (FOX3's) girlfriend to arrive. When FOX2 asked him to leave
immediately FOX3 did so and there is no mention of the girlfriend. Did FOX3
just leave the girlfriend to show up and find him gone without explanation?
What happened?

Anyway, Martin, you are to be commended for doing a tremendous job of
investigation which involved a great deal of effort and thought.

Brad Sparks

Oops, the Clearwater case was not the military's doing, but a
private pilot wanting to brighten up the 4th of July festivities
with some red flares on parachutes. He had no idea of the trouble
it would cause until after he had landed. It was, however, a
lesson for UFOlogy. The witnesses described accurately what the
lights DID (no description was outside the capabilities of the
flares). The one place over half of the witnesses did err was to
see the flares as being on one object. Some even saw a gray or
dark red "body" holding the lights. The description of this was
usually either a double convex lens on edge, or a cigar.

The Condon report covers the Cape Ann case. Again, many witnesses
saw the yellow lights as being on something, and some said a dark
gray shape was behind the lights.

The Phoenix case was revealed as a series of flare drops by the
men who dropped the flares. The delay was caused by the fact that
they had returned to their home state in the east long before the
news reached them (I found out about it two months later, and
that was before they did). Again, many witnesses described a dark
gray or black shape containing the lights, vee shaped, since the
lights formed a rough vee. One witnesses said the stars blanked
out as the object passed. This could either be caused by the
parachutes, or by a contrast effect causing the eyes to
desensitize in the area of the much brighter flares.

@Some people need an alien body or alien hardware in their hands

Emotional fears of scientists have nothing to do with it, because
there are other causes for many of the items you cite. A kaboodle
of marginal cases is nothing but a kaboodle of marginal cases.
They do not compound into the equivalent of one airtight case.
Here are some alternate causes for the things you cite:

1. Fire balloons explain many of the night cases where objects
are seen to do fantastic things. They rotate, wobble, swing like
a pendulum, and change speed, all at the mercy of the wind. The
reason they are not identified as such is that they are farther
away than the 30 foot limit on binocular vision against a uniform
background. Most people imagine them to be a lot larger and
farther away, because they assume they are piloted, controlled
vehicles.

2. How "credible" the witness is has absolutely NO effect on the
human inability to determine size or distance against a uniform
background when the object is farther away than 30 feet (and that
is the best case -- some people lose it at 15 feet). No amount of
training can fix this problem, but it can alert people that it
exists. A cop near here reported a fire balloon (approximately 1.5
feet in diameter at the base and 4 feet high) as a flying
transparent two-story house. Two more cops in a helicopter in
Kentucky chased an identical object, saying it was lens shaped,
extremely maneuverable, and much bigger than the helicopter.

3. Ground traces may or may not have anything to do with the UFO.
One set of traces that appeared near here a few years ago,
supposedly linked to a UFO seen by a child, was actually made by
a telephone company arm-and-bucket truck two days earlier. Pads
sticking out of the truck to stabilize it when the bucket is
raised made a triangle of three square imprints in the relatively
hard ground. The tires made no imprints in the same ground.

4. The National Enquirer prizes and other financial enticements
generate UFO occupant cases. A LOT of people will fake sightings
for a chance to collect a million dollars.

5. The Brookings Institute is a liberal think-tank for political
policy, not a body of true scientific inquiry. Everything they do
is as suspect as a 3 dollar bill with Bill Clinton's picture on
it. Their political belief is that "ordinary people are like
little children, and government must take care of them." That
report is typical of what they put out as "objective research."
The RAND Corporation is a similar entity.

6. The "real" reason many companies do not consider UFOs to be a
serious subject is that their customers tend to evaporate
whenever they start doing something in a UFO vein of research.
This is probably because bookstores and magazine racks throw UFOs
into the occult bins along with witchcraft, ghosts, and psychics.
7. My big question is: Whenever someone sees an unidentified
object in the sky, why do they think of space aliens first????

I don't care whether there are aliens or not. It would be
interesting to find out. But true scientific methods must be used
to do so. Too many "UFOlogists" sidestep this little requirement.

Scientific proof demands that nothing be assumed to be true. But
it is impossible to prove that aliens are NOT visiting the Earth.
So the burden of proof must be on those who say that aliens are
visiting the Earth. And reports by people who thought the UFOs
were from outer space just don't add up to proof, no matter how
many there are. I don't see any established causal link between
things seen in the sky and alien intelligences. I could prove a
bunch of Smurfs caused the sighting using the same faulty logic.


@> I do know of cases where the military used UFOs to cover up
@> something else secret. Many unsolved cases have been generated by
@> spy satellite film capsule retrievals. Those ARE done in remote
@> areas, many times in the Arctic. Sometimes, one comes down in a
@> bad place due to a malfunction or an urgent need for information.

@> I know of the existence of a case where a fake military report of
@> a fantastic UFO sighting with dead witnesses was actually a
@> security clearance test designed to weed out whistle blowers.

@> I know of another case where a military crash investigator told a
@> 50's UFO book author a wild story just to get him to leave the
@> crash site.

@Such a large object and effort?

That depends on what the military's real intent was.

And it could always be a civilian prank of some kind. In early
20th Century England, some people went to the trouble and expense
of dressing themselves and hired actors up in exotic costumes.
They did this to fool royalty into entertaining them as
emissaries from a fictitious African country. It really worked.
Imagine what people could do with some money, a car battery, some
lights, imagination, and a lot of weather balloons (which can be
had for $5 each in a scientific supply catalog -- which also
sells helium).

And never underestimate the power of a wager. I have several
cases of pranks in my files that were the results of either
making a bet on whether someone could pull off a fake UFO, or
of losing a bet with the prank as the payoff.
A supposition: Suppose FOX2 and FOX3 were in cahoots on their
own stories, and also released fire balloons along the
highway that all of the the others saw.

@> I do know of several cases where horizontal bending of light

I don't mean that nine different locations got the same mirage. I
mean that people in one location saw the same mirage repeated
nine times, simultaneously, side by side, like they were looking
between two parallel mirrors. I will get the info and pass it on
(the book isn't here and the internet isn't there).

There is no reason why a mirage can't be seen over a large area.
All it requires is that the atmospheric lens or mirror causing
the effect be large. And if a mirror effect can cause a
multiplication of images, it can also cause the image to be seen
in different directions at the same time.

Also, didn't the sightings in the three locations happen at three

I did a survey of most of the copies of the Trent photos I have.
Here are the results:



The following published works cropped the areas containing the
anomalies out, since they were nowhere near the UFO:

* Look 1967 special "FLYING SAUCERS"

* The Condon report

* Peter Brookesmith "UFOs - The Government Files

* Jenny Randles "UFOs and How to See Them" (Trent2 only)

* Jenny Randles "Alien Contact: The first fifty years"

* J A Hynek "The Hynek UFO Report"

* Hynek and Vallee "The Edge of Reality"

* Paris Flammonde "UFO Exist
* Time-Life "The UFO Phenomenon" (Trent2 - see below)



The following published works printed the photo too lightly for
the anomalies to appear if they existed in those copies. Other
than the phone wires and pole, the background is white:

* The true report on Flying Saucers (1967 - only Trent2)

* Philip Klass "UFOs Explained" (only Trent1)

* Ronald Story "Encyclopedia of UFOs" (Trent1 - see below)



The following published works printed copies with the pickup
truck actually visible:

* Bob Larson: UFOs and the Alien Agenda

* Time-Life "The UFO Phenomenon" - Not only is the pickup truck
visible, but other cars are parked to the left of it.

* Sagan and Page "UFOs - a Scientific Debate" The pickup truck is
cropped out, but the other cars visible in the Time-Life print
are there, but very faint.



The following published works printed copies with the "Adamski
object" visible.

* Ronald Story "Encyclopedia of UFOs"



The following published works printed the colorized fake:

* Brookesmith "UFO -- The complete Sightings"

* John Spencer "The World Atlas of UFOs"

* "The World's Greatest UFO Mysteries"

* "UFO II" CD ROM for Windows



After further investigation, I think the "Adamski object"
happened when developer was dripped on the negative, then wiped
off. The "three ball effect" was an artifact of pixelation and
was visible in only one magnification.

The pickup trick looks similar to what happens when a photo is
taken through a sheet of glass reflecting another scene faintly.

As for the effect being created in the mind, I have experimented
with this, and I find that, if the effect is psychological, I can
make it change into something else. I can't make the pickup truck
change.

and distance to the closest part of the object (since FOX2 was on the closest edge) you
would get very different object sizes if
relatively close to the objects. The sphere gives an object size several times larger
than a narrow cigar (It helps to draw a picture for this). I chose the narrow cigar to be
conservative in the size calculation.

cigar (We don't know what the actual shape was). So I made the ellipse the same
length that I got from the cigar calculation. This

can construct a graphic to illustrate this if needed. The short story is that this gives a
conservative length for the UFO.

Hi Martin,

Thanks for your comments and additional info. I do understood the point I
think you're making about closeness to a sphere reducing the amount of sphere
that is visible but this has nothing to do with different methods of
measuring ANGULAR width. An angle is an angle, you're talking about the
LINEAR width derived from the angle which is a different matter. If you take
a given ANGULAR width and draw in a large sphere or a somewhat smaller
ellipse or cigar shape on a map (smaller in LINEAR dimensions), that is your
choice, but the ANGLE stays the same. Only the linear width varies depending
on your choice or model of object shape.

And the linear visibility effect with a sphere is much smaller than you say.
For example if someone is so close to a sphere that its angular size is 90
degrees (close to the case with FOX3), then the observer sees about a 29%
smaller diameter of sphere than its full diameter, if 120 degrees then 50%
smaller, but certainly not a factor of "several times."

The plot of the object's dimensions on a map where there is some rough
reference to landmarks is more accurate for determining angular size than
holding out the arms. So I think the 80-degree figure from your map could be
more reliable and accurate (if you did the map correctly) than the 113-degree
figure from the arms.

As for the discrepancies in witness accounts I'm glad you'll be able to ask
questions to see if the witnesses can clarify things. My impression of FOX3
is he has/had too much of a storytelling aspect to his account, whereby he
fixates on a point (such as emerging from the UFO encounter in "Silence") and
then for dramatic purposes ignores or neglects bringing up anything that may
clash with that point. As for this being due to the trauma of the UFO
incident and its size and proximity, why weren't they terrified instead of
just awestruck?

Regards,

Brad

I interrupt this most interesting discussion to clear up some
misinformation
about the famous "Phoenix Lights"


>@> Phoenix AZ 2/13/97

Date was 3/13/97

(SNIP)

>The Phoenix case was revealed as a series of flare drops by the
>men who dropped the flares. The delay was caused by the fact that
>they had returned to their home state in the east long before the
>news reached them (I found out about it two months later, and
>that was before they did). Again, many witnesses described a dark
>gray or black shape containing the lights, vee shaped, since the
>lights formed a rough vee. One witnesses said the stars blanked
>out as the object passed. This could either be caused by the
>parachutes, or by a contrast effect causing the eyes to
>desensitize in the area of the much brighter flares.
<

The March 13, 1997 sightings consist of TWO separable events.
The event which grabbed the media was at 10 PM plus or minus
minutes and resulted in four videos by witnesses at widely separated
locations in Phoenix. All of these witnesses were looking south or
south westward during their sightings. After dozens or a hundred
or more (?) hours of study using copies of the videos, maps and
information derived from being at the sites of the observations
I determined by triangulation that these lights were 60 or more miles
south of Phoenix over the Barry Goldwater Test range....
Furthermore, except for their extreme brightness, they obeyed the
"laws of flares" : careful analysis of the videos (frame capture,
position shift analysis) I determined that they dropped downward and
to the left during the several minute videos. This was consistent with
the general drift of the wind at the time. A short report was published
in
the MUFON journal in 1998. A full report including frame grabs for
illutration and maps was on the internet. Unfortunately the site with the
illustrations has now evaporated into thin cyber air, so I have attached
a text version. Use a variable width font.

NOW, comes a main point of this discussion: whereas the 10 PM sightings
were likely all caused by flares many miles south, it is clear from
witnesses
descriptions (MULTIPLE witness descriptions) that the event (s) that
started it
all off, which occurred between about 8 PM and 9 PM were NOT flares
south of the city of Phoenix. This is because this series of sightings
started
with witness reports of something flying overhead at a location over 50
miles
north northwest of Phoenix. Witness reports to the National UFO Reporting
Center were made within minutes of th sightings and the plot of the
witness locations showed an object or a group of objects (lights) moving
southward. This "object" eventually was seen moving southward by many
residents of Phoenix. See the shorter two attached files for initial
reports.
  I have not investigated THIS series of events because
many investigators have done so (e.g., Bill Hamilton). However, the
"bottom
line" is that this series of sightings between 8 and 9 PM are as yet
unexplained.

NOTE: the two events, 8-9 PM and 10 PM, because thoroughly mixed in the
media reports.

Bruce wrote;

"Witness reports to the National UFO Reporting
Center were made within minutes of th sightings and the plot of the
witness locations showed an object or a group of objects (lights) moving
southward. This "object" eventually was seen moving southward by many
residents of Phoenix. See the shorter two attached files for initial
reports.
  I have not investigated THIS series of events because
many investigators have done so (e.g., Bill Hamilton). However, the
"bottom line" is that this series of sightings between 8 and 9 PM are as yet
unexplained.
"


In 1997, I became curious about the events of Phoenix and quickly was able to
determine that there were two different events. This is something that has
been confused by the media AND many "investigators". Your work on the 10 pm
events seem to have cleared up any further concern for those videos (although
Hamilton still contends they were orbs in front of the mountains). This had
been pretty much determined in 1997 by Captain Bienz of the AZ ANG and the
Discovery Channel (Dr. Rudin).
The 8-8:30PM event consisted of sightings that started in the northern part
of the state and proceded south over Phoenix. They were last reported around
9PM in the Tuscon area. What becomes clear in many of the reports is that
there were 5 lights moving south (the number varies but 5 seems to be the
most consistent) at a constant rate of speed that was determined to be "blimp
speed". Some observers determined that there was an object behind the lights
but it appears that there was none. Witness Mike Fortson saw the lights pass
in front of the moon and there was no object. All he reported was the moon
changed color (he assumed the object was transparent but it appears this is
an incorrect assumption based on other data). The timing of the lights
moving south indicated the lights moved about 350-400 mph. Since witnesses
felt they moved at about 1/10th that speed it becomes apparent they were
incorrect in their assumptions of speed in altitude. When taking Fortson's
observation of the lights and the moon and others who saw the lights pass
overhead to his west, the altitude of the lights were about 30-40,000 feet!
This describes the low apparent speed to the observers on the ground. The
estimates of low altitude were completely off and also explains why no sounds
were heard. Lastly, the sighting by Mitch Stanley of the lights through his
telescope appears to clear up the matter even more. Mitch used a 10"
dobsonian reflector to catch the lights that night. He reports straight wing
aircraft with lights underneath the wings and fuselage. This would also
explain the fact that Fortson reported the moon changed color and appeared
like gas fumes leaving a can (exhaust from the aircraft).
Several witnesses reported the lights appearing to be two lights each and it
seems that the lights merged into one for observers without optical aid.
Since early investigators ignored Mitch's report and instead focused on the
more extraordinary claims, we are left with an "unexplained case". The
frenzy associated with this event seems to mirror Dr. Hartmann's look at the
Zond IV incident in 1968. The "excitedness effect" (some of the more
interesting reports are quite lengthy and seem to incorporate more
imagination than careful observation) coupled with the "airship effect"
(connecting the lights to form one object) seems to have created a UFO out of
the event.

Tim Printy
